orderingVariable: COURSE ORDER — 4 stages that run alongside the versatility list's stages (a chunk in Stage N is learned during versatility Stage N). The most common, most typical sets first; each stage mixes several areas of daily life; within a topic, chunks run from the most common sets to less common ones.
whyThatVariable: Selected on how common and how typical each set is: measured in 3.17M lines of Japanese film and TV subtitles (OpenSubtitles 2018, counted on dictionary forms), corrected by native judgement where foreign-film subtitles over-count plot sets and under-count Japanese daily life. Whether English misleads the learner is a note on the entry (trap), not a reason to keep or cut.

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (koohii, juuden, sou), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t.
conventions.register: romaji = the plain dictionary form of the whole set; polite = its desu/masu form, or null for adjective + noun. Examples use the form people say most (ame futteru), often without ga/o.
conventions.parts: noun + particle + verb (verb also holds the adjective in se ga takai or koi koohii); verbSense = what the verb means on its own.
conventions.measured: count = occurrences in the subtitle corpus (with any particle, or none); perMillion = per million lines; shareN = typicality, the share of everything said with the noun that goes to this verb; shareV = the noun's share of the verb's nouns; logDice = association (10+ strong); particles = the particle mix (∅ = dropped). null = too rare in films to count.
conventions.ranks: nounRank / verbRank = ranks of the parts in the jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0).
conventions.trap: the mistake an English speaker would make, or null. englishVerb = the English word they would reach for.
conventions.listLinks: ids of items in 20-list-versatile.json that the set builds on.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; groups can span topics.

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Talk about the weather, being hungry or in pain, going out and coming home, the bathroom, catching a train, school and work days, chatting and making friends, simple hobbies, how you feel, and what people look like and are good at.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Talk about meals and drinks, catching a cold and getting better, doors, lights and bedtime, TV and photos, what you're wearing, family and friends, noticing and understanding things, and what you like.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Make plans and say when you're free, pay and spend, phone and message people, go out to drink, take trips and pick people up, find your way, tidy up, take time off, and handle favours, apologies and thanks.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Talk about breakfast and the fridge, housework, gadgets and apps, glasses and accessories, exams, job hunting and getting work done, long-term health and injuries, errands and promises, moods and worries, and outings through the seasons.

blocks.label: Rain and snow
blocks.rationale: What rain and snow do and what you do about it: it's coming down, it has stopped, the umbrella's own verb, and getting rained on.
blocks.interference: ame ga furu and yuki ga furu share furu, so drill them in one frame (soto, ___ futteru yo), and set ame ni furareta (it rained on me) against plain ame futta. Keep ame ga yamu (it stops by itself) apart from yameru (a person quits), and kasa o sasu (have it up) apart from kasa motsu (carry it).

items.use: You hear ame futteru (it's raining) most, usually without ga. Plain ame furu points ahead, as in ashita ame furu kana (will it rain tomorrow?).
items.verbSense: fall from the sky (rain, snow, hail)
items.trap: Not ame ga ochiru: rain falls with furu. Once the topic is weather, furu alone means rain: futte kita (it's started raining), furisou da ne (looks like rain).

example.ja: 外、雨降ってるよ。
example.english: It's raining outside.

examplePolite.romaji: soto, ame ga futtemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 外、雨が降ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's raining outside.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 雨が降る is also listed as a set expression at #5450. Kana あめ also covers 飴 (candy), and ふる covers 振る (wave/dump), so the kanji ranks are used. Hail 雹 is #67652, hence 'rare' in partners.
items.notes: ame furisou = looks like rain; ame futte kita = it's started raining.

items.use: Same shape as ame ga furu: yuki futteru is 'it's snowing', and ashita yuki furu kamo is 'it might snow tomorrow'.
items.verbSense: fall from the sky (rain, snow, hail)
items.trap: Not yuki ga ochiru: snow takes the same furu as rain, so yuki futteru is 'it's snowing'.

example.ja: 外、雪降ってるよ！
example.english: It's snowing outside!

examplePolite.romaji: soto, yuki ga futtemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 外、雪が降ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's snowing outside.

items.freqNote: Kana ゆき also covers place names and 行き, so the kanji rank is used.
items.notes: Snow lying on the ground is yuki ga tsumoru (yuki tsumotteru = the snow's settled / there's snow on the ground).

items.use: Mostly heard as ame yanda? (has it stopped?) or ame yamu made matou (let's wait till it stops). Ima wa yanderu means it has stopped for now, not 'it is stopping'.
items.verbSense: stop or die down by itself (rain, wind, noise)
items.trap: Not ame ga tomaru, and not yameru (a person quitting something): rain stops with intransitive yamu.

example.ja: もう雨やんだ？
example.english: Has the rain stopped yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ame, mou yamimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨、もうやみましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has the rain stopped yet?

items.freqNote: Rank is for kana やむ (#3517), the usual spelling of this verb; 病む (#9762) and やむを得ない (#17615) have their own rows, though the kana row may still hold a little kana-written 病む. The kanji 止む alone is #14280.
items.notes: ame ga agaru (the rain lifts) is a common alternative: ame agatta ne.

items.english: put up (open) an umbrella; have an umbrella up
items.use: Said about having an umbrella up over you: kasa sashite aruku (walk with an umbrella up), kasa sasanakute ii yo (no need to put it up). Kasa sashiteru means someone has one up. Taking one with you is kasa motte iku, not sasu: kasa motte itta hou ga ii yo (you'd better take an umbrella).
items.verbSense: hold something up over you (an umbrella, a parasol)
items.trap: Not kasa o akeru: an umbrella you hold up over you is sasu. Hiraku is only the moment of opening it, motsu is carrying it (kasa motteru? = got an umbrella?), and tsukau fits offering one (kasa tsukau? = want to use my umbrella?).

example.romaji: kasa sashita hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 傘さしたほうがいいよ。
example.english: You'd better put your umbrella up.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o sashita hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 傘をさしたほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better put your umbrella up.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 差す (#7696). 傘をさす is usually written in kana, and kana さす (#3059) also holds the causative and other kana-written senses (刺す #1780 and 指す #6552 have their own rows), so the umbrella sense ranks somewhere between the two.
items.notes: Closing it is kasa o tojiru, or kasa o tatamu (fold it up). A different sasu from the 'sting' in ka ni sasareru, though they sound the same.

items.use: Almost always past, usually with -chatta: ame ni furarechatta (I got rained on). Ame ga futta just reports the weather; furareta says it happened to you.
items.verbSense: furu = fall from the sky; the passive furareru means it fell on you, to your cost
items.trap: 'Get caught in the rain' points to tsukamaru, but Japanese says the rain fell on you, with furu's suffering passive: ame ni furareta. Ame ni au (run into rain: ame ni atchatta) is just as natural.

example.romaji: kinou kaeri ni ame ni furarechatta.
example.ja: 昨日帰りに雨に降られちゃった。
example.english: I got caught in the rain on the way home yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kaeri ni ame ni furarechaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日帰りに雨に降られちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I got caught in the rain on the way home yesterday.

items.freqNote: The passive 降られる is not a dictionary form, so it isn't in the list. The rank is for the base 降る. The alternative's verb 遭う (au, run into) is #2225.
items.notes: Getting soaked is nureru: ame ni nurechatta (I got wet in the rain). Ame ni au sounds like au 'meet' but is a different verb (遭う, run into).

blocks.label: Hungry, full, thirsty
blocks.rationale: Everyday appetite signals: hungry (two ways), full and thirsty.
blocks.interference: onaka suita and onaka hetta mean the same, but hetta sounds blunter, so learn suita first and hetta as its casual twin. Both use the past tense for hunger you feel now, and so does nodo kawaita. onaka ippai has no verb of its own (add ni natta for the past).

items.use: Said in the past for hunger you feel now: onaka suita (I'm hungry), ga usually dropped. Onaka suiteru? asks if someone is hungry, and onaka suitenai is 'I'm not hungry'.
items.verbSense: become empty, thin out (densha ga suiteru = the train isn't crowded)
items.trap: No everyday 'hungry' adjective (himojii is old-fashioned): the stomach empties, onaka suita, in the past tense for hunger you feel now.

example.ja: ああ、お腹すいた。なんか食べよう。
example.english: I'm so hungry. Let's get something to eat.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, onaka ga sukimashita ne. nanika tabemashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、お腹がすきましたね。何か食べましょうか。
examplePolite.english: I'm hungry, aren't you? Shall we get something to eat?

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758). Verb rank is kana すく #2947. 好く 'like' (#1880, mostly 好かれる / 好かない) is a separate word and is not counted, though the tokenizer may file some kana すいた under it, so #2947 may undercount this sense. Kanji 空く read すく is #47898 (read あく it is #1498). Phrase entries: お腹が空く #22626, お腹がすく #27605. The rough 腹が減る is #6497 and 腹減った #4970.
items.notes: Onaka hetta (onaka ga heru) means the same but sounds a little blunter; hara hetta is the rough, mostly male version. Onaka pekopeko (I'm starving) sounds childish or cute.

items.use: Said at the end of a meal and to turn down more food, usually without ga: mou onaka ippai (I'm full). It has no verb of its own: add desu to be polite, and ni natta for the past, as in onaka ippai ni natta? (are you full?).
items.verbSense: full, filled up; also 'a lot' (ippai aru = there's lots)
items.trap: English 'I'm full' names no body part; Japanese says the stomach is full, onaka ippai. Keep onaka in: ippai alone mostly means 'a lot', and mou ippai can be heard as 'one more (drink)'.

example.ja: ああ、お腹いっぱい。もう食べられない。
example.english: I'm so full. I can't eat another bite.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ippai desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹いっぱいです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm full. Thank you for the meal.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); いっぱい #512 counts every sense ('a lot', 'full'); 一杯 #2892 and １杯 #2744 are mostly 'one cup'. Ippai is a noun or adverb, not a verb or adjective; it goes in the partner slot. Phrase entry お腹いっぱい #14252 (particle dropped); 満腹 #18617.
items.notes: Hara ippai is the rougher, mostly male version; hara ippai taberu = eat your fill. Mou onaka ippai can also mean 'I've had enough of that'.

items.use: Said in the past for thirst you feel now: nodo kawaita (I'm thirsty), ga usually dropped. Nodo kawaiteru? asks if someone is thirsty.
items.verbSense: become dry (of the throat); the same-sounding kawaku is also used for laundry or paint drying
items.trap: No 'thirsty' adjective: the throat dries, nodo kawaita, in the past tense for thirst you feel now.

example.ja: 喉渇いた。水ある？
example.english: I'm thirsty. Is there any water?

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita. omizu o moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きました。お水をもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Could I have some water?

items.freqNote: 喉 #3552 (kana のど #7553); 渇く #6159 (its homophone 乾く 'dry' is #6556); phrase entry 喉が渇く #14507.
items.notes: The same nodo is the throat in nodo ga itai (sore throat).

items.use: Like onaka suita, said in the past for hunger you feel now: onaka hetta, with ga often dropped. It's a bit blunter and more casual than suita, and the rough, mostly male hara hetta is the form heard most in film. In desu/masu talk onaka ga sukimashita is the safer default; herimashita sounds blunt and a little male.
items.verbSense: decrease, go down (taijuu ga heru = lose weight)
items.trap: Hunger is a past-tense verb, not an adjective: onaka hetta (I'm hungry); onaka heru sounds like 'I'll get hungry'.
partners: hara (belly: hara hetta = rough, mostly male)

example.romaji: onaka hetta. nanka tabe ni ikanai?
example.ja: お腹減った。なんか食べに行かない？
example.english: I'm hungry. Want to go grab something to eat?

examplePolite.romaji: onaka ga herimashita ne. nanika tabe ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: お腹が減りましたね。何か食べに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: I'm hungry, aren't you? Shall we go and get something to eat?

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 減る #1173 counts every 'decrease' use. Phrase entry お腹が減る #60005, far below the rough 腹減った #4970 and 腹が減る #6497 (腹 #1216).
items.notes: Same meaning as onaka ga suku. Among friends onaka hetta is just as everyday; hara hetta is its rough, mostly male twin.

blocks.label: Out and back
blocks.rationale: Leaving the house, stepping outside, running errands and getting home (late or not): the trip that starts and ends every day.
blocks.interference: The particle shows direction: o for the place you leave (uchi o deru), ni for where you end up or what you go to do (soto ni deru, uchi ni kaeru, kaimono ni iku). 'Go home' is kaeru, because uchi ni iku means visiting someone's house.

items.use: Covers 'go home', 'come home' and 'get home': mou kaeru (I'm off home), uchi kaettara (once I'm home). uchi and ni are often dropped. mou kaetteru means they've already gone home, while ima kaetteru is casual for 'I'm on my way home' (also ima kaeri, kaeru tochuu).
items.verbSense: go back to where you belong (home, your country)
items.trap: Not uchi ni iku for going home yourself: iku is for going to someone else's place (tomodachi no uchi ni iku) or taking a friend along to yours (uchi iku?). Your own return home is kaeru, which also covers 'come home' and 'get home'.

example.ja: もううち帰った？
example.english: Are you home yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanji goro uchi ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何時ごろうちに帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Around what time are you going home today?

items.freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152.
items.notes: Going back somewhere that isn't home (your desk, your seat) is modoru; for the office after a client visit, both kaisha ni modoru and kaisha ni kaeru are heard.

items.use: For setting off from home, usually saying or asking when: nanji ni uchi deru?, ima uchi deta (I've just left). Casual speech drops o; dekakeru (go out) is the single-verb alternative.
items.verbSense: go out, leave; also come out, appear
items.trap: English 'leave' leads to saru or hanareru, which sound like leaving for good (uchi o hanareru = leave home to live elsewhere); heading out for the day is deru: uchi o deru, and uchi kara deru is also fine.

example.ja: 何時にうち出る？
example.english: What time are you leaving the house?

examplePolite.romaji: nanji ni uchi o demasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何時にうちを出ますか？
examplePolite.english: What time do you leave the house?

items.freqNote: うち #113 also counts 内 'among/while'; 家 read いえ is #152. 出かける (dekakeru) is #1420.
items.notes: Said with ie instead, ie o deru can mean moving out for good; iede is running away from home.

items.use: For stepping out of a building or room, often just for a moment: chotto soto deyou (let's go out for a bit, get some air). Casual speech drops ni (soto deta); setting off for the day is uchi o deru or dekakeru.
items.verbSense: go out, leave; also come out, appear

example.ja: 寒いから外出たくない。
example.english: It's cold, I don't want to go out.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node, soto ni detakunai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので、外に出たくないです。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so I don't want to go outside.

items.freqNote: 外 #437 is the そと reading; 出る #81 counts every sense of deru.
items.notes: Going inside is naka ni hairu (back in: naka ni modoru). soto also means away from home: soto de taberu (eat out).

items.use: Covers groceries as much as clothes: chotto kaimono itte kuru (I'm popping out to the shops). Casual speech drops ni. kaimono itteru means someone has gone shopping and is out now (okaasan nara kaimono itteru yo), not on the way; kaimono shiteru is being in the middle of shopping.
items.verbSense: go (kaimono = kau 'buy' + mono 'things')
items.trap: Not kaimono suru ni iku: the noun goes straight before ni iku (kaimono ni iku); with the verb it's the stem, kaimono shi ni iku.

example.ja: 買い物行くけど、なんかいる？
example.english: I'm going shopping, need anything?

examplePolite.romaji: kaimono ni ikimasu kedo, nanika irimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 買い物に行きますけど、何かいりますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm going shopping. Do you need anything?

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted (the tokenizer splits it). The loanword ショッピング is #13644.
items.notes: shoppingu (the loanword) leans to browsing malls for fun; kaimono covers any buying errand.

items.use: Said about family, worried or annoyed: otousan kaeri osoi ne. Your own heads-up is kyou kaeri osoku naru (I'll be home late today), with ga usually dropped.
items.verbSense: late; also slow
items.trap: Not okureru for 'I'll be late tonight': okureru is being late for something with a set time (a train, a meeting). Getting home late is kaeri ga osoku naru, or just osoku naru.

example.ja: 今日帰り遅くなるから。
example.english: I'll be home late today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaeri ga osoku narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は帰りが遅くなります。
examplePolite.english: I'll be home late today.

items.freqNote: 帰り #1209 also counts 'on the way home' (kaeri ni); 遅い #328 covers both late and slow.
items.notes: The opposite is kaeri ga hayai; the same noun gives kaeri ni (on the way home): kaeri ni konbini yoru.

blocks.label: Looks and voice
blocks.rationale: Describing what someone looks and sounds like: tall, short, loud, long hair, a good figure.
blocks.interference: Each noun picks its own size word: height is takai/hikui (never ookii or mijikai), hair is nagai, and a loud voice is ookii, since koe ga takai means high-pitched. sutairu ga ii is a good figure, not fashion (that's oshare).

items.use: The plain way to call someone tall: ano hito, se takai ne, with ga dropped in casual speech. Before a noun, ga often becomes no: se no takai hito (a tall person).
items.verbSense: takai: high; also expensive
items.trap: Not kare wa takai: takai on its own is for things (high, expensive), so a person's height needs se ga takai.

example.romaji: uchi no ani, se takai n da.
example.ja: うちの兄、背高いんだ。
example.english: My big brother's tall.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ani wa se ga takai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちの兄は背が高いんです。
examplePolite.english: My older brother is tall.

items.freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388, plus 背 (せい) #39147 for the sei ga takai variant. The bare noun ranks low because se almost only occurs inside this phrase. 身長 shinchou #4523.
items.notes: Sei ga takai is a common spoken variant. The 'tall' sense of takai applies to a person only inside this phrase. For an exact height, use shinchou: shinchou nan senchi? (how tall are you?).

items.use: The opposite of se ga takai, often said about yourself: watashi, se hikui kara... Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: hikui: low, not high
items.trap: Not se ga mijikai: in Japanese height is high or low, so short is hikui. Mijikai is for length and duration, never height.

example.romaji: watashi, se hikui kara, ue no tana todokanai n da.
example.ja: 私、背低いから、上の棚届かないんだ。
example.english: I'm short, so I can't reach the top shelf.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa se ga hikui node, ue no tana ni todokanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私は背が低いので、上の棚に届かないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm short, so I can't reach the top shelf.

items.notes: Casual speech also says chiisai (chiisai hito); chibi is teasing slang.

items.english: have a loud voice, be loud
items.use: Said about someone who talks loudly (ano hito, koe ookii yo ne) or to quieten someone: chotto, koe ookii! Casual speech drops ga, and friends often say koe dekai (dekai is blunter and more slangy than ookii). The opposite, koe ga chiisai, means quiet or soft-spoken (koe chiisai yo = speak up, I can't hear you).
items.verbSense: ookii: big; for sounds and voices, loud
items.trap: Not koe ga takai, which in everyday speech means high-pitched. urusai also works for 'you're being noisy', but it sounds annoyed (urusai! = shut up) and calls the person noisy or nagging, not their voice loud. To describe a loud voice, say koe ga ookii (casually koe dekai).

example.ja: ちょっと、声大きいよ！
example.english: Hey, you're being loud!

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto koe ga ookii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと声が大きいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, you're being a bit loud.

items.freqNote: 声 #327; 大きい #536 (大きな #538); でかい #1836; 大声 oogoe #5023; うるさい #517. The film count (67) includes ookii koe before a noun (ADJ:19).
items.notes: 'Speak up' is motto ookii koe de, and 'in a loud voice' is ookina koe de. In older speech and period dramas, shh, koe ga takai! means 'keep your voice down'.

items.use: Describes someone's hair in the person wa kami ga nagai frame: imouto, kami nagai yo, with ga dropped. Before a noun ga becomes no (kami no nagai hito), and 'your hair's got long' is kami nobita ne.
items.verbSense: nagai: long (length or time)
items.trap: Not nagai kami o motte iru ('has long hair'): Japanese doesn't 'have' hair. Say kami ga nagai, the same frame as se ga takai, or nagai kami o shite iru, nagai kami no hito.

example.romaji: imouto, kami nagai n da yo.
example.ja: 妹、髪長いんだよ。
example.english: My little sister's got long hair.

examplePolite.romaji: imouto wa kami ga nagai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 妹は髪が長いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My younger sister has long hair.

items.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 kami no ke #3658); 長い #467; 短い #1621. The kana かみ is shared with 神 #1988 and 紙 #2672. The film count (20) is mostly nagai kami before the noun (ADJ:14); the kami ga nagai frame is judged.
items.notes: Short hair is kami ga mijikai, but people often just say shooto (shooto ni shita = I went short).

items.use: A common compliment on someone's figure, usually meaning slim and well-proportioned: sutairu ii ne, with ga dropped. It's said of men and women alike, and an amazing figure is sutairu batsugun.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: False friend: sutairu ga ii is about the body, not fashion. To praise how someone dresses, say oshare or fuku no sensu ga ii.

example.ja: スタイルいいね！モデルみたい。
example.english: You've got a great figure! Like a model.

examplePolite.romaji: sutairu ga ii desu ne! moderu mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: スタイルがいいですね！モデルみたいです。
examplePolite.english: You have a great figure! You look like a model.

items.freqNote: スタイル #3954 covers both senses of the loanword, so it is not a count of this phrase. いい #24; おしゃれ #3483; 体型 taikei #19649.
items.notes: For a toned build, kitaeteru ne (you work out, don't you) is the usual compliment.

blocks.label: Getting on and off
blocks.rationale: The ride itself: one frame, X ni noru, for train, bus, car and bike, and oriru for getting off.
blocks.interference: Getting on takes ni and getting off takes o (densha ni noru, densha o oriru), so drill them as a pair. You never take a bus or ride a bike with toru or o noru, and how you travel takes de: jitensha de iku.

items.use: The riding and boarding itself: densha notteru (I'm on the train now), densha nottara (once I'm on). To say how you get somewhere, natives use de: densha de iku (I'll go by train), densha de kayotteru (I commute by train). Casual speech often drops ni.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not densha o toru or densha o noru: you ride on a vehicle with ni noru, and 'take' is never toru here.

example.ja: 電車乗ったら、連絡するね。
example.english: I'll text you once I'm on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ni nottara, renraku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 電車に乗ったら、連絡しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll let you know once I'm on the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted, so noun and verb are ranked separately. The same frame covers basu (#2466), takushii (#1987), hikouki (#3222) and jitensha (#2927) ni noru.
items.notes: norikaeru (change trains) is a single verb. The transitive is noseru, giving someone a ride: nosete kureru? (can you give me a lift?)

items.use: Same frame as densha ni noru: basu notta (I've got on the bus, the usual text), basu notteru (I'm on the bus now), basu nottara (once I'm on), often chained as basu notte iku / kaeru. To say how you get there, use de: basu de iku. Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not basu o toru: 'take the bus' is ni noru, as with every vehicle.

example.ja: バス乗って帰ろうか。
example.english: Shall we take the bus home?

examplePolite.romaji: basu ni notte kaerimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: バスに乗って帰りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we take the bus home?

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. In film subtitles basu pairs with noru a third of the time.
items.notes: On local buses you press the button for your stop (botan o osu); a bus that won't come is basu konai.

items.english: get in / ride in a car
items.use: Covers getting in and riding along: kuruma notte (get in the car), kuruma nottara (once we're in). kuruma notteru is 'I'm in the car' (as in the example) and also 'drive / own one': donna kuruma notteru? (what car do you drive?). To say how you get there, use de: kuruma de iku.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not kuruma ni hairu or kuruma o noru: getting in is ni noru (kuruma no naka ni hairu is only for ducking inside, say out of the rain). 'What car do you drive?' is kuruma nani notteru? or donna kuruma notteru?, while unten suru is the act of driving (unten dekiru? = can you drive?).

example.ja: 先に車乗ってるね。
example.english: I'll wait in the car.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni kuruma ni nottemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先に車に乗ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wait in the car.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. unten (driving) is #2725; asking what someone drives uses notteru.
items.notes: Getting out is kuruma kara oriru; giving someone a ride is the transitive noseru: nosete kureru?

items.use: Once the train is clear, people usually name only the stop, with de: tsugi de oriru (I'm getting off at the next one). The vehicle takes o, or kara. On a packed train, sumimasen, orimasu! (excuse me, getting off) clears the way.
items.verbSense: come down; get off (a vehicle, stairs)
items.trap: Not densha ni oriru or densha kara deru: getting off is oriru, with the vehicle marked by o (kara also works). Only a car also allows kuruma kara deru, 'climb out'.

example.ja: 電車降りたら、連絡するね。
example.english: I'll text you when I get off the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha o oritara, renraku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 電車を降りたら、連絡しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll let you know when I get off the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. In speech the noun usually drops: tsugi de oriru.
items.notes: Missing your stop is eki o norisugosu: nete te norisugoshita (I fell asleep and missed my stop). The same verb goes down stairs: kaidan o oriru.

items.use: Used for being able to ride (jitensha noreru? = can you ride a bike?) and for riding one now (jitensha notteru). To say how you get somewhere, use de: jitensha de iku. Casual speech drops ni, and the slangy chari (charinko) often replaces jitensha.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not jitensha o noru: English 'ride a bike' takes an object, but a bike takes ni noru like every other vehicle.

example.ja: 自転車乗って、コンビニ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to bike over to the convenience store.

examplePolite.romaji: jitensha ni notte, konbini ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 自転車に乗って、コンビニに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to ride my bike to the convenience store.

items.freqNote: The tokenizer splits 自転車 into 自転 + 車, so its ~42 hits (自転車に乗) are counted inside kuruma ni noru's 458. The casual chari is #15668.
items.notes: Pedalling is kogu (jitensha o kogu), and the everyday shopping bike with a basket is a mamachari.

blocks.label: School and work days
blocks.rationale: The daily round, guessable sets first: going to school, going to work, getting off work, being busy with it.
blocks.interference: gakkou ni itteru and shigoto ni itteru mean you attend or are there now, not that you're on the way; owaru and isogashii make the work the subject with ga, where English says 'I'.

items.use: Said about the daily trip and about being a student at all, so you hear itteru a lot: nihongo gakkou itteru (I go to a Japanese language school). Casual speech drops ni, and e also works (gakkou e iku).
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: 'I'm going to school' (on the way) isn't gakkou ni itteru, which means you're there now or that you attend it. On the way is ima gakkou iku tochuu (or ima gakkou ni mukatteru), and about to leave is plain: ima kara gakkou iku.

example.ja: 最近日本語学校行ってる。
example.english: I've been going to a Japanese language school lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nihongo gakkou ni ittemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近日本語学校に行ってます。
examplePolite.english: I've been going to a Japanese language school lately.

items.freqNote: 学校 #661, 行く #40. No phrase entry. 通う kayou (attend regularly) is #1026.
items.notes: For a regular routine, kayou also works: juku ni kayotteru.

items.use: Said about the daily trip: ja, shigoto itte kuru (I'm off to work). itteru is the state, 'they're at work': papa wa shigoto itteru. Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: 'He's at work' tempts shigoto ni iru, which doesn't work. He has gone and is there: shigoto itteru or shigoto ni deteru (or shigoto-chuu, in the middle of work).

example.ja: 今から仕事行く。
example.english: I'm heading off to work now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima kara shigoto ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今から仕事に行きます。
examplePolite.english: I'm heading off to work now.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 行く #40. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 172 of 192 hits keep ni; 会社 + 行く (go to the office) has 12, and 仕事に出て (out at work) 11.
items.notes: Coming back is shigoto kara kaeru; on the way home is shigoto no kaeri.

items.use: Said when making plans around someone's workday: shigoto nanji ni owaru? Once you're done, you say shigoto owatta. Casual speech usually drops ga.
items.verbSense: end, be over (the thing itself finishes)
items.trap: English makes you the subject ('I finish work'), which tempts o with a transitive verb (shigoto o owaraseru means getting a job done). For clocking off, the work itself ends: shigoto ga owaru, so 'I'm done' is shigoto owatta.

example.ja: 今日仕事何時に終わる？
example.english: What time do you get off work today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa shigoto nanji ni owarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は仕事何時に終わりますか？
examplePolite.english: What time do you finish work today?

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 終わる #190, 上がる agaru #503. Same frame: gakkou ga owaru, jugyou ga owaru.
items.notes: Leaving the building is kaisha o deru. The stiffer transitive is shigoto o oeru. Among coworkers, clocking off is also agaru: kyou nanji ni agaru?

items.use: The standard reply to saikin dou? and the standard excuse: shigoto isogashikute (work's been busy, so...). Casual speech drops ga, and shigoto de isogashii means the same.
items.verbSense: busy (a person, their work or schedule)
items.trap: English 'busy' also covers crowds and phone lines. A shop packed with customers, from the customer's side, is konderu (mise ga komu); mise ga isogashii is how the staff put it. A busy phone line is hanashi-chuu.

example.ja: 最近仕事忙しくて、全然休めない。
example.english: Work's been so busy lately, I never get a break.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin shigoto ga isogashikute, zenzen yasumemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 最近仕事が忙しくて、全然休めません。
examplePolite.english: Work's been so busy lately, I never get a break.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 忙しい #447. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 34 of 47 hits use ga and 5 use de.
items.notes: The usual reply to someone's busy spell: taihen da ne.

blocks.label: Feels good or bad
blocks.rationale: How something feels to you (kimochi), your mood (kibun), someone's temper (kigen) and a place you like being in (igokochi).
blocks.interference: English 'feel good/bad' covers all of these: kimochi ii is a physical sensation, kibun ii is your mood, igokochi ii is a place you're at ease in. kimochi warui is queasy or gross, while a grumpy mood others can see is kigen ga warui, not kibun ga warui (feel sick).

items.use: A reaction to a bath, a breeze, a massage or a stretch, almost always said as one word without ga: aa, kimochi ii. kimochi ii ne asks the other person to agree.
items.verbSense: good, fine; here the feeling is good
items.trap: English 'feel good' covers mood and health, but kimochi ii is only a physical sensation: a bath, a breeze, a massage. For 'I feel good today', say kyou choushi ii or kibun ii. A bath isn't tanoshii (fun) either; it's kimochi ii.
partners: kibun (kibun ga ii: in a good mood)
choushi (choushi ga ii: in good shape)

example.romaji: aa, kaze ga kimochi ii ne.
example.ja: ああ、風が気持ちいいね。
example.english: Ah, the breeze feels nice.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, kaze ga kimochi ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、風が気持ちいいですね。
examplePolite.english: Ah, the breeze feels nice, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: Usually said without ga: 気持ちいい #2005 vs 気持ちがいい #13062.
items.notes: Also used for 'satisfying', like a tidy desk or a crisp sound.

items.english: feel queasy, feel nauseous; gross, creepy
items.use: Usually said as one word, kimochi warui. It covers both 'gross/creepy' (a bug, a weird message) and 'I feel queasy' (chotto kimochi warui).
items.verbSense: bad
items.trap: English 'feel sick' covers both nausea and illness, but kimochi warui is only nausea or disgust. With a cold or the flu, say guai ga warui; kimochi warui sounds like you're about to throw up. For 'gross', learners say kirai, which only means dislike.
partners: guai (guai ga warui: feel unwell, not queasy)
kibun (kibun ga warui: feel sick, without the 'gross' sense)

example.ja: 飲みすぎてちょっと気持ち悪い。
example.english: I drank too much, I feel a bit sick.

examplePolite.romaji: nomisugite, chotto kimochi ga warui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲みすぎて、ちょっと気持ちが悪いです。
examplePolite.english: I drank too much, I feel a bit sick.

items.freqNote: Usually said as one word: 気持ち悪い #1740 (気持ちが悪い #23002). The slang clip キモい is #4580.
items.notes: About a person, kimochi warui means creepy and is insulting, and the slang clip kimoi (キモい), which only means gross or creepy, is ruder still. To say someone looks unwell, say guai warui sou.

items.english: be in a good mood; feel well
items.use: About your mood, usually with ga dropped: kyou kibun ii (I'm in a good mood today). It also covers feeling well again after feeling sick: kibun yoku natta? (feeling better?). After a shower or a walk, sukkiri shita is more usual.
items.verbSense: good, fine; here your mood is good
items.trap: English 'feel good' covers everything, but kimochi ii is how something feels to you (a bath, a breeze, finally finishing), while kibun ii is your mood or how you feel overall. The negative isn't the mirror: kibun warui means feel sick, or feel put off (sonna koto iwarete kibun warui). Someone else being grumpy is kigen ga warui (kachou kigen warui); for yourself, iraira shiteru (I'm irritable) is more usual.
partners: choushi (condition: choushi ga ii, doing well)

example.romaji: kyou wa nanka kibun ii n da.
example.ja: 今日はなんか気分いいんだ。
example.english: I'm in a good mood today for some reason.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanka kibun ga ii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はなんか気分がいいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm in a good mood today for some reason.

items.freqNote: The phrase entry 気分がいい is #13225; the tokenizer usually splits it, and the ga-less 気分いい has no entry.
items.notes: ii kibun (a nice feeling) is common too: nanka ii kibun. gokigen da ne means 'you're in a good mood'.

items.english: be in a bad mood, grumpy
items.use: Said mostly about someone whose mood shows, with ga often dropped: kyou kachou kigen warui. It's also the word for a fussy, cranky baby or child (nemukute kigen warui); for yourself, iraira shiteru (I'm irritable) is more usual.
items.verbSense: bad; here someone's mood is bad and it shows
items.trap: For 'in a bad mood', learners say kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick or put off. A mood others can see is kigen ga warui: kare kyou kigen warui.
partners: kibun (kibun ga warui: feel sick, not grumpy)

example.ja: 今日課長機嫌悪いね。
example.english: The boss is in a bad mood today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kachou, kigen ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は課長、機嫌が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is in a bad mood today, isn't he.

items.freqNote: Phrase entries 機嫌が悪い #12058 and 機嫌がいい #23070; ご機嫌 #4177 and 不機嫌 #8467 rank higher. 期限 'deadline' #4825 shares the sound.
items.notes: fukigen (sulky, grumpy) is common too, and kigen naoshite asks someone to stop sulking. For a good mood, kigen ii (kyou kigen ii ne) and gokigen (gokigen da ne) both work.

items.use: Said about a place or a group you feel at ease in, usually without ga: kono kafe igokochi ii. It also works for people: kare to iru to igokochi ii (I feel at ease with him).
items.verbSense: good, nice; here being there feels good
items.trap: For a place or people you feel at ease with, learners reach for kaiteki (comfortable), which is physical comfort and sounds like an ad; say igokochi ii. Don't stretch it to objects: a comfy chair is raku or suwarigokochi ii, comfy shoes are hakiyasui.

example.romaji: kono mise, nanka igokochi ii yo ne.
example.ja: この店、なんか居心地いいよね。
example.english: There's something really cosy about this place.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mise, igokochi ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この店、居心地がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: This place is so cosy, isn't it?

items.freqNote: The bare noun ranks low because it almost only occurs in this phrase, which has entries of its own: 居心地がいい #18169, 居心地いい #22077.
items.notes: The opposite, igokochi warui, means you feel awkward or out of place.

blocks.label: Read, watch, sing, draw
blocks.rationale: The everyday pastimes whose English verb carries straight across: a book is read, a film watched, a song sung, a picture drawn or painted.
blocks.interference: Little between them. e o kaku uses the same sound as kaku (write) and covers painting too, never hiku as in sen o hiku (draw a line). miru is 'watch' for films and TV alike (eiga mita, terebi miteru).

items.use: Said about reading as a habit or right now: hon toka yomu? asks if someone reads, and hon yonderu is 'is reading' (or, with mainichi, 'reads every day'). Casual speech drops o, as in hon yomu no suki (I like reading).
items.verbSense: read, silently or aloud

example.ja: 最近なんか面白い本読んだ？
example.english: Read any good books lately?

examplePolite.romaji: saikin nanika omoshiroi hon o yomimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近何か面白い本を読みましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you read any good books lately?

items.freqNote: manga 漫画 #3363 and zasshi 雑誌 #2341 take the same yomu.
items.notes: Reading named as a hobby is dokusho (shumi wa dokusho desu); in chat, hon yomu no ga suki sounds more natural.

items.use: Said about films at home or at the cinema, often without o in casual speech (eiga miru). 'Have you seen it yet?' is the past tense mou mita?, and 'have you ever seen it?' is mita koto aru?
items.verbSense: see, look at, watch
items.trap: 'Not yet' is mada mitenai, not mada minai, which means 'I'm not going to watch it yet'.

example.ja: あの映画、もう見た？
example.english: Have you seen that movie yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ano eiga, mou mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの映画、もう見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you seen that movie yet?

items.freqNote: 観る, a spelling often used for films and shows, is ranked separately at #10463; it is the same miru.
items.notes: Going to the cinema is its own set, eiga ni iku. The invitation is eiga ikanai? or eiga mi ni ikanai?, which mean the same.

items.use: utau already means sing, so uta is often dropped when the song is obvious, as in karaoke de nani utau? (what'll you sing at karaoke?). The full uta (o) utau is for singing in general: uta utau no suki (I like singing).
items.verbSense: sing

example.romaji: ofuro de uta utau no suki.
example.ja: お風呂で歌うたうの好き。
example.english: I like singing in the bath.

examplePolite.romaji: ofuro de uta o utau no ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: お風呂で歌を歌うのが好きです。
examplePolite.english: I like singing in the bath.

items.freqNote: 曲 (kyoku, a particular song or track) #2119 takes the same utau: kono kyoku utaeru?
items.notes: Praise usually names uta: uta umai ne! (casual) or uta ga ojouzu desu ne (polite), both meaning 'you're a great singer'. utau no umai ne is also fine.

items.use: Use it for drawing or painting a picture, as a hobby or right now. Casually o is dropped: e kaiteru means you are drawing now or draw as a hobby.
items.verbSense: draw or paint a picture; it sounds the same as kaku (write)
items.trap: Not e o hiku (hiku draws a line: sen o hiku) or e o nuru (nuru paints a surface). A picture takes kaku whether it is drawn or painted.

example.ja: 絵描くの好き？
example.english: Do you like drawing?

examplePolite.romaji: e o kaku no ga suki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 絵を描くのが好きですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you like drawing?

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 絵を描く is listed on its own at #4836 (えをかく). Bare 描く (#1092) is filed under the reading えがく, but the subtitles can't separate kaku from egaku, so that rank counts both. 書く (かく, write) #233 is the homophone.
items.notes: egaku is the written reading of the same kanji; in conversation it is kaku.

blocks.label: Talking to people
blocks.rationale: The four everyday hanashi sets: talking, listening, opening a serious talk, and someone who goes on and on.
blocks.interference: All four share hanashi, so drill them together: hanashi o suru (you talk), hanashi o kiku (you listen, or do what someone says), hanashi ga aru (I need to talk to you) and hanashi ga nagai (they go on forever), which is not nagai hanashi (a long story: nagai hanashi ni naru kedo...).

items.use: Used for having a conversation, with to for the person and no for the topic: kare to sono hanashi shita (I talked to him about that), shigoto no hanashi shiteta (we were talking about work). X ni tsuite hanasu is fine too but sounds more structured. Casual speech drops o when hanashi has a word in front of it.
items.verbSense: do; with a noun, carry out that activity (here, have a talk)
partners: uwasa (talking about someone who isn't there: X no uwasa shiteta = we were just talking about X)

example.ja: 何の話してたの？
example.english: What were you guys talking about?

examplePolite.romaji: nan no hanashi o shiteta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何の話をしてたんですか？
examplePolite.english: What were you talking about?

items.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; する #15. Phrase entry 話をする #994.
items.notes: nan no hanashi? on its own means 'what are you talking about?', when you're lost or denying something.

items.english: listen to someone, hear someone out
items.use: The everyday way to ask for or offer an ear: chotto hanashi kiite (just hear me out), hanashi kiku yo (I'm happy to listen). hito no hanashi kiitenai desho is the complaint 'you're not listening to me' (hito here means me, the speaker). It also covers hearing about something: sono hanashi kiita (I heard about that).
items.verbSense: listen, hear; also ask
items.trap: English 'listen to me' leads to watashi o kiite, but kiku takes what is said, not the person: watashi no hanashi kiite, or just chotto kiite. And kare ni kiku means ask him (or hear it from him), never listen to him.
partners: guchi (venting: guchi kiku yo = I'll hear you vent)
uwasa (rumour: sonna uwasa kiita = I heard a rumour like that)

example.ja: ちょっと、話聞いてよ。
example.english: Hey, just listen to me.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto hanashi o kiite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと話を聞いてください。
examplePolite.english: Please just hear me out.

items.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; 聞く #67 (聴く #1930 separately).
items.notes: X no iu koto o kiku = do what X says (oya no iu koto kikinasai). Listening to a friend's problem and helping them think it through is soudan ni noru.

items.use: Opens a serious or personal talk and usually trails off with n da kedo: chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo... Natives usually keep the ga here, though chotto hanashi aru n da kedo is heard too. Politely it's hanashi ga aru n desu kedo, and to a boss or client often ohanashi ga aru n desu ga.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
items.trap: English 'I need to talk to you' leads to hanasu hitsuyou ga aru, which sounds stiff and official; the everyday opener is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
partners: youji (something to see to: kimi ni youji ga aru = I need you for something)

example.romaji: chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo, ima ii?
example.ja: ちょっと話があるんだけど、今いい？
example.english: I need to talk to you. Got a minute?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo, ima ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお話があるんですけど、今いいですか？
examplePolite.english: There's something I'd like to discuss. Do you have a moment?

items.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; お話 #654 (the polite ohanashi); ある #21. No phrase entry.
items.notes: ii hanashi ga aru n da kedo = I've got a good offer for you (a classic sales opener). Plain good news is more often ii shirase.

items.use: A stock grumble about bosses, principals and relatives: buchou no hanashi nagai n da yo (my boss goes on forever), with ga dropped. Before a noun it becomes nagai hanashi (a long talk), and 'it's a long story' is hanaseba nagaku naru.
items.verbSense: long (length or time)
partners: denwa (phone calls: denwa nagai = always on the phone for ages)
ofuro (baths: ofuro nagai ne = you take long baths)

example.romaji: buchou no hanashi, honto nagai yo ne.
example.ja: 部長の話、ほんと長いよね。
example.english: The boss's talks go on forever, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou no hanashi wa hontou ni nagai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長の話は本当に長いですよね。
examplePolite.english: The manager's talks really do go on, don't they.

items.freqNote: 話 #96 counts every hanashi use; 長い #467. Only about 10 of the 73 pair hits are the predicate hanashi ga nagai (63 are nagai hanashi); an everyday grumble that films under-count. 長話 (nagabanashi) #29859.
items.notes: nagabanashi = a long chat: nagabanashi shichatte gomen (sorry for keeping you). Someone who just talks a lot is oshaberi, or yoku shaberu.

blocks.label: No time, no money
blocks.rationale: Being busy or broke in one frame: no time, no free time, no money, not enough money, nothing to spare.
blocks.interference: All take ga nai, never o mottenai. jikan nai is no time now or for this, hima nai is no free time at all; okane nai is broke, okane tarinai is short for one thing; yoyuu nai covers money, time or headspace and alone means 'I'm swamped'.

items.use: Said when you're in a hurry (mou jikan nai! = we're out of time) and as an excuse (ima jikan nai n da). Casual speech often drops ga. The past jikan nakatta and the -te form jikan nakute (no time, so...) are also common.
items.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
items.trap: Not jikan o mottenai: time exists or doesn't, so it's jikan ga nai.

example.romaji: gomen, ima chotto jikan nai n da.
example.ja: ごめん、今ちょっと時間ないんだ。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really have time right now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima chotto jikan ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今ちょっと時間がないんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I don't really have time right now.

items.freqNote: ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807). The list has no phrase entry for 時間がない.
items.notes: jikan aru? (got a minute?) is the question it answers; jikan ga aku (aiteru) is having a free slot. hima ga nai is the wider 'no free time these days', while jikan nai is about now or this one thing. 'No time to cook' puts the verb first: ryouri suru jikan ga nai.

items.use: Said about being too busy, with a verb in front naming what you have no time for: ...teru hima wa nai is the commonest shape (nonbiri shiteru hima wa nai), and a plain verb usually takes mo (asobu hima mo nai, neru hima mo nai). As a brush-off it's sonna hima (wa) nai (I've got no time for that); plain ga is heard less than wa.
items.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)

example.romaji: saikin isogashikute, asobu hima mo nai.
example.ja: 最近忙しくて、遊ぶ暇もない。
example.english: I've been so busy lately I don't even have time to go out.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin isogashikute, asobu hima mo nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近忙しくて、遊ぶ暇もないんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been so busy lately I don't even have time to go out.

items.freqNote: 暇 #909 also counts the adjective hima (free, bored). ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807). Phrase entry 暇がない #16117. Pair count 327 (wa 198, ga 47, mo 41, none 40); films inflate it with 'we don't have time for this' lines (...teru hima wa nai).
items.notes: hima is also an adjective: hima? (are you free?), hima da naa (I'm bored). Unlike jikan ga nai, it never means you're running late: in a hurry it's mou jikan nai!, not mou hima nai!

items.use: The everyday 'I'm broke', usually okane nai in casual speech, often with ima or kongetsu. As a reason it's okane nai kara... (I'm broke, so...).
items.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
items.trap: okane mottenai is natural too, but it usually means no cash on you right now (ima okane mottenai), and about someone else, okane motteru means they're well-off. 'I'm broke' is plain okane nai, which can also mean no cash on you.
partners: genkin (cash: genkin nai = no cash on me)

example.ja: 今月、もうお金ない。
example.english: I'm already broke this month.

examplePolite.romaji: kongetsu wa mou okane ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今月はもうお金がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm already broke this month.

items.freqNote: お金 #422; the blunter 金 (kane) is #670. ない #43 is the kana form (無い #6807).
items.notes: kane nai, without o-, is blunter and mostly men's speech. For one purchase it's okane tarinai (not enough money).

items.use: Said at the till or when you're short for something: are, gohyaku en tarinai (oh, I'm 500 yen short). The amount often takes the place of okane. As a general state, okane tarinai means money's tight.
items.verbSense: not be enough (negative of tariru, be enough)
items.trap: Not okane ga sukunai, which is having little money in general. Being short for something is tarinai (not enough): gohyaku en tarinai.
partners: ninzuu (headcount: ninzuu tarinai = we're a person short)

example.ja: ごめん、お金足りないから貸して。
example.english: Sorry, I'm short. Can you lend me some?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, okane ga tarinai node kashite moraemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、お金が足りないので貸してもらえませんか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm short. Could you lend me some?

items.freqNote: 足りる #764 pools its forms; 足りない also has its own entry at #3974. お金 #422.
items.notes: okane nai is being broke; tarinai is being short for something. Enough is tariru: kore de tariru? (will this cover it?).

items.use: Says you have no spare money, time or energy. A noun before it says which: okane no yoyuu, jikan no yoyuu. Plain ima yoyuu nai means 'I'm swamped right now'.
items.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
items.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'afford'. For one item it's kaenai (takakute kaenai = I can't afford it). For having no money to spare in general it's okane no yoyuu ga nai (or just okane nai), and yoyuu nai alone means 'I'm swamped'.
partners: okane (money: okane no yoyuu ga nai)
jikan (time: jikan no yoyuu ga nai)
kokoro (headspace: kokoro no yoyuu ga nai = too stressed to deal with anything)

example.romaji: ima okane no yoyuu nai n da
example.ja: 今お金の余裕ないんだ
example.english: Money's a bit tight right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima okane no yoyuu ga nai n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今お金の余裕がないんです
examplePolite.english: Money's a bit tight right now.

items.notes: jikan ni yoyuu ga aru = there's still plenty of time. In slang, yoyuu means 'easy': yoyuu desho / yoyuu da yo = piece of cake.

blocks.label: Weather and wind
blocks.rationale: The remarks people trade about conditions outside: nice weather, a strong wind, heavy rain, a breeze, and stepping out for some air.
blocks.interference: kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi both use tsuyoi where English says 'windy' and 'heavy', so learn them in one frame (kyou ___ tsuyoi ne). kaze (wind) sounds exactly like kaze (a cold) and only the verb tells them apart: kaze ga fuku and kaze ni ataru are the wind, kaze o hiku is catching a cold.

items.use: The default weather opener, usually as ii tenki da ne (nice weather, huh?); bad weather is tenki ga warui.
items.verbSense: good, fine
items.trap: English 'beautiful/lovely weather' pushes kirei na tenki, which sounds odd: nice weather is ii tenki, bad is tenki ga warui.

example.ja: 今日いい天気だね。
example.english: Nice weather today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ii otenki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はいいお天気ですね。
examplePolite.english: Nice weather today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: いい is #24 (the spelling 良い is #1474). Native judgement: the attributive ii tenki (da ne) is the more common spoken shape. The list has no phrase count.
items.notes: Polite speech usually says otenki. The past is yokatta, not iikatta: tenki yokatta ne. tenki ga kuzureru = the weather turns bad; tenki motsu kana = will the weather hold? Sunny and cloudy are single verbs: hareteru (it's clear), kumotteru (it's cloudy).

items.use: The normal way to say 'it's windy': kyou kaze tsuyoi ne. When it picks up, kaze tsuyoku natte kita.
items.verbSense: strong (wind, rain, sun, a person)
items.trap: There is no Japanese adjective for 'windy': say the wind is strong (kaze ga tsuyoi), or kaze ga aru for 'there's some wind'.

example.ja: 今日風強いね。
example.english: It's windy today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze ga tsuyoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風が強いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's windy today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 風 (kaze, wind) is #1532. The homophone 風邪 (kaze, a cold) is a separate entry at #2666. 強風 (strong wind) is #22617 but belongs to news register.
items.notes: kaze ga dete kita = the wind's picking up. For no wind at all people say kaze ga nai.

items.use: Said as ame tsuyoi ne or ame tsuyoku natte kita (it's really coming down now). Tsuyoi ame is the same pairing before the noun. Just as often you hear ame sugoi ne or hidoi ame.
items.verbSense: strong (wind, rain, sun, a person)
items.trap: Not omoi ame: omoi is only weight, so heavy rain is strong rain; ame ga hidoi and ooame are also fine.

example.ja: 今日雨強いね。
example.english: The rain's heavy today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ame ga tsuyoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は雨が強いですね。
examplePolite.english: The rain's heavy today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: The attributive tsuyoi ame is the same pairing. The single nouns 大雨 (#11181) and 土砂降り/どしゃ降り (#30415–32931) are alternatives, not collocations.
items.notes: When it eases off: ame yowaku natta; a downpour is doshaburi.

items.use: Mostly heard as kaze fuiteru with a describing word: ii kaze fuiteru (there's a nice breeze), tsumetai kaze fuiteru (a cold wind's blowing). For 'it's windy', people say kaze ga tsuyoi.
items.verbSense: blow (wind; also blowing air from your mouth)
items.trap: kaze is both 'wind' and 'a cold', and only the verb tells you which: kaze ga fuku is the wind blowing, kaze o hiku is catching a cold. kaze ni ataru (get some air) is the wind too.

example.ja: いい風吹いてるね。
example.english: There's a nice breeze.

examplePolite.romaji: ii kaze ga fuitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: いい風が吹いてますね。
examplePolite.english: There's a nice breeze.

items.freqNote: Kana ふく is dominated by 服 and 拭く, so the kanji 吹く is used.
items.notes: kaze ga yamu = the wind dies down.

items.use: Mostly as chotto kaze ni atatte kuru (I'm going to get some air), said when stepping out of a stuffy, hot or boozy room. The ni always stays.
items.verbSense: hit, be struck by; be exposed to (wind, sun, rain)
items.trap: Nothing in 'get some air' leads to ataru: you let the breeze hit you, kaze ni ataru. Soto no kuuki o suu (breathe the outside air) is just as natural; kuuki o ireru is airing out a room, not you.
partners: hi (sun: hi ni ataru, get some sun)
ame (rain: ame ni ataru, get rained on)

example.romaji: chotto kaze ni atatte kuru ne.
example.ja: ちょっと風に当たってくるね。
example.english: I'm just going to get some air.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kaze ni atatte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと風に当たってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to get some air.

items.freqNote: The phrase 風に当たる is listed at #18645. 風 #1532; the homophone 風邪 (a cold) is #2666. 当たる #719 counts every sense (hit, win, be right). soto no kuuki o suu has 23 corpus hits.
items.notes: It is also a warning: anmari kaze ni atatteru to, kaze hiku yo (stay out in the wind too long and you'll catch a cold).

blocks.label: Washing and grooming
blocks.rationale: Looking after your body day to day: washing your hands, face and hair, and cutting your hair and nails.
blocks.interference: arau covers every kind of washing, from hands to hair, so there's no separate shampoo verb. The kiru in kami o kiru and tsume o kiru means cut (kitta), not wear (fuku o kiru, kita), and kami kitta is said even when a stylist cut it.

items.use: Said every day, before meals and on coming in: te aratte kite (go wash your hands), te aratta? O often drops in these reminders.
items.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.romaji: gohan da yo. te aratte kite.
example.ja: ごはんだよ。手洗ってきて。
example.english: Dinner's ready. Go wash your hands.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan desu yo. te o aratte kite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ごはんですよ。手を洗ってきてください。
examplePolite.english: The meal's ready. Please go and wash your hands.

items.freqNote: 手 #259; 洗う #1246. No phrase entry; お手洗い otearai (toilet) #5898 is built from the same two words.
items.notes: Only literal. Ashi o arau (wash your feet) is the idiom for quitting a shady line of work; pulling out of a deal or matter is te o hiku.

items.use: Part of the morning routine, and the way to wake yourself up: kao aratte kuru (I'll go wash my face). O often drops in casual talk.
items.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.ja: 眠いから、顔洗ってくる。
example.english: I'm sleepy, so I'll go wash my face.

examplePolite.romaji: nemui node, kao o aratte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 眠いので、顔を洗ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm sleepy, so I'll go and wash my face.

items.freqNote: 顔 #174; 洗う #1246. No phrase entry; 洗顔 sengan #29643 is the word on face-wash labels.
items.notes: Kao aratte denaoshite koi (go wash your face and come back) is a rough, stock brush-off for someone not ready.

items.use: Talk of the bath or shower routine: kami aratte kara neru, or kami arau no mendokusai (washing my hair is a pain). At home people say atama arau just as often (atama aratta?, especially to kids). O drops in casual speech.
items.verbSense: wash with water (hands, dishes, a car)

example.ja: 髪洗ってから寝る。
example.english: I'll wash my hair, then go to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: kami o aratte kara nemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 髪を洗ってから寝ます。
examplePolite.english: I'll wash my hair before I go to bed.

items.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 #3658); 洗う #1246; シャンプー #7199 is the product and the salon word.
items.notes: Drying it afterwards is kami o kawakasu (kami kawakashite). Shanpuu suru is also everyday (shanpuu shite kara neru).

items.use: Mostly heard in the past tense with o dropped: kami kitta? (did you get a haircut?), a stock small-talk line. For the salon trip itself, say kami kiri ni iku (go get a haircut).
items.verbSense: kiru: cut (with a blade or scissors)
items.trap: English 'get a haircut' suggests kitte morau or the dictionary word sanpatsu suru (old-fashioned). Kitte morau works, but natives just say kami kitta (or katto shita), even when a stylist did it.

example.ja: あれ、髪切った？
example.english: Oh, did you get a haircut?

examplePolite.romaji: are, kami kirimashita?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、髪切りました？
examplePolite.english: Oh, did you get your hair cut?

items.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 kami no ke #3658); 切る #546; カット #3084; 散髪 sanpatsu #24840.
items.notes: Don't mix it up with kiru 'wear' (fuku o kiru): cut is kitta / kirimasu, wear is kita / kimasu. By ear, cut drops after ki (KI-tta) and wear is flat (kita). Kami (hair) sounds the same as kami 'paper' (10-list-nouns #14), so kami o kiru can also mean cut paper. Context decides, and kami no ke makes 'hair' explicit.

items.use: Said as a reminder or a chore: tsume kitte (cut your nails), tsume kiranakya. O often drops; the clippers are tsumekiri.
items.verbSense: cut (with a blade or scissors)

example.ja: そろそろ爪切らなきゃ。
example.english: It's about time I cut my nails.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro tsume o kiranai to ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ爪を切らないといけませんね。
examplePolite.english: It's about time I cut my nails.

items.freqNote: 爪 #4532; 切る #546; 爪切り tsumekiri (nail clippers) #36115.
items.notes: Many people still know the superstition against cutting your nails at night (yoru tsume o kiru to...).

blocks.label: Bathroom
blocks.rationale: The washroom routine people mention morning and night: the toilet, a shower, a bath, teeth, a shave.
blocks.interference: shawaa o abiru and ofuro ni hairu are both 'take a ___' in English, but a shower is poured over you (o abiru) and a bath is gone into (ni hairu); drill them in one frame, saki ni ___ kuru ne. Teeth are polished (migaku), and a shave names what comes off (hige o soru).

items.use: The plain way to excuse yourself, usually with -te kuru since you'll be back: chotto toire itte kuru. Casual speech drops ni. toire itteru means someone has gone and is in there now (tanaka-san nara toire itteru yo), not that they're on the way. With strangers or at work, otearai ni itte kimasu sounds softer.
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: Not ofuro or basuruumu for 'bathroom': those mean the room you bathe in, which in most Japanese homes is separate from the toilet, so 'go to the bathroom' is toire ni iku.

example.ja: ちょっとトイレ行ってくる。
example.english: I'm just going to the bathroom.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto toire ni itte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとトイレに行ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go to the restroom.

items.freqNote: お手洗い (otearai) #5898 is the politer word.
items.notes: Asking where it is: toire doko? to friends, otearai wa doko desu ka? to staff.

items.use: Used for showering at any time of day. You mostly hear shawaa abite kuru (I'll go shower) or shawaa abita (I've showered), usually without o.
items.verbSense: pour over yourself, bathe in (water, sunlight)
items.trap: Not shawaa o toru: 'take' points to toru, but a shower is poured over you, so the verb is abiru.

example.romaji: saki ni shawaa abite kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にシャワー浴びてくるね。
example.english: I'll go shower first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni shawaa o abite kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にシャワーを浴びてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and take a shower first.

items.freqNote: Both parts ranked. abiru is used mostly for showers, sunlight and criticism, so this phrase is where learners meet it.
items.notes: Casual shawaa suru is also heard.

items.use: The everyday way to talk about bathing at home, usually at night. You hear ofuro haitte kuru and ofuro haitta? (have you had your bath?) all the time, mostly without ni.
items.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
items.trap: Not ofuro o toru or ofuro o abiru: a bath is something you go into, so it's ni hairu.

example.romaji: saki ni ofuro haitte kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にお風呂入ってくるね。
example.english: I'll go have my bath first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni ofuro ni haitte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にお風呂に入ってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and have my bath first.

items.freqNote: お風呂 #1921 (plain 風呂 #2586); 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.
items.notes: Running the bath is ofuro o ireru or ofuro o wakasu; the water heater announces ofuro ga wakimashita.

items.use: Part of the morning and bedtime routine: ha migaita? (did you brush your teeth?), ha migaite neru (brush and go to bed). The noun form hamigaki suru is just as common.
items.verbSense: polish, scrub until it shines (teeth, shoes)
items.trap: Not ha o arau ('wash'): teeth are polished, migaku. hamigaki suru is just as common.

example.ja: まだ歯磨いてない。
example.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada ha o migaite imasen.
examplePolite.ja: まだ歯を磨いていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

items.freqNote: 歯磨き #16183 (hamigaki suru) is the competing noun form.
items.notes: 10-list-nouns leaves out bare ha (too many homophones) and names ha o migaku as the collocation card that carries it. hamigaki (brushing) and haburashi (toothbrush) are the related nouns.

items.use: The daily shave, mostly heard as hige sotta? or hige soranakya; o is often dropped. Stubble is hige ga nobiteru (your beard's grown).
items.verbSense: shave off (hair)
items.trap: Not hige o kiru, which sounds like trimming it with scissors; shaving it off is soru. soru takes the hair (hige, ke, mayu) or the place (atama o soru).

example.ja: 今日ひげ剃るの忘れた。
example.english: I forgot to shave today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hige o soru no o wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はひげを剃るのを忘れました。
examplePolite.english: I forgot to shave today.

items.freqNote: ひげ #10683; the katakana spelling ヒゲ is #9045 and 髭 #35748. 剃る #18134.
items.notes: Growing one is hige o hayasu; hige hayashiteru = he has a beard.

blocks.label: Smart and skilled
blocks.rationale: Praise for what someone is good at: brains, Japanese, their job, taste.
blocks.interference: Each noun takes its own word for 'good': atama ga ii (never jouzu), nihongo ga jouzu (a skill done well), shigoto ga dekiru (capable, not jouzu), sensu ga ii. nihongo ga dekiru only says you can speak it; jouzu says you speak it well.

items.use: The everyday 'smart': ano hito, atama ii ne, with ga dropped in casual speech. Ii conjugates from yoi, so the past is atama yokatta and the negative is atama yokunai.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not sumaato (in Japanese that means slim or sleek): 'smart' is atama ga ii. Kashikoi is also correct but less everyday, and often said to children or pets.

example.ja: 田中さん、頭いいよね。
example.english: Tanaka's smart, right?

examplePolite.romaji: tanaka-san wa atama ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 田中さんは頭がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka is smart, right?

items.freqNote: 頭 #375; いい #24 (良い #1474, よい #120). The fused casual form 頭いい appears as its own entry at #7901, which is direct evidence for the phrase. 賢い kashikoi #3471; スマート #11064.
items.notes: Atama ga warui is fine about yourself but rude about others. For someone who is good at their job, say shigoto ga dekiru.

items.use: The compliment every learner hears, often after a single sentence: nihongo jouzu desu ne! Casual speech drops ga, and friends also say nihongo umai ne. The usual reply is iie, mada mada desu or sonna koto nai desu.
items.verbSense: jouzu: skilful, good at (praise for someone else's skill)
items.trap: Jouzu is for praising others: watashi wa nihongo ga jouzu desu sounds like boasting. About yourself, say nihongo ga sukoshi dekimasu, or mada mada desu when complimented.

example.ja: 日本語上手になったね！
example.english: Your Japanese has got really good!

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo ga jouzu ni narimashita ne!
examplePolite.ja: 日本語が上手になりましたね！
examplePolite.english: Your Japanese has improved!

items.freqNote: 日本語 #3651; 上手 #1309, お上手 #5903; うまい #246 also covers 'tasty'. Films rarely compliment anyone's Japanese (3 hits), so commonness is judged.
items.notes: It's said after a single konnichiwa, so it's politeness more than a verdict.

items.english: be capable, good at one's job
items.use: Praise for a capable coworker, usually shigoto dekiru (ga dropped), or before a noun, where ga often becomes no: shigoto ga dekiru hito / shigoto no dekiru hito (someone good at their job). Dekiru alone can carry it (dekiru hito da ne), and shigoto ga dekinai is blunt criticism. It's said about someone: telling a superior to their face that they're capable sounds presumptuous.
items.verbSense: dekiru: can do; here, be capable, perform well
items.trap: Not shigoto ga jouzu. Jouzu praises how skilfully something is done (nihongo ga jouzu, ryouri ga jouzu), while dekiru says someone is capable. Being good at your job is shigoto ga dekiru, usually as shigoto ga dekiru hito.
partners: benkyou (benkyou ga dekiru: do well at school)
undou (undou ga dekiru: be good at sports, athletic)

example.romaji: atarashii buchou, sugoku shigoto dekiru n da yo.
example.ja: 新しい部長、すごく仕事できるんだよ。
example.english: The new manager's really good at her job.

examplePolite.romaji: atarashii buchou wa totemo shigoto ga dekiru kata na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 新しい部長はとても仕事ができる方なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Our new manager is extremely capable.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134; できる #73 (出来る #1313). No phrase entry. 優秀 yuushuu #1364; 有能 yuunou #7229; 上手 jouzu #1309.
items.notes: Outside of praise it's literal: ashita shigoto dekinai (I can't work tomorrow). Yuushuu (excellent) is the formal word.

items.english: have good taste, a good eye
items.use: A stock compliment on clothes, a gift, a room or a playlist: sensu ii ne! Ga is usually dropped. The opposite is sensu nai (no taste), and sensu ga aru means a flair for something (ryouri no sensu ga aru).
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: 'Good taste' isn't aji (flavour). Sensu is a false friend: sensu nai means 'no taste', not 'that doesn't make sense' (imi wakannai). 'That makes sense' is naruhodo, and common sense is joushiki.

example.ja: その服、センスいいね。
example.english: Great taste, that outfit.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, sensu ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、センスがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That outfit shows great taste.

items.freqNote: センス #2690; いい #24. No phrase entry; 趣味がいい #53080; おしゃれ #3483. The film count (17) is too low to use, so commonness is judged.
items.notes: Shumi ga ii also means good taste, but shumi mostly means 'hobby', and ii shumi shiteru ne is often sarcastic. Keep it apart from sutairu ga ii, which means a good figure, not style; someone who dresses well is oshare.

blocks.label: Going out for fun
blocks.rationale: Everyday plans to go out and do something, all built the same way: the activity noun goes straight before ni iku.
blocks.interference: English 'go for a walk' or 'go to karaoke' tempts a verb before ni iku, but the noun goes straight in: sanpo ni iku, karaoke ni iku. eiga ni iku is the outing and eiga o miru the watching. asobi ni iku also means dropping by someone's place (asobi ni kite ne).

items.english: go out for fun; go visit
items.use: Covers a fun day or night out and a visit to someone's home: shuumatsu shibuya ni asobi ni itta, tomodachi no uchi ni asobi ni iku. Casual speech often drops ni (asobi iku?). The mirror image, kondo asobi ni kite, is the standard 'come over sometime'.
items.verbSense: go (asobi is the noun of asobu, have fun, hang out)
items.trap: English 'play' makes asobu sound childish, but adults say asobi ni iku all the time for a fun outing or a visit to a friend's place. And 'I'll come and visit' is asobi ni iku, not asobi ni kuru: as with mukae ni iku, you are the one going.
partners: omimai (visiting someone sick: omimai ni iku)
aisatsu (dropping by to say hello: aisatsu ni iku)

example.ja: 今度、遊びに行くね！
example.english: I'll come and visit sometime!

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, asobi ni ikimasu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 今度、遊びに行きますね！
examplePolite.english: I'll come and visit sometime!

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 遊びに行く has its own entry at #4009 and 遊びに来る (come over) at #3038; the verb 遊ぶ is #674. The tokenizer tags 遊び as a verb stem, so the pair count is only 11, but the written form 遊びに行 counts 47, and 遊びに来 outnumbers it at 64 (asobi ni kite alone 33).
items.notes: Among friends kondo asobou (let's hang out sometime) is the plain invitation, often a friendly maybe rather than a fixed plan.

items.use: Said about going to the cinema, usually as a plan or an invitation: eiga ikanai? Casual speech drops ni. eiga mi ni iku says the same with the watching spelled out; at home it is just eiga o miru.
items.verbSense: go; with an event noun + ni, go out to see it

example.ja: 週末、映画行かない？
example.english: Want to go to a movie this weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu, eiga ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末、映画に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go to a movie this weekend?

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. In the subtitles 映画に行 (24) is more common than 映画を見に (14).
items.notes: eigakan is the building: eigakan de mita (I saw it at the cinema).

items.use: Said when popping out for a walk, often as chotto sanpo itte kuru (I'm off for a little walk). Casual speech drops ni. sanpo suru puts the focus on the walk itself and takes the place you walk through with o: kouen o sanpo shita.
items.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
items.trap: Not sanpo o toru, copied from 'take a walk': you go on one (sanpo ni iku) or just do one (sanpo suru). With a dog it is inu no sanpo ni iku, never inu o aruku.

example.ja: ちょっと散歩行ってくるね。
example.english: I'm just popping out for a walk.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto sanpo ni itte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと散歩に行ってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going out for a walk.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. The pair count is 52 (ni 46). The written form 散歩に行 counts 43 against 133 for all forms of sanpo suru, which is the more frequent verb but a plain noun + suru; ni iku is the set built on the noun.
items.notes: Walking the dog is inu no sanpo (ni iku); aimless wandering about town is burabura suru.

items.use: Usually a plan or an invitation (karaoke ikanai?), often as the second stop after dinner. Casual speech drops ni: karaoke iku.
items.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
items.trap: karaoke is where you sing, so the usual phrasing is karaoke de utau, karaoke suru, or just karaoke iku. karaoke o utau, copied from 'sing karaoke', is heard but sounds off to many speakers.

example.ja: 昨日カラオケ行って、声枯れた。
example.english: Went to karaoke yesterday and lost my voice.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou karaoke ni itte, koe ga karemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日カラオケに行って、声が枯れました。
examplePolite.english: I went to karaoke yesterday and lost my voice.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. Films mention karaoke only 39 times, so the pair count (4) says little; in Japan it is an everyday night out.
items.notes: At a work do, karaoke is the classic nijikai (second stop); going alone is hitori karaoke, or the slang hitokara.

blocks.label: Questions and learning
blocks.rationale: Class talk: having a question, answering one, speaking English, then the thanks phrase benkyou ni naru.
blocks.interference: shitsumon ga aru (have one) takes ga and shitsumon ni kotaeru (answer it) takes ni, never o; benkyou ni natta (I learned from it) is not benkyou shita (I studied).

items.use: Said to open a question, usually with n da kedo, and here the ga mostly stays: shitsumon ga aru n da kedo. After nanika it's often dropped or becomes wa: teachers and presenters ask the room nanika shitsumon (wa) arimasu ka?
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
items.trap: English 'have' leads to motsu, but a question you have is aru: shitsumon ga aru. Asking it is shitsumon suru, or simply kiku.

example.romaji: hitotsu shitsumon ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: 一つ質問があるんだけど。
example.english: I've got a question for you.

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu shitsumon ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 一つ質問があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: I've got a question for you.

items.freqNote: 質問 #1058, ある #21. No phrase entry. 聞く kiku #67 is the everyday verb for asking.
items.notes: To check before asking: shitsumon ii? (can I ask something?). Answering one is shitsumon ni kotaeru.

items.use: Said in class, interviews and arguments, often as a demand (chanto shitsumon ni kotaete) or a refusal (sono shitsumon ni wa kotaerarenai). The ni almost always stays.
items.verbSense: answer, reply
items.trap: English 'answer the question' has a direct object, which tempts shitsumon o kotaeru. In Japanese you answer to a question: shitsumon ni kotaeru. Answering the phone is a different verb: denwa ni deru.

example.ja: その質問には答えられない。
example.english: I can't answer that question.

examplePolite.romaji: sono shitsumon ni wa kotaeraremasen.
examplePolite.ja: その質問には答えられません。
examplePolite.english: I can't answer that question.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 質問に答える has its own entry in the drama list at #6167 (質問 #1058, 答える #646). In the subtitles 362 of 367 hits keep ni.
items.notes: Asking is shitsumon suru or just kiku; the answer itself is kotae (kotae wa?).

items.use: Mostly heard about ability, in the potential: eigo hanaseru? (can you speak English?). With the potential, ga is as common as o: eigo ga hanaseru. Casual speech drops o. eigo de hanasu means talking in English at that moment: eigo de hanashite mo ii?
items.verbSense: speak, talk; tell
items.trap: 'Do you speak English?' is a plain present in English, but asking whether someone can takes the potential: eigo hanaseru? or eigo dekiru? Plain eigo hanasu? is understood, but it asks whether someone does speak it somewhere (ie de eigo hanasu no? = do you speak English at home?) or is about to, not whether they can.

example.ja: 英語はちょっとだけ話せる。
example.english: I can speak a little English.

examplePolite.romaji: eigo wa chotto dake hanasemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 英語はちょっとだけ話せます。
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little English.

items.freqNote: 英語 #2574, 話す #151, potential 話せる #1219. しゃべる shaberu #745 is the casual twin (eigo shaberu). No phrase entry.
items.notes: eigo dekiru? asks the same thing. Whether English gets you by somewhere is tsuujiru: eigo tsuujiru?

items.use: Said as thanks when someone explains or shows you something: benkyou ni narimasu as a reply on the spot, especially to a senior, and benkyou ni natta or benkyou ni narimashita afterwards.
items.verbSense: become, turn into
items.trap: benkyou shita means you sat down and studied. 'I learned a lot from that' is benkyou ni natta: the thing becomes a lesson.

example.romaji: kyou no hanashi, sugoku benkyou ni natta.
example.ja: 今日の話、すごく勉強になった。
example.english: I learned a lot from today's talk.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no ohanashi, hontou ni benkyou ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日のお話、本当に勉強になりました。
examplePolite.english: I learned a lot from today's talk.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 勉強になる has its own entry in the drama list at #4175 (勉強 #729, なる #29).
items.notes: Often comes after naruhodo: naruhodo, benkyou ni narimasu.

blocks.label: Aches and pains
blocks.rationale: Saying what hurts: body part + ga itai for any pain, plus stiff shoulders.
blocks.interference: X ga itai covers every pain (atama itai, nodo itai), and koshi is the lower back, which English just calls 'my back'. kata ga koru is stiffness and takes the verb koru, never itai.
