items.use: Body part + ga itai is the pattern for any pain, usually said without ga: atama itai. Add n da or n desu when it's the reason you can't do something.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts; on its own, 'ouch!'
items.trap: Not a 'have' sentence: the head hurts, atama ga itai. The noun zutsuu exists (zutsuu ga suru, zutsuuyaku), but in conversation atama itai comes first.

example.ja: 朝からずっと頭いたい。
example.english: I've had a headache since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara zutto atama ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝からずっと頭が痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had a headache since this morning.

items.freqNote: 頭 #375; 痛い #336; phrase entry 頭が痛い #8807, a partial count that also includes the figurative 'it's a headache'. 頭痛 #7624.
items.notes: Also used, as in English, for a problem that's a headache.

items.use: Covers any pain in the belly; usually said without ga, onaka itai, often with n da or n desu to explain. Often a polite hint that you need the toilet.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts
items.trap: Dictionaries give i for 'stomach'; i ga itai is said too, but the everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai.

example.ja: なんかお腹痛い。食べすぎたかも。
example.english: My stomach kind of hurts. Maybe I ate too much.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka onaka ga itai n desu. tabesugita kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんかお腹が痛いんです。食べすぎたかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: My stomach kind of hurts. I might have eaten too much.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.
items.notes: An upset stomach from something you ate is onaka o kowasu (onaka kowashita). Onaka no choushi ga warui is the discreet way to mention it.

items.use: Often the first sign of a cold: nanka nodo itai, with ga dropped. Add n da or n desu when it explains a rough voice or skipping karaoke.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts

example.ja: なんか喉痛い。風邪かも。
example.english: My throat's kind of sore. Might be a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka nodo ga itai n desu. kaze kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんか喉が痛いんです。風邪かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: My throat is a bit sore. It might be a cold.

items.freqNote: 喉 #3552 (kana のど #7553); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.
items.notes: The same nodo is in nodo ga kawaku (thirsty); a scratchy throat is nodo ga igaiga suru.

items.use: The everyday back-pain complaint after lifting, sitting all day or sleeping badly: koshi itai, with ga dropped. Older people say it constantly.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts
items.trap: 'My back hurts' usually means the lower back, which is koshi. Senaka is the upper and middle back, so senaka ga itai points higher.

example.romaji: omoi mono motte, koshi itaku natta.
example.ja: 重いもの持って、腰痛くなった。
example.english: I lifted something heavy and now my back hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: omoi mono o motte, koshi ga itaku narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 重いものを持って、腰が痛くなりました。
examplePolite.english: I lifted something heavy and hurt my back.

items.freqNote: 腰 #2126; 痛い #336. No phrase entry; 腰痛 youtsuu #15563 is the clinic word, and ぎっくり腰 gikkurigoshi (a sudden back spasm) is #17355.
items.notes: Koshi covers the lower back and hips together.

items.use: Said as kata kotta (my shoulders have gone stiff) or kata kotteru (they're stiff); the noun katakori is just as common.
items.verbSense: stiffen, harden; also be really into something (ryouri ni koru)
items.trap: English uses the adjective 'stiff', so learners look for one; Japanese uses the verb koru: kata ga kotteru.

example.ja: 一日中パソコンで、肩凝った。
example.english: A whole day at the computer, and my shoulders are stiff.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichijuu pasokon o tsukatte ite, kata ga korimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一日中パソコンを使っていて、肩が凝りました。
examplePolite.english: I was on the computer all day, and my shoulders have gone stiff.

items.freqNote: 肩 #1811; kana こる #4566 (kanji 凝る #6722), the higher-ranked spelling as for the other verbs here; phrase entry 肩が凝る #35013; the noun 肩こり is #33119 and 肩凝り #32224.
items.notes: Japanese complain of stiff shoulders where English speakers often say neck or back. Lower-back pain is koshi ga itai.

blocks.label: Making friends
blocks.rationale: Meeting someone new: making friends, becoming friends with one person, swapping names, going up to someone, and chances to meet people.
blocks.interference: tomodachi ga dekiru is gaining friends in general (tomodachi dekita), while one person is X to tomodachi ni naru; neither is tomodachi o tsukuru. 'Tell me your name' is namae oshiete, not iu, and going up to someone is koe o kakeru, not hanasu.

items.use: Said once a friendship has formed, so mostly in the past: tomodachi dekita (I've made a friend). kareshi / kanojo dekita (got a boyfriend / girlfriend) works the same way.
items.verbSense: come into being, be made; also 'can do' and 'be ready'
items.trap: English 'make' leads to tomodachi o tsukuru, which natives use for setting out to make friends (tomodachi tsukuritai); 'I've made a friend' is tomodachi dekita.
partners: kodomo (child: kodomo dekita = we're expecting; akachan works too)

example.ja: こっちでもう友達できた？
example.english: Made any friends here yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kochira de tomodachi wa dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: こちらで友達はできましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you made any friends here?

items.freqNote: dekiru: kana できる #73 pools every sense, mostly 'can do' (出来る #1313 listed separately).
items.notes: Wanting friends is usually tomodachi hoshii or tomodachi tsukuritai. Having them takes ga iru, as in kodomo ga iru: dekita is the moment it happens, iru is having them (tomodachi iru?). Becoming friends with one person is X to tomodachi ni naru.

items.use: Takes to for the other person: kare to tomodachi ni natta (I became friends with him). Mostly told in the past, about where or how a friendship started.
items.verbSense: become (with ni after a noun)
items.trap: English 'make friends with him' leads to tomodachi o tsukuru, which is setting out to make friends in general (tomodachi tsukuritai). With a particular person it's kare to tomodachi ni natta, and 'I've made a friend' is tomodachi dekita.
partners: koibito (a couple; tsukiau is the usual 'start going out')

example.romaji: kanojo to wa daigaku de tomodachi ni natta.
example.ja: 彼女とは大学で友達になった。
example.english: She and I became friends at uni.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa daigaku de tomodachi ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とは大学で友達になりました。
examplePolite.english: She and I became friends at university.

items.freqNote: 友達 #405; naru: kana なる #29 (成る #13300). No phrase entry.
items.notes: nakayoku naru (get close) is the near twin: sugu nakayoku natta (we hit it off right away). tomodachi ni narou = let's be friends.

items.use: Mostly the request namae oshiete (what's your name?), a friendly alternative to onamae wa? or namae nante iu no?. The same oshieru asks for any personal details: bangou oshiete (give me your number).
items.verbSense: teach; also tell, let someone know (information)
items.trap: English 'tell me your name' leads to iu, and namae o iu is real Japanese: it's saying a name out loud (in a roll call, or saying your own). Asking someone to share their name, number or the way takes oshieru: namae oshiete.
partners: michi (the way: michi o oshieru = give directions)

example.ja: よかったら、名前教えてくれる？
example.english: If you don't mind, what's your name?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, onamae o oshiete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、お名前を教えてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Would you mind telling me your name?

items.freqNote: 名前 #256; 教える #196 (all senses, mostly 'tell'). No phrase entry. Written 名前を教 119; 名前を言 182 is mostly saying a name aloud.
items.notes: onamae wa? is the plain polite question (at a counter, or to a child); between friends namae nante iu no? is common.

items.english: speak to, call out to; ask along
items.use: Used for going up to someone, or asking to be told: nanka attara koe kakete (give me a shout if anything comes up). Also the everyday way to invite someone along: tanaka-san ni mo koe kakeyou ka? (shall we ask Tanaka too?). koe kakerareta can mean someone came up to you, including being hit on.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, direct your voice at someone
items.trap: 'Talk to someone' leads to hanasu, which is fine once you're talking: X to hanasu is chatting with X, X ni hanasu is telling X something. Going up to someone, calling them over or giving them a shout is koe o kakeru (hanashikakeru also works for starting a chat).
partners: kotoba (words: yasashii kotoba o kakeru = say something kind to someone)

example.ja: なんかあったら声かけてね。
example.english: Give me a shout if you need anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara koe o kakete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったら声をかけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know if you need anything.

items.freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools all senses.
items.notes: hanashikakeru (start talking to someone) is the close single verb. Same kakeru as denwa o kakeru (make a call) and meiwaku o kakeru, in a different sense.

items.use: Mostly in the negative, the stock complaint deai ga nai (I never meet anyone), and in good wishes: ii deai ga arimasu you ni (hope you meet someone great). Often about romance, but it also covers new friends at a new job or school.
items.verbSense: there is; have (events, chances)
items.trap: English 'I never meet anyone' leads to dare ni mo awanai, which sounds like you never see people at all. Meeting someone new is talked about as a deai (an encounter): deai ga nai.

example.romaji: shokuba ni zenzen deai nai n da yo.
example.ja: 職場に全然出会いないんだよ。
example.english: I never meet anyone at work.

examplePolite.romaji: shokuba ni wa zenzen deai ga nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 職場には全然出会いがないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I never get to meet anyone at work.

items.freqNote: 出会い #1993; ある #21. The verb 出会う (deau) #608. Written 出会いがあ 15, 出会い(が)な 11.
items.notes: deau is the verb, for meeting for the first time or by chance: daigaku de deatta (we met at uni).

blocks.label: Play and lessons
blocks.rationale: English 'play' splits in two: games and sports take suru (casually yaru) and instruments take hiku. Taking lessons in any of them is narau.
blocks.interference: asobu tempts for all of them. suru/yaru names the activity or hobby (piano yatteru), hiku is actually playing (piano hikeru?), and narau is lessons with a teacher (piano naratteta), never benkyou suru. Keep this hiku apart from kaze o hiku and omikuji o hiku, which sound the same.

items.english: play games (video games, cards and the like)
items.use: Use it for video games, and for card or party games too. Casually it is geemu shiteru or geemu yatteru with o dropped, and zutto geemu shiteta means you were gaming the whole time.
items.verbSense: do; the general verb, and sports and games are things you 'do'
items.trap: English 'play' pulls toward asobu. For gaming in general, friends say geemu suru or yaru (geemu yatteru). With a specific title, gamers also say kono geemu asonda?, and geemu de asobu (play around with a game) is fine.

example.ja: 昨日ずっとゲームしてた
example.english: I was gaming all day yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa zutto geemu o shitemashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はずっとゲームをしてました
examplePolite.english: I was playing games all day yesterday.

items.freqNote: yaru #45 is the common casual alternative (geemu yaru); asobu is #674. toranpu #9541 takes the same suru.

items.use: Use it for playing any sport, whether regularly or right now. In speech you mostly hear sakkaa shiteru or sakkaa yatteru with o dropped, and yatteta means used to play.
items.verbSense: do; the general verb, and sports and games are things you 'do'
items.trap: Not sakkaa o asobu: asobu means playing around, so a sport takes suru, or casually yaru (sakkaa yatteru).

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa sakkaa shiteru
example.ja: 休みの日はサッカーしてる
example.english: On my days off I play soccer.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa sakkaa o shitemasu
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日はサッカーをしてます
examplePolite.english: I play soccer on my days off.

items.freqNote: suru #15; yaru #45 is the casual partner for sports. tenisu #9450, yakyuu #3911 and gorufu #5148 take the same verb.

items.use: Use it for actually playing the instrument. The common forms are piano hikeru? (can you play the piano?) and piano hiiteru (is playing now, or plays regularly). With hikeru, ga often replaces o: piano ga hikeru.
items.verbSense: play a string or keyboard instrument (plucked, bowed or keyed); wind and drums take other verbs
items.trap: Not piano o asobu, and not piano o suru carried over from sakkaa o suru: playing the instrument is hiku (piano hiiteru, piano hikeru?). piano yatteru ('I do piano') names it as a hobby, and lessons with a teacher are piano o narau (piano naratteta); neither means playing it right now.

example.ja: ピアノ弾ける？
example.english: Can you play the piano?

examplePolite.romaji: piano o hikemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ピアノを弾けますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you play the piano?

items.freqNote: 弾く (ひく) #5832. The kana spelling ひく #2982 mixes every hiku sense, and 引く #1039 is the homophone hiku (pull; kaze o hiku). gitaa #7059 takes the same verb.
items.notes: Wind instruments take fuku (fue o fuku) and drums take tataku (taiko o tataku).

items.use: Said about lessons with a teacher, now or as a child: piano naratteru (I take lessons), naratteta (I used to). Casual speech drops o. Childhood lessons like this are a standard getting-to-know-you topic.
items.verbSense: learn from a teacher, take lessons in
items.trap: English 'learn' leads to benkyou suru, but piano o benkyou shita sounds like studying it as a subject. Lessons with a teacher are narau: piano naratteta. oboeru is memorising or picking something up yourself (shigoto oboeta = I've learned the job).

example.ja: 小さい頃、ピアノ習ってた。
example.english: I took piano lessons when I was little.

examplePolite.romaji: chiisai koro, piano o narattemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 小さい頃、ピアノを習ってました。
examplePolite.english: I took piano lessons when I was little.

items.freqNote: 習い事 (naraigoto, lessons taken as a hobby) #15541. 弾く (hiku, play the piano) is #5832.
items.notes: The teacher's side is oshieru (piano o oshiete iru); after-school lessons like this are called naraigoto.

blocks.label: Feeling unwell
blocks.rationale: Saying you feel off, from the general guai ga warui and the work-safe taichou ga warui to being in or out of form.
blocks.interference: guai ga warui and taichou ga warui both mean 'I don't feel well', and taichou is the safer word at work. choushi ga warui / ii is being off or on form, and also a device acting up. kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now. kimochi warui (in senses) is queasy or gross.

items.use: The general 'I'm not feeling well', usually softened to chotto guai warui; others ask guai warui no? or guai dou? (how are you feeling?).
items.verbSense: bad
items.trap: 'I'm sick' as byouki desu sounds like a real illness; for just feeling unwell, the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
partners: kibun (feeling; kibun ga warui = feel sick, also 'be put off')

example.romaji: chotto guai warui kara, saki ni kaeru ne.
example.ja: ちょっと具合悪いから、先に帰るね。
example.english: I'm not feeling great, so I'll head home early.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto guai ga warui node, kyou wa saki ni kaette mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと具合が悪いので、今日は先に帰ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I'm not feeling well. Would it be all right if I went home early today?

items.freqNote: 具合 #1423; 悪い #139; phrase entry 具合が悪い #5837, high for a phrase.
items.notes: The sets next to it split the job. Taichou ga warui means the same in a more careful word, and it's the safe phrase for calling in sick at work. Choushi ga warui is being off form, and also a machine acting up (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now (in a car, in a crowd). Kimochi warui (in the senses list) is queasy, but also 'gross, creepy'.

items.english: not feel well, be under the weather (the safe phrase at work)
items.use: The stock phrase for calling in sick or cancelling: taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai. Casual talk drops ga (chotto taichou warui), and others ask taichou dou? or taichou daijoubu?
items.verbSense: bad, in poor condition

example.romaji: gomen, taichou warui kara kyou yasumu.
example.ja: ごめん、体調悪いから今日休む。
example.english: Sorry, I'm not feeling well, so I'm taking today off.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、体調が悪いので、今日は休ませてください。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I'm not feeling well. Could I have today off?

items.freqNote: 体調 #1944; 悪い #139. No phrase entry (体調を崩す is #9388).
items.notes: A little more neutral than guai ga warui, so it's the safe choice at work; the opposite is taichou ga ii.

items.use: About yourself it's a vague 'I'm off' (kyou chotto choushi warui). Put a body part or a device before no: onaka no choushi ga warui, sumaho no choushi ga warui (my phone's acting up). Ga often drops in casual talk, the opposite is choushi ii, and choushi dou? asks how things are going.
items.verbSense: bad, in poor condition
items.trap: A glitchy phone or PC isn't kowareta, which means it has stopped working (sumaho kowareta? is also said as an exaggeration). If it still works, just badly, it's choushi ga warui: sumaho no choushi warui.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga warui = look pale)
me (eyes: me ga warui = poor eyesight)

example.romaji: saikin, pasokon no choushi warui n da yo ne.
example.ja: 最近、パソコンの調子悪いんだよね。
example.english: My computer's been acting up lately.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara chotto onaka no choushi ga warui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からちょっとお腹の調子が悪いんです。
examplePolite.english: My stomach's been a bit off since yesterday.

items.freqNote: 調子 #1124; 悪い #139; phrase entry 調子が悪い #8863 (調子がいい #16780). The ga-dropped 調子悪い has no entry of its own.
items.notes: Onaka no choushi ga warui is the discreet way to mention stomach trouble. Choushi ni noru (get carried away) is a separate idiom with the same noun.

items.english: be in good shape, going well
items.use: The opposite of choushi ga warui, for your body, your form or a device: kyou choushi ii (I'm on form today), and choushi dou? asks how things are going. Ga often drops.
items.verbSense: good, fine, OK
partners: guai (condition: guai ga ii = feel well; of a thing, work properly)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga ii = look well)
kigen (mood: kigen ga ii = be in a good mood)

example.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ii n da.
example.ja: 最近、体の調子いいんだ。
example.english: I've been feeling good lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ga ii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、体の調子がいいんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been in good shape lately.

items.freqNote: 調子 #1124; いい #24; phrase entry 調子がいい #16780 (調子が良い #43063), well below 調子が悪い #8863.
items.notes: About someone's words it means glib: choushi ii koto bakari iu (always says whatever suits them).

items.english: feel sick (queasy or faint); feel put off
items.use: For feeling sick right now, in a crowd, a hot room or a car: chotto kibun ga warui (ga can drop, but it's kept far more than in kimochi warui), and kibun waruku natta when it comes on. Said about something someone did, it means it left you feeling put off: ano iikata, kibun warui.
items.verbSense: bad
items.trap: English 'I feel bad (about it)' is guilt, which is warui na or moushiwake nai, never kibun ga warui. Kibun ga warui is feeling sick, or feeling put off by something someone did; a grumpy mood that others can see is kigen ga warui.
partners: kigen (mood: kigen ga warui = be grumpy)
igokochi (comfort: igokochi ga warui = uncomfortable somewhere)

example.ja: 電車混んでて、気分悪くなっちゃった。
example.english: The train was packed and I started feeling sick.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ga sugoku konde ite, kibun ga waruku natte shimatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 電車がすごく混んでいて、気分が悪くなってしまったんです。
examplePolite.english: The train was really packed, and I started feeling sick.

items.freqNote: 気分 #804; 悪い #139; phrase entry 気分が悪い #10247. Compare 気持ち悪い #1740 (one word, also 'gross') and 機嫌 #3757 (機嫌が悪い #12058).
items.notes: Kimochi warui is the queasier twin with a 'gross' sense; guai ga warui is general unwellness.

blocks.label: What's on
blocks.rationale: The timetable: a class, meeting or exam you have (all ga aru), then plans shifting: work coming up, something postponed.
blocks.interference: jugyou, kaigi and shiken all take ga aru, never motsu; shigoto ga hairu and enki ni naru say what happened to the plan, with no 'I' or 'they' doing it.

items.use: How students explain their day or turn down plans: ashita ichigen kara jugyou aru (I've got class from first period). Casual speech drops ga; jugyou nai means a free day or period.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: 'Have class' tempts jugyou o motsu, which only fits a teacher's teaching load. A class you go to just exists: jugyou ga aru.

example.romaji: ashita asa kara jugyou aru n da.
example.ja: 明日朝から授業あるんだ。
example.english: I've got class first thing tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa asa kara jugyou ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は朝から授業があるんです。
examplePolite.english: I've got class first thing tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 授業 #2326, ある #21. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 19 of 23 hits keep ga; school life is under-counted in foreign films.
items.notes: In class right now is jugyou-chuu; skipping it is jugyou o saboru.

items.use: Said when explaining your schedule or why you can't talk: kore kara kaigi aru kara. Casual speech drops ga, and smaller team or client meetings are uchiawase, with the same verb.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: 'Have a meeting' tempts kaigi o motsu, which only works as stiff 'hold a meeting' (the everyday 'hold' is kaigi o hiraku). A meeting on your calendar just exists: kaigi ga aru. Attending is kaigi ni deru; kaigi o deru is leaving the room.

example.romaji: gomen, kore kara kaigi aru n da.
example.ja: ごめん、これから会議あるんだ。
example.english: Sorry, I've got a meeting now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kore kara kaigi ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、これから会議があるんです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I've got a meeting now.

items.freqNote: 会議 #1612, ある #21, 打ち合わせ uchiawase #2320. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 80 of 81 hits keep ga; 会議 + 開く has 23.
items.notes: Someone in one right now is kaigi-chuu: ima kaigi-chuu desu.

items.use: Said when explaining plans or turning things down: raishuu shiken aru kara muri. Casual speech drops ga, and for school tests students say tesuto more than shiken.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: 'Have an exam' tempts shiken o motsu. An exam on your calendar exists: shiken ga aru. Sitting it is shiken o ukeru.

example.ja: 来週試験あるから、無理。
example.english: I've got an exam next week, so I can't.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu shiken ga aru node, chotto muri desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週試験があるので、ちょっと無理です。
examplePolite.english: I've got an exam next week, so I'm afraid I can't.

items.freqNote: 試験 #3067, ある #21, テスト #2539. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 22 of 23 hits keep ga; テスト + ある adds 15.
items.notes: Wishing someone luck before it: shiken ganbatte!

items.use: The standard reason for cancelling: kyuu ni shigoto haitchatta (work came up suddenly). Mostly in the past, or as haitteru (I've got work booked); ga is usually dropped.
items.verbSense: go in, enter; get put into something

example.ja: ごめん、急に仕事入っちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, something came up at work.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kyuu ni shigoto ga haitchaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、急に仕事が入っちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, something came up at work.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 入る #115. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 18 of 30 hits keep ga.
items.notes: Same frame as yotei ga hairu (see there for why not okiru). Freelancers and shops also use it for work coming in: atarashii shigoto ga haitta, yoyaku ga haitta.

items.use: Said when an event moves because of rain, illness or schedules: shiai, ame de enki ni natta. Mostly in the past (natta, natchatta), and the ni stays.
items.verbSense: become, turn into
items.trap: English 'was postponed' tempts the passive enki sareta, which sounds like an official notice. In conversation the event becomes postponed: enki ni natta, like chuushi ni naru (called off).

example.romaji: ame de shiai enki ni natta.
example.ja: 雨で試合延期になった。
example.english: The game got postponed because of rain.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de shiai ga enki ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨で試合が延期になりました。
examplePolite.english: The game was postponed because of rain.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 延期になる has its own entry in the drama list at #20128 (延期 #6376, なる #29). In the subtitles 延期になる itself has 13 hits, all with ni; 延期する (91) is more common, much of it official announcements; 中止になる has 24.
items.notes: Moving it yourself is enki suru, or casually zurasu: raishuu ni zurasou.

blocks.label: Luck and help
blocks.rationale: Quick verdicts on how something went: lucky, unlucky, that helped, that did me good.
blocks.interference: un ga ii and un ga warui are one pair, so drill them in one frame (un ii ne! / un warui na). yaku ni tatsu is practical help with a task (not benri, handy); tame ni naru is something that does you good over time, like a talk, a book or an experience.

items.use: Said when luck goes someone's way: un ii ne! (lucky you), with ga dropped. The past un yokatta (that was lucky) is just as common. Ii becomes yo- in its other forms, so it's never un iikatta.
items.verbSense: ii: good (past yokatta)
items.trap: English 'lucky' is an adjective on the person. Japanese usually makes luck the subject, un ga ii (your luck is good), though rakkii! and tsuiteru are just as natural in casual speech. 'Good luck!' before a test or game is ganbatte, not anything with un.
partners: engi (engi ga ii: a good omen)

example.romaji: ichiban mae no seki? un ii ne!
example.ja: 一番前の席？運いいね！
example.english: Front-row seats? Lucky you!

examplePolite.romaji: ichiban mae no seki desu ka? un ga ii desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 一番前の席ですか？運がいいですね！
examplePolite.english: Front-row seats? You're lucky!

items.freqNote: 運 #4015 (kana うん #49 is mostly 'yeah'); いい #24. The phrase has its own entries: 運がいい #11653, 運が良い #16963. ラッキー #2636; ツイてる #8862; 幸運 kouun #4863.
items.notes: Un ii ne (lucky you) sounds the same as un, ii ne (yeah, nice), so context decides. Kouun (幸運) is the written word.

items.use: Said about your own bad luck (kyou un warui naa) or to console someone: un warukatta ne (that was just bad luck). Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: warui: bad
items.trap: As with un ga ii, luck is the subject: un ga warui (my luck is bad). For your own bad day, tsuitenai is the more natural casual choice (kyou tsuitenai naa); un warukatta ne is the usual consolation.
partners: engi (engi ga warui: a bad omen)

example.ja: 今日、ほんと運悪いなあ。
example.english: I'm having such bad luck today.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa un ga warukatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは運が悪かったですね。
examplePolite.english: That was just bad luck.

items.freqNote: 運 #4015; 悪い #139. The phrase entry 運が悪い #10068 ranks above 運がいい #11653. 不運 fuun #9351; アンラッキー #37260.
items.notes: Fuun (不運) is the written word, and anrakkii is rare.

items.use: Said about advice, information, tools or people being of real use. You hear the past yaku ni tatta (that helped) most, then yaku ni tatenakute gomen (sorry I couldn't help) and the negative yaku ni tatanai (no use; harsh if said of a person).
items.verbSense: stand (here: serve a purpose)
items.trap: 'Useful' leads to benri, which means handy or convenient to use. yaku ni tatsu means it actually helped you with something, and it's the one for advice and information: advice that helped is yaku ni tatta, not benri datta.

example.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, sugoku yaku ni tatta yo.
example.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、すごく役に立ったよ。
example.english: That app you told me about the other day was really useful.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, hontou ni yaku ni tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、本当に役に立ちました。
examplePolite.english: The app you told me about the other day was really useful.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 役に立つ has its own entry in the drama list at #1516 (役 #1534, 立つ #610). 助かる tasukaru #542.
items.notes: tasukatta (you saved me) is the warmer thanks when someone helps you. To offer help: nanika yaku ni tateru koto attara itte ne. A talk, book or experience that does you good in the longer run is tame ni naru (tame ni naru hanashi), and to thank a senior for a talk, say benkyou ni narimashita.

items.use: Said about a book, show, talk or piece of advice you come away from knowing more: ano bangumi, tame ni naru yo. Ni is kept, and before a noun it's tame ni naru hanashi (a talk worth hearing). With a person, X no tame ni naranai means it does X no good.
items.verbSense: naru: become; here, turn out to be of benefit
partners: sankou (sankou ni naru: useful as a reference)
kusuri (ii kusuri ni naru: a setback that teaches you a lesson)

example.romaji: ano hon, honto ni tame ni naru yo.
example.ja: あの本、ほんとにためになるよ。
example.english: That book's really worth reading.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hon wa hontou ni tame ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの本は本当にためになりますよ。
examplePolite.english: That book is really worthwhile.

items.freqNote: ため #203 is mostly the grammar word (-tame ni, 'in order to'). The phrase ためになる has its own entry at #4007, just above 勉強になる #4175. なる #29.
items.notes: Not the grammar -tame ni (in order to): here the phrase ends in naru, and tame means benefit. benkyou ni narimashita is the thank-you said on the spot; tame ni naru judges a book, show or advice as good for you; yaku ni tatsu says it was of practical use (a tool, a tip that helped).

blocks.label: Drinks
blocks.rationale: Water, coffee, alcohol and tea all take nomu. These are the four drinks people offer and ask about every day.
blocks.interference: All four take nomu, so drill them in one frame (mizu nomu? koohii nomu?); medicine and soup take nomu too. Making the tea or coffee is ocha o ireru (in Breakfast), never ocha o tsukuru.

items.use: Often heard as care and advice, after drinking alcohol or in the heat: mizu nonda? (have you had some water?), mizu nonde ne (make sure you drink water). Also when thirsty: nodo kawaita, mizu nomitai (I'm thirsty, I want some water). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing

example.romaji: atsui kara, mizu chanto nonde ne.
example.ja: 暑いから、水ちゃんと飲んでね。
example.english: It's hot, so make sure you drink enough water.

examplePolite.romaji: atsui node, omizu o chanto nonde kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑いので、お水をちゃんと飲んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: It's hot, so please make sure you drink enough water.

items.freqNote: 水 #797; the polite お水 (omizu) is counted separately (#3032). 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
items.notes: mizu is cold or room-temperature water; hot water is oyu, not atsui mizu. In restaurants ask for omizu, which is free. In polite heat warnings you hear komame ni suibun o totte kudasai (keep taking fluids).

items.use: Used to offer a cup and to talk about habits: koohii nomu? (want a coffee?), koohii wa nomanai (I don't drink coffee). Casual speech drops o, and koohii demo nomu? (a coffee or something?) softens an invitation.
items.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing

example.romaji: asa wa koohii nomanai to dame na n da.
example.ja: 朝はコーヒー飲まないとダメなんだ。
example.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa koohii o nomanai to dame na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝はコーヒーを飲まないとダメなんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

items.freqNote: コーヒー #1154 (珈琲 #36261). 飲む #229 counts all drinking, medicine included.
items.notes: To order, say koohii (o) onegaishimasu or koohii ni shimasu (I'll have coffee). Making it is koohii o ireru.

items.use: Used to ask about and describe drinking: osake nomu? or osake nomeru? (do you drink?), anmari nomanai (I don't drink much). Casual speech drops o, and once drinking is the topic nomu alone means alcohol: kinou nomisugita (I drank too much last night).
items.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing
items.trap: Learners take osake to mean Japanese sake, but it covers any alcohol, beer and wine included; rice wine is nihonshu.

example.romaji: kyou kuruma da kara, osake wa nomenai.
example.ja: 今日車だから、お酒は飲めない。
example.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kuruma na node, osake wa nomenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は車なので、お酒は飲めないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

items.freqNote: お酒 #1229; bare 酒 (sake) #1131 and ビール #1481 are counted separately. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
items.notes: nomi ni iku (go out for drinks) and nomikai (a drinking party) use the same nomu. How much you can take is osake ni tsuyoi / osake ni yowai, casually osake yowai n da (I'm a lightweight). Bare sake (sake nomou ze) is rougher, mostly male speech; osake is the everyday default for everyone.

items.use: Said at home and at work, and as a soft offer or invitation: ocha demo nomu? (fancy a cup of tea?). Casual speech drops o, and ocha means whatever Japanese tea is on hand, including cold mugicha.
items.verbSense: drink; swallow without chewing
items.trap: English 'tea' means black tea, but ocha is green or other Japanese tea (mugicha, houjicha); black tea, with or without milk, is koucha.

example.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomou.
example.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲もう。
example.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.

items.freqNote: お茶 #978 (bare 茶 #5292); 紅茶 (koucha) #5258 is counted separately. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
items.notes: ocha ni shiyou / ocha ni shimashou ka (let's stop for tea) is the usual way to call a tea break. ocha shinai? / ocha shiyou (go for tea) means a café break, coffee included. Making the tea is ocha o ireru.

blocks.label: Meals at home
blocks.rationale: A meal at home from start to finish: cooking it, calling out that it's ready, eating it, and letting it go cold.
blocks.interference: gohan means the meal here, not only rice: gohan tsukuru is cooking dinner and gohan dekita yo means it's ready. Hot food cooling off is sameru (samechau yo), not samuku naru, which is for weather and people.

items.use: Said about any meal, not just rice. gohan tabeta? (have you eaten?) is a real question between family, partners and close friends, not a greeting as in Korean or Chinese; answer un, tabeta, or mada (tabetenai) for 'not yet', because tabenakatta means you skipped the meal. Casual speech drops o; the meal is named only when it matters (asagohan, ohiru, bangohan).
items.verbSense: eat
items.trap: Learners who know gohan as 'rice' avoid it for a pasta or burger dinner, but it is the everyday word for any meal (it means rice only when set against pan or men); shokuji (o) suru is stiffer.

example.ja: ご飯食べてから行くね。
example.english: I'll head over after I eat.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan o tabete kara ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯を食べてから行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll come over after I've eaten.

items.freqNote: ご飯 #1225; kana ごはん #2244, the rough 飯 (meshi) #1398 and the stiffer 食事 (shokuji) #860 are counted separately. 食べる #130.
items.notes: meshi kuu (meshi kutta?) is the rough, mostly male version. Skipping a meal, by choice or habit, is nuku: asagohan nuita (I skipped breakfast).

items.use: The everyday way to say who's cooking: kyou wa watashi ga gohan tsukuru, or gohan tsukutte kureta (they made me dinner). Casual speech drops o, and the meal is named only when it matters (bangohan, obentou). ryouri suru also works for tonight's cooking (kyou wa boku ga ryouri suru), but it leans toward cooking as an activity (ryouri suru no ga suki).
items.verbSense: make; with food, prepare or cook

example.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gohan tsukuru ne.
example.ja: 今日は私がご飯作るね。
example.english: I'll make dinner tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa watashi ga gohan o tsukurimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は私がご飯を作りますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll make dinner tonight.

items.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately); 作る #146 counts all making. 料理 (ryouri) is #856. In the subtitles o is dropped in 11 of 14 hits.
items.notes: Cooking the rice itself is gohan o taku (in a rice cooker).

items.english: the meal gets ready (dekita = it's ready)
items.use: Called out from the kitchen: gohan dekita yo! (dinner's ready!), in the past tense and usually without ga. mou sugu dekiru yo (it's nearly ready) uses the non-past dekiru for what's coming.
items.verbSense: come into being, get done; also 'can do' and 'be ready'
items.trap: English 'dinner's ready' is in the present, but the kitchen call says the meal has come into being: gohan dekita yo; plain gohan dekiru yo means it'll be ready soon. The other everyday call is gohan da yo! (food's on!). If you reach for junbi, it's gohan no junbi (ga) dekita, the same dekiru as junbi dekita? (are you ready?).
partners: ryouri (a dish: ryouri dekita; ryouri dekiru? asks if you can cook)

example.ja: ご飯できたよ！早く来て。
example.english: Dinner's ready! Come quick.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan ga dekimashita yo. douzo, samenai uchi ni.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯ができましたよ。どうぞ、冷めないうちに。
examplePolite.english: Dinner's ready. Please, have it while it's hot.

items.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately). できる #73 is the kana form and pools every sense, mostly 'can do' (出来る #1313).
items.notes: gohan dekiteru kara (the food's made) means it's already waiting for you. gohan yo! is the motherly, feminine version of gohan da yo. The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa.

items.use: Said to get people to the table (hayaku, samechau yo) or about a drink left too long (koohii sameta). Hosts say samenai uchi ni douzo (eat it while it's hot).
items.verbSense: lose heat and cool down (food, drinks, bath water)
items.trap: Not samuku naru: samui is for weather and how you feel, and hot food or drink cooling off is sameru. tsumetaku naru is for something that has gone fully cold.

example.ja: 早く食べよう、ご飯冷めちゃうよ。
example.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku tabemashou, gohan ga samechaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 早く食べましょう、ご飯が冷めちゃいますよ。
examplePolite.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

items.freqNote: 冷める #2747 also counts feelings cooling. The verb goes with any hot food or drink, so gohan is only the headword noun. ご飯 + 冷める has no subtitle hits; お茶 + 冷める (5) and スープ + 冷める (3) show the pattern, and most bare 冷めた hits are about feelings cooling.
items.notes: samasu (let it cool) is the transitive partner. The sameru of me ga sameru (wake up) is a different word.

blocks.label: Getting sick
blocks.rationale: Coming down with something: catching a cold, catching one from someone, a real illness, getting run down and an upset stomach.
blocks.interference: kaze o hiku is getting a cold; kaze ga utsuru is catching it from someone. byouki ni naru sounds like a real illness, so for a rough few days say taichou kuzushita. kuzusu and kowasu both mean break: taichou o kuzusu for your health in general, onaka o kowasu for your stomach. kaze 'cold' sounds like kaze 'wind'.

items.use: Kaze hiita (or hiichatta) = I've caught a cold; kaze hiiteru = I have a cold right now, not 'I'm catching one'. Usually said without o.
items.verbSense: pull, draw; with a cold it means come down with
items.trap: Not kaze o toru or tsukamu (catch a ball): you 'pull' a cold, kaze o hiku (kaze hiichatta).

example.ja: 風邪ひいちゃったみたい。
example.english: I think I've caught a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hiita mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいたみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I think I've caught a cold.

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666 (風 'wind' is #1532; kana-only かぜ #20653 mixes both); 引く #1039. Phrase entries: 風邪ひく #3998, 風邪をひく #10899, 風邪を引く #27734. These are partial counts because the tokenizer usually splits; the particle-dropped form ranking highest supports the casual drop.
alsoIn: 10-list-nouns #88 (homophone kaze 'wind'; rule S2 makes kaze o hiku the card for 'a cold')
items.notes: Kaze 'cold' sounds exactly like kaze 'wind' (kaze ga fuku = the wind blows), so this phrase is how 'a cold' is learned. Flu doesn't take hiku: infuru ni kakatta, infuru ni natta. Getting over a cold is kaze ga naoru (kaze, mou naotta?).

items.use: Heard as utsuru yo (you'll catch it) and kaze utsutta or utsutchatta (I caught it off someone). Say who from with kara (kodomo kara utsutta) or no (kodomo no kaze ga utsutta). Just as common: kaze o morau, 'receive' the cold (kodomo kara kaze moratchatta).
items.verbSense: move, spread (to another place or person)
items.trap: Kaze o hiku is just getting a cold; to say you caught it from someone, the cold moves to you, kaze ga utsuru.

example.ja: 子供の風邪、うつっちゃった。
example.english: I caught my kid's cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no kaze ga utsutta mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 子供の風邪がうつったみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I think I caught my child's cold.

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666; verb rank is kanji 移る #2350, which also counts 'move house or office'; kana うつる #34832 is the usual spelling for this sense. 映る #2111 and 写る #2975 are other words.
items.notes: Giving your cold to someone else is kaze o utsusu: kaze utsushichatta, gomen (sorry, I gave you my cold).

items.use: For falling ill with something real (byouki ni natta), or as a warning about overdoing it. The ni always stays.
items.verbSense: become, turn into
items.trap: English 'I got sick' is usually something minor, but byouki ni natta sounds like a real illness: for a cold or a rough few days say kaze hiita, guai ga waruku natta or taichou kuzushita. Byouki desu ('I'm sick') sounds more serious still.

example.romaji: muri suru to byouki ni naru yo.
example.ja: 無理すると病気になるよ。
example.english: You'll make yourself sick if you push too hard.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen, chichi ga byouki ni natte, shibaraku taihen datta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年、父が病気になって、しばらく大変だったんです。
examplePolite.english: My father got sick last year, and things were hard for a while.

items.freqNote: 病気 #1019; なる #29 (成る #13300); phrase entry 病気になる #4880, high for a phrase.
items.notes: Byouki ni kakaru (contract an illness) is more formal; getting better is byouki ga naoru.

items.use: The standard way to explain a minor illness, mostly in the past: taichou kuzushichatte (I came down with something). It fills excuses for missing work or school, and the send-off taichou kuzusanai you ni ne (look after yourself). O often drops.
items.verbSense: knock down, break up (a wall, a pose); upset, throw off (balance, health, pace); also break a note into change
items.trap: Byouki ni naru isn't wrong but sounds like a proper illness; for a passing bug or being run down, people say taichou (o) kuzushita.
partners: choushi (form: choushi o kuzusu = go off form)

example.ja: ちょっと体調崩して、昨日休んだ。
example.english: I got a bit run down and took yesterday off.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto taichou o kuzushite, kinou wa yasumimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと体調を崩して、昨日は休みました。
examplePolite.english: I was a bit under the weather, so I took yesterday off.

items.freqNote: 体調 #1944; 崩す #3822; phrase entry 体調を崩す #9388, high for a phrase.
items.notes: Taichou ga warui is the state; taichou o kuzusu is falling into it.

items.use: The discreet everyday way to mention diarrhoea or a bad stomach, mostly past: onaka kowashita. Also a warning: sonna ni tabetara onaka kowasu yo. O often drops.
items.verbSense: break, damage (a thing); with the body, harm it
items.trap: English 'have an upset stomach' gives no usable verb. Japanese 'breaks' the stomach with kowasu, transitive, with the speaker as subject: onaka kowashita.
partners: karada (health: karada o kowasu = ruin your health)

example.ja: 冷たいもの飲みすぎて、お腹壊した。
example.english: I drank too much cold stuff and upset my stomach.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumetai mono o nomisugite, onaka o kowashimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 冷たいものを飲みすぎて、お腹を壊しました。
examplePolite.english: I had too many cold drinks and upset my stomach.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 壊す #1284. Phrase entries お腹を壊す #76983 and the rougher 腹を壊す #50251.
items.notes: Onaka no choushi ga warui is the vaguer, more discreet version; geri (diarrhoea) is the clinic word.

blocks.label: Clothes and shoes
blocks.rationale: The everyday on/off pairs for what you're dressed in: clothes go on with kiru, shoes with haku, and both come off with nugu.
blocks.interference: kiru vs haku: kiru for the torso or whole body, haku for anything you step into; nugu takes both off, so drill kiru/haku against the one nugu (fuku kite / kutsu haite / kutsu nuide).

items.use: Mostly heard as kiteru (is wearing, a state, not 'putting on now') or kiteku (wear when going out); casual speech drops o. kiteru 'wearing' is flat (ki-TE-RU) while kiteru 'has come' falls after ki (KI-te-ru), so pitch as well as context tells them apart.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the body (tops, coats, dresses)
items.trap: kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which take other verbs (haku, kaburu, kakeru).

example.ja: 明日どんな服着てく？
example.english: What are you wearing tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa donna fuku o kite ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はどんな服を着ていきますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you wearing tomorrow?

items.freqNote: Rank is for 着る #754. Kana きる is mostly 切る 'cut' (#546), the same sound. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Off: fuku o nugu. Changing into other clothes is fuku o kigaeru; looking good in them is fuku ga niau (niau ne).

items.use: Said as kutsu haite (put your shoes on) at the door; casual speech drops o. haiteru means already has them on, not 'putting them on now'.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the feet and legs
items.trap: Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.

example.romaji: chotto matte, ima kutsu haku kara.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、今靴履くから。
example.english: Hang on, I'm putting my shoes on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima kutsu o hakimasu node, chotto matte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今靴を履きますので、ちょっと待ってください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm just putting my shoes on, one moment please.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 履く #3474. Kana はく is mostly 吐く 'throw up' (#1739), so the kana count was not used. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Spelled like haku 'throw up' and haku 'sweep', but the pitch differs: haku 'put on' is flat (ha-KU), the other two fall after ha (HA-ku). Context helps too.

items.use: Heard as kutsu nuide (kudasai) at home entrances, some restaurants and clinics. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: take off (clothes, shoes)
items.trap: Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.

example.ja: ここで靴脱いでね。
example.english: Take your shoes off here, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de kutsu o nuide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここで靴を脱いでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please take your shoes off here.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 靴 #1818 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; kutsu o nuide kudasai is heard at Japanese entrances every day.
items.notes: A hat comes off with boushi o toru or nugu; glasses and accessories with hazusu.

items.use: Heard as nuide (take them off) or nuida hou ga ii (you'd better take them off), and ofuku nuide (with the o- used to children) is what kids hear at bath time. When it's one layer, people name it: uwagi nuidara? (why not take your jacket off?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: take off (clothes, shoes)
items.trap: Not fuku o toru, which sounds like picking clothes up (fuku totte = pass me my clothes). Whatever goes on with kiru or haku (tops, trousers, shoes, socks) comes off with nugu. A hat comes off with toru or nugu. Glasses, masks, watches, ties and belts come off with hazusu, and casual toru works for most of them.

example.romaji: nureta fuku, hayaku nuida hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 濡れた服、早く脱いだ方がいいよ。
example.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.

examplePolite.romaji: nureta fuku wa, hayaku nuida hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 濡れた服は、早く脱いだ方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better get out of those wet clothes.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; in speech the garment is often named instead (上着 #6098).
items.notes: Once it's clear which garment, nugu alone is enough: atsui kara nuijaou (it's hot, I'll take it off).

blocks.label: TV and music
blocks.rationale: Watching and listening at home: TV and the news, music you listen to or put on, and switching channels.
blocks.interference: ongaku o kiku (you listen) vs ongaku o kakeru (you put it on): same noun, different verb. TV and the news both take miru, English 'play' is never asobu here, and channeru o kaeru uses kaeru 'change', not kaeru 'go home'.

items.use: Said about evenings and downtime, mostly as a habit or in the -teru form: terebi miteru (I'm watching TV), terebi miteta (I was watching TV), anmari terebi minai (I don't watch much TV). Casual speech drops o, and something you saw on TV is terebi de mita.
items.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: 最近全然テレビ見ないな。
example.english: I don't watch TV at all these days.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin wa zenzen terebi o mimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 最近は全然テレビを見ません。
examplePolite.english: I don't watch TV at all these days.

items.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, check); the shows-and-films spelling 観る is #10463.
items.notes: On and off are terebi o tsukeru and terebi o kesu, as with denki; a show on TV is terebi de yatteru, a person terebi ni deteru.

items.use: Said about listening habits and what you're listening to now, often in hobby talk (donna ongaku kiku?) and with nagara: ongaku kikinagara benkyou suru (study with music on). Casual speech drops o; putting music on for everyone is ongaku o kakeru.
items.verbSense: listen, hear; ask
items.trap: Not ongaku ni kiku: English 'listen to' has a 'to', but kiku takes o; kiku with ni means asking a person (sensei ni kiku).

example.ja: どんな音楽聞くの？
example.english: What kind of music do you listen to?

examplePolite.romaji: donna ongaku o kikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どんな音楽を聞きますか？
examplePolite.english: What kind of music do you listen to?

items.freqNote: verbRank is 聞く pooling listen, hear and ask; the listening spelling 聴く is #1930.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: school-subjects (ongaku, as a subject)
items.notes: Music you happen to hear is ongaku ga kikoeru; music playing in a shop is ongaku ga kakatteru or nagareteru.

items.use: Said about keeping up with the news, often in the past as a conversation opener: nyuusu mita? (did you see the news?). Something you learned from it is nyuusu de mita (I saw it on the news) or nyuusu de yatteta (it was on the news). It covers news apps on a phone too. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: 今朝のニュース見た？
example.english: Did you see the news this morning?

examplePolite.romaji: kesa no nyuusu o mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今朝のニュースを見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see the news this morning?

items.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, watch).
items.notes: nyuusu ni naru = make the news: ano jiko, nyuusu ni natteta.

items.use: Said when you start music on a speaker or in the car: ongaku kakete ii? (mind if I put music on?). Music that's already playing is ongaku ga kakatteru. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set something going (a record, a call)
items.trap: Not asobu: playing music on a speaker is ongaku o kakeru (nagasu is also fine); asobu is play for fun, hiku is play an instrument.

example.ja: なんか音楽かけていい？
example.english: Mind if I put some music on?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika ongaku o kakete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か音楽をかけてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Mind if I put some music on?

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かける pooling all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742. nagasu (流す) is #1234.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: school-subjects (ongaku, as a subject)
items.notes: nagasu (let flow) is the alternative in shops and at events: biijiiemu o nagasu. Listening is ongaku o kiku; kakeru only starts it playing.

items.use: Said in front of the TV, mostly as a request: channeru kaete ii? (mind if I change the channel?). Casual speech drops o, and the show you switch to takes ni: nyuusu ni kaete.
items.politeJa: チャンネルを変えます
items.verbSense: change, switch (one thing for another)

example.ja: チャンネル変えてもいい？
example.english: Mind if I change the channel?

examplePolite.romaji: channeru o kaete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: チャンネルを変えてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you mind if I change the channel?

items.freqNote: verbRank is the 変える spelling; 替える (#2801) is the same verb and is also written for channels.
items.notes: kaete (change it) and kaette (go home) differ by one t. A YouTube channel is channeru too: channeru touroku shita (I subscribed).

blocks.label: Doors and locks
blocks.rationale: The front door both ways, opening and shutting, plus locking up: each act paired with the state it leaves.
blocks.interference: Each act with o has a ga partner for what the door does or how it is now: akeru/aku, shimeru/shimaru, kakeru/kakaru. Keep doa akete (open it) apart from doa aiteru (it's open), and kagi kakete (lock it) apart from kagi kakatteru (it's locked).

items.use: For opening a door yourself or asking someone to: doa akete (open the door), often with kureru when your hands are full. Casual speech drops o; a door that is open is doa aiteru.
items.verbSense: open something (a door, a box, your eyes)
items.trap: English 'open' does both jobs. Someone opening it is akeru (doa akete); the door opening or being open is aku (doa aiteru).

example.ja: ごめん、ドア開けてくれる？
example.english: Sorry, can you open the door for me?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, doa o akete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ドアを開けてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you open the door?

items.freqNote: 開ける #480 covers every kind of opening; the sound-alike 空ける (leave empty, make room) is #3596.
items.notes: On the intercom, hai, ima akemasu ne (I'll let you in now) is a common reply when buzzing someone through the entrance; at your own front door it's usually hai, ima ikimasu.

items.use: Mostly a request or reminder: doa shimete (shut the door), chanto shimete ne. Casual speech drops o; a door that is shut is doa shimatteru.
items.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock
items.trap: Not tojiru: dictionaries give it for 'close', but tojiru is for eyes, books and apps. Doors, windows and lids are shimeru.

example.ja: 寒いから、ドア閉めて。
example.english: It's cold, shut the door.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node, doa o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので、ドアを閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so please close the door.

items.freqNote: 閉める #1764; the sound-alike 締める (tighten, fasten) is #4630.
items.notes: With kagi the same verb means lock: kagi shimeta? = did you lock up?

items.use: Mostly heard as doa aiteru (the door's open) or doa aita (it opened). Train and lift announcements usually say doa ga hirakimasu instead, so expect both sounds. When a person opens it, use doa o akeru.
items.verbSense: come open, be open; also become free or empty
items.trap: Not doa ga akeru: when the door opens by itself or is open, use aku (doa aiteru). akeru needs someone doing it.

example.ja: 玄関のドア開いてるよ。
example.english: The front door's open.

examplePolite.romaji: genkan no doa ga aite imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 玄関のドアが開いていますよ。
examplePolite.english: The front door is open.

items.freqNote: 開く splits by reading: ひらく #624, あく #14086. Kana あく is #3508 (it may include other words), and 空く #1498 is the 'free/vacant' aku. The tokenizer probably files most 開く under ひらく, so あく is likely understated (unverified).
items.notes: Closing follows the same pattern: doa ga shimaru / doa o shimeru.

items.use: Heard in every train and lift announcement: doa ga shimarimasu (the doors are closing). At home it's mostly the state, doa shimatteru (the door's shut), or doa shimatchatta when it swings shut by itself.
items.verbSense: of a door, window or lid: close by itself, or be shut
items.trap: Not doa ga shimeru: with ga the verb is shimaru (doa shimatteru). shimeru needs someone doing the shutting, as in doa shimete.

example.ja: 玄関のドア、ちゃんと閉まってる？
example.english: Is the front door properly shut?

examplePolite.romaji: genkan no doa wa chanto shimatte imasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 玄関のドアはちゃんと閉まっていますか？
examplePolite.english: Is the front door properly closed?

items.freqNote: 閉まる #3722; 締まる (tighten) #14106 is another kanji for the same sound.
items.notes: A door that won't shut is doa ga shimaranai; the opening half is doa ga aku.

items.use: Said when leaving the house or going to bed: kagi kaketa? (did you lock it?), kagi kakete ne (lock up, okay?).
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
items.trap: English 'lock' has no single verb here: the object is kagi (the lock), not the door, and you put it on with kakeru. In casual speech kagi o shimeru (kagi shimeta?) is just as common. rokku suru is mostly for cars and phones.

example.ja: あれ、鍵かけたっけ？
example.english: Wait, did I lock the door?

examplePolite.romaji: are, kagi o kakemashita kke?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、鍵をかけましたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Hmm, did I lock the door?

items.freqNote: かける #244 is the kana spelling across all senses (掛ける #2742); カギ #9849 is a variant spelling of the noun.
items.notes: Unlocking is kagi o akeru. The locked state is kagi ga kakaru, nearly always heard as kagi kakatteru (it's locked); kagi shimatteru is just as common.

items.english: (a door) locks, gets locked (kakatteru = is locked)
items.use: Nearly always kagi kakatteru (it's locked) or kagi kakattenai (it's not locked). It describes the state, while kagi o kakeru is the act.
items.verbSense: hang, be put on; also take (time) and cost (money)
items.trap: 'It's locked' is a verb state, kagi ga kakatteru (kagi shimatteru is just as common). Not kagi ga kaketeru: with ga the verb is kakaru. kagi ga kakete aru, 'someone has locked it', is also fine.

example.ja: 大丈夫、鍵かかってるよ。
example.english: It's fine, it's locked.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, kagi ga kakatte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、鍵がかかっていますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's fine, it's locked.

items.freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses, including 'take time' and 'cost' (掛かる #5316).
items.notes: The opposite state is kagi ga aiteru (it's unlocked).

blocks.label: Noticing
blocks.rationale: A smell, a sound or a voice reaches you, and you notice something.
blocks.interference: The smell, sound or voice is the subject (nioi suru, oto shita, koe ga kikoeru), so you don't use kagu or kiku; kikoeru? (can you hear me?) is not kiiteru? (are you listening?). ki ga tsuku (notice) sounds almost like ki o tsukeru (be careful).

items.use: Said the moment you notice a smell, usually without ga: ii nioi suru! or nanka hen na nioi shinai? To name the source, add no: gasu no nioi ga suru (I smell gas).
items.verbSense: do; here, be perceived: a smell, sound, taste or feeling makes itself felt
items.trap: For 'I smell something', learners use kagu, but kagu means sniffing on purpose. The smell is the subject: nanka nioi ga suru. ii nioi! on its own is also fine.

example.ja: なんかいい匂いするね。
example.english: Something smells good.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika ii nioi ga shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かいい匂いがしますね。
examplePolite.english: Something smells good, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling におい; 匂い is #2171 and 臭い (bad smell) #7168. The expression 匂いがする is #7128.
items.notes: For a bad smell, natives often just say kusai (it stinks).

items.english: hear a noise, there's a sound
items.use: The normal way to report a noise, with the noise as the subject, not you: nanka oto shita (I heard something). Use the past shita for a sound just now. ga is usually dropped.
items.verbSense: do; here, be perceived: a sound, smell or taste makes itself felt
items.trap: For 'I heard a noise' just now, learners say oto o kiita. That works when you tell the story later, but in the moment natives make the sound the subject: oto shita, or oto ga kikoeta.

example.ja: 今なんか音しなかった？
example.english: Did you just hear something?

examplePolite.romaji: ima nanika oto ga shimasen deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今何か音がしませんでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you just hear a noise?

items.freqNote: The expression 音がする is #5813.
items.notes: Often comes with a sound word: gatan tte oto shita (there was a thud). For 'can hear', the verb is kikoeru: oto ga kikoeru, and koe ga kikoeru for voices and calls.

items.english: hear a voice; (on a call) can hear someone
items.use: The voice that reaches you is the subject: tonari no heya kara koe ga kikoeru. On calls and video meetings it's the check koe kikoeteru? (can you hear me?), or just kikoeru?, and the reply chotto kikoenai (I can't really hear you).
items.verbSense: can be heard, reach your ears; also 'sound like' (X ni kikoeru)
items.trap: For 'I can hear a voice' or 'can you hear me?', learners use kiku, but kiku is listening on purpose: kiiteru? means 'are you listening?'. A sound reaching you is kikoeru, with the voice as subject: koe kikoeru?

example.ja: もしもし、声聞こえてる？
example.english: Hello? Can you hear me?

examplePolite.romaji: moshimoshi, koe kikoemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もしもし、声聞こえますか？
examplePolite.english: Hello? Can you hear me?

items.freqNote: 声+聞こえる 242 in the subtitles (ga 212), a strong pairing. The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately. The bare call check is frequent too: 聞こえる？ 286, 聞こえますか 212.
items.notes: X ni kikoeru means 'sounds like X': iiwake ni kikoeru (that sounds like an excuse). koe ga suru (there's a voice) says a voice is there; kikoeru is whether it reaches you, which is why calls use kikoeru. On a bad line, koe ga tooi (you sound far away) is the other stock complaint.

items.use: Mostly past: ki ga tsuita (I noticed, I realised) and zenzen ki ga tsukanakatta (I didn't notice at all). The thing noticed takes ni: machigai ni ki ga tsuita. ki ga tsuitara is the everyday 'before I knew it': ki ga tsuitara asa datta (next thing I knew, it was morning).
items.verbSense: stick, get attached; here your attention catches on something
items.trap: For 'I noticed', learners say mita or wakatta. The phrase is ki ga tsuita. Keep it apart from ki o tsukeru (be careful), which sounds almost the same.

example.ja: ごめん、全然気つかなかった。
example.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, zenzen ki ga tsukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、全然気が付きませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

items.freqNote: verbRank is 付く; kana つく (#355) mixes several tsuku verbs. The list also holds the whole expression, 気が付く #2832 and 気がつく #3139. The one-word kizuku ranks higher: 気付く #1083, 気づく #1239.
items.notes: The one-word kizuku means the same and is even more common in drama speech: zenzen kizukanakatta.

blocks.label: Kids and growing up
blocks.rationale: Family life: having kids, a baby arriving, growing up, raising children and looking after someone.
blocks.interference: kodomo iru? (got kids?) is having them and kodomo umareta (the baby came) is the birth, with the child as subject in both, not kodomo o motsu. sodateru is raising (sodatsu is being raised), otona ni naru is growing up, and mendou o miru (look after) is not mendokusai (what a hassle).

items.use: Among friends, the get-to-know-you question is kodomo iru? (got kids?), answered un, hitori iru. Politely you ask okosan imasu ka? (or okosan wa irasshaimasu ka?), answered futari imasu. The number goes after the noun: kodomo futari iru (I have two kids). kyoudai iru? and kanojo iru? work the same way.
items.verbSense: be, exist (people and animals); with ga, have (people, pets)
items.trap: English 'have' leads to kodomo o motte iru or the thing-verb aru; in talk, kids, siblings and partners take iru: kodomo iru?, kyoudai iru? (kodomo o motsu oya, parents with children, is written style).

example.romaji: uchi wa kodomo futari iru n da.
example.ja: うちは子供二人いるんだ。
example.english: We've got two kids.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa kodomo ga futari iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは子供が二人いるんです。
examplePolite.english: We have two children.

items.freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate spelling); kana いる #42 merges the -te iru auxiliary (居る #6802).
items.notes: kodomo dekita = we're having a baby, or we've had kids (kekkon shite kodomo mo dekita). The birth itself is kodomo ga umareru: kodomo umareta (the baby's here).

items.use: The way to share baby news, with the child as subject: kodomo ga umareta (we had a baby), raigetsu umareru n da (it's due next month). akachan works the same way, and kodomo dekita is the earlier 'we're expecting'.
items.verbSense: be born
items.trap: English 'we had a baby' leads to kodomo ga atta, which isn't said. kodomo o motsu is real but means being a parent as a stage of life (kodomo o motte kara = since I became a parent). Birth news makes the baby the subject: kodomo ga umareta. kodomo o umu (give birth) is said about the mother.

example.romaji: senshuu, kodomo ga umareta n da.
example.ja: 先週、子供が生まれたんだ。
example.english: We had a baby last week.

examplePolite.romaji: senshuu, kodomo ga umareta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 先週、子供が生まれたんです。
examplePolite.english: We had a baby last week.

items.freqNote: 子供 #589 (子ども #2264 separate); 生まれる #534 (産まれる #6622 separate). 赤ちゃん #2204.
items.notes: Your own birth takes the same verb: toukyou de umareta (I was born in Tokyo).

items.use: Two everyday uses: growing up over the years (otona ni nattara = when you're grown up) and acting mature: otona ni natta ne (you've really grown up), motto otona ni natte yo (grow up a bit).
items.verbSense: become (with ni after a noun)
items.trap: English 'grow up' leads to sodatsu, which is being raised or growing as a child (toukyou de sodatta = I grew up in Tokyo); becoming an adult, or acting like one, is otona ni naru.

example.ja: 大人になったら分かるよ。
example.english: You'll understand when you're older.

examplePolite.romaji: otona ni nattara wakarimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大人になったら分かりますよ。
examplePolite.english: You'll understand when you're older.

items.freqNote: 大人 #898; naru: kana なる #29. Phrase entry 大人になる #1753, high for a phrase.
items.notes: otonappoi = mature for your age; otonagenai = childish (of an adult). To a child, 'when you grow up' is usually ookiku nattara (ookiku nattara nani ni naritai?).

items.use: Used about parenting as a whole: hitori de kodomo o sodateta (she raised her kids alone), kodomo sodateru no tte taihen da yo. Everyday talk often uses the noun kosodate (parenting) instead: ima kosodate-chuu (I'm busy raising kids).
items.verbSense: raise, bring up, grow (children, plants, juniors)
partners: buka (subordinates: buka o sodateru = bring your team on)

example.romaji: kodomo sodateru no tte taihen da yo ne.
example.ja: 子供育てるのって大変だよね。
example.english: Raising kids is tough, isn't it.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo o sodateru no wa taihen desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 子供を育てるのは大変ですよね。
examplePolite.english: Raising children is hard work, isn't it.

items.freqNote: 子供 #589; 育てる #894. 子育て (kosodate) #4148; 育つ #1371.
items.notes: sodatsu is the intransitive side: inaka de sodatta (I grew up in the countryside). Having a dog is inu o kau; inu o sodateru is only raising one from a puppy.

items.use: Used for looking after kids, pets, juniors or ageing parents; o is often dropped in speech: kodomo no mendou mite kureru? (can you watch the kids?). Most often heard with te kureru or te ageru: zutto mendou mite kureta (they always looked out for me).
items.verbSense: see, look; here, see to, look after
partners: kodomo (kids: chotto kodomo mitete = keep an eye on the kids)
nimotsu (bags: nimotsu mitete = watch my bags)
mise (the shop: mise mitete = mind the shop)

example.ja: 子供の面倒見てくれる？
example.english: Can you look after the kids?

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no mendou o mite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 子供の面倒を見てもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you look after the children?

items.freqNote: 面倒 #1114 counts mostly the 'hassle' sense (mendou da); 見る #55. Phrase entries 面倒見る #4146 and 面倒を見る #4508, high for a phrase. Written 面倒を見 268 vs 面倒見 98.
items.notes: mendoumi ga ii = good at looking after people, a common compliment for a senpai or big sister. sewa o suru (kodomo no sewa) is the near twin; mendou o miru adds taking responsibility for someone. It shares the noun with mendokusai (what a hassle) but not the feel.

blocks.label: Cold symptoms
blocks.rationale: Describing a cold or flu: a fever, a cough, a runny nose and that heavy, run-down feeling.
blocks.interference: Symptoms 'come out' with deru (netsu deta, seki ga deru, hanamizu ga deru); netsu ga aru is having a fever right now, never motsu. karada ga darui uses the adjective darui, and darui on its own also means 'can't be bothered'.

items.use: For a fever you have now: netsu aru (I've got a temperature), netsu aru no? (have you got a fever?). Netsu deteru also works; netsu deta is the moment it came on.
items.verbSense: there is, exist (for things)
items.trap: Not netsu o motsu: a fever 'exists', netsu ga aru (netsu aru mitai).

example.ja: 今朝からちょっと熱ある。
example.english: I've had a bit of a fever since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa kara chotto netsu ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今朝からちょっと熱があるんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had a slight fever since this morning.

items.freqNote: 熱 #1641; ある #21. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Often given in Celsius: sanjuuhachido aru (I'm running 38). Nausea and chills take suru: hakike ga suru, samuke ga suru. Taking your temperature is netsu o hakaru, not toru.

items.use: For a fever coming on, mostly past: netsu deta (I came down with a fever). For one you have now, netsu aru and netsu deteru both work. Coughs and runny noses work the same way: seki ga deru, hanamizu ga deru.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
items.trap: English 'get' pulls toward morau or naru, but a fever 'comes out': netsu ga deru (netsu deta). Morau is for catching a cold from someone (kaze o morau).

example.ja: 今朝急に熱出た。
example.english: I suddenly came down with a fever this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa kyuu ni netsu ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今朝急に熱が出ました。
examplePolite.english: I suddenly came down with a fever this morning.

items.freqNote: 熱 #1641; 出る #81. No phrase entry.
items.notes: The opposite is netsu ga sagaru (the fever goes down). For coughing right now, seki shiteru is also natural.

items.use: For a cough you've had a while, said to friends or at the doctor's: seki ga deru n desu, or seki ga tomaranai (I can't stop coughing). For coughing right now, seki shiteru is just as natural.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out

example.romaji: netsu wa nai kedo, seki ga deru.
example.ja: 熱はないけど、咳が出る。
example.english: No fever, but I've got a cough.

examplePolite.romaji: netsu wa nai n desu kedo, seki ga demasu.
examplePolite.ja: 熱はないんですけど、咳が出ます。
examplePolite.english: I don't have a fever, but I have a cough.

items.freqNote: 咳 #21022 is the kanji only. Kana せき #11682 probably holds most spoken uses but can't be told apart from kana 席/関, so it is not used. 出る #81; phrase entry 咳が出る #70272.
items.notes: Seki (o) suru, coughing as an action, is more frequent in films (31 hits to 4). Clinics ask netsu ya seki wa arimasu ka? too.

items.use: Said of a cold or hay fever, often as hanamizu ga tomaranai (my nose won't stop running). Hanamizu deteru yo, ga dropped, tells someone their nose is running.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
items.trap: 'Runny' has nothing to copy: the noun is hanamizu (nose water), and it comes out, hanamizu ga deru (hanamizu deteru yo).

example.ja: 鼻水出てるよ。はい、ティッシュ。
example.english: Your nose is running. Here, a tissue.

examplePolite.romaji: hanamizu ga dete imasu yo. tisshu, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 鼻水が出ていますよ。ティッシュ、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: Your nose is running. Here's a tissue.

items.freqNote: 鼻水 #12653; 出る #81. No phrase entry; 鼻 hana #2627.
items.notes: A blocked nose is hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru); blowing it is hana o kamu.

items.use: The heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on or a bad night: nanka karada darui, with ga dropped. Darui alone is just as common, and about a task it's a casual, youthful 'what a drag' (gakkou darui), not for use with superiors.
items.verbSense: heavy, sluggish, listless; casually, 'what a drag'
items.trap: Tsukareta isn't wrong, but it points to effort; the heavy, achy feeling with no clear cause, as when a cold is coming, is karada ga darui.

example.ja: 朝からなんか体だるい。
example.english: I've felt heavy and sluggish since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara nanka karada ga darui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝からなんか体がだるいんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been feeling sluggish since this morning.

items.freqNote: 体 #371; だるい #10091 (怠い #97383). No phrase entry; しんどい #3271 is the near-synonym.
items.notes: Shindoi (rough, worn out) overlaps; it comes from western Japan but is heard everywhere.

blocks.label: Windows and curtains
blocks.rationale: The same open/close pair on windows and curtains: airing the room, shutting out rain or cold, closing up for the night.
blocks.interference: English 'draw the curtains' hides the direction; Japanese names it: kaaten o shimeru (close) or kaaten o akeru (open). Windows take the same akeru/shimeru as doors, with mado aiteru for the open state.

items.use: Usually an offer or a question: mado akete ii? (mind if I open the window?), mado akeyou ka. Casual speech drops o; a window that is open is mado aiteru.
items.verbSense: open something (a door, a box, your eyes)
items.trap: Not mado ga akete iru for 'the window's open': that is mado ga aiteru, or mado ga akete aru if someone left it open on purpose. akeru needs someone doing the opening (mado akete ii?).

example.ja: 暑いね、窓開けていい？
example.english: It's hot, mind if I open the window?

examplePolite.romaji: atsui desu ne, mado o akete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 暑いですね、窓を開けてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: It's hot, isn't it? May I open the window?

items.freqNote: 開ける #480 also counts doors, boxes and eyes.
items.notes: In a car, mado akete just means put the window down.

items.use: Said when it turns cold or noisy or starts to rain: mado shimete (shut the window). Casual speech drops o; a shut window is mado shimatteru.
items.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock
items.trap: Not mado o shimaru: shimaru is the window closing or being shut (mado shimatteru); someone shutting it is shimeru (mado shimete).

example.ja: 雨降ってきた、窓閉めて！
example.english: It's started raining, shut the windows!

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga futte kita node, mado o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降ってきたので、窓を閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's started to rain, so please close the windows.

items.freqNote: The intransitive 閉まる (shimaru) is #3722.
items.notes: mado shimeta? is a standard check before going out, alongside kagi kaketa?

items.use: Said in the evening or when the sun is in your eyes: kaaten shimete (close the curtains). Casual speech drops o; opening them in the morning is kaaten o akeru.
items.verbSense: shut something (a door, a window, a lid); with kagi, lock

example.ja: まぶしいから、カーテン閉めて。
example.english: It's too bright, close the curtains.

examplePolite.romaji: mabushii node, kaaten o shimete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: まぶしいので、カーテンを閉めてください。
examplePolite.english: It's bright, so please close the curtains.

items.freqNote: 閉める #1764; the sound-alike 締める (tighten, fasten) is #4630.
items.notes: The state is kaaten shimatteru (the curtains are shut) or kaaten aiteru (open).

blocks.label: Photos and your phone
blocks.rationale: The phone as camera and album: taking photos, looking at them, sending them, and idle time on the phone in between.
blocks.interference: Three verbs on shashin: toru (take), miru (look at), okuru (send). Idle phone use is ijiru, not asobu or tsukau, and shashin o okuru shares okuru with meeru o okuru.

items.use: Said whenever photos come up, mostly as requests: shashin totte (take a photo of me or us), and shashin totte moraemasu ka? to a stranger. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: take (a photo or video)

example.ja: 一緒に写真撮ろうよ。
example.english: Let's take a picture together.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni shashin o torimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に写真を撮りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take a picture together.

items.freqNote: verbRank is the 撮る spelling (photo/film sense); 取る 'take' is #228. Phrase entry 写真を撮る is #4201 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: The one English 'take' that is toru. Take medicine is kusuri o nomu, a shower shawaa o abiru, a train densha ni noru, time jikan ga kakaru. toreru = come out in the photo: yoku toreta (it came out well).

items.use: Said when people share photos, mostly as kono shashin mite (look at this photo) while holding out a phone, or shashin mita? (did you see the photo I sent?). Casual speech drops o. Something you've only seen in pictures is shashin de mita.
items.verbSense: see, look at, watch

example.ja: ちょっとこの写真見て。
example.english: Take a look at this photo.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kono shashin o mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとこの写真を見てください。
examplePolite.english: Please take a look at this photo.

items.freqNote: verbRank is 見る pooling every sense (see, look, watch).
items.notes: Asking to see someone's photos uses miseru: shashin misete (show me).

items.use: Said about idly using a phone, usually in the -teru form: zutto sumaho ijitteru (always on their phone). About someone else it often carries a mild complaint; about yourself it admits a habit. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: fiddle with, tinker with
items.trap: Not tsukau or sumaho o asobu: idly being on your phone is sumaho (o) ijiru, and zutto sumaho miteru is just as common. tsukau is understood but sounds like using it for a task; sumaho de asobu is fine but means playing games on it.

example.ja: またスマホいじってる。
example.english: You're on your phone again.

examplePolite.romaji: neru mae ni, tsui sumaho o ijitchaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 寝る前に、ついスマホをいじっちゃいます。
examplePolite.english: I always end up on my phone before bed.

items.freqNote: nounRank is スマホ; keitai (#1458) is the older word and still common. verbRank is kana いじる; 弄る barely appears.
items.notes: With a person as the object, ijiru means tease (slangy): ijiranaide yo (stop teasing me).

items.use: Said after outings and when sharing on LINE, mostly as a promise or a request: ato de shashin okuru ne (I'll send you the photos later), shashin okutte. The person takes ni and the app takes de. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: send; see someone off

example.romaji: kinou no shashin, rain de okutte.
example.ja: 昨日の写真、LINEで送って。
example.english: Send me yesterday's photos on LINE.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shashin, rain de okutte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の写真、LINEで送ってください。
