examplePolite.english: Please send me yesterday's photos on LINE.

items.freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels.
items.notes: Photos arriving take kuru, like meeru ga kuru: shashin kita yo (got the photos).

blocks.label: Understanding
blocks.rationale: The wakaru family: you get what something means, how someone feels, or the difference between two things.
blocks.interference: All three take ga + wakaru, never shitteru, which is knowing a fact; 'tell the difference' is wakaru, not iu. imi nai (it's pointless) is not imi wakannai (it makes no sense).

items.english: understand what something means; (negative) make no sense
items.use: Mostly heard in the negative as a casual reaction, with ga dropped: imi wakannai (that makes no sense) about a rule, a joke or someone acting strangely. Aimed at what someone just said, it's blunt, close to 'you're not making sense'; with someone above you, ask dou iu imi desu ka? instead. imi wakaru? (you get what I mean?) checks that someone is following you.
items.verbSense: understand, be clear; here the meaning gets through to you
items.trap: For 'that makes no sense', learners say imi ga nai, but imi nai means 'it's pointless' (yatte mo imi nai). Something that doesn't add up is imi wakannai: you can't get the meaning. wake wakannai and the slangy imifu say the same.

example.ja: 何それ、意味分かんない。
example.english: What? That makes no sense.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto imi ga yoku wakaranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと意味がよく分からないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I don't quite follow what you mean.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for 意味が分かる or 意味分かんない, since the tokenizer splits them; the contraction 分かんない alone is #1567.
items.notes: For 'oh, that makes sense', the usual reply is naruhodo; aa, imi wakatta means 'oh, now I get it'.

items.use: The everyday empathy line, with ga dropped: sono kimochi wakaru (I know how you feel), often flipped as wakaru, sono kimochi. With wa it sets up a 'but': kimochi wa wakaru kedo... (I get it, but...), the gentle way to disagree.
items.verbSense: understand; here, relate to how someone feels
items.trap: For 'I know how you feel', learners say kimochi o shitteru, but shiru is knowing a fact: kimi no kimochi shitteru means 'I know what your feelings are' (say, a crush). Relating to someone is wakaru: sono kimochi wakaru.

example.ja: 分かる分かる、その気持ち。
example.english: Oh, I totally know how you feel.

examplePolite.romaji: sono kimochi, yoku wakarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: その気持ち、よく分かります。
examplePolite.english: I know exactly how you feel.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately. In the subtitles wa (261 of 437) outnumbers ga (105), as in kimochi wa wakaru kedo.
items.notes: hito no kimochi ga wakannai (has no idea how other people feel) is a common complaint about someone tactless. To a customer or someone senior it's okimochi: okimochi wa wakarimasu ga... (I understand, but...).

items.use: Mostly negative, after tasting or comparing two things: zenzen chigai wakannai (I can't tell the difference at all), with ga dropped. The things compared take no: kono futatsu no chigai.
items.verbSense: understand, be clear; here you can make out the difference
items.trap: Learners put o on it (chigai o wakaranai), but wakaru takes ga, or drops it in speech: chigai wakannai. 'Tell' isn't iu or oshieru here either: chigai o oshiete asks someone to explain the difference. kubetsu tsukanai (can't tell them apart) also works.
partners: aji (aji ga wakaru: have a palate)
yosa (yosa ga wakaru: see what's good about it)

example.ja: 正直、全然違い分かんない。
example.english: Honestly, I can't tell the difference at all.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, zenzen chigai ga wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、全然違いが分かりません。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I can't tell the difference at all.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately; the verb 違う chigau (#94) carries most talk about differences. Subtitle pair count 53 (ga 40).
items.notes: The verb chigau does much of this work too: nani ga chigau no? (what's the difference?). In the positive it praises a discerning palate: chigai ga wakaru hito (someone who can tell good from ordinary).

blocks.label: Eating out
blocks.rationale: A meal out: suggesting it, finding the place packed, saying it's your treat, and remarking on a big portion.
blocks.interference: gohan ni iku needs no taberu. mise ga komu is said as konderu and is not mise ga aiteru (open). Treating someone is ogoru (kyou wa ogoru yo); being treated is gochisou ni naru (in People). A big portion is ryou ga ooi, not ookii.

items.use: The everyday invitation: gohan ikou (let's get food) or kondo gohan ikanai? (want to get dinner sometime?), usually without ni in casual speech. Whether it means lunch or dinner comes from context.
items.verbSense: go; with a purpose noun + ni, go out for it (kaimono ni iku)
items.trap: English 'go out for dinner' pushes learners to spell it all out (yuushoku o tabe ni ikimasen ka, which is stiff) or to name the place (resutoran ni iku, which means a Western-style restaurant). Friends just say gohan ikou or gohan ikanai?, with no taberu; gohan tabe ni ikou also works.

example.ja: 仕事終わったら、ご飯行かない？
example.english: Want to grab dinner after work?

examplePolite.romaji: shigoto ga owattara, gohan ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 仕事が終わったら、ご飯に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for dinner after work?

items.freqNote: ご飯 #1225 (kana ごはん #2244 counted separately); 行く #40 counts all going. In the subtitles ni is dropped in nearly every case.
items.notes: kondo gohan ikou ne is often a friendly 'let's get dinner sometime', not a fixed plan. At work the polite invitation is often shokuji ni ikimasen ka. For drinks it's nomi ni iku.

items.use: Said when choosing where to eat or go. You mostly hear konderu (it's packed now) or kondeta (it was), often without ga; plain komu means 'gets crowded', as in yoru wa komu yo.
items.verbSense: fill up with people or traffic
items.trap: English 'crowded' is an adjective, but Japanese uses the verb komu, said as konderu; komu alone means 'gets crowded'. hito ga ooi and ippai (full) are also fine.

example.ja: この店、いつも混んでるね。
example.english: This place is always packed.

examplePolite.romaji: kono omise, itsumo kondemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このお店、いつも混んでますね。
examplePolite.english: This place is always packed.

items.freqNote: 混む #5984. The spelling 込む (#10624) is counted separately and likely includes compound-verb tails (-komu), so it isn't added in. How often the pairing comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: Opposite: mise ga suiteru (not crowded). Keep it apart from mise ga aiteru (the shop is open), from mise ga aku.

items.use: Said when offering to pay and when telling who paid: kyou wa ogoru yo (it's on me), senpai ni gohan ogotte moratta (my senpai bought me dinner). The meal is often left out, and casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: pay for someone else, treat
items.trap: ogoru is the payer's verb, like 'treat'. When you are the one treated, add kureta or moratta (senpai ga ogotte kureta, senpai ni ogotte moratta); ogotta with no subject named is heard as 'I paid'.

example.romaji: tetsudatte kureta kara, kondo gohan ogoru ne.
example.ja: 手伝ってくれたから、今度ご飯おごるね。
example.english: You helped me out, so I'll buy you dinner sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: tetsudatte moratta node, kondo gohan o ogorimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 手伝ってもらったので、今度ご飯をおごりますね。
examplePolite.english: You helped me out, so I'll buy you dinner sometime.

items.freqNote: ご飯 #1225; the kana おごる (#2743) is far more common than 奢る (#15720). Forms of the verb ogoru occur about 340 times in the subtitles (about 490 counting the noun ogori), ogoru yo 52 of them, mostly with the object left out.
items.notes: In polite speech the usual offer is gochisou shimasu (kondo gochisou shimasu ne). To a senior, ogorasete kudasai (let me treat you) also works; the noun is ogori: kyou wa watashi no ogori.

items.use: Said about servings in restaurants and when sharing food: koko ryou ooi ne (the portions here are big), ryou ooi kara hanbunko shiyou (it's a lot, let's share). Casual speech drops ga, and the opposite is ryou ga sukunai.
items.verbSense: many, much, a lot (number or amount)
items.trap: English 'a big portion' leads to ookii, which is the size of a thing (ookii sara, a big plate). An amount of food is ooi or sukunai: ryou ga ooi.
partners: shigoto (work: shigoto no ryou ga ooi)

example.romaji: koko no raamen, ryou ooi ne.
example.ja: ここのラーメン、量多いね。
example.english: The ramen here comes in big portions.

examplePolite.romaji: koko no raamen wa, ryou ga ooi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここのラーメンは、量が多いですね。
examplePolite.english: The ramen here comes in big portions.

items.freqNote: 量 #1956; 多い #360 counts every sense of many and much. All 17 subtitle hits keep ga. Most are compounds such as koutsuuryou (traffic volume), and only a few are about food, which the films under-count.
items.notes: When ordering, ask for oomori (a large serving) or sukuname (a smaller one): gohan sukuname de onegai shimasu.

blocks.label: Lights and buttons
blocks.rationale: Switching things on and off and pressing a button: the on/off pair, the light's own state, then the press.
blocks.interference: Don't carry akeru and shimeru over from doors: lights go on with tsukeru and off with kesu (not shimeru or tomeru). Drill the pair in one frame: denki ___te.

items.use: Said whenever a room gets dark: denki tsukete (put the light on), denki tsukeyou ka. Here denki means the light itself, and the same tsukeru works for the TV and air conditioner.
items.verbSense: attach; light or switch on (a light, fire, TV)
items.trap: Not denki o ireru: ireru (turn on) goes with suitchi (switch) and dengen (power). The room light is called denki (literally 'electricity') and takes tsukeru, like terebi and eakon: denki tsukete.

example.ja: 暗いね、電気つけようか。
example.english: It's dark, shall I put the light on?

examplePolite.romaji: kurai desu ne, denki o tsukemashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 暗いですね、電気をつけましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's dark, shall I turn the light on?

items.freqNote: つける #393 is the kana spelling across all senses (付ける #1452, 点ける #52228); 電気 also counts 'electricity'.
items.notes: suitchi o ireru / dengen o ireru is how you switch a machine on; eakon o ireru is also heard, but tsukeru is the everyday choice. Intransitive pair: denki ga tsuku, mostly heard as denki tsuiteru (the light's on) and denki tsukanai (it won't come on). denki tsukete ends like ki o tsukete (take care), the same verb in another sense.

items.use: The other half of denki o tsukeru, used for the TV, heater and air conditioner too. You hear it as denki keshite (turn the light off) and denki keshita? (did you turn it off?).
items.verbSense: put out, make disappear (light, fire, writing)
items.trap: Not denki o tomeru, which means cutting off the power supply (denki tomerareta = they cut off my electricity). Lights and TVs are put out with kesu; for the air conditioner or a fan, kesu, kiru (eakon kitte) and tomeru are all used.

example.ja: 部屋の電気消した？
example.english: Did you turn off the light in your room?

examplePolite.romaji: heya no denki o keshimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 部屋の電気を消しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you turn off the light in your room?

items.freqNote: 消す #964 also covers erase and delete.
items.notes: Intransitive pair: denki ga kieru (the light goes out; denki kieta! = the lights went out). A phone or computer is powered off with dengen o kiru.

items.english: the light comes on (tsuiteru = is on)
items.use: Describes the light itself, almost always as denki tsuiteru (the light's on) or denki tsukanai (it won't come on). Use tsukeru only when someone switches it on.
items.verbSense: come on, catch light; also stick, be attached
items.trap: Not denki ga tsuketeru: with ga the verb is tsuku (denki tsuiteru). denki o tsuketeru means someone is keeping it on.

example.ja: 部屋の電気ついてるよ。
example.english: The light's on in your room.

examplePolite.romaji: heya no denki ga tsuite imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋の電気がついていますよ。
examplePolite.english: The light is on in your room.

items.freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570, 点く #45903); 着く 'arrive' is ranked separately at #957.
items.notes: Sounds like tsuku 'arrive' (eki ni tsuku); the particle and context tell them apart.

items.use: For lifts, buses, ticket machines and intercoms: botan oshite (press the button), kono botan osu dake (you just press this button). Casual speech drops o; on a bus, pressing it asks for the next stop.
items.verbSense: push, press

example.romaji: tsugi de oriru kara, botan oshite.
example.ja: 次で降りるから、ボタン押して。
example.english: We get off at the next stop, press the button.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, tsugi de orimasu node, botan o oshite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、次で降りますので、ボタンを押してもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, I'm getting off at the next stop. Could you press the button?

items.freqNote: 押す #1149 also covers pushing a door or a person.
items.notes: Shirt buttons take other verbs: botan o tomeru (do up), hazusu (undo).

blocks.label: Catching the train
blocks.rationale: Train timing: a late train, making it, when it leaves, missing it, and the last train gone.
blocks.interference: densha ga okureru (the train runs late) and densha ni okureru (you're late for it, so you miss it) differ only in ga or ni. 'Miss' is never misu suru: say nogashita, or make the train the subject, shuuden nakunatta (the last train's gone).

items.use: Heard as okureteru (it's running late) or okurete (because it was late), as in gomen, densha okurete... Casual speech drops ga, so densha okureta means the train was late. Swap ga for ni and you are the one who was late: densha ni okureta (I missed the train).
items.verbSense: be late; fall behind time
items.trap: Not densha ga chikoku suru (chikoku is people being late for school or work), and not densha ga osoi for reporting a delay: osoi works as a grumble while you wait (basu osoi ne = the bus is late), but a train running behind schedule, the one you message about, is okureteru. densha osoi can also just mean a slow train.

example.ja: ごめん、電車遅れてる。
example.english: Sorry, the train's delayed.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, densha ga okuretemasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、電車が遅れてます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, the train is running late.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. okureru's rank also covers people being late.
items.notes: When the line has stopped altogether: densha tomatteru. A clock running slow is also tokei ga okureteru (fast is susunderu).

items.use: Mostly heard as a check or a result: maniau? (will we make it?), maniatta (made it), maniawanai (we won't make it). The noun drops once the train is clear. Once it has gone, say densha ni okureta, or more casually nogashita or noriokureta (I missed it). For the last train people usually say shuuden nakunatta (the last train's gone) or shuuden nogashita.
items.verbSense: be in time (for something); be enough
items.trap: Not densha o tsukamaeru or densha o toru: making a train in time is ni maniau ('be in time for'). 'I missed the train' is not misu shita (misu is a mistake): say maniawanakatta or nogashita.

example.romaji: isoganai to, densha ni maniawanai yo.
example.ja: 急がないと、電車に間に合わないよ。
example.english: If we don't hurry, we won't make the train.

examplePolite.romaji: isoganai to, densha ni maniaimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急がないと、電車に間に合いませんよ。
examplePolite.english: If we don't hurry, we won't make the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. maniau's rank covers every deadline, not just trains. For missing one: nogasu #2510, noriokureru #13876, shuuden #8326.
items.notes: maniattemasu also means 'we're fine, no thanks', a common way to turn away a door-to-door or phone salesperson.

items.use: Mostly a timetable question: tsugi no densha nanji ni deru? As it pulls away, densha itchatta or densha dechatta (the train's just gone). Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: go out; leave (a place)
items.trap: For 'what time does it leave?', not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: those describe it pulling away (densha ga hoomu o hanareru). The departure itself is deru, the same verb as leaving the house. shuppatsu suru also works, and hassha is the announcement word.

example.romaji: tsugi no densha, nanji ni deru?
example.ja: 次の電車、何時に出る？
example.english: What time does the next train leave?

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no densha wa nanji ni demasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次の電車は何時に出ますか？
examplePolite.english: What time does the next train leave?

items.freqNote: No film hits. deru's rank covers every sense of going out or appearing; the formal shuppatsu is #2505 and hassha #14705.
items.notes: The first train of the day is shihatsu: shihatsu made nomu (drink until the first train).

items.english: be late for the train (and so miss it)
items.use: Mostly said beforehand while rushing: densha ni okurechau! (I'll miss my train!), densha ni okurenai you ni (so we don't miss it). Keep the ni: with no particle, densha okureta is heard as the train running late, which is the usual excuse. Once it has gone, natives usually say noriokureta or nogashita: nebou shite densha noriokureta (I overslept and missed my train).
items.verbSense: be late; fall behind time
items.trap: Not densha o misu suru (misu is a mistake). And the particle flips it: densha ni okureru is you being late for it, densha ga okureru is the train running late.

example.romaji: sorosoro denai to, densha ni okurechau yo.
example.ja: そろそろ出ないと、電車に遅れちゃうよ。
example.english: We'd better head out soon or we'll miss the train.

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro denai to, densha ni okuremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ出ないと、電車に遅れますよ。
examplePolite.english: We'd better head out soon or we'll miss the train.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. For a train that has already gone natives use noriokureru (#13876) and nogasu (#2510).
items.notes: With a class or meeting the same frame just means late (jugyou ni okureta); a train doesn't wait, so late means missed.

items.english: the last train is gone (no way home)
items.use: Said as a warning or an excuse near midnight: shuuden nakunatchau (I'll miss the last train), shuuden nakunatta (the trains have stopped for the night). Casual speech drops ga. shuuden nogashita (I missed the last train) is just as common and makes it your miss.
items.kana: しゅうでんがなくなる
items.verbSense: run out; be gone (nai 'none' + naru 'become')
items.trap: Not shuuden o misu suru (misu is a mistake): Japanese says the last train 'is gone', with the train as the subject. shuuden nogashita and shuuden ni maniawanakatta also work.

example.romaji: shuuden nakunatchau kara, mou kaeru ne.
example.ja: 終電なくなっちゃうから、もう帰るね。
example.english: I'll miss the last train, so I'm heading home.

examplePolite.romaji: shuuden ga nakunaru node, mou kaerimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 終電がなくなるので、もう帰りますね。
examplePolite.english: The last train will be gone soon, so I'll head home now.

items.freqNote: Rare in films (10 hits for 終電 alone). 397 is the kana spelling なくなる, which covers running out of anything (無くなる #8961).
items.notes: shuuden nanji? (when's your last train?) is the usual question as a night out winds down.

blocks.label: Doctor and medicine
blocks.rationale: Getting treated: going to the doctor, taking medicine and the medicine working.
blocks.interference: English 'see' and 'take' pull toward miru and toru, but a doctor visit is byouin ni iku and medicine is drunk, kusuri o nomu. The kiku in kusuri ga kiku (it works) sounds the same as kiku 'hear, ask'.

items.use: The normal way to say 'see a doctor', often as advice: byouin itta hou ga ii yo. Casual speech usually drops ni: byouin itta?
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: English 'hospital' sounds serious, but byouin is any clinic: for a cold you still go to the byouin, byouin ni iku. Isha ni iku also works; isha o miru or isha ni au doesn't.

example.romaji: sore, byouin itta hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: それ、病院行った方がいいよ。
example.english: You should get that looked at by a doctor.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, byouin ni itta hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それ、病院に行った方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You should have a doctor look at that.

items.freqNote: 病院 #651; 行く #40. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Byouin de mite morau (get it looked at) is the other natural way.

items.use: Used for pills, powders and syrups alike, often as a check: kusuri nonda? (did you take your medicine?).
items.verbSense: drink, swallow
items.trap: Not kusuri o toru, which would mean fetching it: medicine is 'drunk', kusuri o nomu, even pills.

example.ja: 薬飲んで、早く寝てね。
example.english: Take your medicine and get to bed early.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri o nonde, yukkuri yasunde kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 薬を飲んで、ゆっくり休んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Take your medicine and get some rest.

items.freqNote: 薬 #1283; 飲む #229. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Eye drops take sasu (megusuri o sasu); cream takes nuru (kusuri o nuru). When it works, the medicine kiku: kono kusuri, yoku kiku (this medicine works well).

items.use: Asked after a pill as kusuri kiita? and said as it kicks in, kusuri kiite kita. Ga often drops; when the effect wears off, the medicine kireru (kusuri ga kireta).
items.verbSense: take effect, work (medicine, air con, a remedy); sounds the same as kiku 'listen, ask'
items.trap: Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, which sounds just like kiku 'listen'.
partners: eakon (air con: eakon kiitenai = the AC isn't doing anything)

example.ja: 薬効いてきた。だいぶ楽。
example.english: The medicine's kicking in. I feel much better.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri ga kiite kimashita. daibu raku ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 薬が効いてきました。だいぶ楽になりました。
examplePolite.english: The medicine is starting to work. I feel much better.

items.freqNote: 薬 #1283; 効く #1822 (its homophone 聞く 'listen' is #67); phrase entry 薬が効く #19852.
items.notes: Kiku~! is also what people say when wasabi or a strong drink hits.

blocks.label: Close and in touch
blocks.rationale: How things stand with people: close or on bad terms, staying in touch, and hearing from them.
blocks.interference: naka ga ii and naka ga warui say the relationship is good or bad, where English uses a verb (get along). renraku o toru is getting or staying in touch; renraku ga kuru (renraku kita?) is them getting in touch with you, like meeru ga kuru.

items.use: Said about two people or a group (ano futari naka ii yo ne), or with to for you and someone: tanaka-san to naka ii n da (I'm close with Tanaka). ii becomes yo- in other forms: naka yokatta (we used to be close), nakayoku shite ne (be nice to each other). The opposite is naka ga warui.
items.verbSense: good, fine (adjective; past yokatta)
items.trap: English 'get along' splits in two: the state 'we get along' is naka ga ii (our relationship is good), and the action 'get along, be nice to each other' is nakayoku suru (nakayoku shite ne). This naka is not naka 'inside'.

example.romaji: ano futari, naka ii yo ne.
example.ja: あの二人、仲いいよね。
example.english: Those two are close, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa naka ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は仲がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: Those two get along well, don't they.

items.freqNote: 仲 #1305; kana なか #4046 mixes in 中 'inside'. ii: kana いい #24. nakayoku (仲良く) #1816.
items.notes: Opposite: naka ga warui; close friends are nakayoshi. nakayoku suru = get along (as an action), nakayoku natta = we became friends. 10-list-nouns #23 is the homophone naka 'inside'; under its rule S2, 仲 is carded only as this phrase.

items.use: Said about two people or groups (ano futari, naka warui no?), or with to for you and someone: oya to naka warui n da (I don't get on with my parents). Falling out is naka ga waruku naru, and plain 'not close' is often softened to amari naka yokunai.
items.verbSense: bad (adjective; past warukatta)
partners: aishou (compatibility: aishou ga warui = we just don't click)

example.ja: あの二人、仲悪いの？
example.english: Do those two not get along?

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa naka ga warui n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は仲が悪いんですか？
examplePolite.english: Are those two on bad terms?

items.freqNote: 仲 #1305; 悪い #139. Phrase entry 仲が悪い #13246; 仲良く #1816. Written 仲が悪 18, 仲悪 7.
items.notes: The opposite of naka ga ii. kenka shiteru (they've fallen out) is a current fight; naka ga warui is the lasting state.

items.use: Mostly about staying in touch or managing to reach someone: mada renraku totteru? (still in touch?), renraku ga torenai (I can't get hold of them). renraku tsukanai means the same and is just as common (renraku ga tsuku is the intransitive side). For a single message or call, renraku suru is the everyday verb.
items.verbSense: take, get hold of
items.trap: English 'keep in touch' leads to renraku suru for everything. That's right for the goodbye line (mata renraku suru ne, renraku shite ne) and for a single message, but being in contact over time or managing to reach someone is renraku o toru: mada renraku totteru?, renraku ga torenai. renraku o tsuzukeru sounds off, and renraku o tamotsu is stiff written style.
partners: kyori (distance: kyori o toru = keep your distance)
baransu (balance: baransu o toru = keep your balance)

example.ja: 彼とまだ連絡取ってる？
example.english: Are you still in touch with him?

examplePolite.romaji: kare to wa mada renraku o tottemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 彼とはまだ連絡を取ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you still in touch with him?

items.notes: Hearing from someone is renraku ga kuru or renraku moratta.

items.use: The everyday way to ask or report whether someone got in touch: renraku kita? (did they get in touch?), mada renraku konai (still nothing from them), with ga dropped. The sender takes kara: kare kara renraku kita.
items.verbSense: come, arrive
items.trap: English 'hear from him' leads to kare kara kiku, which means being told something by him. Getting a message or call from him is kare kara renraku ga kita. renraku o morau also works, but kita is what you hear most.

example.ja: 彼からまだ連絡来ない。
example.english: I still haven't heard from him.

examplePolite.romaji: kare kara mada renraku ga kimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 彼からまだ連絡が来ません。
examplePolite.english: I still haven't heard from him.

items.freqNote: 連絡 #326; 来る #52 counts all coming (kana くる #429 is mostly -te kuru). No phrase entry. Written 連絡が来 37, 連絡がき 6, 連絡来 2.
items.notes: renraku kitara oshiete = let me know if you hear from them.

blocks.label: Likes, interest, confidence
blocks.rationale: How you feel about a thing or a plan: you like it, you're into it, you can't wait, you're sure you can do it.
blocks.interference: English 'interested' and 'confident' are adjectives, but here they are nouns that exist: kyoumi aru, jishin aru (or nai). ki ni itta (I love it) sounds like ki ni natta (it bugged me).

items.use: Nearly always past or -te ru: ki ni itta (I love it, about a gift, purchase or place) and ki ni itteru (I really like it, I've taken to it). The thing you like takes ga or o, and casual speech drops both: kore ki ni itta. Giving a gift: ki ni itte kureru to ii na (I hope you like it).
items.verbSense: enter, go in (an old reading of hairu); the thing gets into your heart
items.trap: English says 'I love it' in the present, but Japanese says the past, ki ni itta. iru here conjugates like hairu (itta, irimasu), not like iru 'be' (ita, imasu).

example.ja: これすごい気に入った！
example.english: I love this!

examplePolite.romaji: kore, sugoku ki ni irimashita.
examplePolite.ja: これ、すごく気に入りました。
examplePolite.english: I really love this.

items.freqNote: 入る read iru (#63142) survives almost only inside this phrase; the whole expression 気に入る is #889, and the noun お気に入り (favourite) #3558.
items.notes: The negative ki ni iranai (I don't like it) is mostly said about someone's attitude and sounds combative: ano taido ga ki ni iranai. okiniiri means favourite: kore, okiniiri na no.

items.use: The topic takes ni, and casual speech often drops ga: X ni kyoumi aru? The blunt reply kyoumi nai (not interested) is very common.
items.verbSense: there is, exist; here you have (an) interest
items.trap: For 'I'm interested', learners say watashi wa omoshiroi, which means 'I'm funny', or kyoumi desu. Japanese says the interest exists, and the topic takes ni: X ni kyoumi ga aru. X ga omoshiroi (X is interesting) is also fine, but it describes the thing, not you.

example.ja: アニメとか興味ある？
example.english: Are you into anime or anything?

examplePolite.romaji: anime toka ni kyoumi ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: アニメとかに興味がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you interested in anime or anything like that?

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the ga-aru expression because its tokenizer splits it. 興味ない is #1906 and 興味を持つ #4531.
items.notes: kyoumi o motsu (take an interest in) is the version for an interest someone develops: anime ni kyoumi o motta.

items.use: Nearly always in -te ru for how you feel now: tanoshimi ni shiteru (I'm looking forward to it). The thing takes o, often dropped: ryokou tanoshimi ni shiteru. Polite tanoshimi ni shitemasu closes many messages and plans.
items.verbSense: do, make; with X ni, make something into X (here, a pleasure ahead), not the 'go with' of kore ni suru
items.trap: English 'look forward to' has no matching verb, and 'I can't wait' as matenai sounds like you've run out of patience. Say tanoshimi ni shiteru or just tanoshimi!; machikirenai (can't wait) is also fine.

example.romaji: jaa, raishuu tanoshimi ni shiteru ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、来週楽しみにしてるね。
example.english: Okay, looking forward to next week!

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, raishuu tanoshimi ni shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、来週楽しみにしてますね。
examplePolite.english: Well then, I'm looking forward to next week.

items.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 楽しみにする #1435, high for a phrase; suru's #15 covers every use of suru.
items.notes: tanoshimi ni shitete ne (look forward to it!) is what you say when you've planned a surprise.

items.use: Heard as often in the negative as the positive, with ga dropped: jishin nai (I'm not sure I can) before a test, an interview or a date. What you're confident in takes ni: ryouri ni wa jishin aru (I'm good at cooking and I know it).
items.verbSense: there is, exist; here you have it (confidence)
items.trap: 'Confident' is an adjective in English, but Japanese has confidence: jishin aru / jishin nai, and a confident person is jishin aru hito. For 'I'm not sure I can do it', a bare wakaranai sounds like 'I don't know'; say jishin nai, or dekiru ka wakaranai, which is also fine.

example.romaji: ashita no mensetsu, anmari jishin nai na.
example.ja: 明日の面接、あんまり自信ないな。
example.english: I'm not too confident about tomorrow's interview.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no mensetsu, amari jishin ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の面接、あまり自信がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm not very confident about tomorrow's interview.

items.freqNote: 自信 #839 is its own entry, apart from 自身 'oneself' #1355 and 地震 'earthquake' #7156. No phrase entry. Subtitle pairs: 自信+ある 143, 自信+ない 118, 自信+持つ 112. 自信満々 is #10967.
items.notes: To encourage someone it's motto jishin motte (yo), with motsu, not aru. jishin manman (full of confidence) can sound teasing; the same sound jishin also means earthquake.

blocks.label: Ready and how long
blocks.rationale: Getting things done: are you ready, it takes a while, time's gone by, it's a hassle.
blocks.interference: kakaru vs tatsu: ichinen kakatta = it took a year, ichinen tatta = a year has gone by; tema ga kakaru is effort, not minutes. Readiness is asked in the past (junbi dekita?), never junbi dekiru?.

items.use: Asked and answered in the past: junbi dekita? / dekita yo / mou chotto. junbi dekitara oshiete = let me know when you're ready.
items.verbSense: be able to; come into being, get done
items.trap: English asks 'are you ready?' in the present. Japanese asks whether it is done: junbi dekita? or junbi dekiteru?. junbi dekiru? means 'can you get ready?'. Casual junbi ii? also works.
partners: shitaku (getting ready; sounds a bit old-fashioned or parental)

example.ja: もう準備できた？
example.english: Are you ready yet?

examplePolite.romaji: mou junbi dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう準備できましたか？
examplePolite.english: Are you ready yet?

items.freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form; 出来る #1313.
items.notes: Getting ready yourself is junbi suru; junbi ga dekiru is being done with it. The main list's dekiru already covers 'be ready'; the new point is asking in the past: junbi dekita?

items.use: Said about how long anything takes, often with an amount in place of jikan: eki made juppun kakaru, dore gurai kakaru?. On its own, jikan kakaru means 'it takes a while'.
items.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time or money: be needed, be used up
items.trap: English 'take' leads to toru, but jikan o toru mostly means making time for someone (jikan totte kurete arigatou). How long something takes is kakaru.

example.ja: これ、けっこう時間かかるよ
example.english: This takes quite a while.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa kekkou jikan ga kakarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: これはけっこう時間がかかりますよ
examplePolite.english: This takes quite a while.

items.freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses; 掛かる #5316.
items.notes: jikan o kakeru = spend time on something on purpose (jikan kakete tsukutta). tema ga kakaru is the same frame for effort: it's a hassle.

items.use: Mostly in the past, about time that has gone by: mou ichinen tatta (it's already been a year). The fixed remark is jikan tatsu no hayai ne (time flies).
items.verbSense: of time: pass, go by (sounds the same as tatsu 'stand')
items.trap: 'It's been a year' is ichinen tatta, not kakatta, which means 'it took a year'. For 'pass', use tatsu or sugiru, not tooru (pass through).

example.ja: 時間経つの早いね
example.english: Time flies, doesn't it.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga tatsu no wa hayai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 時間が経つのは早いですね
examplePolite.english: Time flies, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: 経つ #3603 is the time sense. The kana たつ is dominated by 立つ #610. sugiru (過ぎる) #701 covers all senses, including 'too much'.
items.notes: ichinen kakatta = it took a year; ichinen tatta = a year has gone by.

items.use: Said about cooking, chores and paperwork that eat up effort: kore, kekkou tema kakaru n da yo. Before a noun, ga becomes no: tema no kakaru ryouri (a fiddly dish).
items.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time, money or effort: be needed, be used up
items.trap: English 'it takes a lot of effort' leads to doryoku, which is effort as in trying hard. A chore that's fiddly or slow is tema ga kakaru, with the same kakaru as jikan ga kakaru.

example.romaji: kono ryouri, kekkou tema kakaru n da.
example.ja: この料理、けっこう手間かかるんだ。
example.english: This dish takes quite a bit of work.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ryouri wa kekkou tema ga kakaru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: この料理はけっこう手間がかかるんです。
examplePolite.english: This dish takes quite a bit of work.

items.freqNote: 手間 #4541; かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses. Phrase entry 手間をかける #19815; no entry for 手間がかかる. Pair counts: ga kakaru 18, o kakeru 40 (films over-count kakesaseru plot lines); kakaru leads here because daily talk about chores and cooking uses it.
items.notes: tema o kakeru is going to the trouble on purpose: tema kakete tsukutta. Apologising for someone's trouble: otesuu o okake shimashita.

blocks.label: Bed and waking
blocks.rationale: Bedtime to morning: dreaming, waking, getting under the covers and setting the alarm, plus the kotatsu people crawl under on winter evenings.
blocks.interference: okiru from the versatility list gets mixed up with me ga sameru: okiru can mean getting out of bed, but me ga sameru never does. Getting into bed is going in, futon ni hairu, the same ni hairu as kotatsu ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu.

items.use: Used for dreams in your sleep, usually in the past: hen na yume mita (I had a weird dream). A life ambition is yume ga aru instead.
items.verbSense: see, watch, look at
items.trap: Not yume o motsu or yume ga aru, which mean having an ambition: dreams in your sleep are 'seen', yume o miru.

example.ja: 昨日変な夢見た。
example.english: I had a weird dream last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou hen na yume o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日変な夢を見ました。
examplePolite.english: I had a strange dream last night.

items.freqNote: 夢 #351 covers both night dreams and ambitions; 夢見る #4121 is the one-word 'dream of' verb.
items.notes: Bedtime set phrase: oyasumi, ii yume mite ne (good night, sweet dreams).

items.english: wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)
items.use: For the moment of waking, often unplanned: yonaka ni me ga sameta (I woke in the night). It also means feeling wide awake, e.g. after coffee. Getting out of bed is okiru.
items.verbSense: wake, come out of sleep or a daze
items.trap: English 'wake up' covers two things. okiru is waking or getting up (yonaka ni okichatta is fine), but me ga sameru is only the waking and never getting out of bed: yoji ni me ga sameta kedo, okita no wa shichiji.

example.ja: 夜中に目が覚めちゃった。
example.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

examplePolite.romaji: yonaka ni me ga samete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夜中に目が覚めてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

items.freqNote: 覚める #6527; 目覚める #3028 is the one-word narrative/written form.
items.notes: Not the sameru of gohan ga sameru (food gets cold). mezamashi (alarm) comes from the transitive me o samasu (wake up, wake someone).

items.english: get into bed, get under the covers
items.use: For getting under the covers, not necessarily asleep yet: mou futon haitta (I'm in bed now). Casual speech drops ni. futon also means the covers on a bed, so it's said with any bed; beddo ni hairu is also common.
items.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)

example.ja: もう布団入ったけど、眠れない。
example.english: I'm in bed, but I can't sleep.

examplePolite.romaji: futon ni haitte mo, nakanaka nemurenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 布団に入っても、なかなか眠れないんです。
examplePolite.english: Even after I get into bed, I can't get to sleep.

items.freqNote: 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu; ベッド beddo is #2222.
items.notes: Laying the futon out is futon o shiku; folding it away in the morning is futon o tatamu.

items.use: Said the night before, often as mezamashi kaketoku (I'll set the alarm). For phone alarms, araamu o kakeru and araamu o setto suru are just as common.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
items.trap: English 'set' gives no hint of kakeru: alarms and timers take kakeru (araamu o setto suru is also fine).

example.ja: 明日早いから、目覚ましかけとく。
example.english: I'm up early tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa hayai node, mezamashi o kakete okimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は早いので、目覚ましをかけておきます。
examplePolite.english: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

items.freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 is the everyday short form; アラーム #12854 competes (araamu o kakeru / setto suru). かける #244 counts every sense.
items.notes: Shutting it off is mezamashi o tomeru; the alarm going off is mezamashi ga naru (mezamashi naranakatta = my alarm didn't go off).

items.use: Winter at home: sitting with your legs under the heated table's quilt, often with mikan. Mostly heard as kotatsu haitte (get in) or kotatsu kara derarenai (I can't get out of the kotatsu).
items.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)

example.ja: 寒い！早くこたつ入ろう。
example.english: It's freezing! Let's get under the kotatsu.

examplePolite.romaji: samui desu ne. hayaku kotatsu ni hairimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いですね。早くこたつに入りましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's cold. Let's get under the kotatsu.

items.freqNote: こたつ #18598 (コタツ #37599); no film hits, since foreign films have no kotatsu.
items.notes: Same hairu as futon ni hairu and ofuro ni hairu. Dozing off in it (kotatsu de neru) is the classic way to catch a cold.

blocks.label: Storms and quakes
blocks.rationale: The big events people warn each other about, and the forecast that got it wrong: a typhoon on the way, an earthquake, thunder, a missed forecast.
blocks.interference: English 'hit' fits none of them: a typhoon kuru (comes), an earthquake okiru (happens; jishin kita as it shakes) and thunder naru (sounds), so drill the three verbs side by side. kaminari ga naru is 鳴る 'sound', not naru 'become', and a forecast hazureru (misses) or ataru (is right), never machigaeru.

items.use: Mostly said without ga, about one in the forecast: shuumatsu taifuu kuru kamo (a typhoon might come this weekend). Taifuu kiteru means one has already come close and is nearby or heading in, not a forecast for later in the week; taifuu chikazuiteru stresses that it's getting closer, and taifuu kita means it has arrived. Often there's no verb at all: ashita taifuu da tte (they say there's a typhoon tomorrow).
items.verbSense: come, arrive
items.trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to taifuu ga utsu or taifuu ga ataru, which don't work: with the typhoon as subject it just comes (taifuu kita). Ataru is fine the other way round, with your plans as subject and ni: ryokou ga taifuu ni atatchatta (our trip ran into a typhoon). Chokugeki (direct hit) is everyday talk too: toukyou chokugeki rashii yo (apparently it's heading straight for Tokyo); jouriku (landfall) mostly comes from the forecast.
partners: jishin (earthquake: jishin kita! as it shakes; the usual set is jishin ga okiru)

example.ja: 明日台風来るらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently a typhoon's coming tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita taifuu ga kuru rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日台風が来るらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently a typhoon's coming tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 台風 is only #8171 because drama dialogue rarely turns to the weather; in typhoon season (roughly July to October) it is everywhere whenever one approaches, so commonness is a judgement. 来る is #52 (kana くる #429 is mostly -te kuru).
items.notes: The cause takes de: taifuu de densha tomatta (the trains stopped because of the typhoon); once it's passed, taifuu sugita ne.

items.use: Used when talking about a quake: jishin ga okita toki (when the earthquake hit), ookii jishin ga okitara (if a big one hits). In the moment people shout jishin da! or jishin kita!, and afterwards say kinou jishin atta ne.
items.verbSense: happen, occur; also wake up, get up
items.trap: English 'an earthquake hit' has no matching verb, and utsu or ataru don't work. It happens (okiru), or casually it comes or there is one (jishin kita!, jishin atta).

example.ja: 大きい地震起きたらどうする？
example.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

examplePolite.romaji: ookii jishin ga okitara dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大きい地震が起きたらどうしますか？
examplePolite.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

items.freqNote: Rank is for the kanji 地震, because kana じしん is dominated by 自信 (#839) and 自身 (#1355). 起きる #329 also covers waking and getting up. 揺れる (shake) is #3717.
items.notes: The shaking is yureru: ima yureta? (did it just shake?), kekkou yureta ne.

items.use: Said when you hear thunder: kaminari natteru (it's thundering), or kaminari natta! for a single clap. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: make a sound, ring (thunder, a phone, a bell, an alarm)

example.ja: あ、雷鳴ってる。
example.english: Oh, it's thundering.

examplePolite.romaji: a, kaminari ga nattemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あ、雷が鳴ってますね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, it's thundering.

items.freqNote: The phrase 雷が鳴る is listed at #42945. Rank is for the kanji 鳴る, because kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'. 雷 covers both thunder and lightning.
items.notes: Naru here is 鳴る 'ring' (as in denwa ga naru), said flat (na-RU), while naru 'become' falls (NA-ru). A strike is kaminari ga ochiru: chikaku ni ochita! The flash is kaminari ga hikaru.

items.use: A grumble, almost always in the past: tenki yohou hazureta (the forecast got it wrong), usually without ga, or just yohou hazureta once the weather is already the topic. When it gets it right: yohou atatta.
items.kana: てんきよほうがはずれる
items.verbSense: miss, come off; turn out wrong (a forecast, guess, lottery ticket)
items.trap: A forecast misses (hazureru) or hits (ataru), like a guess or a lottery ticket. Machigaeru is a person's slip, so yohou ga machigaeta doesn't work; yohou machigatteta (it was wrong) is also fine, but hazureta is the usual word.

example.ja: 天気予報、また外れたね。
example.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

examplePolite.romaji: tenki yohou, mata hazuremashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 天気予報、また外れましたね。
examplePolite.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

items.freqNote: Rank is for the compound 天気予報; 予報 alone is #13931. 外れる #1999 counts every sense (come off, miss). Its partner 当たる is #719. No corpus hits for the pair, so commonness is a judgement.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: weather-terms (tenki, inside tenki yohou)
items.notes: What it says: yohou de wa ame da tte (the forecast says rain).

blocks.label: Personality and mood
blocks.rationale: What someone is like and how they seem: nice, mean, pleasant to deal with, down today.
blocks.interference: seikaku is who someone is underneath, kanji is the impression their manner gives, and genki ga nai is how they seem right now. seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty, far stronger than 'not nice', and genki ga nai is low and flat, not kibun ga warui (feel sick).

items.use: The plain way to say someone is a good, kind person: ano hito, seikaku ii yo ne, with ga dropped. Before a noun it's seikaku no ii hito, and it often pairs with looks: kao mo ii shi seikaku mo ii. Seikaku warui (mean, nasty) is harsh and common in gossip.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not ii seikaku: in that order, ii seikaku shiteru ne is usually sarcastic ('you've got some nerve'). The compliment keeps seikaku first: seikaku ii, seikaku no ii hito. Seikaku warui is far stronger than 'not nice': it means mean or nasty.
partners: tsukiai (tsukiai ga ii: sociable, always up for things)

example.romaji: ano hito, honto ni seikaku ii yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんとに性格いいよね。
example.english: She's such a nice person, isn't she?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni seikaku ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に性格がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: She really is a lovely person, isn't she?

items.freqNote: 性格 #1670; いい #24. The negative is much more frequent in dramas: 性格悪い #14102 and 性格が悪い #30468, against 性格がいい #47898. 人柄 hitogara #7228.
items.notes: Ii hito also means 'a nice person', but ii hito na n da kedo... is the classic brush-off (nice, but not for me).

items.use: Gossip about someone mean or spiteful, almost always with ga dropped: ano hito, seikaku warui yo ne. It judges who a person is, so it's said about people far more than to them; before a noun it's seikaku no warui hito.
items.verbSense: warui: bad
items.trap: Not warui hito, which judges someone as a bad person in the moral sense (warui hito ja nai kedo... = he's not a bad guy, but...): mean or nasty by nature is seikaku ga warui. ijiwaru (mean, spiteful) works for a person or an act: ijiwaru shinaide = don't be mean.

example.romaji: ano senpai, honto seikaku warui n da yo.
example.ja: あの先輩、ほんと性格悪いんだよ。
example.english: That senior is seriously mean.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai wa hontou ni seikaku ga warui n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩は本当に性格が悪いんですよ。
examplePolite.english: That senior is really mean.

items.freqNote: 性格 #1670; 悪い #139. The phrase has its own entries, 性格悪い #14102 and 性格が悪い #30468, both above 性格がいい #47898. 意地悪 ijiwaru #4005.
items.notes: Among friends, the clipped seikaku waru! is a playful 'that's so mean!'.

items.use: The verdict on someone's manner, a shop's staff or a place: ano ten'in-san, kanji ii ne, with ga dropped. Before a noun, ga often becomes no: kanji no ii hito (a pleasant person). The opposite, kanji warui (rude, off-putting), is at least as common.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: English 'nice' pulls toward yasashii, but yasashii is a kind, gentle nature. The pleasant impression a person's manner or a place gives is kanji ga ii, and yasashii is wrong for a place. Rude or off-putting is kanji warui.
partners: inshou (inshou ga ii: make a good impression)
taido (taido ga warui: have a bad attitude)

example.romaji: ano mise no ten'in-san, kanji ii ne.
example.ja: あの店の店員さん、感じいいね。
example.english: The staff at that shop are so pleasant.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise no ten'in-san wa kanji ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの店の店員さんは感じがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: The staff at that shop are very pleasant.

items.freqNote: 感じ #305, though much of that is ii kanji and tte kanji; いい #24. いい感じ has its own entry at #1668 and the opposite 感じ悪い is #8684, but 感じがいい / 感じいい are not listed. The film count (441) is mostly ii kanji (ADJ:410), so commonness is judged.
items.notes: In the reverse order, ii kanji (いい感じ) means 'going well, looking good': ii kanji da ne! For the mood of a café or a room, the usual set is ii fun'iki. Kanji (感じ, feeling) sounds the same as kanji (Chinese characters).

items.use: Said when you notice someone seems low: genki nai ne, dou shita no? Casual speech drops ga. In polite speech genki nai desu ne is just as common as genki ga arimasen. The opposite is genki ga aru (full of energy).
items.verbSense: nai: there isn't, have none (negative of aru)
items.trap: Not kanashii (sad, too strong), and not genki ja nai, which leans toward 'unwell': for 'you seem down', say genki nai ne. If something has upset them, ochikonderu? (are you feeling down?) is also natural.

example.romaji: genki nai ne. dou shita no?
example.ja: 元気ないね。どうしたの？
example.english: You seem down. What's up?

examplePolite.romaji: genki nai desu ne. dou shita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 元気ないですね。どうしたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You seem down. Is something wrong?

items.freqNote: 元気 #297; ない #43 (無い #6807); 落ち込む ochikomu #1647.
items.notes: Here genki is a noun (energy), not the adjective genki da. Genki dashite (cheer up) is the usual response. Keep apart: genki nai = low, flat; kigen warui = grumpy; kibun warui = feel sick; guai warui = unwell.

blocks.label: Lies, jokes and complaints
blocks.rationale: What friends say to each other: lies, jokes, complaints, venting and secrets.
blocks.interference: Lying takes tsuku (uso tsuita), but joking, complaining and venting take iu. monku o iu is complaining at someone or about something wrong, while guchi o iu is grumbling to let off steam. naisho takes ni suru, not mamoru.

items.use: Heard as denial or accusation: uso tsuitenai yo (I'm not lying), uso tsukanaide (don't lie to me). Bare uso! is the 'no way!' reaction, not an accusation.
items.verbSense: let out (breath); in speech it survives mainly in uso o tsuku and tameiki o tsuku (sigh)
items.trap: English 'tell' leads to uso o iu, which natives also say (uso bakkari itte, uso iwanaide), but the set phrase for lying is uso o tsuku: uso tsuita, uso tsukanaide.

example.romaji: uso tsuitenai yo, honto da yo.
example.ja: 嘘ついてないよ、ほんとだよ。
example.english: I'm not lying, it's true.

examplePolite.romaji: uso wa tsuitemasen. hontou desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 嘘はついてません。本当ですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not lying. It's true.

items.freqNote: uso #1544 (kana うそ #2305 counted separately). tsuku: kana つく #355 pools every kana tsuku sense (付く, 点く, 吐く); 吐く read as つく sits at the list floor (#173635, effectively unranked), so this sense has no clean rank.
items.notes: A liar is usotsuki.

items.use: Heard in teasing: mata joudan itte (there you go joking again), joudan itteru dake (I'm only joking). The short replies joudan da yo (just kidding) and joudan desho? (you're kidding, right?) leave the verb out. joudan ja nai yo is the annoyed opposite: this is no joke / you've got to be kidding me.
items.verbSense: say
items.trap: English 'make a joke' leads to joudan o tsukuru, which doesn't work; jokes are said (joudan o iu), and 'just kidding' is joudan da yo.

example.ja: 冗談言ってるだけだよ。
example.english: I'm only joking.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan o itteru dake desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談を言ってるだけですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm only joking.

items.use: Heard mostly as a rebuke: monku iwanaide (stop complaining), monku bakkari (always complaining). Complaining to a shop or a neighbour is also monku o iu, and being on the receiving end is monku iwareta (someone complained to me). Casual speech often drops o.
items.verbSense: say
items.trap: English has one verb, 'complain'; Japanese says the complaint: monku o iu, not monku suru. Dictionary picks sound formal: kujou o iu is lodging a complaint with a landlord or company, fuhei o iu is bookish, and kureemu (from 'claim') is a customer complaint to a business. Venting about your day is guchi o iu.

example.ja: 文句ばっかり言わないでよ。
example.english: Stop complaining all the time.

examplePolite.romaji: monku bakari iwanaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 文句ばかり言わないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please stop complaining so much.

items.freqNote: 文句 #1359; 言う #28. Phrase entry 文句を言う #7153.
items.notes: monku aru? (got a problem with that?) is the confrontational retort, and monku nai yo (no complaints, fine by me) the easy-going reply; both belong to monku ga aru.

items.use: Venting about work, family or your lot, usually to a friend over a drink: guchi itte gomen (sorry for moaning), guchi bakkari (always moaning). The listener's side is guchi o kiku (guchi nara kiku yo), and guchiru is the one-word casual verb. monku o iu is objecting to someone or something; guchi is letting off steam about your situation.
items.verbSense: say

example.ja: ごめん、愚痴ばっかり言って。
example.english: Sorry, all I do is moan.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, guchi bakari itte shimatte.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、愚痴ばかり言ってしまって。
examplePolite.english: Sorry for complaining so much.

items.freqNote: 愚痴 #4194; 言う #28. The verb 愚痴る (guchiru) #10411. 愚痴 appears 68 times in the subtitles, 愚痴を言 7.
items.notes: guchi o kobosu means the same and sounds a little more literary.

items.use: Almost always a request: kore naisho ni shite ne (keep this between us). On its own, naisho da yo means 'it's a secret' when you won't tell.
items.verbSense: do; with ni, make something into X (kore ni suru = I'll take this one)
items.trap: English 'keep a secret' leads to mamoru. himitsu o mamoru is fine (himitsu mamotte ne works too), but naisho doesn't take mamoru: 'keep this between us' is naisho ni shite (or himitsu ni shite).

example.ja: これ内緒にしてね。
example.english: Keep this between us, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa naisho ni shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: これは内緒にしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please keep this to yourself.

items.freqNote: 内緒 #2414; kana ないしょ #4442 counted separately; suru #15.
items.notes: himitsu ni suru is the neutral twin.

blocks.label: Rest and recovery
blocks.rationale: Lying down and getting better: the fever drops, the cold clears up, the tiredness goes.
blocks.interference: sagaru, naoru and toreru say the thing goes away by itself, so they take ga; their o twins mean someone does it (netsu o sageru, kaze o naosu). yoko ni naru is lying down to rest, not neru (sleep).

items.use: For lying down to rest rather than to sleep: chotto yoko ni naru (I'll lie down a bit); to someone unwell, yoko ni natta hou ga ii yo. The ni always stays: never yoko naru.
items.verbSense: become, turn into; with yoko (side) it's 'become horizontal'
items.trap: Dictionaries give yokotawaru, which sounds written; in speech you 'become sideways', yoko ni naru. Neru also works but suggests going to sleep.

example.ja: ちょっと横になっていい？
example.english: Mind if I lie down for a bit?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto yoko ni natte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと横になってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Would it be all right if I lie down for a bit?

items.freqNote: 横 #2228; なる #29 (kanji 成る #13300); phrase entry 横になる #4874, high for a phrase.
items.notes: Related single verb: nekorobu (lie down casually, sprawl).

items.use: The follow-up to any fever: netsu sagatta? answered with sagatta or mada sagaranai. Ga often drops; a fever going up is netsu ga agaru.
items.verbSense: go down, drop (temperature, prices); also step back
items.trap: Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).

example.ja: 薬飲んだら、熱下がった。
example.english: I took some medicine and my fever went down.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri o nondara, netsu ga sagarimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 薬を飲んだら、熱が下がりました。
examplePolite.english: After I took the medicine, my fever came down.

items.freqNote: 熱 #1641; 下がる #1064 (上がる #503, for a fever going up). No phrase entry.
items.notes: Bringing a fever down is netsu o sageru; the medicine for it is genetsuzai. Netsu ga hiku (the fever subsides) is also fine.

items.use: Asked after someone's cold as kaze naotta? and answered mou naotta or mada naoranai. Ga drops, and kaze itself is often left out once the topic is clear.
items.verbSense: heal, get better (an illness, an injury); the same-sounding naoru also means a thing gets fixed

example.ja: 風邪、もう治った？
example.english: Are you over your cold yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kaze wa mou naorimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 風邪はもう治りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you got over your cold?

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666; 治る #1604 (transitive 治す #2761; 直る 'be fixed' #4537 is a homophone). No phrase entry.
items.notes: Hayaku naoshite ne (get well soon) uses the transitive naosu; odaiji ni is the stock polite wish.

items.use: Most often heard in the negative: nete mo tsukare ga torenai (I sleep and still feel tired). After a bath, a massage or a holiday it's tsukare toreta, and ga often drops.
items.verbSense: come off, come out (a button, a stain); also can get (potential of toru)
items.trap: Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness isn't cured, it 'comes off' (toreru).

example.ja: 寝ても、全然疲れ取れない。
example.english: Even after sleeping, I can't shake the tiredness.

examplePolite.romaji: nete mo, zenzen tsukare ga toremasen.
examplePolite.ja: 寝ても、全然疲れが取れません。
examplePolite.english: Even after sleeping, I still feel tired.

items.freqNote: 疲れ #3920; 取れる #631 counts all its senses (come off, can get, be taken). No phrase entry; transitive 疲れを取る #62068.
items.notes: Tsukare o toru is doing something about it: onsen de tsukare o toru (soak it away at a hot spring). Tsukare ga nukenai (the tiredness won't leave) is also common.

blocks.label: Costs and paying
blocks.rationale: Money at the till and the table: what it costs overall, one item's price, pricey, paying, and splitting the bill.
blocks.interference: No single verb for 'cost': okane ga kakaru is the overall cost (kekkou kakatta), ikura suru is an item's price (ikura shita?), nedan ga takai says the price is high. okane o harau is you handing it over, and warikan ni suru is splitting evenly, not wakeru.

items.use: For what a trip, a hobby, a repair or daily life costs overall, often with an amount: ichiman en gurai kakatta. For the price of a thing you bought, use ikura suru.
items.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time or money: be needed, be used up
items.trap: There is no one Japanese verb for 'cost'. A thing's price is suru (ikura shita?). What something costs you overall is kakaru, the same verb as time: shuuri ni ichiman en kakatta.

example.romaji: kuruma tte kekkou okane kakaru yo
example.ja: 車ってけっこうお金かかるよ
example.english: Having a car costs quite a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma wa kekkou okane ga kakarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 車はけっこうお金がかかりますよ
examplePolite.english: Having a car costs quite a bit.

items.freqNote: お金 #422; the blunter 金 (kane) is #670. かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses.
items.notes: okane o tsukau = spend (your choice); okane ga kakaru = something costs.

items.use: The shape is price + suru: ichiman en suru = it costs 10,000 yen. In the past about something bought: sore ikura shita? or ikura datta? (both common). In the present for what a thing goes for: are tte ikura suru no?, ikura suru n darou, or sanman en mo suru n da (it's a whole 30,000 yen). In a shop, the plain kore ikura desu ka is the usual question.
items.verbSense: do, make; after a price or amount: cost, be priced at
items.trap: The main list teaches kakaru as 'cost', but that is for overall spending. A single thing's price takes suru: kore ikura shita? / ichiman en shita. ikura datta? also works.

example.ja: これ、いくらした？
example.english: How much did this cost?

examplePolite.romaji: kore, ikura shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、いくらしましたか？
examplePolite.english: How much did this cost?

items.freqNote: いくら #553 counts all uses, including 'no matter how'. The shape is price + suru, so an amount often takes the place of ikura.
items.notes: kekkou suru ne = that's pricey.

items.use: Said when comparing shops or weighing up a buy: koko, nedan chotto takai ne. Day to day people just say takai! about a thing; nedan comes in when the price itself is the point, often with mo: oishii kedo nedan mo takai.
items.verbSense: high; expensive
items.trap: A low price isn't hikui in speech: cheap is yasui (nedan ga yasui). hikui turns up only in written kakaku ga hikui.

example.romaji: koko, oishii kedo nedan chotto takai ne.
example.ja: ここ、おいしいけど値段ちょっと高いね。
example.english: This place is good, but it's a bit pricey.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa oishii kedo, nedan ga chotto takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここはおいしいけど、値段がちょっと高いですね。
examplePolite.english: This place is good, but it's a bit pricey.

items.freqNote: 値段 #2953; 高い #421 also covers 'high' and 'tall'. Pair count 16 (mo 6, ga 6).
items.notes: nedan no wari ni = for the price: nedan no wari ni oishii. kakaku is the written word on signs and sites.

items.use: For whether someone has paid, usually in the past: okane haratta? / mou haratta yo. When the amount, bill or method is said, okane drops: sen en haratta, kaado de harau.
items.verbSense: pay; also brush or sweep off (dust, snow)
items.trap: Paying back money you borrowed is kaesu (give back), not harau: ashita kaesu ne. When a friend covered your share, ato de harau ne works too.

example.ja: お金、もう払った？
example.english: Have you paid already?

examplePolite.romaji: okane, mou haraimashita?
examplePolite.ja: お金、もう払いました？
examplePolite.english: Have you paid already?

items.freqNote: 払う #760. 支払う shiharau #2842 is the formal word used on bills and at the register.
items.notes: Offering to pay is dasu (koko wa watashi ga dasu yo), and treating someone is ogoru. At the register staff ask oshiharai wa dou nasaimasu ka? (how will you pay?).

items.use: Said when the bill comes: warikan ni shiyou, warikan de ii?, or just warikan shiyou. People often follow with each person's share: hitori sen en ne. Between two people, hanbunko also works.
items.verbSense: do; X ni suru = make it X, go with X
items.trap: English 'split' leads to wakeru, which is fine with staff for separate bills (kaikei wakete moraemasu ka?). Splitting the total evenly is one noun, warikan: warikan ni shiyou. Each paying their own is betsubetsu.

example.ja: じゃあ、割り勘にしよう
example.english: OK, let's split it.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, warikan ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、割り勘にしましょう
examplePolite.english: OK, let's split it.

items.freqNote: 割り勘 #12038 is low in drama subtitles; commonness is judged from how often it's said at meals out.
items.notes: Paying for someone is ogoru (kyou wa ogoru yo = it's on me); being treated is gochisou ni naru.

blocks.label: Trying clothes on
blocks.rationale: Dressing past plain on/off, the mirror and fitting-room talk: trousers take haku, getting changed is kigaeru, then whether it suits you (niau) and whether it fits (saizu ga au).
blocks.interference: zubon takes haku like shoes, not kiru; niau (looks good on you) vs saizu ga au (right size), which English both calls 'fit' or 'suit', and this au also sounds like au 'meet'; changing clothes is kigaeru, not fuku o kaeru.

items.use: Heard as zubon haiteru (is wearing trousers) or haite mite (try them on). Same verb as shoes; casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the feet and legs
items.trap: Not zubon o kiru: trousers, skirts, socks and tights take haku, like shoes (anything you step into).

example.ja: このズボン、履いてみていい？
example.english: Can I try these trousers on?

examplePolite.romaji: kono zubon, haite mite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: このズボン、履いてみてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I try these trousers on?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for ズボン #6081 and 履く #3474. sukaato (#6710) and kutsushita (#5748) take the same verb.
items.notes: pantsu with a flat pitch is trousers (younger speakers prefer it; zubon can sound a little old to them), but PA-ntsu, falling, is underpants, so zubon is the safe word. sutokkingu = sheer stockings or pantyhose. In shops, 'try on' is shichaku: shichaku shite mo ii desu ka?

items.use: kigaeru already means 'change clothes', so fuku is often dropped: chotto kigaete kuru (I'll just go and get changed). What you change into takes ni: pajama ni kigaeru.
items.verbSense: change clothes (kiru 'wear' + kaeru 'change')
items.trap: fuku o kaeru isn't wrong, but it's about switching to a different outfit (are, fuku kaeta? = oh, you've changed your outfit?). The everyday verb for getting changed is kigaeru, and English 'change into' becomes ni (seifuku ni kigaeru).

example.ja: ちょっと服着替えてくる。
example.english: I'm just going to go and get changed.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto fuku o kigaete kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと服を着替えてきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just go and get changed.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 着替える #1536. The verb usually comes without fuku (着替えて alone has 158 corpus hits, against 27 for the pair); the noun 着替え kigae is #5293.
items.notes: The noun kigae is a change of clothes: kigae motteku (I'll bring a change of clothes). Some speakers say kikaeru; it's the same word.

items.english: suit someone, look good on someone
items.use: Mostly said as a compliment: sono fuku niau ne, or yoku niatteru (it really suits you). ga is dropped, and so is the noun once it's clear. The person it looks good on takes ni: watashi ni niau kana? (would it suit me?). Politely, and from every shop assistant, it's (yoku) oniai desu ne.
items.verbSense: suit, look good on someone
items.trap: Suit and fit are different verbs: niau is about looks, saizu ga au is about size (niau ne vs saizu atteru?). What looks good takes ga, and the person takes ni (watashi ni niau kana?) or comes first as the topic (kanojo wa aka ga niau ne = red suits her).

example.ja: その服、よく似合ってるね。
example.english: That outfit really suits you.

examplePolite.romaji: sono fuku, yoku oniai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: その服、よくお似合いですね。
examplePolite.english: That outfit really suits you.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 服 #1051 and 似合う #941. The pair count is low (8) because the noun is usually dropped or replaced by sore; 似合ってる alone has 178 corpus hits. お似合い oniai is #2476 (181 corpus hits).
items.notes: It works for any look, not just clothes: kami mijikai no mo niau ne (short hair suits you too). oniai also describes a well-matched couple (oniai no futari), and said with a sneer it means 'it's what you deserve' (omae ni wa oniai da).

items.use: Mostly heard as a check or a complaint when trying things on or ordering online: saizu atteru? (does it fit?), saizu awanai (it's not my size). Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: match, fit together
items.trap: English 'it fits' makes the clothes the subject. Japanese usually makes the size the subject: saizu ga au, mostly heard as saizu awanai. Don't reach for niau, which is about looks (it suits you). fitto suru exists but means snug, close to the body.
partners: kutsu (shoes: kono kutsu, ashi ni awanai)
megane no do (glasses' prescription: do ga awanai = wrong prescription)
makura (pillow: makura ga awanai = it isn't right for me)

example.ja: これ、ちょっとサイズ合わないかも。
example.english: I don't think this is quite my size.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa chotto saizu ga awanai kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: これはちょっとサイズが合わないかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: This might not be quite the right size.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for サイズ #3308 and 合う #563; kana あう is mostly 会う 'meet' (#110). Shop and online-order talk is under-counted in film subtitles, so pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: If you can't get it on at all, say hairanai (kono zubon hairanai). Too tight is kitsui, too loose yurui, and a perfect fit pittari. This au sounds exactly like au 'meet' (same pitch); saizu, or the thing being tried on, tells you which.

blocks.label: Are you free?
blocks.rationale: Setting a time: are you free, have you got plans, and whether a time suits.
blocks.interference: aiteru (got a gap) vs yotei aru (got plans) is the yes/no; tsugou ii / warui is the tactful pair for whether a time suits, not benri / fuben.

items.use: Asking about or offering free time, nearly always as aiteru: ashita aiteru? / doyoubi nara aiteru yo. Plain aku means 'come free': jikan aitara renraku suru (I'll get in touch when I get a moment).
items.verbSense: become empty or free; open up (a seat, a room, a gap in time)
items.trap: Not jiyuu (free as in liberty) or tada (free of charge). A free slot is aku, 'open up': ashita aiteru?. ashita jikan aru? also works, and hima? is fine with friends but blunt to a senior.

example.ja: 明日時間空いてる？
example.english: Are you free tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa jikan aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は時間空いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you free tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 空く (あく) #1498. The kana あく #3508 mixes senses, and 開く read as aku (a shop or door opens) is ranked separately.
items.notes: aku also means a shop is open (mise ga aku); both come out as aiteru. Asking someone politely, people say ojikan: ojikan aitemasu ka?

items.use: Asked before an invitation (shuumatsu yotei aru?) and given as the reason for saying no (sono hi wa chotto yotei aru n da). Casual speech drops ga, and yotei nai means 'I'm free'.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: Not yotei o motteru: plans exist, so it's yotei ga aru. And 'got plans?' is yotei aru?, not keikaku aru?, which sounds like asking about a worked-out scheme (a project, a trip itinerary).

example.ja: 週末、なんか予定ある？
example.english: Got any plans for the weekend?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa nanika yotei ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末は何か予定がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have any plans for the weekend?

items.freqNote: 予定 #843; ある #21. No phrase entry. 計画 keikaku #1502 counts every sense of 'plan', including projects.
items.notes: A booked plan is yotei haitteru, and the politer excuse is senyaku ga atte (a prior engagement). Drawing up a schedule (a trip, a study plan) is yotei o tateru, like keikaku o tateru; fixing a day with friends is hi o kimeru, and arranging to meet is yakusoku suru.

items.use: The tactful way to set a time, itsu ga tsugou ii? (when suits you?), and to decline, sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute (that day doesn't quite work). Casual speech drops ga. Among close friends, ashita daijoubu? is more usual.
items.verbSense: good, fine, OK
items.trap: Not benri, which is for tools and places. A time that suits someone is tsugou ga ii, and 'can't make it' is tsugou ga warui.

example.ja: 明日都合いい？
example.english: Does tomorrow work for you?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa tsugou ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は都合いいですか？
examplePolite.english: Does tomorrow work for you?

items.freqNote: いい #24 is the spoken form (良い #1474); 悪い #139 for tsugou ga warui.
items.notes: Asking someone above you: gotsugou ii desu ka? Declining politely: sono hi wa tsugou ga tsukanakute... (I can't make that day). tsugou ga tsuitara oshiete = let me know if you can make it. Said about a person, tsugou ii ne can be a dig: 'how convenient for you'.

items.english: not suit someone, can't make it (a time)
items.use: For turning down a time: ashita tsugou warui (tomorrow's no good), or politely sumimasen, sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute..., left trailing. Mostly for schedules; about a person it means 'doesn't suit them': jibun ni tsugou no warui koto wa kikanai (he won't listen to anything that doesn't suit him). With close friends, ashita chotto muri is also common.
items.verbSense: bad, not good
items.trap: English 'inconvenient' leads to fuben, which is for places and tools (eki kara tookute fuben = it's a pain, being so far from the station). A time that doesn't suit you is tsugou ga warui.
partners: taimingu (taimingu warui = bad timing, an unlucky moment; not a way to decline)

example.romaji: ashita tsugou warui kara, asatte wa?
example.ja: 明日都合悪いから、あさっては？
example.english: Tomorrow's no good for me. How about the day after?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa chotto tsugou ga warui node, asatte wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はちょっと都合が悪いので、あさってはどうですか？
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow doesn't really work for me. How about the day after?

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 都合が悪い #16199. 不便 fuben #6936.
items.notes: Often cut short to chotto tsugou ga..., with warui left unsaid.

blocks.label: Seeing people
blocks.rationale: Getting together: meeting up with a friend, seeing someone home, going back to your parents', and birthdays.
blocks.interference: au takes ni (tomodachi ni au), not o. Seeing someone home is okuru (okutte iku yo), not tsurete iku. jikka ni kaeru is going back to your parents' place, while uchi ni kaeru is just going home.

items.use: The everyday way to say what you're doing on a day off: kyou wa tomodachi ni au (I'm seeing a friend today). tomodachi to au is also heard and stresses a meet-up you both arranged; asobu (hang out) is the other weekend verb.
items.verbSense: meet, see (a person)
items.trap: English 'meet a friend' or 'see a friend' leads to tomodachi o au or tomodachi o miru. People you meet take ni or to (tomodachi ni au, tomodachi to au), and miru with a person means watching or minding them (kodomo mitete = keep an eye on the kids).

example.romaji: ashita tomodachi ni au n da.
example.ja: 明日友達に会うんだ。
example.english: I'm seeing a friend tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa tomodachi ni au n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は友達に会うんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 友達 #405; 会う #110 (合う #563 is 'fit, match'). Written 友達に会 37 vs 友達と会 6.
items.notes: Bumping into a friend by chance is also au: eki de guuzen atta.

items.use: The offer at the end of an evening is okutteku yo (I'll walk or drive you home), often without naming the place, and the thanks is okutte kurete arigatou. made marks how far you go: eki made okuru (see someone to the station). The one taken home says uchi, their own home: uchi made okutte kureta (they saw me home).
items.verbSense: send; also see someone off or take them somewhere
items.trap: English 'take you home' leads to tsurete iku, which sounds like leading someone who can't go alone (a child, a drunk friend). Seeing someone home as a courtesy, on foot or by car, is okuru: okutteku yo.
partners: genkan (the front door: genkan made okuru = see someone to the door)

example.romaji: osoi kara, ie made okutteku yo.
example.ja: 遅いから、家まで送ってくよ。
example.english: It's late, I'll see you home.

examplePolite.romaji: osoi node, ie made okurimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 遅いので、家まで送りますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's late, so I'll take you home.

items.freqNote: Noun is 家 (ie) #152. 送る #324 also counts sending things; 見送る (miokuru) #3407. Written 家まで送 109, うちまで送 1; 送ってく 384 vs 送っていく 29. The pair counter does not see made, so there is no measured count.
items.notes: miokuru is seeing someone off at the door, station or airport.

items.use: The holiday question and answer: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru? (going home for New Year?), obon wa jikka kaeru yo. It takes kaeru because it's a return, even after years of living away.
items.verbSense: go back to where you belong (home, your country)
items.trap: English 'go to my parents' place' leads to oya no uchi ni iku, which sounds like a visit. The home you grew up in is jikka, and you kaeru to it. Your spouse's family home takes iku: tsuma no jikka ni iku.
partners: inaka (your home region in the country)

example.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaeru no?
example.ja: お正月は実家に帰るの？
example.english: Are you going home for New Year?

examplePolite.romaji: oshougatsu wa jikka ni kaerimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お正月は実家に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going back to your family's for New Year?

items.freqNote: 実家 #1109; 帰る #101 (変える #450 is 'change'). 里帰り (satogaeri) #15496. Written 実家に帰 17.
items.notes: satogaeri = a trip back to your family home, also a mother-to-be going home to give birth.

items.use: Mostly about others doing it for or with you: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta (everyone celebrated my birthday), or planning: kanojo no tanjoubi, dou iwaou? The greeting itself is tanjoubi omedetou.
items.kana: たんじょうびをいわう
items.verbSense: celebrate, mark a happy occasion

example.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi iwatte kureta n da.
example.ja: みんなが誕生日祝ってくれたんだ。
example.english: Everyone celebrated my birthday for me.

examplePolite.romaji: minna ga tanjoubi o iwatte kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: みんなが誕生日を祝ってくれたんです。
examplePolite.english: Everyone celebrated my birthday.

items.freqNote: 誕生日 #1370; 祝う #3023. お祝い (oiwai) #1674 is more frequent than the verb. Written 誕生日(を)祝 18 hits; the pair counter misses it.
items.notes: oiwai suru is the softer noun form: tanjoubi no oiwai shiyou (let's do something for the birthday).

blocks.label: Drinking out
blocks.rationale: A night out drinking: the invitation, asking about smoking, and whether you can hold your drink.
blocks.interference: nomi ni iku is the drinking version of gohan ni iku, and nomi means alcohol without saying osake. osake ga tsuyoi and osake ga yowai describe the drinker, while kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is strong. Tobacco takes suu, not nomu.

items.use: The standard invitation and plan for a night out: kondo nomi ni ikou (let's go for a drink sometime), kyou nomi ni ikanai? Bare nomi already means alcohol. Naming the drink is fine too (osake nomi ni iku, koohii nomi ni iku), and a café break is ocha shi ni iku. Casual speech sometimes drops ni (nomi iku).
items.verbSense: go; with a verb stem or activity noun + ni, go (out) to do it (tabe ni iku, kaimono ni iku)

example.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikou yo.
example.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行こうよ。
example.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

items.freqNote: The noun 飲み is #15171 (kana のみ #1942 is mostly the particle 'only'); 飲み会 (nomikai) is #4920. 行く #40 counts all going. The phrase 飲みに行 occurs 141 times in the subtitles, and only 7 times without ni.
items.notes: A drinking party with colleagues or a club is a nomikai, and moving on to a second place afterwards is the nijikai (second round).

items.use: Used to ask about smoking and to say whether you smoke: tabako suu? (do you smoke?), sutte mo ii? (mind if I smoke?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: breathe in, suck in (air, smoke)
items.trap: Dictionaries give kitsuen suru for 'smoke', but that is the word on signs and forms (kitsuenjo, kin'en); in speech you inhale the tobacco: tabako (o) suu. kemuri names only the smoke itself.

example.ja: タバコ吸ってもいい？
example.english: Mind if I smoke?

examplePolite.romaji: tabako o sutte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: タバコを吸ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you mind if I smoke?
