items.freqNote: タバコ #4158 is the most frequent spelling (たばこ #7069, 煙草 #28060). 吸う #1684 also counts breathing in. 喫煙 (kitsuen) is only #18056, which fits it being a sign-and-form word.
items.notes: Restaurants ask kitsuen seki ka kin'en seki (smoking or non-smoking seat?); kin'en on a sign means no smoking. tabako o nomu is dated (older speakers); don't use it.

items.use: Said about yourself to turn down drinks gently (osake yowai n desu) or about someone who gets drunk fast. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
items.trap: English has no set phrase here, so learners fall back on amari nomenai (fine, but blunt). Japanese says the drinker is weak: osake ga yowai (or osake ni yowai). Careful: kono osake tsuyoi is about the drink (high proof), not the drinker.
partners: asa (mornings: asa ga yowai, not a morning person)
i (stomach: i ga yowai, a delicate stomach)

example.romaji: osake yowai kara, ippai dake ni shitoku.
example.ja: お酒弱いから、一杯だけにしとく。
example.english: I'm a lightweight, so I'll just have one.

examplePolite.romaji: osake yowai n de, ippai dake ni shitokimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お酒弱いんで、一杯だけにしときます。
examplePolite.english: I'm not much of a drinker, so I'll just have the one.

items.freqNote: お酒 #1229; bare 酒 is counted separately (#1131). 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: osake ni yowai is equally fine; osake ga tsuyoi is the opposite. With conditions only ni works: samusa ni yowai (can't take the cold), atsusa ni yowai (can't take the heat), norimono ni yowai (get travel-sick); samusa ga yowai would mean the cold is mild.

items.use: Said about people at drinking parties, often as surprised praise: osake tsuyoi ne! (you can really drink!), or as a question, osake tsuyoi n desu ka? Casual speech drops ga, and osake ni tsuyoi is equally common.
items.verbSense: strong; with something you take or face, able to handle it
partners: kikai (machines: kikai ni tsuyoi, good with tech)

example.romaji: osake tsuyoi ne. zenzen kao ni denai.
example.ja: お酒強いね。全然顔に出ない。
example.english: You can really drink. It doesn't even show on your face.

examplePolite.romaji: osake ga tsuyoi desu ne. zenzen kao ni demasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: お酒が強いですね。全然顔に出ませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can really drink. It doesn't show on your face at all.

items.freqNote: お酒 #1229 (bare 酒 #1131 counted separately); 強い #310 counts every sense of strong. In the subtitles 酒 + 強い is mostly tsuyoi sake (strong liquor), and the drinker sense shows up only about five times, so its commonness is judged.
items.notes: osake ga yowai is the opposite. With the drink as the subject, kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is high-proof. Someone who never seems to get drunk is jokingly called a zaru (a sieve).

blocks.label: Phone calls
blocks.rationale: One phone call on the noun denwa: calling, picking up and hanging up, then the phone ringing and calls that came in for you.
blocks.interference: The o/ni sets are things you do (kakeru, deru, kiru) and the ga sets happen to you (naru, aru, kakaru): denwa o kakeru vs denwa ga kakaru differ only in o/ga, with kara for the caller. This naru is 'ring', not naru 'become', and kiru ends the call.

items.use: Said when you phone someone, with the person marked by ni. For a plain 'I'll call you', denwa suru is the everyday default (ato de denwa suru ne); kakeru is what you hear for dialing and trying: kakete miru, nankai kakete mo denai (they don't pick up however many times I call). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set something going (a call, a record)
items.trap: Not yobu or iu: phoning someone is denwa o kakeru (or simply denwa suru); yobu is summon, iu is call something a name.

example.romaji: chotto okaasan ni denwa kakete miru.
example.ja: ちょっとお母さんに電話かけてみる。
example.english: Let me try calling my mom.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto haha ni denwa o kakete mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと母に電話をかけてみます。
examplePolite.english: Let me try calling my mother.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かける, which pools every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742. Phrase entry 電話をかける is #7088 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: kakenaosu = call again (after a dropped or missed call). The number takes ni: kono bangou ni kakete.

items.use: Said about picking up, mostly in the negative: denwa denai (they're not picking up). Casual speech drops ni, and denwa dete means 'can you get the phone?'
items.verbSense: come out, go out; appear
items.trap: Not denwa ni kotaeru: picking up is denwa ni deru ('come out to the phone'); kotaeru answers a question. denwa o toru (lift the receiver) is also natural, especially for office phones: denwa totte!

example.romaji: zenzen denwa denai n da kedo.
example.ja: 全然電話出ないんだけど。
example.english: They're not picking up at all.

examplePolite.romaji: zenzen denwa ni denai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 全然電話に出ないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: They're not picking up at all.

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電話に出る is #3584 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).

items.use: Said at the end of a call (jaa, kiru ne = OK, I'll hang up) and for being hung up on (kirareta). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: cut; cut off
items.trap: Not kakeru ('hang'): denwa o kakeru makes the call; ending it is kiru ('cut').

example.ja: ごめん、間違えて電話切っちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I hung up by mistake.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, machigaete denwa o kitchaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、間違えて電話を切っちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I hung up by mistake.

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電話を切る is #16284 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: Not kiru 'wear' (fuku o kiru): a different verb with different pitch and conjugation. Hung up = kitta, kirimasu; wore = kita, kimasu. Intransitive: denwa ga kireta = the call cut off.

items.use: Said as a heads-up when a phone rings, in the -teru form: denwa natteru yo (your phone's ringing), often just natteru yo. Casual speech drops ga. The past natta is for a ring that already happened: sakki denwa natta yo.
items.verbSense: ring, sound (a phone, bell or alarm)
items.trap: Spelled like naru 'become' and conjugated alike (natteru, natta), but the pitch differs: naru 'ring' is flat (na-RU), while naru 'become' falls after na (NA-ru). So keitai natteru yo means 'your phone's ringing'. Ringing something yourself is the transitive narasu (chaimu o narasu).

example.ja: ねえ、電話鳴ってるよ。
example.english: Hey, your phone's ringing.

examplePolite.romaji: denwa ga nattemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 電話が鳴ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: Your phone's ringing.

items.freqNote: verbRank is 鳴る only; kana なる (#29) is almost all 'become'.
items.notes: Alarms and stomachs use it too: mezamashi naranakatta (my alarm didn't go off), onaka natta (my stomach rumbled).

items.english: (someone) called, there was a call from X
items.use: Said when passing on who called, in the past with the caller marked by kara: obaachan kara denwa atta yo (Grandma called). At work, passing on a call takes the polite odenwa: tanaka-san kara odenwa ga arimashita. Casual speech often drops ga.
items.verbSense: there is, exist; have; happen
items.trap: 'Your mom called' is okaasan kara denwa atta yo, with the caller marked by kara; okaasan ni denwa atta means a call came for her. okaasan ga denwa shita sounds like she called someone else.

example.romaji: tanaka-san kara denwa atta yo. orikaeshite hoshii tte.
example.ja: 田中さんから電話あったよ。折り返してほしいって。
example.english: Tanaka called. He wants you to call him back.

examplePolite.romaji: sakihodo tanaka-san kara odenwa ga arimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 先ほど田中さんからお電話がありました。
examplePolite.english: Mr. Tanaka called earlier.

items.freqNote: verbRank pools every use of ある (there is, have, happen). The count also holds 'there's a phone' uses; the call forms 電話(が)あった and 電話がありました alone are 233.
items.notes: denwa kakatte kita tells the call coming in to you; denwa atta reports that a call happened, often to pass it on. denwa kita is the casual short form, and renraku atta covers word by any channel.

items.use: Said of an incoming call, almost always as denwa kakatte kita (I got a call), with the caller marked by kara. The -te kuru shows the call coming toward you.
items.verbSense: hang, be put onto; get going (the intransitive of kakeru)
items.trap: Not okaasan kara denwa kaketa: kaketa says you made the call. An incoming call makes either the call the subject (okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita) or the caller the subject with -te kuru (okaasan ga denwa kakete kita). denwa kita and denwa moratta are also natural.

example.romaji: sakki okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita.
example.ja: さっきお母さんから電話かかってきた。
example.english: My mom called a little while ago.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki haha kara denwa ga kakatte kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: さっき母から電話がかかってきました。
examplePolite.english: My mother called a little while ago.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる (掛かる alone is #5316). Phrase entries 電話がかかる #10203 and 電話がかかってくる #32857.
items.notes: denwa kita is the short everyday version. Passing on a call that came while someone was out is denwa ga aru: tanaka-san kara denwa ga arimashita. This -te kuru means 'toward me', not the 'go and do' sense of -te kuru. The partners take kakaru in its 'running' sense.

blocks.label: On the way
blocks.rationale: Updates from the journey: I'm at the station, the roads are jammed, a seat's come free, I rode past my stop.
blocks.interference: Crowded is konderu and a free seat is aiteru, while a whole empty train or road is suiteru, never isogashii or hima. Arriving takes ni (eki ni tsuku), but the stop you ride past takes o (eki o norisugosu).

items.use: Mostly a phone or text update: ima eki tsuita (I'm at the station now), eki tsuitara renraku suru (I'll text when I get there). The past tsuita is how you say 'I'm here'; casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: arrive; get to (a place)
items.trap: eki ni touchaku suru is correct but stiff, the language of announcements and work emails; in conversation you arrive with tsuku, and 'I'm here' is the past tsuita.

example.romaji: eki tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de matteru ne.
example.ja: 駅着いたら、改札の前で待ってるね。
example.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

examplePolite.romaji: eki ni tsuitara, kaisatsu no mae de mattemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅に着いたら、改札の前で待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: When I get to the station, I'll wait in front of the ticket gates.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. 着く is ranked apart from kana つく (#355), which mixes in the other tsuku verbs.
items.notes: nanji ni tsuku? (what time do you get in?) and mou sugu tsuku (almost there) are the other everyday forms.

items.use: Heard as konderu (busy now) or kondete (because it was busy), usually without ga: michi konderu kara okureru kamo. Plain komu is for patterns: kono jikan wa michi komu yo (the roads get busy at this hour). Same verb as mise ga komu and densha konderu. (sugoi konderu, with sugoi as an adverb, is casual; sugoku is the standard form.)
items.verbSense: get crowded; konderu = be crowded, packed
items.trap: Not michi ga isogashii: isogashii is for people and their time (isogashii hi, a busy day), never for a place full of people or cars. A busy road, train or shop is konderu ('has got packed').

example.ja: 今日、道すごい混んでるね。
example.english: The roads are really busy today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa michi ga sugoku kondemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は道がすごく混んでますね。
examplePolite.english: The roads are really busy today.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. komu is written 混む or 込む, and the list splits them (#5984 / #10624). juutai (traffic jam) is #8673.
items.notes: A full jam is juutai: juutai ni hamatta (I got stuck in traffic). Clear roads are suiteru: michi suiteta.

items.english: a seat frees up (aiteru = a seat is free)
items.use: Almost always heard as aiteru: koko aitemasu ka? (is this seat free?) or seki aiteru (there's a free seat). aita is the moment one frees up: a, seki aita.
items.verbSense: become empty or vacant; open up (a space, a slot)
items.trap: Not kono seki tada? (that asks if it costs nothing) or seki ga hima: hima is a person or a quiet shop with nothing going on, and a free seat is aiteru ('has come open'). For your own schedule both work: ashita aiteru? / ashita hima?

example.ja: あ、あそこ席空いてるよ。
example.english: Oh, there's a free seat over there.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono seki aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、この席空いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, is this seat free?

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 空く (aku) is ranked separately from 開く (#14086, a door opening).
items.notes: A whole train being empty or packed is densha ga suiteru / konderu, not aiteru.

items.use: Nearly always in the past, norisugoshita or norisugoshichatta, and usually without eki: nechatte norisugoshita (I fell asleep and missed my stop). How far you went is counted in stops: hitoeki norisugoshita. When the noun is said, it's oriru eki: oriru eki norisugoshita (I went past my stop).
items.verbSense: ride past (noru 'ride' + sugosu 'let go by')
items.trap: Not eki o nogasu or eki o misu shita: staying on past your stop is norisugosu (ride past), and nogasu is for a train that left without you. orisokoneta (didn't manage to get off) also works, say on a packed train.

example.ja: 寝ちゃって、一駅乗り過ごした。
example.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.

examplePolite.romaji: nete shimatte, hitoeki norisugoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 寝てしまって、一駅乗り過ごしました。
examplePolite.english: I fell asleep and went one stop too far.

items.freqNote: No film hits, and norisugosu ranks #51053 in drama, yet it is everyday commuter talk. nesugosu (sleep past) is #25205.
items.notes: Sleeping through the stop is also nesugoshita; oversleeping in the morning is nebou shita.

blocks.label: Can't make it
blocks.rationale: The stock reasons for saying no or heading off: something on, an early start, already booked, a prior engagement.
blocks.interference: All use aru or hairu, never motsu. youji ga atte is the vague errand excuse, yotei haitteru says the day is taken, senyaku ga atte is the politer 'prior engagement'; asa hayai kara makes the morning the subject. Something 'comes up' as youji ga dekita or yotei ga haitta, not okita.

items.use: The vague, polite reason for saying no or leaving: chotto youji ga atte..., left unfinished so the listener hears 'so I can't'. Nobody asks what the youji is. When something comes up, the verb is dekiru: kyuu ni youji ga dekichatte (something came up).
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: English 'have' leads to motsu, but having plans or errands is aru (youji ga aru). And 'something came up' is youji ga dekita, not kita or okita.

example.ja: 明日はちょっと用事あって…
example.english: Tomorrow I've got something on, so...

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa chotto youji ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: 明日はちょっと用事があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I've got something on tomorrow, I'm afraid...

items.use: The standard reason to leave or go to bed early: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne. ga is nearly always dropped, and ashita hayai kara alone is common too. Said about someone's routine, asa hayai ne means they're up early.
items.verbSense: early; also fast, quick
partners: kaeri (getting home: kyou kaeri hayai ne)

example.romaji: ashita asa hayai kara, mou neru ne.
example.ja: 明日朝早いから、もう寝るね。
example.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'm off to bed.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa asa ga hayai node, mou nemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は朝が早いので、もう寝ますね。
examplePolite.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'll go to bed now.

items.freqNote: 朝 #453; 早い #396 (速い 'fast' is #2346). Phrase entry 朝が早い #41988.
items.notes: The opposite is asa ga osoi (a late start), and asa yowai means you're not a morning person. ashita hayaku okinakya (I have to get up early) works just as well.

items.use: Mostly as haitteru (is booked) or haitta (got booked): sono hi wa mou yotei haitteru. A sudden clash is kyuu ni yotei haitchatte.
items.verbSense: go in, enter; get put into something
items.trap: 'Something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita or kyuu ni yotei ga haitta, not okita (that sounds like an accident). Plain 'I have plans' is yotei ga aru, never yotei o motteru; haitteru adds that the day is already taken.

example.ja: 明日はもう予定入ってる
example.english: I've already got plans tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa mou yotei ga haittemasu
examplePolite.ja: 明日はもう予定が入ってます
examplePolite.english: I've already got plans tomorrow.

items.notes: Transitive partner: yotei o ireru (book something in).

items.use: The polite way to turn down an invitation for a particular day: sumimasen, sono hi wa sen'yaku ga atte..., left trailing, since a flat ...kara sounds like an excuse. Friends say it too (gomen, sen'yaku aru n da) when the plan is with someone else; yotei aru is vaguer.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)

example.romaji: gomen, sono hi wa senyaku ga atte...
example.ja: ごめん、その日は先約があって…
example.english: Sorry, I've already got plans that day...

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sono hi wa senyaku ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: すみません、その日は先約があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I already have plans that day...

items.freqNote: 先約 #13651 is rare as a word because it lives almost only in this set (74% of its uses). ある #21. Pair count 17.
items.notes: Same trailing shape as youji ga atte...: the 'so I can't' is left unsaid.

blocks.label: Trash and tidying
blocks.rationale: Keeping the place in order: binning things, trash day, the messy room and putting things back.
blocks.interference: gomi o suteru is throwing something away; gomi o dasu is putting the bags out for collection. A messy room is chirakatteru, not kitanai (dirty), and the fix is katazukeru (put away), not souji (scrub).

items.use: For getting rid of anything, at home or out: kono gomi doko ni suteru? (where does this go?). Casual speech drops o, and the thing itself often replaces gomi: kore sutete ii? (can I throw this out?).
items.verbSense: throw away, discard; also abandon
items.trap: 'Throw' points to nageru, which is throwing through the air (a ball). Throwing away is suteru; only in Hokkaido and Tohoku dialect does gomi o nageru mean this.

example.romaji: kono gomi, doko ni sutetara ii?
example.ja: このゴミ、どこに捨てたらいい？
example.english: Where should I throw this away?

examplePolite.romaji: kono gomi wa doko ni sutetara ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: このゴミはどこに捨てたらいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Where should I throw this rubbish away?

items.freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); 捨てる #436 also covers abandoning people and plans.
items.notes: Putting the bags out on collection day is gomi o dasu; the bin is gomibako.

items.use: Used for the household chore and for collection days: gomi dashite kite (go put the trash out). gomi sutete kuru is also said for the same trip; gomi o suteru alone is throwing something away.
items.verbSense: put out, take out, send out
items.trap: English 'take out' points to toru, but gomi o toru means picking off fluff or dirt. Putting trash out for collection is dasu.

example.ja: ちょっとゴミ出してくる。
example.english: I'm just going to take the trash out.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto gomi o dashite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとゴミを出してきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just take the trash out.

items.freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); ゴミ出し #17427 is the noun form.
items.notes: gomidashi is the chore's name.

items.use: Putting things back where they belong (moto ni modosu), as in the parent's nag heya katazukenasai. Casual speech drops o; cleaning is souji suru (vacuuming is soujiki o kakeru), and heya o kirei ni suru covers both.
items.verbSense: put away, tidy; also clear (the table) or get (a job) done
items.trap: 'Clean your room' points to souji suru, which is vacuuming, wiping and dusting; putting things away is katazukeru. Both are right, for different jobs.

example.ja: 今日は部屋片付けなきゃ。
example.english: I have to tidy my room today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa heya o katazukenakya ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は部屋を片付けなきゃいけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I have to tidy my room today.

items.freqNote: 片づける #2251 (片付ける #2543); 掃除 (souji) is #1393.
items.notes: The mess it fixes is heya ga chirakaru (chirakatteru); a tidied room is katazuiteru.

items.english: (a room) gets messy, is a mess
items.use: Nearly always the state chirakatteru: heya chirakatteru (my room's a mess), or the host's apology chirakatteru kedo gomen ne as a guest comes in. Casual speech drops ga; making the mess is chirakasu.
items.verbSense: get scattered, become cluttered

example.ja: ごめん、部屋散らかってるけど。
example.english: Sorry, the place is a mess.

examplePolite.romaji: heya ga chirakatte ite, sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋が散らかっていて、すみません。
examplePolite.english: Sorry the room is such a mess.

items.freqNote: 散らかる #5946; the transitive 散らかす chirakasu (make a mess) is #9673.
items.notes: heya kitanai is also said of a messy room (kitanai covers dirty and messy, and is blunter); chirakatteru is stuff lying everywhere. The fix is heya o katazukeru; a tidy room is katazuiteru or kirei.

items.use: For putting something back where it was or how it was: tsukattara moto ni modoshite ne. It also covers undoing a change (a setting, an edit); things going back to normal by themselves is moto ni modoru.
items.verbSense: return something to where or how it was
items.trap: Not moto ni modoru when you do the putting: modoru is the thing (or you) going back. Putting something back yourself is modosu: moto ni modoshite.

example.ja: 使ったら元に戻してね。
example.english: Put it back when you're done with it.

examplePolite.romaji: tsukattara moto ni modoshite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 使ったら元に戻してくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please put it back after you use it.

items.freqNote: 元 #642 counts every sense of moto (origin, former); the intransitive 戻る modoru is #166.
items.notes: Giving a borrowed thing back to its owner is kaesu (hon o kaesu), not modosu.

blocks.label: Favours, sorry, cheer up
blocks.rationale: Asking a favour, apologising for the trouble or worry you caused, and cheering someone up.
blocks.interference: onegai ga aru is asking a favour and onegai o kiku is granting one. meiwaku o kakeru and shinpai o kakeru put trouble or worry on someone else, while shinpai suru means you are the one worrying. genki dashite (cheer up) is not ganbatte (hang in there).

items.use: Opens a request and usually trails off with n da kedo: chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo... Natives often keep the ga in this one.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
items.trap: English 'ask a favour' leads to onegai o kiku, which means granting one; asking opens with onegai ga aru (tanomi ga aru is a blunter twin, mostly heard from men).

example.romaji: chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっとお願いがあるんだけど。
example.english: Can I ask you a favour?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto onegai ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお願いがあるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: I have a small favour to ask.

items.freqNote: お願い #258 mostly counts onegai (shimasu) as 'please'; aru #21.
items.notes: hanashi ga aru n da kedo = I need to talk to you; soudan ga aru n da kedo = can I ask your advice?

items.use: Mostly in apologies: meiwaku kakete gomen (sorry for the trouble), meiwaku kaketakunai (I don't want to be a burden). Bare meiwaku da means 'what a nuisance'.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, put a burden on someone
items.trap: English 'cause' leads to okosu: mondai o okosu is fine for causing an incident, but meiwaku o okosu doesn't work; trouble you put on others is kakeru (meiwaku suru means you are the one being bothered).
partners: tesuu (bother: otesuu o okake shimasu, polite/business)

example.ja: 迷惑かけてごめんね。
example.english: Sorry for all the trouble.

examplePolite.romaji: gomeiwaku o kakete sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: ご迷惑をかけてすみません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry for the trouble.

items.freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools every sense (call, put on, spend); 掛ける #2742 listed separately.
items.notes: In business you'll hear the humble gomeiwaku o okake shite sumimasen.

items.use: Said apologetically after you've had people worried: shinpai kakete gomen. Different from shinpai shinaide (don't worry), where the other person is the worrier.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, put worry on someone
items.trap: English 'worry you' leads to shinpai suru, which means you are the one worrying; worrying someone else is shinpai o kakeru (shinpai sasete gomen also works).

example.ja: 心配かけてごめんね。
example.english: Sorry I made you worry.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai o kakete sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 心配をかけてすみません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry to have worried you.

items.freqNote: 心配 #210 counts every shinpai use (shinpai da, shinpai suru); kakeru kana #244 pools all senses.

items.use: Almost always the request genki dashite (cheer up!), said to someone who is down. The intransitive genki ga deru means feel better or perk up: kore tabetara genki deta.
items.verbSense: put out, bring out
items.trap: For 'cheer up', learners say ganbatte, which means 'hang in there' and can feel like pressure to someone who's sad. genki ni natte is said mostly to someone ill (get well). For someone down right now, the set phrase is genki dashite.

example.ja: 大丈夫だよ、元気出して。
example.english: It's okay, cheer up.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo, genki o dashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ、元気を出してください。
examplePolite.english: It's okay, please cheer up.

items.freqNote: The expression 元気を出す is #13529, the request 元気出して #7639, and the intransitive 元気が出る #8964.
items.notes: Pairs with genki ga nai (feeling down), which is in the describing-people set. To a superior, genki o dashite kudasai can sound presumptuous, like ganbatte kudasai.

blocks.label: On a trip
blocks.rationale: Going away: the trip, the flight, the hotel, the gifts you bring back and the hot spring.
blocks.interference: Each place takes ni with its own verb: noru for the plane (English 'fly' is not tobu), tomaru for staying the night (not iru, and not yoru, which is dropping in), hairu for the hot spring.

items.use: The usual way to talk about trips and plans: dokka ryokou iku? Casual speech drops the ni after ryokou, and a trip you're back from is ryokou itte kita. Going abroad is kaigai ryokou ni iku.
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: Not ryokou o toru ('take a trip'): you go on a trip, ryokou ni iku, or just ryokou suru.

example.ja: 夏休み、どっか旅行行かない？
example.english: Want to go on a trip somewhere over the summer break?

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi, dokoka ryokou ni ikimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 夏休み、どこか旅行に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go on a trip somewhere over the summer break?

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. tabi (#2626) is the more emotive 'journey', heard in set words (hitoritabi, tabi ni deru); plans and chat use ryokou.
items.notes: A work trip is shutchou, not ryokou: ashita kara shutchou nan da.

items.use: Used for the flight itself: hikouki notta koto aru? (have you ever flown?), hikouki notteru aida (during the flight). To say how you get somewhere, use de: hikouki de iku. Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not hikouki o toru for 'take a plane': hikouki totta? means 'have you booked your flight?'. Being on board is ni noru, like every vehicle, and how you get there takes de: hikouki de iku. oosaka ni tobu (fly off to Osaka) is real too, but casual, with a sudden, business-trip feel.

example.ja: 飛行機乗ってる間、ずっと寝てた。
example.english: I slept the whole flight.

examplePolite.romaji: hikouki ni notteru aida, zutto netemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 飛行機に乗ってる間、ずっと寝てました。
examplePolite.english: I slept the whole flight.

items.freqNote: The tokenizer splits 飛行機, so the pair isn't counted. 飛行機に乗 has 197 literal film hits, more than バスに乗 (160).
items.notes: A flight is a bin: nanji no bin? (what time's your flight?).

items.use: Mostly asked and planned: doko tomaru? (where are you staying?), kyou wa hoteru ni tomaru. Casual speech can drop ni, and the same verb covers a sleepover: tomodachi no uchi ni tomaru.
items.verbSense: stay the night (away from home)
items.trap: Not hoteru ni nokoru, which is staying in rather than going out. hoteru ni iru says where you are or are based, not where you sleep: 'where are you staying?' is doko ni tomatteru?, and taizai suru is the formal word.

example.romaji: ekimae no hoteru ni tomaru yo.
example.ja: 駅前のホテルに泊まるよ。
example.english: I'm staying at a hotel by the station.

examplePolite.romaji: ekimae no hoteru ni tomarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅前のホテルに泊まります。
examplePolite.english: I'm staying at a hotel by the station.

items.freqNote: 泊まる is ranked apart from 止まる (#776, stop).
items.notes: Booking a room is hoteru o toru; putting someone up is tomeru: hitoban tomete kureru? (can you put me up for the night?).

items.use: Comes up on every trip: omiyage kawanakya (I need to get gifts to take back), omiyage nani ga ii? Casual speech drops o. A small gift you bring when visiting someone's home is also omiyage.
items.verbSense: buy
items.trap: English 'souvenir' is often something for yourself, but omiyage are mainly gifts for others, family and coworkers above all, often boxed local sweets and close to expected. One for yourself is jibun-you (or jokingly jibun e no omiyage), and a keepsake is kinenhin.

example.romaji: kaisha no hito ni, omiyage kawanakya.
example.ja: 会社の人に、お土産買わなきゃ。
example.english: I need to get gifts for the people at work.

examplePolite.romaji: kaisha no hito ni, omiyage o kawanai to ikenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 会社の人に、お土産を買わないといけないんです。
examplePolite.english: I need to buy gifts for the people at work.

items.freqNote: Films under-count it (6 pair hits), yet kau takes a sixth of omiyage's verbs there. Plain 土産 is #6311.
items.notes: Handing one over: kore, omiyage (here, a little something from my trip).

items.use: Heard on trips and at an inn: onsen haitta? (been in the hot spring yet?), onsen haitte kuru, mostly without ni. Going to a hot-spring town or bathhouse is onsen ni iku: onsen ikitai na.
items.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
items.trap: Not onsen o abiru: abiru is for showers. You get into a hot spring the way you get into a bath, with ni hairu (ofuro ni hairu).

example.romaji: gohan no mae ni, onsen haitte kuru.
example.ja: ご飯の前に、温泉入ってくる。
example.english: I'm going to soak in the hot spring before dinner.

examplePolite.romaji: gohan no mae ni, onsen ni haitte kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ご飯の前に、温泉に入ってきます。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to have a dip in the hot spring before dinner.

items.freqNote: Only 3 film hits (onsen ni iku has 6 of the noun's 16), but hairu is the verb for the bathing itself. 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.
items.notes: A long soak is tsukaru: yukkuri onsen ni tsukaritai (I want a good long soak).

blocks.label: Spending and saving
blocks.rationale: Two verb pairs for money going out and piling up: spend money, pay by card, save up, collect points.
blocks.interference: Spending money is tsukau (use), never sugosu, which is only for time; the same tsukau asks about cards (kaado tsukaemasu ka?). tameru is saving money and collecting points alike, not hozon suru or setsuyaku.

items.use: Mostly about spending too much, or on what: kongetsu okane tsukaisugita, nani ni sonna ni tsukatta no?. Once an amount is said, okane drops: ichiman en tsukatchatta.
items.verbSense: use; spend (money, effort)
items.trap: Dictionaries give tsuiyasu for 'spend', which is formal, and sugosu, which is only for time. Everyday spending is tsukau, 'use': ryokou de ichiman en tsukatta.

example.ja: 今月、お金使いすぎちゃった。
example.english: I've spent too much this month.

examplePolite.romaji: kongetsu wa okane o tsukaisugichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今月はお金を使いすぎちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I've spent too much this month.

items.freqNote: お金 #422; 使う #171 covers every sense of 'use'.
items.notes: Wasting money is mudazukai: mudazukai shichatta.

items.use: Mostly as the question at a till or before going in: kaado tsukaemasu ka? (or kaado daijoubu desu ka?), answered hai, daijoubu desu or hai, otsukai itadakemasu, or genkin nomi desu (cash only). The particle often drops, or becomes ga with the potential: kaado ga tsukaeru.
items.verbSense: use
items.trap: 'Do you take cards?' is kaado tsukaemasu ka? (can I use a card?), not kaado torimasu ka?.

example.ja: ここ、カード使える？
example.english: Do they take cards here?

examplePolite.romaji: koko, kaado tsukaemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ここ、カード使えますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you take cards here?

items.freqNote: カード #2450 counts every card (ID cards, game cards). 使う #171. Pair count 79 (o 48, ga 14); films undercount till talk.
items.notes: When paying, you say kaado de onegai shimasu. For a credit card, staff may ask oshiharai kaisuu wa?; the answer is ikkatsu de or ikkai de (in one payment).

items.use: For saving toward something, usually as tameteru (I'm saving): ryokou no okane tameteru. okane ga tamatta means you've finally saved enough.
items.verbSense: let something build up; store up
items.trap: English 'save' leads to hozon suru (save a file), tasukeru (rescue) or setsuyaku (cut back). Saving up is tameru, 'pile up'. chokin suru also works.

example.romaji: ima ryokou no okane tameteru n da
example.ja: 今旅行のお金貯めてるんだ
example.english: I'm saving up for a trip.

examplePolite.romaji: ima ryokou no okane o tameteru n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今旅行のお金を貯めてるんです
examplePolite.english: I'm saving up for a trip.

items.freqNote: 貯める #10930 is the money spelling; the kana ためる #3410 covers every sense.
items.notes: Intransitive partner: okane ga tamaru (the money builds up). Points work the same way: pointo o tameru. The same sound also means letting things pile up through neglect: shigoto o tameru, sutoresu ga tamaru (溜める).

items.use: Said about the point cards and apps at konbini, drugstores and supermarkets: itsumo koko de pointo tameteru. At the till staff ask pointo kaado omochi desu ka? (do you have a points card?).
items.verbSense: let something build up; store up

example.romaji: itsumo koko de pointo tameteru n da.
example.ja: いつもここでポイント貯めてるんだ。
example.english: I always collect points here.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo koko de pointo o tameteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: いつもここでポイントを貯めてるんです。
examplePolite.english: I always collect points here.

items.freqNote: ポイント #2464 counts every 'point' (score, main point). 貯める #10930 is the saving spelling; the kana ためる #3410 covers every sense. No count in the subtitles; commonness is judged from how often point cards come up at Japanese tills.
items.notes: Same verb as okane o tameru; kasegu is for racking points up fast (poikatsu de pointo kasegu). pointo ga tsuku = points get added; to spend them, staff ask pointo otsukai ni narimasu ka? (hai, tsukaimasu).

blocks.label: Numbers and messages
blocks.rationale: Keeping in touch in writing: swapping numbers, then a message's round trip of send, receive and reply.
blocks.interference: meeru o okuru (you send, o) vs meeru ga kuru (it comes to you, ga) is the same out/in split as the phone calls. 'Give me your number' is bangou oshiete, not kudasai, and kaesu 'send back' sounds like kaeru 'go home'.

items.use: Said when swapping numbers, mostly as the request bangou oshiete (give me your number), softened to bangou oshiete kurenai? Here bangou means denwa bangou (phone number). Casual speech drops o, and asking someone for theirs is bangou o kiku.
items.verbSense: teach; tell, let someone know
items.trap: English 'give' pulls toward ageru or kudasai, but the everyday set is oshieru ('tell'): 'give me your number' is bangou oshiete and 'I gave him my number' is bangou oshieta. bangou ageru is heard, bangou choudai works among close friends, and bangou o kudasai sounds stiff.

example.ja: よかったら、番号教えてくれない？
example.english: Could I get your number?

examplePolite.romaji: yokattara, bangou o oshiete kuremasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: よかったら、番号を教えてくれませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you mind giving me your number?

items.freqNote: 電話番号 (denwa bangou) is #4138 and 連絡先 (renrakusaki, contact details) #2550.
items.notes: Among friends, contacts now go over LINE: rain koukan shiyou (let's swap LINE).

items.use: Said when you send or promise an email, with the person marked by ni: senpai ni meeru okutta (I emailed my senpai), ato de meeru okuru ne (I'll email you later). Sending something by email is meeru de okuru (shiryou meeru de okuru ne). Between friends, messages usually go by LINE: rain suru ne, rain okutta yo. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: send; see someone off

example.ja: 後でメール送るね。
example.english: I'll email you later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de meeru o okurimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後でメールを送りますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll email you later.

items.freqNote: verbRank 送る also counts seeing someone off and sending parcels; 送信 (soushin, the 'send' button) is #6591.
items.notes: The same okuru is seeing someone off or giving them a lift (eki made okuru); meeru suru is the shorter casual version.

items.use: Said when an email arrives, mostly as meeru kita (I got an email), with the sender marked by kara. The negative henji ga konai means there's no reply yet.
items.verbSense: come, arrive
items.trap: Not uketoru: English makes you the subject of 'got', but Japanese makes the email the subject: meeru (ga) kita ('an email came'). meeru moratta is also fine, but kita is what you hear most; uketoru sounds stiff and is for parcels and documents.

example.ja: なんか変なメール来た。
example.english: I got a weird email.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka hen na meeru ga kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: なんか変なメールが来ました。
examplePolite.english: I got a weird email.

items.notes: meeru now means email; a text from a friend is a rain (LINE): rain kita. henji and renraku work the same way: henji kita. Sending is meeru o okuru: okutta yo (I sent it).

items.use: Said about answering emails or texts, often about being slow: kaesu no wasureteta (I forgot to reply). For chat messages the noun is rain (LINE): rain kaeshite. With henji the usual verb is suru: henji shite.
items.verbSense: give back, return something
items.trap: Not meeru ni kotaeru: replying to an email or text is kaesu ('send back'); kotaeru answers questions. henshin suru and henji suru are also fine.

example.ja: ごめん、メール返すの忘れてた。
example.english: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your email.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, meeru o kaesu no wasuretemashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、メールを返すの忘れてました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your email.

items.freqNote: nounRank is メール and verbRank is 返す, which also counts returning things; 返事 (henji) is #1075 and 返信 (henshin) #5122.
items.notes: To call someone back, the verb is orikaesu: ato de orikaeshimasu.

blocks.label: How it tastes
blocks.rationale: The everyday comments on flavour: what it tastes like, and seasoning that is too light or too strong.
blocks.interference: A taste you notice uses suru (hen na aji suru), not aru. Seasoning is usui (light) or koi (strong), never yowai or tsuyoi, which are kept for osake.

items.use: Used to say what something tastes like: hen na aji suru (tastes weird), ichigo no aji ga suru (tastes of strawberry). Casual speech drops ga, and aji shinai means it tastes of nothing.
items.verbSense: do; with a taste, smell or sound, be sensed or give off
items.trap: English 'it has a weird taste' pulls toward hen na aji ga aru, which sounds off; a taste you notice 'does': hen na aji ga suru. hen na aji da is also fine. Tasting something on purpose is ajimi suru or aji o miru, not aji ga suru.

example.ja: なんか変な味する。
example.english: This tastes kind of weird.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka hen na aji ga shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: なんか変な味がしますね。
examplePolite.english: This tastes a bit strange.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only; suru's #15 covers every use of suru. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: nioi ga suru and oto ga suru use the same frame.

items.use: The everyday verdict on food that needs more salt or soy sauce: chotto aji usui ne. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: thin, faint, weak (paper, colour, taste)
items.trap: Not aji ga yowai: food short on salt is usui (thin), the same word as weak coffee. aji ga nai is fine for food with no taste at all.

example.ja: これ、ちょっと味薄いね。
example.english: This is a bit bland.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, chotto aji ga usui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、ちょっと味が薄いですね。
examplePolite.english: This is a bit bland.

items.freqNote: 薄い #2547 also counts thin (paper, walls) and pale (colour).
items.notes: aji ga koi is the opposite: strongly seasoned, often too salty. usuaji (light seasoning) is often praise (usuaji de oishii); aji ga usui on its own is usually a complaint.

items.use: Said about food with a lot of salt, soy sauce or sauce, often as a mild complaint (chotto aji koi ne) and sometimes as praise for food that goes with rice. Casual speech drops ga, and before a noun it is koi aji.
items.verbSense: dense, strong in concentration (taste, colour, coffee)
items.trap: English 'strong flavour' leads to aji ga tsuyoi, which is said of a pungent, distinctive taste. Heavy seasoning is koi (dense), the same word as strong coffee and dark colour. 'Too salty' on its own is shoppai.

example.romaji: aji koi kara, gohan susumu ne.
example.ja: 味濃いから、ご飯進むね。
example.english: It's richly seasoned, so it goes great with rice.

examplePolite.romaji: aji ga koi node, gohan ga susumimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 味が濃いので、ご飯が進みますね。
examplePolite.english: It's richly seasoned, so it goes great with rice.

items.freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い (#3669); kana こい also matches 来い and 恋. Only 3 subtitle hits, because food talk is daily life the films miss.
items.notes: aji ga usui is the opposite; aji koisugiru (way too strong) is a clear complaint.

blocks.label: Picking someone up
blocks.rationale: Collecting someone and driving them: going to get them, taking their bags, giving them a lift, parking, and stopping at the konbini on the way.
blocks.interference: For mukae ni iku Japanese says iku where English says 'I'll come'. noseru (give a lift) is the transitive of noru. tomeru (park) gets mixed up with yoru (drop in) and with tomaru (a car pulling up, or staying the night).

items.use: Paired with kuru for the other direction: mukae ni iku ne (I'll come get you) and mukae ni kite (come get me). Japanese says iku where English says 'I'll come'.
items.verbSense: go (mukae is the noun of mukaeru, meet and welcome)
items.trap: Not mukae ni kuru for 'I'll come get you': you are the one going, so it is mukae ni iku (only 'come get me' is mukae ni kite). 'Pick up' is not toru here either. Among friends with a car, hirou also works for grabbing someone on the way (tochuu de hirotteku yo), but not for meeting a guest or collecting a child.

example.romaji: eki made mukae ni iku ne.
example.ja: 駅まで迎えに行くね。
example.english: I'll come pick you up at the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made mukae ni ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで迎えに行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll come and pick you up at the station.

items.freqNote: Bare 迎え is #8575; the polite and childcare form お迎え is #2913 and the verb 迎える #1366.
items.notes: Collecting a child from nursery is omukae: hoikuen ni omukae ni iku.

items.use: Mostly an offer: nimotsu motsu yo, or motou ka? (shall I take that?). Casual speech drops o, and nimotsu motteru means you have bags with you.
items.verbSense: hold, carry (in your hands); have with you
items.trap: English 'carry' points to hakobu, which is moving things to a place (a porter, a removal van). Taking a bag off someone's hands, or carrying your own, is motsu.

example.ja: 重いでしょ、荷物持つよ。
example.english: That must be heavy, let me take your bag.

examplePolite.romaji: omoi desu yo ne, nimotsu mochimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 重いですよね、荷物持ちますよ。
examplePolite.english: That looks heavy, let me carry your bag.

items.freqNote: motsu's rank covers holding, owning and lasting.
items.notes: nimotsu is also a parcel: nimotsu todoita (my package came).

items.use: Mostly a request or an offer: nosete kureru? (can you give me a lift?), eki made nosete tte (give me a lift to the station), nosete ku yo (I'll give you a lift), nosete moratta (I got a lift). Once the car is clear the noun often drops.
items.verbSense: put on board; give someone a ride (the transitive of noru)
items.trap: Not raido o ageru or kuruma o ageru (that gives the car away): giving a lift is noseru (put on board), the transitive of noru, with kureru or iku only as helpers after it (nosete kureru?, nosete ku yo). norasete means 'let me ride it', as with a friend's new bike, not 'give me a lift'.

example.ja: 帰り、車乗せてくれる？
example.english: Can you give me a lift back?

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri, kuruma ni nosete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 帰り、車に乗せてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you give me a lift back?

items.freqNote: 乗せる is ranked apart from 載せる (#3380, put on top or publish). okuru (#324) also covers sending mail and messages.
items.notes: Driving someone all the way somewhere is often okuru: ie made okuru yo (I'll take you home).

items.use: The everyday word for parking, with ni for the spot: doko ni tomeru? (where shall we park?), koko tomete ii? (can I park here?). The same verb stops any car, so in a taxi you say koko de tomete kudasai.
items.verbSense: stop (something moving); park (a car, a bike)
items.trap: Not paaku suru (paakingu is a car park, as in koin paakingu) and not yameru (quit): parking is tomeru, 'stop' the car. chuusha suru is correct but formal, the word on signs (chuusha kinshi) and in polite asks; in everyday talk people still say chuushajou (car park) and chuusha ga nigate (I'm bad at parking).

example.ja: 車、どこに止めればいい？
example.english: Where should I park the car?

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma wa doko ni tomereba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車はどこに止めればいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Where should I park the car?

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. 止める covers stopping anything, so its rank overstates the parking sense; the parking spelling 停める is #22793 and chuushajou (car park) #4816.
items.notes: A car sitting there is the intransitive tomatteru: mise no mae ni kuruma tomatteru.

items.use: Almost always followed by a direction verb: konbini yotteku (I'll stop at the konbini on the way) or yotte kaeru (stop off on the way home). Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: drop in on the way; come close to
items.trap: Not konbini ni tomaru: that tomaru is a car pulling up there (konbini de tomatte = pull over at the konbini; parking is kuruma o tomeru), and the overnight tomaru never fits a shop. Dropping in on the way is yoru: konbini yotteku.

example.ja: ちょっとコンビニ寄ってくね。
example.english: I'm just going to stop by the konbini.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto konbini ni yotte ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとコンビニに寄っていきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to stop by the convenience store.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 寄る also covers 'come closer'.
items.notes: Sounds the same as yoru (night) and -ni yoru (it depends on); yotteku? also invites someone to drop in.

blocks.label: Breaks and time off
blocks.rationale: Stepping away from work, commonest first: missing a day, booking leave, a short break, quitting for good.
blocks.interference: yasumu (stay off) and yameru (quit) sound alike; yasumi o toru is days off, while a few minutes' rest is kyuukei o toru.

items.english: take time off work, miss work
items.use: Said when you stay away from work, sick or not, for a day or longer: kyou shigoto yasumu. It's usually heard in the past (yasunda), and gakkou o yasumu works the same way.
items.verbSense: rest, take a break; stay away from (work, school)
items.trap: yasumu sounds like 'rest', and 'off work' or 'from work' suggests kara, giving shigoto kara yasumu. Work is the object: shigoto o yasumu, like gakkou o yasumu (miss school). yasumi o toru (take time off) is also fine.

example.ja: 今日風邪で仕事休んだ。
example.english: I took today off work with a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze de shigoto o yasumimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風邪で仕事を休みました。
examplePolite.english: I took today off work with a cold.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 休む #584. Same frame with gakkou (#661) and kaisha (#474): kyou gakkou yasunda.
items.notes: Planned leave is yasumi o toru. 'I'm off tomorrow' is just ashita yasumi.

items.use: Said about days off arranged with work, usually once they're booked: raishuu yasumi totta. The o is often dropped, and paid leave works the same way: yuukyuu totta. The everyday complaint is yasumi torenai (I can't get time off).
items.verbSense: take; get (here: take time away from work, booked ahead or on the spot)
items.trap: 'Take a break' for a few minutes isn't yasumi o toru, which on its own means time off, or rest in general (chanto yasumi totte ne, make sure you get some rest). For a few minutes, say chotto yasumou, kyuukei shiyou or kyuukei torou.

example.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi totta n da.
example.ja: 来週三日休み取ったんだ。
example.english: I've booked three days off next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu mikka yasumi o totta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週三日休みを取ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I've booked three days off next week.

items.freqNote: 休み #1322, 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is counted separately at #649). 有給 yuukyuu #13555, 休暇 kyuuka #5687. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 休み + 取れる (can get time off) is the strongest pairing (log_dice 9.20).
items.notes: A sick day is yasumu instead: kyou kaze de yasumu.

items.use: Said about breaks at work or while studying, especially the ones you're owed: chanto kyuukei totte ne, juppun kyuukei torou. Casual speech drops o, and for calling a break on the spot kyuukei shiyou or chotto yasumou is more common.
items.verbSense: take; set aside (time for rest)
items.trap: 'Take a break' tempts yasumi o toru, which means time off or proper rest (chanto yasumi totte ne). A few minutes' break is kyuukei: kyuukei torou.

example.ja: ちゃんと休憩取ってね。
example.english: Make sure you take your breaks.

examplePolite.romaji: chanto kyuukei o totte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと休憩を取ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Make sure you take your breaks.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 休憩を取る has its own entry in the drama list at #60724 (休憩 #1948, 取る #228). In the subtitles 休憩 is mostly a suru verb: 休憩する 164 hits against 18 with 取る.
items.notes: On a break right now: ima kyuukei-chuu. Going on your break at work is kyuukei ni hairu: kyuukei hairimasu.

items.use: Said about leaving a job for good, mostly as yameta (I quit) or as a complaint, yametai (I want to quit). Casual speech drops o, and shigoto o yameru means the same.
items.verbSense: quit, leave (a job, school or club); same sound as yameru 'stop'
items.trap: 'Leave the company' suggests kaisha o deru, but that normally means walking out of the office building (going home, heading out to lunch). Leaving the job is kaisha o yameru. Likewise daigaku o deru means graduating; dropping out is yameru.

example.ja: 去年会社辞めたんだ。
example.english: I quit my job last year.

examplePolite.romaji: kyonen kaisha o yameta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 去年会社を辞めたんです。
examplePolite.english: I quit my job last year.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 会社を辞める has its own entry in the drama list at #6363, and 仕事を辞める at #8598. 辞める #604 is the 'resign' spelling; kana やめる #117 mixes both senses.
items.notes: Getting fired is kubi ni naru: kubi ni natta.

blocks.label: Out and about
blocks.rationale: Remarks about a shop, a place or a day out: crowded, popular, a nice vibe, well reviewed, heavy bags.
blocks.interference: ninki ga aru means lots of people like it, hyouban ga ii means people speak well of it (reviews, word of mouth). Crowded is hito ga ooi or konderu, never isogashii. ii fun'iki puts ii first, though fun'iki ga ii is just as natural.

items.use: The everyday comment on a crowded place: kyou, hito ooi ne, usually with ga dropped. Said of stations, festivals, shops and tourist spots; for a place packed right now, konderu is just as common. The opposite is hito ga sukunai, or suiteru (not crowded).
items.verbSense: ooi: many, a lot (used as a predicate)
items.trap: Not ooi hito ga iru: ooi rarely goes before a noun, so 'there are lots of people' is hito ga ooi (or hito ga ippai), and before a noun it's takusan no hito.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa hito ooi kara, heijitsu ni ikou.
example.ja: 週末は人多いから、平日に行こう。
example.english: Weekends are crowded, so let's go on a weekday.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa hito ga ooi node, heijitsu ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 週末は人が多いので、平日に行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Weekends are crowded, so let's go on a weekday.

items.freqNote: 人 (ひと) #60; 多い #360; 少ない #1076. No phrase entry. 混む #5984; 人混み hitogomi #18818.
items.notes: hitogomi (a crowd) is the noun: hitogomi nigate (I can't stand crowds).

items.use: For people, shops, shows and products: ano mise, ninki aru yo ne. Casual speech drops ga, and also says ninki da yo or sugoi ninki da yo. 'Popular with X' is X ni ninki ga aru, very popular is ninki ga takai, and unpopular is ninki nai. Before a noun: ninki no aru mise, or just ninki no mise (a popular shop).
items.verbSense: aru: there is; have (things, qualities)
items.trap: Not popyuraa: in Japanese it's for things that are widely known or standard (popyuraa na kyoku), never for a person. A person or shop that people like ninki ga aru.

example.romaji: ano sensei, seito ni ninki aru yo.
example.ja: あの先生、生徒に人気あるよ。
example.english: That teacher's popular with the students.

examplePolite.romaji: ano sensei wa seito ni ninki ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの先生は生徒に人気がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: That teacher is popular with the students.

items.freqNote: 人気 #1303; ある #21. Ninkimono (#5320, 'a popular person') is a related noun, noted only; モテる #2224; ポピュラー #37551.
items.notes: Popular with the opposite sex is the single verb moteru. Hyouban ga ii is different: people speak well of it (reviews, word of mouth), while ninki ga aru means lots of people like it or go there.

items.use: Said about cafes, restaurants, shops and towns: kono mise, ii fun'iki da ne, or with the noun first and ga dropped, fun'iki ii ne. About a person, fun'iki is their air: ano hito, fun'iki ii yo ne (he/she has a nice vibe), or yasashii fun'iki no hito (someone with a gentle air). About two people, ii fun'iki means they seem into each other.
items.verbSense: ii: good, nice
items.trap: 'Atmosphere' isn't kuuki here: ii kuuki or kuuki ga ii means fresh air, and kuuki as a mood is mostly kuuki o yomu or kuuki ga omoi (an awkward mood). A place's nice feel is ii fun'iki.

example.romaji: kono kafe, ii fun'iki da ne.
example.ja: このカフェ、いい雰囲気だね。
example.english: This café has a nice vibe.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kafe wa ii fun'iki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このカフェはいい雰囲気ですね。
examplePolite.english: This café has a lovely atmosphere.

items.freqNote: 雰囲気 #1448; いい #24. Neither いい雰囲気 nor 雰囲気いい has its own entry. The film count (32) is mostly ii fun'iki before the noun (ADJ:27).
items.notes: fun'iki kawatta ne (you look different) is the usual remark on a new hairstyle; many natives say fuinki.

items.use: Said when recommending a shop, restaurant, doctor or teacher: ano mise, hyouban ii yo, with ga dropped. Before a noun ga becomes no (hyouban no ii mise), and the opposite is hyouban ga warui.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not ii hyouban o motte iru ('has a good reputation'): the reputation is the subject, hyouban ga ii (hyouban no ii mise). yuumei only says famous, not that people speak well of it.
partners: uke (uke ga ii: go down well)

example.ja: あの歯医者さん、評判いいよ。
example.english: That dentist's got a good reputation.

examplePolite.romaji: ano haisha-san wa hyouban ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの歯医者さんは評判がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That dentist has a good reputation.

items.freqNote: 評判 #1932; いい #24. No phrase entry; 口コミ kuchikomi #16520. Film count 23, with hyouban ga warui at 14.
items.notes: For online reviews, kuchikomi is the word: kuchikomi mo ii yo.

items.use: Said while carrying shopping or luggage, often before an offer to help: nimotsu omoi desho, motou ka? Casual speech drops ga, and before a noun it's omoi nimotsu (heavy bags).
items.verbSense: omoi: heavy; also serious, weighing on you

example.ja: 荷物重いでしょ？持とうか？
example.english: Your bags must be heavy. Want me to carry them?

examplePolite.romaji: onimotsu, omoi desu yo ne. mochimashou ka?
examplePolite.ja: お荷物、重いですよね。持ちましょうか？
examplePolite.english: Your bags must be heavy. Shall I carry them for you?

items.freqNote: 荷物 #1140; 重い #1004 (the kana おもい is mostly 思い #616); 重たい omotai #5482; 軽い #1175. The film count (17) is mostly omoi nimotsu before the noun (ADJ:12), some of it figurative ('a heavy burden'); the everyday remark is judged.
items.notes: omotai is a spoken variant that stresses how heavy it feels: kono kaban, omotai. Shop staff and juniors offer with the humble omochi shimashou ka.

blocks.label: Manners and thanks
blocks.rationale: Being polite and grateful: saying thanks, speaking politely, not making a fuss, and the guest's thanks for care and meals.
blocks.interference: keigo o tsukau (speak politely) and ki o tsukau (fuss over others) share tsukau, and ki o tsukau is not ki o tsukeru (be careful). In osewa ni naru and gochisou ni naru, ni naru puts you on the receiving end; the giver says mendou o miru or ogoru.

items.use: For talking about thanking rather than doing it (arigatou does that): orei iwanakya (I have to thank them), chanto orei itta? (did you thank them properly?), orei iitakute (I wanted to say thanks).
items.verbSense: say
items.trap: English 'thank' leads to kansha suru, which is being grateful (kansha shiteru = I'm grateful), not saying it: 'I have to thank them' is orei iwanakya. orei o suru means giving something back, like a gift or a meal.
partners: oiwai (congratulations: oiwai iitakute = I wanted to congratulate them)

example.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼言わなきゃ。
example.english: I need to thank them properly later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de chanto orei o iwanakya ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 後でちゃんとお礼を言わなきゃいけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should thank them properly later.

items.freqNote: お礼 #968; bare 礼 #3119, so the o- form is the spoken headword. 言う #28.
items.notes: orei ni = as thanks: orei ni gohan ogoru yo (dinner's on me, as thanks).

items.use: Mostly heard as the offer to drop it: keigo tsukawanakute ii yo (no need to be formal with me), often followed by tameguchi de ii yo (talk to me casually). Also for describing relationships: senpai ni wa keigo tsukau (I speak politely to my seniors).
items.verbSense: use
items.trap: English 'speak keigo' leads to keigo o hanasu, on the model of nihongo o hanasu. It is heard (keigo ga hanasenai), but the everyday verb is tsukau (keigo tsukau), or keigo de hanasu.
partners: kotoba (words: warui kotoba o tsukau = use bad language)
eigo (English: eigo o tsukau shigoto = a job using English)

example.ja: 敬語使わなくていいよ。
example.english: No need to be formal with me.

examplePolite.romaji: keigo wa tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 敬語は使わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to speak formally with me.

items.freqNote: 敬語 #6169 (警護 'guard' is listed separately, #8020); 使う #171. タメ口 (tameguchi) #10671. 敬語 appears only 18 times in the subtitles (敬語(を)使 once), so commonness is judged.
items.notes: Sounds like ki tsukawanakute ii yo (don't go to any trouble), the other host line; drill them together.

items.use: Hosts and guests say ki o tsukawanakute ii yo or ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble). About a person, ano hito to iru to ki tsukau means you have to tiptoe around them.
items.verbSense: use, spend; here, spend your attention on others
items.trap: Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): 'don't go to any trouble' is ki o tsukawanaide, and the mix-up gives ki o tsukenaide, 'don't be careful'.
partners: shinkei (nerves: shinkei tsukau = it takes a lot of care, it's nerve-racking)

example.ja: そんな気遣わなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't have to fuss over me like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ki o tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなに気を遣わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't go to any trouble.

items.freqNote: 気 #315. verbRank is 使う #171, which pools all tsukau senses (subtitles often write 気を使う); the 遣う spelling alone is #6992.
items.notes: Also written 気を使う; the noun is kizukai (thoughtfulness).

items.use: Mostly polite and set: kyou kara osewa ni narimasu when you start a stay or a job, osewa ni narimashita (thank you for everything) when you leave a host, job or school. In business you'll hear the humble osewa ni natte orimasu (recognise it, no need to say it). Casual osewa ni natta is used when describing someone who helped you.
items.verbSense: become; here, come to be in someone's care
items.trap: English 'thanks for looking after me' leads to sewa shite kurete arigatou, which fits literal care (nursing you when sick, minding your pet). Friends say iroiro arigatou; to hosts, teachers and colleagues the set thanks is osewa ni narimashita.
partners: gochisou (a treat: be treated to a meal)
yakkai (being a burden: rely on someone)

example.romaji: ano senpai ni wa honto ni osewa ni natta.
example.ja: あの先輩にはほんとにお世話になった。
example.english: That senior really looked out for me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai ni wa hontou ni osewa ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩には本当にお世話になりました。
examplePolite.english: That senior really looked after me.

items.freqNote: お世話 #3633 (bare 世話 #2302); naru: kana なる #29.
items.notes: gochisou ni naru (be treated to a meal) is built the same way: with ni naru, you are the one receiving. The one doing the looking after says mendou o miru (or sewa o suru).

items.use: Said by the one being treated. When someone offers to pay (kyou wa ogoru yo), you accept with jaa, gochisou ni narimasu, and afterwards you thank them with gochisou ni narimashita, to a boss, senpai or host. Among friends gochisousama! does both jobs, and telling someone about it is gochisou ni natta or, more often, ogotte moratta (they paid for me).
items.verbSense: become; here, come to be the one treated
items.trap: English 'I got treated' leads to the passive gochisou sareta, which is heard but less usual; people say gochisou ni natta (like osewa ni naru), ogotte moratta or ogorareta. The payer's verbs are ogoru and gochisou suru.
partners: yakkai (imposing: tomodachi no ie ni yakkai ni naru = stay at a friend's place)

example.romaji: kinou senpai ni gochisou ni natta.
example.ja: 昨日先輩にごちそうになった。
example.english: My senpai treated me to a meal yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa gochisou ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はごちそうになりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for dinner yesterday.

items.freqNote: ごちそう #2702 (kana; ご馳走 #15229); ごちそうさま #2052 is its own entry. naru: kana なる #29. Phrase entry ごちそうになる #6670 (ご馳走になる #43407).
items.notes: gochisou on its own is a feast or treat: sugoi gochisou (what a spread).

blocks.label: Kitchen
blocks.rationale: Round a meal at home: washing up, boiling the kettle, wiping the table.
blocks.interference: Each job has its own verb where English says 'wash' or 'boil': arau is with water, fuku is with a cloth, and the water you boil is already oyu (hot water) and takes wakasu, not niru, which is for cooking food.

items.use: The after-meal chore, often an offer: osara arau ne (I'll do the dishes). Casual speech drops o; the chore nouns sara-arai and araimono (washing-up) are just as common: araimono shitoku ne.
items.verbSense: wash with water (hands, face, dishes, a car)
items.trap: 'Do the dishes' has no do-verb with osara itself: say osara (o) arau, or put suru on a chore noun: sara-arai (o) suru or araimono (o) suru.

example.romaji: osara wa watashi ga arau ne.
example.ja: お皿は私が洗うね。
example.english: I'll do the dishes.

examplePolite.romaji: osara wa watashi ga araimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お皿は私が洗いますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wash the dishes.

items.freqNote: お皿 #5119 (plain 皿 #5569). In films the chore nouns win: 皿洗い sara-arai 40 hits and 洗い物 araimono (#10157) 23, against 15 for (o)sara o arau.
items.notes: Clearing the table first is osara o sageru or katazukeru; shokki o arau (wash the tableware) is the same chore, and a dishwasher is shokusenki.

items.use: For putting the kettle on, for tea, coffee or instant noodles: oyu wakasu kedo, nanka nomu? Casual speech drops o; when it's ready, oyu waita (the water's boiled).
items.verbSense: bring to the boil, heat (water, a bath)
items.trap: 'Boil' points to niru or yuderu, which are for cooking food (yuderu for eggs and pasta). Water is heated with wakasu, and it's usually called oyu (hot water) already; mizu o wakasu is also fine.

example.ja: お湯沸かすけど、なんか飲む？
example.english: I'm putting the kettle on, want anything?

examplePolite.romaji: oyu o wakashimasu kedo, nanika nomimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お湯を沸かしますけど、何か飲みますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm boiling some water. Would you like something to drink?

items.freqNote: 沸く waku #6780 is the intransitive (oyu ga waku = the water boils).
items.notes: The kettle is a yakan or a denki ketoru (electric kettle); the same verb heats the bath (ofuro o wakasu).

items.use: A small chore before and after meals, usually a request: teeburu fuite (give the table a wipe). Casual speech drops o; the cloth is a daifukin (table-wiping cloth) or a damp towel.
items.verbSense: wipe (with a cloth or towel)

example.ja: ちょっとテーブル拭いてくれる？
example.english: Can you give the table a wipe?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto teeburu o fuite moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとテーブルを拭いてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you wipe the table, please?

items.freqNote: 拭く #2732; kana ふく is shared with 服 (clothes) and 吹く (blow).
items.notes: souji suru is for a room or the whole house; a table just gets a wipe.

blocks.label: Hooked, tickets, winning
blocks.rationale: What comes up once a hobby takes hold: being into something right now, managing to get tickets for a concert or game, and a match won or lost.
blocks.interference: geemu ni hamaru and shiai ni katsu both take ni where English uses 'into' or a direct object, never o. chiketto o toru keeps o, and its toru means securing them (toreta! = I got them), not buying (katta) or being given them (moratta).

items.english: be hooked on games; be really into games
items.use: Use it for what you are into right now. It is almost always hamatteru (am hooked), as in saikin X ni hamatteru; hamatta means got hooked. It works with any hobby.
items.verbSense: fit snugly into, get stuck in; hence get hooked on
items.trap: English has no verb for being into something, so learners fall back on suki desu. suki is fine but only says you like it in general; for a current craze natives say X ni hamatteru, with ni, never o.

example.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってる
example.english: I'm hooked on this game lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin kono geemu ni hamattemasu
examplePolite.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってます
examplePolite.english: I've been hooked on this game lately.

items.freqNote: はまる #3789 and ハマる #4047 are one word in two spellings. The subtitles count them separately, so real use is higher than either rank.
items.notes: Colloquial but mainstream (dictionaries mark this sense as slang, and the katakana shows it): fine in casual and friendly polite talk; in a formal setting say X ni kyoumi ga arimasu. Milder: X ni kyoumi ga aru (interested in). Stronger: X ni muchuu ni natteru (completely absorbed in). hamatta also means got stuck: juutai ni hamatta (got stuck in traffic).

items.use: Use it about any match or game you played or watched. It is mostly past tense (katta, or kateta for managed to win). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic and katta stands alone (kinou no shiai, katta yo). Keep ni when the match follows straight on: shiai ni katta.
items.verbSense: win; beat (both the contest and the opponent take ni)
items.trap: Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' takes an object, but Japanese wins at it with ni. shiai de katsu (win in the match) is also fine. The same ni marks who you beat: Kankoku ni katta = we beat Korea (not Kankoku o).

example.ja: 昨日の試合、勝ったよ
example.english: We won yesterday's match.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai ni kachimashita yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に勝ちましたよ
examplePolite.english: We won yesterday's match.

items.freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni katsu.
items.notes: English 'win' is wider: win a prize = shou o morau / toru; win the lottery = takarakuji ga ataru.

items.use: It is mostly past tense: maketa, or makechatta (lost, sadly; makechaimashita among colleagues). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic (kinou no shiai, makechatta), and the team goes unsaid. Otherwise keep ni: shiai ni maketa.
items.verbSense: lose a contest; be beaten
items.trap: Not shiai o nakusu: nakusu is losing an object. A contest is makeru with ni, never o; shiai de makeru is also fine. The same ni marks who beat you: Kankoku ni maketa = we lost to Korea.

example.ja: 昨日の試合、負けちゃった
example.english: Ugh, we lost yesterday's match.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai ni makemashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に負けました
examplePolite.english: We lost yesterday's match.

items.freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni makeru.

items.use: Said about securing tickets for concerts, games, flights or the shinkansen, often ones that sell out. You hear the can-form toreru most, which takes ga (usually dropped in speech): chiketto toreta! (got them!), torenakatta (couldn't get any).
items.verbSense: take; also get hold of, secure (seats, bookings, rooms)
items.trap: Not chiketto o morau, which means someone gave them to you: tickets you secure yourself are toru (kau, buy, is also fine), and 'I got them!' is toreta! (casually also getto shita!).

example.ja: ライブのチケット取れた！
example.english: I got tickets for the concert!

examplePolite.romaji: raibu no chiketto ga toremashita!
examplePolite.ja: ライブのチケットが取れました！
examplePolite.english: I got tickets for the concert!

items.freqNote: 取れる (toreru, the toreta form) is ranked on its own at #631. Films say chiketto o kau (48) far more than toru (9): kau is the plain everyday pairing, and toru lives in Japanese booking talk about hard-to-get tickets, which subtitles under-count. 切符 (kippu) #11210 is far rarer than chiketto.
items.notes: kippu is a train ticket (kippu o kau); for the shinkansen you hear both. chiketto covers concerts, games, flights and anything booked online.

blocks.label: Finding the way
blocks.rationale: Directions and losing your way: turning left at the corner, getting lost, going the wrong way, getting separated.
blocks.interference: The corner takes o and the side takes ni (tsugi no kado o hidari ni magaru), and turning is magaru, not mawaru. mayou means you don't know where you are, machigaeru means you took the wrong road, and maigo means you got separated, like a lost child.

items.use: Heard in directions, mostly as the te-form request hidari ni magatte, often with the corner or light first, which takes o or de (tsugi no kado o / de hidari ni magatte). The side takes ni, sometimes e; migi ni magaru (turn right) works the same. In a taxi the verb often drops: tsugi, hidari de onegaishimasu.
items.verbSense: bend; turn (when moving along a road)
items.trap: Not hidari ni mawaru: mawaru is spin or go round; turning at a corner or light is magaru.

example.romaji: koko, hidari ni magaru n da yo ne?
example.ja: ここ、左に曲がるんだよね？
example.english: We turn left here, right?

examplePolite.romaji: koko o hidari ni magaru n desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: ここを左に曲がるんですよね？
examplePolite.english: We turn left here, don't we?

items.freqNote: 左に曲がる is listed as a phrase at #25158 and 右に曲がる at #18193; migi is #1600. magaru (#3893) also covers bent things (nekutai magatteru).
items.notes: Drivers and car navigation also say sasetsu / usetsu (left / right turn): koko usetsu dekinai yo (you can't turn right here).

items.use: Heard in directions. The corner takes o because you go round it, and the side takes ni: futatsume no kado o migi ni magatte (turn right at the second corner). With no side named, kado magattara (once you turn the corner) says a place is just round it.
items.verbSense: bend; turn (when moving along a road)
items.trap: Not kado ni magaru: ni marks the side (migi ni), so the corner takes o (de also works: kado de migi ni magatte). kado o mawatta tokoro (just round the corner) is also fine, but a turn with a side named is magaru.

example.romaji: ano kado magattara, sugu da yo.
example.ja: あの角曲がったら、すぐだよ。
example.english: It's just round that corner.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kado o magattara, sugu desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの角を曲がったら、すぐですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's just around that corner.

items.freqNote: Both parts rank mid-list because drama talk rarely gives directions, but a quarter of kado's film uses are with magaru.
items.notes: A street corner is kado; the inside corner of a room is sumi (heya no sumi).

items.use: Usually mayotta or mayotchatta (I've got lost) once the context is clear, like English 'I'm lost'. ima mayotteru (I'm lost right now) works just as well, and michi mayotte... explains why you're late. michi ni mayotta spells it out.
items.verbSense: lose your way; also hesitate, can't decide
items.trap: Not michi o nakusu or michi o ushinau: nakusu is for losing things, and being lost is michi ni mayou ('stray on the road').

example.ja: ごめん、道迷って、ちょっと遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I got lost, I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, michi ni mayotte, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、道に迷って、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I got lost, so I'll be a little late.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. mayou's rank also covers its 'can't decide' sense.
items.notes: The place you got lost in takes de: eki no naka de mayotta. Taking the wrong road on a route you know is michi o machigaeru (michi machigaeta). Getting separated from the people you're with, like a child in a shop, is maigo ni naru. Asking the way is michi o kiku: sumimasen, chotto michi o kikitai n desu kedo.

items.use: Mostly in the past, michi machigaeta (I went the wrong way), often as the reason you're late. Casual speech drops o, and the same frame covers the wrong train or exit: densha machigaeta, deguchi machigaeta.
items.verbSense: get wrong; mistake one thing for another
items.trap: A word-for-word machigatta michi ni itta is understood but stiff, and machigatta michi mostly means the wrong path in life. For a route, the road is the object: michi machigaeta (casually also michi machigatteru). michi ni mayou is different: being lost, with no idea where you are.

example.ja: あ、道間違えたかも。
example.english: Oh, I think we went the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: a, michi o machigaeta kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あ、道を間違えたかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Oh, I think we may have gone the wrong way.

items.freqNote: machigaeru's rank covers every kind of mistake, not just routes.
items.notes: Getting on the train going the other way is hantai no densha ni notchatta.

items.english: get lost (wander off, like a lost child)
items.use: Mostly about children who wander off (kodomo no koro, maigo ni natta koto aru = I got lost once as a kid) or a companion lost in a crowd. Adults say it of themselves half-jokingly, in a huge station or mall. For an adult who simply can't find the way, indoors or out, the default is mayotta (michi ni mayou). The ni usually stays.
items.verbSense: become, turn into
items.trap: Not maigo suru: maigo is a noun ('lost child'), so you become one, maigo ni natta.

example.romaji: hito ooi kara, maigo ni naranaide ne.
example.ja: 人多いから、迷子にならないでね。
example.english: There are lots of people, so don't get lost.

examplePolite.romaji: hito ga ooi node, maigo ni naranaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 人が多いので、迷子にならないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: There are lots of people, so please don't get lost.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 迷子になる is listed at #7984, above 迷子 alone (#8524): the noun nearly always comes with naru (83% of its film uses). naru's rank covers every 'become'.
items.notes: Getting separated from your group in a crowd is hagureru: tomodachi to hagurechatta.

blocks.label: Homework and grades
blocks.rationale: Schoolwork from the desk to the report card: doing homework, handing it in, working problems, good grades.
blocks.interference: shukudai o suru is doing it and shukudai o dasu is handing it in (or setting it, when a teacher says it); a problem you work out is toku, not kotaeru.

items.use: Said by and to students, often as a reminder or a groan: shukudai shita? or shukudai shinakya (I've got to do my homework). The o is often dropped, and yaru is just as common: shukudai yatta?
items.verbSense: do; the general verb for tasks

example.romaji: ato de issho ni shukudai shiyou.
example.ja: 後で一緒に宿題しよう。
example.english: Let's do our homework together later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de issho ni shukudai o shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 後で一緒に宿題をしましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's do our homework together later.

items.freqNote: 宿題 #3935, する #15, やる yaru #45. In the subtitles 宿題 goes with する 28 times and やる 22 times, its two most frequent verbs (37% together). The counts are low only because 宿題 itself is rare in foreign-film subtitles.
items.notes: Getting homework is shukudai ga deru (shukudai deta), and handing it in is dasu: shukudai dashita?

items.use: Between students it means handing in: shukudai dashita? From a teacher it means setting it, and being set homework is shukudai ga deru. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put out, take out, send out; here: hand in, or set
items.trap: 'Hand in' tempts watasu, which is only the physical handover to a person. Handing in work is putting it out: shukudai dashita? (teishutsu suru is the word on notices.) Who is talking tells you whether dasu means hand in or set.

example.ja: 宿題、もう出した？
example.english: Have you handed in the homework yet?

examplePolite.romaji: shukudai wa mou dashimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 宿題はもう出しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you handed in the homework yet?

items.freqNote: 宿題 #3935, 出す #163, 提出 teishutsu #2463. No phrase entry. All 9 hits keep o; 宿題 itself is rare in foreign-film subtitles.
items.notes: Forgetting it is shukudai o wasureru: shukudai wasureta.

items.use: Said about test, homework and quiz questions, often in the potential: kono mondai toketa? (did you get this one?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: untie; solve (a question, a puzzle)
items.trap: 'Solve' points to kaiketsu suru, but that's for problems in real life. Test and puzzle questions are untied: mondai o toku, and 'I got it' is toketa.

example.romaji: kono mondai, dou yatte toku no?
example.ja: この問題、どうやって解くの？
example.english: How do you solve this one?

examplePolite.romaji: kono mondai wa dou yatte toku n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: この問題はどうやって解くんですか？
examplePolite.english: How do you solve this one?

items.freqNote: 問題 #347, 解く #2921, 解ける tokeru #3468. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 31 of 34 hits keep o. 問題 also means 'trouble', which takes kaiketsu suru (解決 #1134).
items.notes: A question that came up on a test is shiken ni deta mondai.

items.english: have good grades, do well at school
