items.use: Said about kids, classmates and students, often as praise: seiseki ii ne, usually without ga. About yourself it sounds like bragging, so people say seiseki agatta (my grades went up) or play it down: seiseki yokunai.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: 'Get good grades' pushes toward a verb (ii seiseki o morau). Japanese describes the grades: seiseki ga ii. ii seiseki o toru also works for one term or exam.

example.romaji: otouto, seiseki ii n da yo.
example.ja: 弟、成績いいんだよ。
example.english: My little brother gets good grades.

examplePolite.romaji: otouto wa seiseki ga ii n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 弟は成績がいいんですよ。
examplePolite.english: My little brother gets good grades.

items.freqNote: 成績 #3011, いい #24. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 30% of everything said with 成績 goes to いい/良い (32 hits: 15 of them ii seiseki before the noun, 10 with ga); 成績 + 悪い has 6.
items.notes: ii conjugates from yoi: seiseki yokatta (past), yokunai (not good). The opposite is seiseki ga warui; falling grades are seiseki ga sagaru.

blocks.label: Sun and moon
blocks.rationale: What the sky does through the day: it gets dark, the sun comes up and goes down, the moon comes out.
blocks.interference: hi ga shizumu (the sun sinks) and hi ga kureru (the day closes) both mean evening: shizumu is the sun itself, kureru is the light going, and it isn't kureru 'give'. The sun noboru (climbs) but the moon usually deru (comes out), like a person going out.

items.use: Mostly heard in hi ga kureru mae ni (before it gets dark) and hi ga kureru no ga hayai (it gets dark early). In plain chat people also just say kuraku natte kita.
items.verbSense: (of a day or year) draw to a close; grow dark at dusk
items.trap: Nothing in English points to kureru, and it isn't kureru 'give me': the day 'closes'. Kuraku naru (get dark) is also natural.

example.romaji: hi ga kureru mae ni kaerou.
example.ja: 日が暮れる前に帰ろう。
example.english: Let's head home before it gets dark.

examplePolite.romaji: hi ga kureru mae ni kaerimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 日が暮れる前に帰りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's head home before it gets dark.

items.freqNote: The phrase 日が暮れる is listed as a set expression at #7770, which ranks higher than the bare verb 暮れる (#14744). 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Kana くれる (#565) is mostly 'give'.
items.notes: Classic autumn remark: hi ga kureru no hayaku natta ne (it's getting dark earlier). Joking 'this'll take forever': sonna no yattetara hi ga kurechau yo. Days getting longer: hi ga nobita ne. The sun itself going down is hi ga shizumu; kureru is the light going with it.

items.use: Said about dawn, often after a night without sleep: mou hi ga nobotteru (the sun's already up). Nobotteru means it is up, not 'it is rising'. For the moment it appears, people say hi ga nobotte kita or hi ga dete kita.
items.verbSense: rise, go up (the sun, the moon, smoke)
items.trap: 'Rise' points to agaru, the everyday 'go up', but the usual verb for the sun is noboru: hi ga nobotta.

example.ja: うわ、もう日が昇ってる。
example.english: Whoa, the sun's already up.

examplePolite.romaji: uwa, mou hi ga nobottemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: うわ、もう日が昇ってますね。
examplePolite.english: Whoa, the sun's already up.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 昇る (#8916). Kana のぼる also holds 上る (#3537, the corpus's lemma for this pair) and 登る (climb, #3936). 日 #209 mixes 'day' and 'sun'. taiyou ga noboru adds 29 corpus hits, and 日の出 (sunrise) is #14516.
items.notes: Watching the sunrise uses the noun hinode (hinode mi ni iku); the first one of the New Year is hatsuhinode.

items.use: Mostly in hi ga shizundara (once the sun's down) and hi ga shizumu mae ni (before sunset). In talk hi ga ochiru is just as common: hi ga ochiru no hayaku natta ne (the sun goes down so early now). 'Before it gets dark' is hi ga kureru mae ni or kuraku naru mae ni.
items.verbSense: sink, go under (into water or below the horizon)
items.trap: 'Go down' points to oriru or sagaru, but the sun sinks: hi ga shizumu, the same verb as a ship sinking. Hi ga ochiru (the sun drops) is just as natural in talk.

example.romaji: hi ga shizundara suzushiku naru yo.
example.ja: 日が沈んだら涼しくなるよ。
example.english: It'll cool down once the sun goes down.

examplePolite.romaji: hi ga shizundara suzushiku narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 日が沈んだら涼しくなりますよ。
examplePolite.english: It'll cool down once the sun goes down.

items.freqNote: 沈む #3611 counts every sense of sinking (ships, moods). 日 #209 mixes 'day' and 'sun'. taiyou ga shizumu adds 17 corpus hits to the 22, and 夕日 (the setting sun) is #7509. hi ga ochiru (the sun drops) has 17 corpus hits (日が落ち 13 vs 日が沈 20).
items.notes: The sunset itself is yuuhi (the setting sun) or yuuyake (the red evening sky): yuuhi kirei da ne.

items.use: Said when you notice the moon: tsuki deteru (the moon's out), kyou tsuki detenai ne. Deteru means it's out now, not 'it's coming out'.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out

example.ja: 見て、月出てるよ。
example.english: Look, the moon's out.

examplePolite.romaji: hora, tsuki ga detemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、月が出てますよ。
examplePolite.english: Look, the moon's out.

items.freqNote: 月 #1720 is the 'moon' reading つき; read がつ (month) it is #8752. 出る #81 counts every sense. hoshi ga deru (6 corpus hits) uses the same frame.
items.notes: A full moon is mangetsu: kyou mangetsu da tte (apparently it's a full moon tonight).

blocks.label: Breakfast
blocks.rationale: The morning kitchen: making a cup of tea or coffee, putting sugar in it, making toast, or skipping breakfast.
blocks.interference: ireru works two ways here: ocha o ireru is brewing the cup, and satou o ireru is literally putting sugar in. Neither is tsukuru. Toast is pan o yaku (yaku covers bake, grill and toast), and skipping a meal is nuku, not tobasu.

items.use: Said when offering or asking for a cup: ocha ireru ne (I'll make tea), koohii irete (make me a coffee). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put in; for tea or coffee, brew by pouring on hot water
items.trap: English 'make tea' leads to ocha o tsukuru; for a cup or pot of tea or coffee the verb is ireru. tsukuru is used for a big jug, as in mugicha o tsukuru.

example.ja: お茶入れるけど、飲む？
example.english: I'm making tea, want some?

examplePolite.romaji: ocha iremasu kedo, ikaga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お茶入れますけど、いかがですか？
examplePolite.english: I'm making tea. Would you like some?

items.freqNote: 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on); the tea-only spelling 淹れる (#19863) is rarer only because of how it is written.
items.notes: koohii o ireru works the same way. Serving tea to a guest is ocha o dasu; ireru is the brewing. Sugar or milk going into the cup uses ireru in its plain 'put in' sense: satou ireru? (do you take sugar?).

items.use: Asked when making someone coffee or tea (satou ireru? = sugar?), and also said about adding sugar when cooking. Casual speech drops o, and polite speech says osatou.
items.verbSense: put in; add (to a drink or dish)
items.trap: English 'do you take sugar?' has no 'take' in Japanese: sugar or milk going into a drink is ireru (satou ireru?). Say irete for yes and daijoubu for no; a bare iranai is only for friends.

example.ja: 紅茶に砂糖入れないでね。
example.english: Don't put sugar in my tea, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: koucha ni wa, osatou o irenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 紅茶には、お砂糖を入れないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't put sugar in my tea.

items.freqNote: 砂糖 #4869 (kana さとう #22633); 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru. Only 9 subtitle hits, because offering sugar is daily-life talk the films miss.
items.notes: Black coffee is burakku: burakku de ii yo (black's fine).

items.use: Said at breakfast about toast (pan yaku? = want some toast?) and about baking at home. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: cook with dry heat: grill, roast, bake, toast; also burn

example.romaji: asa wa itsumo pan yaite taberu.
example.ja: 朝はいつもパン焼いて食べる。
example.english: I always have toast in the morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa itsumo pan o yaite tabemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝はいつもパンを焼いて食べます。
examplePolite.english: I always have toast in the morning.

items.freqNote: パン #2129; 焼く #1576 counts all grilling, baking and burning. パン + 焼く occurs 15 times in the subtitles (with o in 14), against 4 for トーストし (toosuto suru). The noun トースト (toast) is #14928.
items.notes: When it's done, the intransitive yakeru: pan yaketa yo (the toast is ready). yaku covers toast, bake and grill alike (keeki o yaku, niku o yaku, sakana o yaku). toosuto suru exists but is mostly recipe and packaging language; at home people say pan yaku.

items.use: Said about busy mornings and diets: asagohan nuita (I skipped breakfast), with o dropped and asagohan often cut to asa (asa nuichatta). For a habit you hear asa wa itsumo nuiteru.
items.verbSense: pull out, take out, leave out
items.trap: English 'skip' leads to tobasu, which is for pages or steps, not meals. Leaving out a meal is nuku; asagohan tabenakatta (didn't eat breakfast) is also fine.

example.ja: 今日朝ご飯抜いちゃった。
example.english: I skipped breakfast today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa asagohan o nuichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は朝ご飯を抜いちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I skipped breakfast today.

items.freqNote: 朝ご飯 #5780; the kana spelling 朝ごはん (#6629), the rough 朝飯 (asameshi, #9447) and the stiff 朝食 (choushoku, #4784) are counted separately. Only 7 subtitle hits, mostly choushoku o nuku in translated dialogue.
items.notes: When ordering, X nuki de means 'without X': sabi nuki de (no wasabi), koori nuki de (no ice).

blocks.label: Housework and laundry
blocks.rationale: The chores beyond the kitchen: housework as a whole, laundry from the line to the drawer, and vacuuming.
blocks.interference: hosu is you hanging the washing out, kawaku is it drying (sentakumono kawaita?), and folding is tatamu, not oru (paper). 'Vacuum' is a verb in English, but Japanese runs the machine with kakeru: soujiki o kakeru, like mezamashi o kakeru.

items.use: Housework as a whole (cooking, cleaning, laundry), mostly in talk about who does what at home: kaji wa futari de yatteru (we both do the housework). Casual speech drops o, and yaru often replaces suru.
items.verbSense: do; the general verb for tasks and chores

example.ja: 今日は一日家事してた。
example.english: I spent all day on housework.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ichinichi kaji o shite imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は一日家事をしていました。
examplePolite.english: I spent the whole day doing housework.

items.freqNote: 家事 #3945; kana かじ is also 火事 'fire' (#3576).
items.notes: Helping with it is kaji o tetsudau; splitting it is kaji o buntan suru.

items.use: A daily chore in Japan, where most laundry is hung up to dry rather than tumble-dried: out on the balcony, or indoors (heyaboshi) when it rains. sentakumono hoshita? (did you hang the washing out?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang out to dry; air in the sun
items.trap: English 'hang' points to kakeru, but laundry put out to dry is hosu. The careful noun is sentakumono (the clothes); casual speech often shortens it to sentaku hosu.
partners: futon (futon: air it in the sun)

example.ja: 天気いいから、洗濯物干そう。
example.english: It's sunny, let's hang the washing out.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tenki ga ii node, sentakumono o soto ni hoshimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は天気がいいので、洗濯物を外に干しました。
examplePolite.english: The weather's nice today, so I hung the laundry outside.

items.freqNote: 洗濯 (sentaku, the washing itself) is #3221.
items.notes: Once it's dry (sentakumono ga kawaku: kawaita?), bringing it in is torikomu (sentakumono torikonde!) and folding it is tatamu (fuku o tatamu).

items.use: Comes up with the weather: sentakumono kawaita? (is the washing dry?), and in the rainy season the complaint sentakumono ga kawakanai. Casual speech drops ga.
items.kana: せんたくものがかわく
items.verbSense: become dry (laundry, paint, hair)
items.trap: Not sentakumono o kawaku: kawaku is the laundry drying by itself. Hanging it out to dry is sentakumono o hosu; drying something yourself with heat is kawakasu (kami o kawakasu, dry your hair).

example.ja: 今日は洗濯物乾かないね。
example.english: The washing won't dry today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa sentakumono ga kawakimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は洗濯物が乾きませんね。
examplePolite.english: The laundry won't dry today, will it?

items.freqNote: 乾く #6556; its homophone 渇く (nodo ga kawaku, thirsty) is #6159.
items.notes: Washing hung indoors on a rainy day is heyaboshi; a tumble dryer is kansouki.

items.use: Usually once the dry washing has been brought in (sentakumono o torikomu): fuku tatande (fold your clothes), with sentakumono as the object just as often (sentakumono tatanda?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: fold up; also close (an umbrella), shut down (a shop)
items.trap: Not oru: oru is folding paper (origami) or snapping something (hone o oru). Clothes, futons and umbrellas are tatamu.

example.ja: 服、ちゃんと畳んでよ。
example.english: Fold your clothes properly.

examplePolite.romaji: fuku wa chanto tatande kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 服はちゃんと畳んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please fold your clothes properly.

items.freqNote: 畳む #6592 (kana たたむ #20410); kana ふく also matches 拭く (wipe).
items.notes: Folded clothes then go away with shimau: tatande shimatte (fold them and put them away).

items.use: The everyday way to say 'vacuum': soujiki kakeru kara chotto doite (I'm vacuuming, move a sec). Casual speech drops o; souji suru (clean) covers it along with the rest of the cleaning.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
items.trap: English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese runs the machine with kakeru: soujiki (o) kakeru. Casual soujiki suru is also heard, and soujiki o tsukau (use the vacuum) is fine but less usual.

example.ja: あとで掃除機かけとくね。
example.english: I'll vacuum later.

examplePolite.romaji: ato de soujiki o kakete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あとで掃除機をかけておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll do the vacuuming later.

items.freqNote: かける #244 counts every sense of kakeru (掛ける #2742); 掃除 souji is #1393.
items.notes: The same kakeru irons a shirt (airon o kakeru) and sets an alarm (mezamashi o kakeru).

blocks.label: Power, battery, sound
blocks.rationale: Switching a device on and off, and the times it stops working: a dead battery or no sound.
blocks.interference: dengen o ireru / kiru (you switch it on or off) vs juuden ga kireru (it runs out on its own) is transitive kiru vs intransitive kireru, as in denwa o kiru / denwa ga kireta. Lights and the TV take tsukeru / kesu, and oto ga deru (sound comes out of a device) is not oto ga suru (you hear a noise).

items.use: Said about switching off a phone or other device, as an excuse (gomen, dengen kitteta = sorry, my phone was off) or a fix (ikkai dengen kitte mite). Cinema and exam announcements say keitai denwa no dengen o okiri kudasai. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: cut; cut off (a call, the power)
items.trap: Not sumaho o kesu: powering a phone or device down is dengen o kiru ('cut the power'), with the device joined by no (sumaho no dengen kitte), or casually just keitai kitte; dengen o otosu is common too. Sumaho kesu can sound like turning only the screen off; kesu is for lights and the TV, though pasokon kesu is heard.

example.ja: 一回電源切ってみて。
example.english: Try turning it off for a moment.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido dengen o kitte mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一度電源を切ってみてください。
examplePolite.english: Please try turning it off for a moment.

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を切る is #16226 (the tokenizer merges only some uses); 電源を入れる is #32795.
items.notes: On is dengen o ireru, and a phone that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai); one that shuts itself off is dengen kireta. Shutting down a computer is often dengen o otosu (pasokon otoshita). The kiru is the one in denwa o kiru.

items.use: Said about switching on a phone, computer or machine, often while troubleshooting: dengen ireta? (did you turn it on?). A device that won't start is dengen ga hairanai (or tsukanai), with intransitive hairu. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put in; switch on (the power, a switch)
items.trap: English 'turn on' pulls toward tsukeru, the verb for the appliance itself (denki, terebi, eakon). The power or a switch usually takes ireru ('put in'); dengen tsukeru is heard, but much less. Join the device with no: sumaho no dengen irete.
partners: eakon (air conditioner; tsukeru is more usual)

example.ja: ちゃんと電源入れた？
example.english: Did you actually turn it on?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, purojekutaa no dengen o irete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、プロジェクターの電源を入れてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you turn on the projector?

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電源を入れる is #32795 (the tokenizer merges only some uses); 電源を切る is #16226.
items.notes: Off is dengen o kiru. For a computer, pasokon tsukeru and kidou suru (boot up) are heard too.

items.use: Said when a phone dies, in the past: juuden kireta / kirechatta (my phone died). About to die is juuden kiresou (or juuden yabai, slangy); low but not dead is juuden ga nai.
items.verbSense: be cut; run out (of a supply, charge or time)
items.trap: Not shinu: a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'). denchi kireta, juuden nakunatta and batterii kireta are also fine; sumaho shinda is slang.

example.ja: ごめん、充電切れちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, my phone died.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, juuden ga kirechaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電が切れちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my phone died.

items.freqNote: juuden ranks low overall (#7708); judgement: most spoken uses are this phrase, juuden suru and juuden ga nai (the list has no phrase counts). batterii is #9633.
items.notes: Charging is the plain verb juuden suru. The same kireru is a dropped call: denwa kireta (the call cut off). Switching the phone off yourself is dengen o kiru, the transitive half.

items.english: sound comes out (of a TV, speaker, phone)
items.use: Said about TVs, speakers, laptops and video calls, most often in the negative or as a check: oto denai (there's no sound), oto deteru? (is there sound?). ga is usually dropped, and on a call oto dete nai yo means your sound isn't coming through.
items.verbSense: come out, go out; appear
items.trap: Not oto ga ugokanai: when a TV, speaker or call goes silent, the sound 'doesn't come out', oto ga denai. oto nai is heard too, and it is the plain way to say a clip has no sound at all: kono douga, oto nai yo.

example.romaji: are, oto denai n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、音出ないんだけど。
example.english: Huh, there's no sound.

examplePolite.romaji: are, oto ga denai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、音が出ないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Huh, there's no sound.

items.freqNote: nounRank is 音 read oto; verbRank 出る pools every sense (leave, appear, answer the phone).
items.notes: Different from oto ga suru (you hear a noise). Muting is oto o kesu; turning it down is oto o sageru.

blocks.label: Masks and glasses
blocks.rationale: Two on/off pairs for the face: a mask goes on with suru, glasses with kakeru, and both come off with hazusu.
blocks.interference: suru vs kakeru for putting on, one shared hazusu for taking off; never nugu, which is for clothes and shoes.

items.use: Usually masuku shiteru (is wearing a mask); casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
items.trap: Not masuku o kiru: small worn items (mask, watch, scarf, tie) just take suru, as in masuku shiteru. masuku o tsukeru is also fine and a little more formal; masuku o kakeru is heard from some speakers too.

example.ja: 風邪ひいたからマスクしてる。
example.english: I've got a cold, so I'm wearing a mask.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hiita node, masuku o shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいたので、マスクをしてます。
examplePolite.english: I've caught a cold, so I'm wearing a mask.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and する #15. マスク may be under-ranked if the drama corpus is mostly pre-2020 (not verified); the rank was not adjusted.
items.notes: Off: masuku o hazusu or toru. The same suru goes with a ring or a tie (yubiwa o suru, nekutai o suru). tsukeru is the catch-all for things put on the body: nekkuresu / piasu / kousui o tsukeru (necklace, earrings, perfume). A scarf is also mafuraa o maku (wrap it).

items.use: Mostly heard as masuku hazushite (take your mask off) or hazushite mo ii? (OK if I take it off?). masuku hazushita kao (someone's face without the mask) comes up a lot too, as in masuku hazushita kao hajimete mita (first time I've seen your face without the mask). masuku hazushiteru means the mask is already off. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: remove, unfasten, detach
items.trap: Not masuku o nugu for a face mask: nugu is for clothes and shoes. Masks, glasses, watches and rings come off with hazusu; casual toru (masuku totte) is just as everyday, though masuku totte can also mean 'pass me a mask'.

example.romaji: koko de masuku hazushite mo ii?
example.ja: ここでマスク外してもいい？
example.english: Is it OK to take my mask off here?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de masuku o hazushite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ここでマスクを外してもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I take my mask off here?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and 外す #1043; 外す also counts 'miss' and 'step away' (seki o hazusu). マスク may be under-ranked if the drama corpus is mostly pre-2020. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Putting one on is masuku o suru (or tsukeru). A mask pulled down under the chin is an ago masuku. A full-head costume or wrestler's mask is the one you nugu.

items.use: Most often megane kaketeru (wears glasses), which describes a person, not the act of putting them on. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something
items.trap: Not megane o kiru: glasses hang on the ears, so the verb is kakeru. Casual megane shiteru is also common.

example.ja: あの眼鏡かけてる人、誰？
example.english: Who's that person with the glasses?

examplePolite.romaji: ano megane o kaketeru hito wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの眼鏡をかけてる人は誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who is that person wearing glasses?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 眼鏡 #4549 (the katakana spelling メガネ is listed separately at #6067) and the kanji 掛ける #2742, used because kana かける (#244) also counts the call, sit and spend senses.
items.notes: Off: megane o hazusu, the same verb as masuku o hazusu. Contact lenses go in: kontakuto o ireru (or tsukeru).

items.use: Often megane hazushite (take your glasses off) or hazusu to (when I take them off). The same verb takes off masks, watches and rings.
items.verbSense: remove, unfasten, detach
items.trap: Not megane o nugu: nugu is for things you are dressed in (clothes, shoes, hats, gloves). Glasses, watches, masks, rings and earrings come off with hazusu. English 'take off' leading to toru is fine in casual speech (megane totte, masuku totte); hazusu is the neutral verb.

example.romaji: megane hazusu to nani mo mienai.
example.ja: 眼鏡外すと何も見えない。
example.english: I can't see a thing without my glasses.

examplePolite.romaji: megane o hazusu to, nani mo mienai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 眼鏡を外すと、何も見えないんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't see a thing without my glasses.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 外す #1043, which also counts 'miss' and 'step away (seki o hazusu)'. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Contact lenses come out with kontakuto o hazusu or toru.

blocks.label: Exams and results
blocks.rationale: An exam from start to finish: you sit it, get your score, the results come out, you pass or fail.
blocks.interference: The exam is ukeru but the score is toru (never shiken o toru); ukeru (take, with o) and ukaru (pass, with ni) sound alike, and ochiru is ukaru's opposite.

items.use: Said about sitting a test, often when talking about plans: raishuu shiken ukeru. o is often dropped, and interviews take the same verb (mensetsu o ukeru).
items.verbSense: receive; undergo
items.trap: 'Take' leads to shiken o toru, but toru is for the score you get (ten o toru), a licence, or signing up for a class (jugyou o toru). Exams, tests and interviews are 'undergone': shiken o ukeru.

example.ja: 来週日本語の試験受ける。
example.english: I'm taking a Japanese exam next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu nihongo no shiken o ukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週日本語の試験を受けます。
examplePolite.english: I'm taking a Japanese exam next week.

items.freqNote: 試験 #3067, 受ける #356. Everyday school tests are more often tesuto (#2539), with the same verb. 面接 mensetsu (#3050, interview) takes ukeru too.
items.notes: Students often just say ashita tesuto aru (there's a test tomorrow). On its own, ukeru! is slang for 'that's hilarious'.

items.use: Said about test results, almost always with the number fused to ten: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (I managed a good score). Casual speech often drops o, and in sport it means scoring.
items.verbSense: take; get, earn (a score, a licence)
items.trap: 'Get a hundred' tempts morau, which only fits a mark someone awards you (sensei ni hyakuten moratta). A score you earn on a test is taken: hyakuten totta. This is the toru that English 'take an exam' wrongly points to; the exam itself is shiken o ukeru.

example.ja: 数学で百点取った！
example.english: I got a hundred in maths!

examplePolite.romaji: suugaku de hyakuten torimashita!
examplePolite.ja: 数学で百点取りました！
examplePolite.english: I got a hundred in maths!

items.freqNote: 点 #1137 also covers 'point, dot'; 点数 tensuu #6480, 満点 manten #9848. In the subtitles 点 + 取る splits evenly with and without o (11 each).
items.notes: Asking how it went: nanten datta?

items.use: Said while waiting on exam, medical or job-application results: kekka itsu deru? Once they're in it's kekka deta, and not yet is mada detenai. The ga is often kept.
items.verbSense: go out; appear; come out (be announced or issued)
items.trap: English 'I got my results' makes you the subject. For results being announced, Japanese says the results come out: kekka deta. kekka moratta only fits when a results sheet is handed to you (kenkou shindan no kekka moratta). kekka o dasu means producing results, at work or in sport.

example.ja: 試験の結果、もう出た？
example.english: Are your exam results out yet?

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka wa mou demashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果はもう出ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have your exam results come out yet?

items.freqNote: 結果 #626; 出る #81 counts every sense of deru. 結果を出す (produce results) has its own phrase entry at #8074; 結果が出る has none.
items.notes: To ask how it went: kekka dou datta? (polite: kekka wa dou deshita ka?)

items.use: Said about a result, almost always in the past: shiken ukatta! Casual speech drops ni, and schools and companies work the same way (daigaku ni ukatta).
items.verbSense: pass, get in (be accepted by an exam, school or employer)
items.trap: 'Pass' gives no hint of ukaru, and the exam takes ni, not o (shiken ni ukatta). goukaku shita is just as common in speech, especially for entrance exams, and shiken ni tootta also works.

example.ja: 日本語の試験受かった！
example.english: I passed the Japanese exam!

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo no shiken ni ukarimashita!
examplePolite.ja: 日本語の試験に受かりました！
examplePolite.english: I passed the Japanese exam!

items.freqNote: 受かる #3494, 合格 goukaku #2357: both are everyday speech. ukaru is the more casual verb; goukaku also turns up in set phrases like goukaku omedetou.
items.notes: The results come out first (kekka ga deru): kekka deta? ukatta?

items.use: Said about a result, usually as ochita or ochichatta (failed, sadly). Also used for schools, interviews and auditions: mensetsu ni ochita.
items.verbSense: fall, drop (here: fail to get through)
items.trap: 'Fail' points to shippai suru. shiken ni shippai shita is possible, but it means you blew it. For the pass/fail result, you 'fall': shiken ni ochita, or just shiken ochita. The exam takes ni, not o.

example.ja: 日本語の試験落ちちゃった。
example.english: I failed the Japanese exam, unfortunately.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo no shiken ni ochichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語の試験に落ちちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I failed the Japanese exam, unfortunately.

items.freqNote: 試験 #3067, 落ちる #490. 落ちる counts every 'fall' sense; the exam sense rests on native judgement. 失敗 shippai #809, 滑る suberu #5017.
items.notes: Before someone's exam, avoid saying ochiru or suberu (slip): it's considered bad luck. Casually, failing is also shiken subetta. The careful polite form is ochite shimaimashita, and failing a course is tan'i o otosu.

blocks.label: Out on errands
blocks.rationale: Running errands: grab some cash, is the shop open yet, has it closed, wait your turn.
blocks.interference: A shop's aiteru means 'open', not 'free' as in ashita aiteru?; shimatteru is 'closed'. orosu is cash from the ATM, not toru. junban o matsu is waiting your turn, while standing in the queue itself is narabu.

items.use: What you say on the way to the ATM or konbini: chotto okane oroshite kuru, okane orosanakya. The o usually drops.
items.verbSense: bring or take down; lower
items.trap: Not okane o toru, which sounds like taking someone's money. Cash from an ATM is orosu, 'bring down'. Casual dasu also works.

example.ja: ちょっとお金下ろしてくる
example.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto okane o oroshite kimasu
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお金を下ろしてきます
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

items.freqNote: 下ろす #2775 covers all senses, including lowering things; 降ろす #4786 is letting people off.
items.notes: hikidasu is the formal word; ATM voice prompts and bank staff say ohikidashi.

items.use: Almost always aiteru (is open), in questions about hours: kono mise nanji made aiteru?. Plain aku is the moment it opens: juuji ni aku. yatteru (is open for business) is just as common: nanji made yatteru?
items.verbSense: of a door or shop: open, by itself
items.trap: About the shop itself, use aiteru: ano mise mou aiteru?. akeru is what the staff do, so aketemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. yatteru also works. mise o hiraku is starting a new shop.

example.ja: あの店、もう開いてる？
example.english: Is that shop open yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう開いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Is that shop open yet?

items.freqNote: 開く read as aku shows #14086, but the tokenizer probably files most 開いてる under 開く read as hiraku (#624), so the real spoken rank of aku 'open' is higher. 空く #1498 is a different word.
items.notes: mise o akeru = the staff open up; mise o hiraku = start a new shop. A door opening uses the same verb: doa ga aku.

items.use: Mostly shimatteru (is closed) and shimatchau (is about to close): hayaku ikanai to shimatchau yo. Plain shimaru gives the time: kuji ni shimaru.
items.verbSense: of a door or shop: close, by itself
items.trap: For the shop's own state, use shimaru: mou shimatteru = it's already closed. shimeru is the staff closing up, so nanji ni shimemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. Casual owaru also works.

example.ja: あの店、もう閉まってるよ
example.english: That shop's already closed.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou shimattemasu yo
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう閉まってますよ
examplePolite.english: That shop's already closed.

items.notes: Closing for good is mise o tatamu, or tsubureru (go bust). Sounds like shimau (put away; the -chau ending): mou shimatta can mean 'I already put it away', and shimatta! alone means 'oops'. Context decides.

items.use: Said to kids (chanto junban matte ne) and as a pointed remark to someone pushing in: minna junban matteru n desu kedo. The noun junban machi is common too (ima sanjuppun junban machi da tte), and when your turn comes it's junban ga kita, or just ban: tsugi, dare no ban?
items.verbSense: wait

example.ja: ちゃんと順番待ってね。
example.english: Wait your turn, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: chanto junban o matte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと順番を待ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please wait your turn.

items.freqNote: 順番 #3213; 待つ #71; 番 ban #1055. Pair count 15; the noun 順番待ち adds 8.
items.notes: Pushing in is warikomi: warikomi shinaide.

blocks.label: Long-term health
blocks.rationale: Health beyond today's symptoms: what's good for you, getting older, quitting smoking and allergies.
blocks.interference: karada ni ii keeps its ni even in casual talk. Getting older is toshi o toru, not furuku naru. tabako o yameru uses the same yameru as quitting a job (kaisha o yameru). An allergy is something you have: ebi no arerugii ga aru.

items.use: Said of food, drinks, sleep and habits: yasai wa karada ni ii. The opposite karada ni warui is just as common (tabako, yofukashi), and since ii conjugates from yoi, the softer negative is karada ni yokunai. Ni is kept even in casual speech.
items.verbSense: good; with ni, good for
items.trap: Not kore wa kenkou desu: kenkou describes a person's health, so food or habits that are good for you are karada ni ii (kenkou ni ii also works). Kenkouteki na shokuji (a healthy diet) and herushii (light, healthy food) are fine too.

example.romaji: yasai mo tabete. karada ni ii kara.
example.ja: 野菜も食べて。体にいいから。
example.english: Have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

examplePolite.romaji: yasai mo tabete kudasai. karada ni ii desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: 野菜も食べてください。体にいいですから。
examplePolite.english: Please have some vegetables too. They're good for you.

items.freqNote: 体 (からだ) #371; いい #24; phrase entries 体にいい #11815 and 体に悪い #13606 (体に良い #44244); 健康 #2531.
items.notes: Okarada ni ki o tsukete kudasai (take care of yourself) is the stock sign-off with karada; casually, karada ni ki o tsukete ne.

items.use: Mostly said in the past for how you feel now: toshi totta naa (I'm getting old). The generic toshi o toru to... (as you get older...) is also common, and toshi totteru means someone is elderly. O often drops in casual talk (toshi totta) but is usually kept in toshi o toru to...
items.verbSense: take, get; with years, take them on
items.trap: Not furuku naru, which is for things: people take on years, toshi o toru, and 'I'm getting old' is the past, toshi totta.

example.romaji: aa, toshi totta naa. sugu tsukareru.
example.ja: ああ、年取ったなあ。すぐ疲れる。
example.english: Man, I'm getting old. I get tired so fast.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi mo toshi o torimashita yo. sugu tsukarete shimau n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私も年を取りましたよ。すぐ疲れてしまうんです。
examplePolite.english: I've gotten old too. I get tired so easily now.

items.freqNote: 年 read とし #1354 (read ねん it is #155); 取る #228. Phrase entries 年を取る #5402 and 年取る #8003 are high for phrases.
items.notes: Keep apart from toshi ga ue (older than someone); otoshiyori is the polite word for the elderly. Mou toshi da kara (I'm not as young as I was) is the everyday shorthand you'll hear alongside toshi totta.

items.use: Heard as news, tabako yameta (I've quit), or advice, tabako yameta hou ga ii yo. Wa is common for contrast (tabako wa yameta), and osake o yameru works the same way.
items.verbSense: stop, give up (a habit, an activity); quitting a job is the same-sounding yameru (辞める), as in kaisha o yameru
items.trap: English 'stop smoking' pulls toward tomeru, which is stopping a machine or a person (kuruma o tomeru). A habit you give up is yameru: tabako yameta.

example.ja: タバコ、去年やめたんだ。
example.english: I quit smoking last year.

examplePolite.romaji: tabako wa kyonen yamemashita.
examplePolite.ja: タバコは去年やめました。
examplePolite.english: I gave up smoking last year.

items.freqNote: タバコ #4158 (たばこ #7069); kana やめる #117 counts every 'stop, quit' use (辞める 'quit a job' #604). Phrase entry タバコをやめる #84839; 禁煙 kin'en #10367.
items.notes: Kin'en-chuu (I'm off cigarettes for now) is the other everyday phrase; kin'en on a sign means no smoking.

items.use: Put the cause in front: tamago arerugii ga aru, or ebi no arerugii ga aru. Restaurants and clinics ask about it (arerugii wa arimasu ka?), and casual talk drops ga.
items.politeJa: アレルギーがあります
items.verbSense: there is, exist (for things); here, have
items.trap: Said the German way, arerugii (a-re-ru-gii), not like English 'allergy'. The cause goes in front: tamago arerugii, or tamago ni arerugii ga aru.

example.ja: エビアレルギーあるから、食べられない。
example.english: I'm allergic to shrimp, so I can't eat it.

examplePolite.romaji: ebi no arerugii ga aru node, taberaremasen.
examplePolite.ja: エビのアレルギーがあるので、食べられません。
examplePolite.english: I have a shrimp allergy, so I can't eat it.

items.freqNote: アレルギー #6251; ある #21. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Hay fever is kafunshou (kafunshou nan desu), the allergy nearly everyone in Japan talks about each spring.

blocks.label: Motivation and mood
blocks.rationale: Your energy and mood: no motivation, getting yourself going, perking up, getting hyped, stress piling up.
blocks.interference: yaruki and genki both 'come out' (deru): yaruki denai is can't get going, genki deta is it gave me a lift, and genki dashite is what you say to someone else. Mood goes up (tenshon agaru) while stress piles up (tamaru); tenshon means hype, not tension.

items.english: have no motivation, can't be bothered
items.use: About yourself it's the flat 'I just don't feel like it': kyou yaruki nai (I just don't feel like doing anything today). About someone else it's a criticism, they're not trying: ano hito yaruki nai yo ne. In polite talk people usually say yaruki nai desu or yaruki ga nai n desu; yaruki ga arimasen sounds stiff.
items.verbSense: nai: there isn't, have none (negative of aru)

example.romaji: kyou maji yaruki nai. nanimo shitakunai.
example.ja: 今日マジやる気ない。何もしたくない。
example.english: I've got zero motivation today. I don't want to do anything.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nanka yaruki nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はなんかやる気ないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: I just don't feel like doing anything today.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase; ない #43 (無い #6807).
items.notes: yaruki denai is 'I can't get going'; yaruki nai is flatter: I just don't feel like it, or, about others, they don't care.

items.use: Mostly said in the negative about yourself, about a task or a day you can't face: yaruki denai (I can't get going). yaruki nai (no motivation at all) is a flatter state and is also said about other people. yaruki aru means keen or motivated; asked as yaruki aru no?, it's a reproach: are you even trying?
items.verbSense: come out, appear
items.trap: Learners look for an adjective for 'motivated', but everyday Japanese has none. The will to do it 'comes out' (deru): yaruki ga denai. yaruki ga aru (be keen) and mochibeeshon ga agaru are also fine.
partners: chikara (strength: chikara ga denai, can't muster the strength)

example.ja: 今日全然やる気出ない。
example.english: I can't get motivated at all today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zenzen yaruki ga demasen.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は全然やる気が出ません。
examplePolite.english: I just can't get motivated today.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately.
items.notes: yaruki is literally 'do-feeling', from yaru + ki.

items.use: Mostly past, about what gave you a lift, with ga often dropped: amai mono tabetara genki deta, or arigatou, genki deta after a kind word. The negative genki denai means you can't shake a low mood.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; here energy wells up in you
items.trap: English 'cheer up' is both 'I cheered up' and 'cheer up!', but Japanese splits it: genki deta about yourself, genki dashite to someone else. genki dete! isn't a request, though genki dete kita (I'm perking up) is fine.

example.ja: ありがとう、なんか元気出た。
example.english: Thanks, that cheered me up.

examplePolite.romaji: arigatou gozaimasu. okage de genki ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます。おかげで元気が出ました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you. That cheered me up.

items.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 元気が出る #8964, near the request genki dashite (元気出して #7639, the kept genki o dasu). 33 subtitle hits (ga 29).
items.notes: genki moratta (it gave me a boost) is a common way to credit a song, a person or a message.

items.use: For being hyped right now: tenshon agaru! or tenshon agatte kita. The opposite is tenshon sagaru (get bummed out), and tenshon takai means hyper. It's an informal word: fine with friends and coworkers, but not in formal speech.
items.politeJa: テンションが上がります
items.verbSense: go up, rise
items.trap: For 'I'm excited', learners say koufun shiteru, which sounds worked-up and, in some contexts, sexual. Say tenshon agaru for hyped right now, and tanoshimi or wakuwaku suru for a plan. False friend: tenshon is energy or mood, not tension.

example.ja: やばい、テンション上がってきた！
example.english: Oh man, I'm getting so hyped!

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne, tenshon ga agatte kimashita!
examplePolite.ja: いいですね、テンションが上がってきました！
examplePolite.english: This is great, I'm getting excited!

items.freqNote: The phrase entry テンションが上がる is #30223 because the tokenizer usually splits it.
items.notes: English 'tension' or 'nervousness' is kinchou (kinchou suru, get nervous).

items.use: Usually in -te ru for how you are now: sutoresu tamatteru (I'm stressed out). Getting rid of it is sutoresu kaishou, and blowing off steam is sutoresu hassan: karaoke de sutoresu hassan shita.
items.politeJa: ストレスが溜まります
items.verbSense: pile up, accumulate
items.trap: For 'I'm stressed', learners turn 'stress' into a verb: sutoresu shiteru, which isn't Japanese. Stress piles up: sutoresu tamatteru. sutoresu o kanjiru (feel stress) and shigoto ga sutoresu (work stresses me out) are also fine.

example.ja: 最近ストレス溜まってる。
example.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin sutoresu ga tamattemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近ストレスが溜まってます。
examplePolite.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

items.freqNote: verbRank is the kana spelling たまる (#1650); 溜まる is #16850. The whole phrase has no entry.
items.notes: The transitive is tameru, as in okane o tameru: sutoresu tamenai you ni ne (don't let the stress build up).

blocks.label: Fridge and microwave
blocks.rationale: Putting food away and getting it out again: into the fridge, a lid on, heating it up, and checking whether it's past its date.
blocks.interference: reizouko ni ireru takes ni for where the food goes, unlike satou o ireru. Heating food up is atatameru (obentou atatamemasu ka? at the konbini), not atsuku suru. A lid goes on with futa o suru; a screw cap is futa o shimeru. Expiry has no verb of its own: the date runs out with kireru, like juuden ga kireru.

items.use: Said about leftovers and shopping, usually with -toku: reizouko ni iretoku ne (I'll put it in the fridge), or as a request, reizouko iretoite. ni is often kept, but casual speech drops it too, and reizouko ni shimau (put away in the fridge) is also common.
items.verbSense: put in, put inside
items.trap: English 'put' leads to oku, which is mainly setting something down on a surface. Into the fridge, a bag or a box, the usual verb is ireru; reizouko ni oite aru (it's been left in the fridge) is also heard.

example.romaji: amatta no, reizouko ni iretoku ne.
example.ja: 余ったの、冷蔵庫に入れとくね。
example.english: I'll put what's left in the fridge.

examplePolite.romaji: amatta no wa, reizouko ni irete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 余ったのは、冷蔵庫に入れておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll put what's left in the fridge.

items.freqNote: 冷蔵庫 #2894; 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on, make tea). The phrase 冷蔵庫に入れ occurs 12 times in the subtitles and 冷蔵庫に置 once; subtitles keep particles more than speech does.
items.notes: Taking it out is reizouko kara dasu; chilling a drink is hiyasu (biiru hiyashitoku).

items.use: Heard at every konbini checkout as a question, obentou atatamemasu ka? (shall I heat it up?), answered with onegai shimasu or daijoubu desu. At home renji de chin suru (zap it) is the casual alternative.
items.kana: おべんとうをあたためる
items.verbSense: warm up, heat (food, a room, hands)
items.trap: English 'heat up' leads to atsuku suru; warming food is atatameru. At the till, daijoubu desu means 'no, thanks', so say onegai shimasu if you want it heated.

example.romaji: obentou, renji de atatamete kuru ne.
example.ja: お弁当、レンジで温めてくるね。
example.english: I'll go heat up my lunch in the microwave.

examplePolite.romaji: obentou, renji de atatamete kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: お弁当、レンジで温めてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go heat up my lunch in the microwave.

items.freqNote: お弁当 #2384; the plain 弁当 (bentou) is #3091 and counted separately. 温める #4658. No subtitle hits, because the konbini question is daily life the films miss.
items.notes: At the same till you'll hear ohashi otsuke shimasu ka? (want chopsticks?).

items.use: Said while cooking and storing food: futa shite gofun (lid on for five minutes), futa shitoite (keep it covered). Casual speech drops o, and taking the lid off is futa o toru or futa o akeru.
items.verbSense: do; with a lid, plug or wrap, put it on (as with worn items: masuku o suru)
items.trap: English 'put the lid on' leads to futa o oku, which means setting the lid down somewhere. Covering a pot is futa (o) suru, the same suru as masuku o suru.
partners: raappu (cling film: raappu shite reizouko ni ireru)
sen (a plug or stopper: ofuro no sen o suru)

example.ja: 蓋して、五分ぐらい煮込んで。
example.english: Put the lid on and let it simmer about five minutes.

examplePolite.romaji: futa o shite, gofun gurai nikonde kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 蓋をして、五分ぐらい煮込んでください。
examplePolite.english: Put the lid on and let it simmer for about five minutes.

items.freqNote: 蓋 #11198 (ふた #18330 and フタ #14988 counted separately); する #15 counts every use of suru. The 24 subtitle hits are almost all figurative (kusai mono ni futa o suru, covering things up); cooking talk is daily life the films miss.
items.notes: futa o shimeru (close the lid) works for pots and boxes too, and is the only choice for a screw-top bottle or jar; opening is futa o akeru.

items.use: Said about food in the fridge and about cards, passports and coupons, mostly as kireteru or kireta: kore, kigen kireteru (this is past its date). For food the full noun is common: shoumi kigen kireteru.
items.verbSense: snap, run out; for a time limit, lapse
items.trap: Dictionaries give shikkou suru or manryou for 'expire', which are legal and formal words. Food, passports and coupons just run out: kigen ga kireta.

example.ja: この牛乳、期限切れてるよ。
example.english: This milk is past its date.

examplePolite.romaji: kono gyuunyuu, kigen ga kiretemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この牛乳、期限が切れてますよ。
examplePolite.english: This milk is past its date.

items.freqNote: 期限 #4825; 賞味期限 (shoumi kigen, best-before) #12993 and the noun 期限切れ (kigengire, expired) #36600 are counted separately. 切れる #1147 counts every sense; 期限が切れ / 期限切れ occur 45 times in the subtitles.
items.notes: Don't mix it up with kigen ga warui (in a bad mood), which is a different kigen (機嫌).

blocks.label: Pride and teasing
blocks.rationale: Looking foolish or cool: being made fun of, embarrassing yourself, and showing off.
blocks.interference: Making fun of someone is baka ni suru (baka ni shinaide), not warau. haji o kaku uses the same kaku as ase o kaku. kakko tsukeru is acting cool, while kakko ii is being cool.

items.english: make fun of, look down on
items.use: Heard most in protest: baka ni shinaide (don't make fun of me), baka ni shiteru no? (are you mocking me?), and in the passive, baka ni sareta (they made fun of me). It covers both mocking and treating someone as stupid.
items.verbSense: do; with X ni, treat as or make into X
items.trap: English 'make fun of' leads to karakau, which is right for playful teasing but too light for contempt. Mocking someone or treating them as stupid is baka ni suru.
partners: nakamahazure (leaving someone out: nakamahazure ni sareta)

example.ja: バカにしないでよ。
example.english: Don't make fun of me.

examplePolite.romaji: baka ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: バカにしないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't make fun of me.

items.freqNote: nounRank is katakana バカ #433 (ばか #2695, 馬鹿 #6994). Phrase entry バカにする #1657, high for a phrase (馬鹿にする #14581). The pair count (39, mostly を) is baka o suru 'do something stupid', not this set; written バカに/馬鹿に/ばかに + する forms (incl. sareta): about 524 hits.
items.notes: baka ni dekinai = not to be underestimated: konbini no bentou, baka ni dekinai yo.

items.english: embarrass yourself, make a fool of yourself
items.use: Mostly told after the fact: minna no mae de haji o kaita (I made a fool of myself in front of everyone), with o kept far more often than in most sets, though haji kaita is heard too. Making someone else look bad is haji o kakaseru: haji o kakasenaide yo (don't embarrass me).
items.verbSense: scratch; with sweat, snoring or shame, give off or come out in
items.trap: English 'I embarrassed myself' leads to jibun o hazukashiku shita, which isn't said. The incident is haji o kaku (the kaku of ase o kaku, not kaku 'write'); hazukashikatta is how it felt.

example.romaji: minna no mae de haji o kaita.
example.ja: みんなの前で恥をかいた。
example.english: I made a fool of myself in front of everyone.

examplePolite.romaji: minna no mae de haji o kakimashita.
examplePolite.ja: みんなの前で恥をかきました。
examplePolite.english: I embarrassed myself in front of everyone.

items.freqNote: 恥 #3019. Verb rank is kana かく #11889, the spelling used for sweat, snoring and shame (掻く #51963). Phrase entry 恥をかく #6752. o is kept in 88 of 91 subtitle hits.
items.notes: hazukashii is the feeling; haji o kaku is the incident that causes it.

items.use: Said with the short vowel and no o: kakko tsukenaide (quit posing), kakko tsuketeru dake (he's just trying to look cool). A poser is a kakkotsuke. The dictionary form is kakkou o tsukeru (格好をつける).
items.verbSense: attach, put on; here, put on a look or front
items.trap: English 'show off' leads to jiman suru, which is bragging in words about what you have or did. Putting on a cool act is kakko tsukeru, and the long-vowel kakkou o suru is about clothes: hen na kakkou shiteru (you're dressed weird).

example.ja: かっこつけなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't need to act cool.

examplePolite.romaji: kakko tsukenakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: かっこつけなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: There's no need to put on a show.

items.freqNote: 格好 #1247 (kana かっこ #7518, カッコ #6594). tsukeru: kana つける #393 pools all senses (付ける #1452). Phrase entries かっこつける #11704 and 格好つける #17512. Pair particles ∅:62 vs を:21.
items.notes: kakkoii (cool) and kakkowarui (uncool, embarrassing) are built on the same noun.

blocks.label: Exercise and outdoors
blocks.rationale: Getting your body moving and getting out into nature at the weekend, plus what people say it does for them: a nice change of pace.
blocks.interference: yama ni noboru takes ni, not the bare object of English 'climb a mountain'. tsuri ni iku and kyanpu ni iku put the activity straight before ni iku. kibun tenkan ni naru (with naru) means something did you good, while kibun tenkan suru is taking the break yourself.

items.english: get some exercise, move your body
items.use: The everyday way to talk about getting exercise, often as something you should do: tama ni wa karada ugokasanakya. Casual speech usually drops o, and karada ugokasu no ga suki means you like being active.
items.verbSense: move something, set it in motion (the transitive of ugoku)
items.trap: Not karada o ugoku. ugoku is the intransitive 'move' (karada ga ugokanai = I can't move), and only ugokasu takes o.

example.ja: たまには体動かさなきゃ。
example.english: I need to get some exercise now and then.

examplePolite.romaji: tama ni wa karada o ugokasanakya ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: たまには体を動かさなきゃいけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should get some exercise now and then.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 体を動かす has its own entry at #13082. 運動 (undou, exercise) is #3290.
items.notes: undou suru is the general word for exercise, from sport to the gym (undou busoku = not enough exercise); karada o ugokasu covers any getting moving, from a walk to cleaning.

items.english: be a nice change of pace, do someone good
items.use: Said to encourage someone or about something that helped: ii kibun tenkan ni naru yo (it'll do you good), ii kibun tenkan ni natta. It often comes with ii. kibun tenkan ni alone means 'for a change': kibun tenkan ni sanpo shite kuru.
items.kana: きぶんてんかんになる
items.verbSense: become, turn into
partners: kibarashi (taking your mind off something: ii kibarashi ni natta)

example.romaji: issho ni ikou yo, ii kibun tenkan ni naru yo.
example.ja: 一緒に行こうよ、いい気分転換になるよ。
example.english: Come with us, it'll be a nice change of pace.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni ikimashou yo, ii kibun tenkan ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょうよ、いい気分転換になりますよ。
examplePolite.english: Do come along, it'll be a nice change of pace.

items.freqNote: 気分転換 #5393 ranks above 気晴らし #8089 in the drama list. The tokenizer splits 気分転換, so there is no pair count; in the subtitles the written forms are 気分転換 85 and 気晴らし 120, with 気分転換になる and 気晴らしになる 9 each.
items.notes: kibarashi works the same way and is about as common in films; it leans to taking your mind off something bad: ii kibarashi ni natta, kibarashi ni sanpo suru. iya na koto o wasureru (forget your troubles) is another natural way to say it.

items.use: Said about hiking up a mountain as much as real climbing, often in the past or as an experience: fujisan nobotta koto aru? The mountain usually takes ni (o is also heard), and casual speech sometimes drops it. The hobby itself is yama nobori (mountain climbing).
items.verbSense: climb, go up (mountains, trees, stairs)
items.trap: English 'climb' takes a direct object, so learners default to yama o noboru. That is fine too, mostly when the way up is the point (kewashii yama o nobotta, climbed a steep mountain), but for having climbed a mountain ni is about three times as common: fujisan ni nobotta.

example.romaji: shuumatsu, tomodachi to yama ni nobotta.
example.ja: 週末、友達と山に登った。
example.english: I climbed a mountain with friends at the weekend.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu, tomodachi to yama ni noborimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 週末、友達と山に登りました。
examplePolite.english: I climbed a mountain with friends at the weekend.

items.freqNote: 登る #3936. The subtitle count files 山に登る under the other spelling 上る (#3537, used for stairs and slopes): 43 hits, ni 26 and o 9. The hobby nouns are 山登り #17609 (26 in the subtitles) and 登山 #14277.
items.notes: An easy walk in the hills is haikingu; climbing as a hobby is yama nobori or tozan (shumi wa tozan desu).

items.use: Said about fishing trips, as plans or as a habit. Casual speech often drops ni (tsuri iku?), and tsuri itteru means someone is out fishing now, not on their way.
items.verbSense: go (tsuri is the noun of tsuru, catch on a line)

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa, yoku tsuri ni iku.
example.ja: 休みの日は、よく釣りに行く。
example.english: I often go fishing on my days off.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa, yoku tsuri ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日は、よく釣りに行きます。
examplePolite.english: I often go fishing on my days off.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 釣りに行く has its own entry at #18346. The verb 釣る (catch on a line) is #3657.
items.notes: A fish on the line is tsureru: nanka tsureta? (catch anything?). tsukamaeru is catching something that could get away, like a bug or a thief, so it fits a fish caught by hand or net, not on a rod.

items.use: Said about camping trips, often family or summer ones. Casual speech drops ni (kyanpu iku?), and being at the campsite is kyanpu shiteru.
items.verbSense: go; with an activity noun + ni, go out to do it
items.trap: Not kyanpingu ni iku: the activity is kyanpu, and kyanpingu turns up mainly in compounds like kyanpingu kaa (camper van).

example.romaji: natsuyasumi, kazoku de kyanpu ni itta.
example.ja: 夏休み、家族でキャンプに行った。
example.english: We went camping as a family over the summer break.

examplePolite.romaji: natsuyasumi, kazoku de kyanpu ni ikimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夏休み、家族でキャンプに行きました。
examplePolite.english: We went camping as a family over the summer break.

items.freqNote: No phrase entry. In the subtitles キャンプ is often a military or summer camp, so the count (53) mixes senses.

blocks.label: Internet and apps
blocks.rationale: Getting online and what you do there: looking things up, connection and signal trouble, and putting apps on your phone.
blocks.interference: netto de shiraberu (look things up, de for the means) vs netto ga tsunagaru (the net connects, ga). Phone signal is denpa, not shingou, and apuri o ireru uses the same 'put in' ireru as dengen o ireru.

items.use: Said about checking facts, words and places online, often as an offer or a report: netto de shirabete miru (I'll look it up online), netto de shirabeta kedo wakannakatta (I looked it up but couldn't work it out). The de stays even in casual speech.
items.verbSense: look into, check, look up

example.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみる。
example.english: Let me look it up online.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto netto de shirabete mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとネットで調べてみます。
examplePolite.english: Let me look it up online.

items.freqNote: ググる (guguru, google it) is #24884 and 検索 (kensaku, search) #4276.
items.notes: o marks what you look up (netto de imi o shiraberu), and netto o shiraberu (search the net) is fine too. To find something like a shop or a flat, the verb is sagasu: netto de sagasu. guguru (google it) is the casual verb: gugutte mita.

items.use: Said mostly in the negative when Wi-Fi fails: netto tsunagaranai (the internet isn't working). The same verb covers a call going through: denwa tsunagaranai.
items.politeJa: ネットがつながります
items.verbSense: be connected, be linked
items.trap: Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect'); ugokanai is for a frozen app or device.

example.romaji: nanka netto tsunagaranai n da kedo.
example.ja: なんかネットつながらないんだけど。
example.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka netto ga tsunagaranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: なんかネットがつながらないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana つながる (繋がる #6342) and also counts people or things being linked.
items.notes: Transitive half: netto ni tsunagu (connect to the internet). Slow internet is netto ga omoi ('heavy'): kyou netto omoi ne. Asking about Wi-Fi: koko waifai tonderu? (tobu 'fly', casual).

items.use: Said when calls break up or pages won't load, usually without ga: koko denpa warui ne (the signal's bad here). On a call it comes as an apology: gomen, denpa warukute kikoenai (sorry, bad signal, I can't hear you).
items.verbSense: bad; poor (quality, condition)
items.trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.

example.ja: ここ、電波悪いね。
example.english: The signal's bad here, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa denpa ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここは電波が悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: The signal's bad here, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 圏外 (kengai, out of range) is #16111; verbRank 悪い pools every sense of bad.
items.notes: A weak signal is denpa ga yowai; no signal at all is usually denpa hairanai, also denpa nai or kengai (out of range).

items.english: install an app, get an app
items.use: Said when recommending or setting up apps: kono apuri irete (get this app), mada irete nai (I haven't got it yet). Casual speech drops o. daunroodo suru is just as everyday (shop staff and signs use it), and younger speakers also say otosu (apuri otoshita). insutooru suru sounds more technical.
items.verbSense: put in; install (an app, software)
items.trap: Not apuri o morau: English 'get the app' pulls toward morau, which sounds like someone handed it to you. Putting it on your phone is ireru ('put in').

example.romaji: kono apuri irete mite, benri da yo.
example.ja: このアプリ入れてみて、便利だよ。
example.english: Try getting this app, it's handy.

examplePolite.romaji: kono apuri, benri desu yo. yokattara irete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: このアプリ、便利ですよ。よかったら入れてみてください。
examplePolite.english: This app is handy. Give it a try if you like.

items.freqNote: No count: the films have no アプリを入れ. インストール (insutooru) is #23611.
items.notes: Deleting an app is apuri o kesu; updating it is appudeeto suru.

blocks.label: Plans and promises
blocks.rationale: How plans go: wait and see, called off, keep your word, plan it out.
blocks.interference: English verbs mislead in all four: 'wait and see' is yousu o miru, not matsu; events are called off with chuushi ni naru rather than kyanseru sareru; promises are mamoru (protect), not motsu; plans stand up with tateru, not tsukuru.

items.use: Said when you hold off acting to see how things go: a cold, a noise in the car, a plan (toriaezu yousu miyou). Doctors say nisannichi yousu o mimashou. It also means going to check on someone: chotto yousu mite kuru.
items.verbSense: see, look, watch
items.trap: English 'wait and see' leads to plain matsu, which says nothing about watching how things go. For holding off on a problem (a cold, a noise in the car, a plan) the set phrase is yousu o miru, 'look at how things are'. mou sukoshi matte miyou also works when you're waiting for something to happen.
partners: keika (progress: keika o mimashou = let's see how it goes, a doctor's line)
joukyou (how things stand: joukyou mite kimeyou = let's decide once we see how things are)
hannou (a reaction: aite no hannou o miru = see how they react)

example.ja: とりあえず様子見ようか。
example.english: Shall we just wait and see for now?

examplePolite.romaji: toriaezu yousu o mimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: とりあえず様子を見ましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we just wait and see for now?

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 様子を見る #3061. 見る #55 covers every sense. Pair count 314 (o 282); the noun 様子見 adds 27.
items.notes: The same noun describes how someone seems: yousu ga hen (he's acting strange). The noun yousumi is everyday too: shibaraku yousumi da ne (let's wait and see for a while).

items.use: How events get cancelled, mostly in the past: ame de shiai chuushi ni natta. Put off to a later date is enki ni naru, in the same frame.
items.verbSense: become; X ni naru = end up as X
items.trap: English 'cancelled' leads to kyanseru, which fits bookings, orders and your own plans (yoyaku kyanseru shita, kyou no yakusoku kyanseru shite ii?). An event that gets called off, such as a match, a festival, a concert or a school trip, is usually chuushi ni natta, and a cancelled flight is kekkou ni natta.

example.romaji: ame de shiai chuushi ni natta.
example.ja: 雨で試合中止になった。
example.english: The game got rained off.

examplePolite.romaji: ame de shiai ga chuushi ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 雨で試合が中止になりました。
examplePolite.english: The game was rained off.

items.freqNote: 中止 #2024; なる #29 is the kana form. 延期 enki #6376; phrase entry 延期になる #20128.
items.notes: Among friends, a plan that's off is often just nakunatta: kyou no nomikai nakunatta.

items.use: Said as a reminder (yakusoku mamotte ne), a reproach (yakusoku mamoranakatta ja nai) or, with wa, a pledge: daijoubu, yakusoku wa mamoru yo (don't worry, I'll keep my word). Being on time works the same way: jikan o mamoru.
items.verbSense: protect, defend; keep to (a promise, a rule, a deadline)
items.trap: English 'keep' leads to motsu or tamotsu, but promises, rules and deadlines are 'protected': yakusoku o mamoru, ruuru o mamoru, shimekiri o mamoru.
partners: jikan (time: jikan o mamoru = be on time)

example.romaji: kondo wa chanto yakusoku mamotte ne.
example.ja: 今度はちゃんと約束守ってね。
example.english: Make sure you keep your promise this time.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo wa chanto yakusoku o mamotte kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今度はちゃんと約束を守ってくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you keep your promise this time.

items.freqNote: 守る #303 also counts its 'protect' sense, inflated by drama plots. Phrase entry 約束を守る #7216. Pair count 247 (o 159, wa 73), with film pledges inflating the wa share.
items.notes: Breaking one is yakusoku o yaburu (yakusoku yabutta!). yakusoku also covers plans with friends: kyou wa tomodachi to yakusoku shiteru (I'm meeting a friend today).

items.use: For working out a plan ahead: a trip, savings, a study schedule. You mostly hear tateta or tateteru: ryokou no keikaku tateteru. The same verb goes with yotei: natsuyasumi no yotei o tateru.
items.verbSense: stand something up; set up (a plan, a goal)
items.trap: English 'make a plan' leads to keikaku o tsukuru, which is heard but far less often (17 against 128 in the subtitles). Plans and goals are 'stood up': keikaku o tateru, mokuhyou o tateru.

example.romaji: ima ryokou no keikaku tateteru n da.
example.ja: 今旅行の計画立ててるんだ。
example.english: I'm planning a trip right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima ryokou no keikaku o tateteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今旅行の計画を立ててるんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm planning a trip right now.

items.freqNote: 計画 #1502 covers every sense of 'plan', including projects. 立てる #1187. Phrase entry 計画を立てる #10041.
items.notes: 'Got plans?' is yotei aru?, not keikaku aru?; keikaku is a worked-out scheme.

blocks.label: Hats and accessories
blocks.rationale: The rest of what you wear, each with its own verb: a hat is pulled on with kaburu, a ring and a tie just take suru, perfume goes on with tsukeru.
blocks.interference: kaburu for anything over the head, suru for small worn items (as in masuku o suru), tsukeru for things put onto the body; a hat comes off with toru or nugu, a ring or tie with hazusu.

items.use: Usually boushi kabutteru (has a hat on) or boushi kabutte (put your hat on). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: pull over or put on the head
items.trap: Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.

example.ja: 今日帽子かぶってるね。
example.english: Oh, you've got a hat on today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa boushi o kabuttemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は帽子をかぶってますね。
examplePolite.english: You're wearing a hat today.

items.freqNote: Rank is for kana かぶる #1926, the usual spelling; the kanji 被る is #7902. The kana count also includes the casual 'clash/overlap' sense (yotei ga kaburu), so it overstates the wearing sense.
items.notes: Off: boushi o toru or nugu. kaburu also means 'clash', as in yotei ga kaburu.

items.use: Mostly heard as yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on) or shitenai, very often about a wedding ring: kekkon yubiwa shiteru. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
items.trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: a ring, like a watch, mask or tie, takes suru (yubiwa shiteru).

example.romaji: ano hito, kekkon yubiwa shiteru ne.
example.ja: あの人、結婚指輪してるね。
example.english: Oh, he's wearing a wedding ring.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa kekkon yubiwa o shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は結婚指輪をしてますね。
examplePolite.english: He's wearing a wedding ring.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 指輪 #3345 and する #15; 結婚指輪 kekkon yubiwa is #12423. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Slipping one on is often yubiwa o hameru, the same verb as for gloves (tebukuro o hameru), and hameteru also means has one on; yubiwa o tsukeru is fine too, a little more formal. The finger takes ni: kusuriyubi ni yubiwa shiteru (has a ring on the ring finger). It comes off with hazusu.

items.use: Mostly heard as nekutai shiteru (has a tie on) or, in dress-code talk, nekutai shinakute ii (no tie needed). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
items.trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie takes suru, like a mask or a watch (nekutai shiteru). nekutai o shimeru is tying it, and shimeteru is also a slightly more formal 'has one on'. It comes off with hazusu or toru.

example.romaji: kyou wa nekutai shinakute ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はネクタイしなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't need a tie today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nekutai o shinakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はネクタイをしなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't need to wear a tie today.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for ネクタイ #5375 and する #15. Office talk is under-counted in film subtitles, so pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Loosening it is nekutai o yurumeru; the summer kuuru bizu dress code means noo nekutai (no tie).

items.use: Heard as kousui tsuketeru? (are you wearing perfume?) or as a complaint, tsukesugi (too much). Casual speech drops o. tsuketeru means it's on, not that someone is putting it on now.
items.verbSense: attach, apply; put on (jewellery, perfume, cream)
items.trap: Not kousui o kiru: perfume takes tsukeru, the verb for anything applied or attached (earrings, a necklace, cream). kiru is only for clothes on the torso or whole body.

example.ja: いい匂い、香水つけてる？
example.english: You smell nice, are you wearing perfume?

examplePolite.romaji: ii kaori desu ne. kousui o tsuketeru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: いい香りですね。香水をつけてるんですか？
examplePolite.english: What a lovely scent. Are you wearing perfume?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 香水 #6814 and kana つける #393, which pools every tsukeru sense (付ける #1452, 着ける #3726). Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: For spraying it on, kousui o kakeru is also common (12 corpus hits against 19 for tsukeru).

blocks.label: University and jobs
blocks.rationale: Getting in somewhere: looking for work, finding it, entering a university or company, the experience you bring.
blocks.interference: Looking is shigoto o sagasu (o) but finding is shigoto ga mitsukaru (ga); daigaku and kaisha both take ni hairu, and keiken takes ga aru, not motsu.

items.use: Said about job hunting, mostly in -teru: ima shigoto sagashiteru (I'm looking for work). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: look for, search

example.romaji: ima atarashii shigoto sagashiteru n da.
example.ja: 今新しい仕事探してるんだ。
example.english: I'm looking for a new job right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima atarashii shigoto o sagashiteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今新しい仕事を探してるんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm looking for a new job right now.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 探す #391. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 64 of 73 hits keep o. 就活 shuukatsu #7063 is graduates' job hunting; 転職 tenshoku #4875 is changing jobs.
items.notes: Changing jobs is tenshoku suru; students' job hunting is shuukatsu.

items.use: The usual way to share or ask job news, almost always in the past: atarashii shigoto mitsukatta? Casual speech drops ga, and mada mitsukaranai means you're still looking.
items.verbSense: be found, turn up (intransitive of mitsukeru)

example.ja: やっと仕事見つかった！
example.english: I finally found a job!

examplePolite.romaji: yatto shigoto ga mitsukarimashita!
examplePolite.ja: やっと仕事が見つかりました！
examplePolite.english: I finally found a job!

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 見つかる #445, 見つける #311. No phrase entry. The subtitles have 23 hits with 見つかる and 61 with transitive 仕事を見つける; both are correct.
items.notes: Both work: shigoto mitsuketa (I found one) and shigoto mitsukatta (one turned up); the question is usually mitsukatta? Congratulating: shigoto mitsukatte yokatta ne.

items.use: Said in life stories, often as haitte kara (since I started) or haitta toki (when I started). Casual speech can drop ni; passing the entrance exam itself is daigaku ni ukaru.
items.verbSense: go in, enter; join (a school, company or club)
items.trap: 'Start university' tempts daigaku o hajimeru. You enter a school: daigaku ni hairu (formally nyuugaku suru). Going there day to day is daigaku ni iku or kayou.

example.ja: 大学入ってから一人暮らししてる。
example.english: I've lived alone since I started university.

examplePolite.romaji: daigaku ni haitte kara hitorigurashi o shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 大学に入ってから一人暮らしをしてます。
examplePolite.english: I've lived alone since I started university.

items.freqNote: 大学 #709, 入る #115, 入学 nyuugaku #4768. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 25 of 31 hits keep ni.
items.notes: Graduating is daigaku o deru or sotsugyou suru.

items.use: Said in self-introductions and work history: kono kaisha ni haitte sannen (three years since I joined). Casual speech can drop ni; the formal word is nyuusha suru.
items.verbSense: go in, enter; join (a school, company or club)
items.trap: 'Join a company' tempts sanka suru, which is taking part in an event. Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitta.

example.ja: この会社入って、もう三年。
example.english: It's been three years since I joined this company.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kaisha ni haitte, mou sannen desu.
examplePolite.ja: この会社に入って、もう三年です。
examplePolite.english: It's been three years since I joined this company.

items.freqNote: 会社 #474, 入る #115, 入社 nyuusha #4711. No phrase entry. Only 5 subtitle hits: films under-count work-history talk.
items.notes: Leaving for good is kaisha o yameru; kaisha ni iku is just going to the office.

items.use: Said in job talk and about life, usually with what kind before it: baito no keiken aru? Casual speech drops ga, and the negative keiken nai (I've never done it) is common too.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, a background)
items.trap: 'Have experience' tempts keiken o motteru, which sounds like a CV. Experience exists: keiken aru? For one thing you've done once, -ta koto aru is more natural: itta koto aru?
partners: buranku (a gap in your work history: buranku ga aru)

example.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken aru?
example.ja: こういう仕事の経験ある？
example.english: Have you done this kind of work before?

examplePolite.romaji: kou iu shigoto no keiken wa arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こういう仕事の経験はありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have experience with this kind of work?

items.freqNote: 経験 #1077, ある #21. No phrase entry. In the subtitles 経験 + ある has 231 hits (133 with ga, 39 with no particle); 経験 + ない has 117; 経験 + 持つ only 16.
items.notes: After a trip or a hard time: ii keiken ni natta (it was a good experience).

blocks.label: Visible signs
blocks.rationale: What shows on your body or someone else's: an injury, blood, sweat, a pale or flushed face. These are often followed by daijoubu?
blocks.interference: An injury takes suru (kega o suru), and blood comes out just like a fever does (chi ga deru, chi deteru yo). Sweat takes kaku (ase o kaku), which is not kaku 'write'. A pale face is kaoiro ga warui (bad colour), while a red face is just kao ga akai.

items.use: Heard as kega shita (I got hurt) and as the worried kega nai? (you're not hurt?) after a fall. Name the body part with o and drop kega's own o (ashi o kega shita), or use ni (ashi ni kega o shita); never two o's.
items.verbSense: do, make; here it turns the noun kega (injury) into something that happens
items.trap: Not itaku naru or kizutsuku (mostly hurt feelings): an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident.

example.ja: サッカーで足怪我しちゃった。
example.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

examplePolite.romaji: sakkaa de ashi o kega shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: サッカーで足を怪我したんです。
examplePolite.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

items.freqNote: けが #3721 (怪我 #7111); する #15. No phrase entry.

items.use: Said when you spot a cut: chi deteru yo (you're bleeding), or chi deta (it bled). Ga often drops in casual talk, and when it stops the blood tomaru (chi tomatta?).
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
items.trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo). Shukketsu suru is the medical word.

example.romaji: are, yubi kara chi deteru yo.
example.ja: あれ、指から血出てるよ。
example.english: Hey, your finger's bleeding.

examplePolite.romaji: are, yubi kara chi ga dete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、指から血が出ていますよ。
examplePolite.english: Oh, your finger is bleeding.

items.freqNote: 血 #1261; 出る #81. No phrase entry; 出血 shukketsu #4944 is the medical and news word.
items.notes: A nosebleed has its own word: hanaji ga deru (hanaji deteru yo).

items.use: Mostly heard in the past, ase kaita or ase kaichatta (I got all sweaty), after heat or exercise. For dripping with sweat natives say asedaku: asedaku ni natta.
items.verbSense: scratch; with sweat or snoring it means to give something off from the body
items.trap: 'Sweat' is a verb in English, but Japanese uses the noun with kaku: ase o kaku, not ase suru (ase ga deru, 'sweat comes out', is also fine). This kaku is not kaku 'write'.

example.ja: 汗かいたから、シャワー浴びたい。
example.english: I'm all sweaty, I want a shower.

examplePolite.romaji: ase o kaita node, shawaa o abite kite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 汗をかいたので、シャワーを浴びてきてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I got all sweaty. Would it be OK if I had a shower?

items.freqNote: 汗 #2650. Verb rank is kana かく #11889, the spelling used here, which mixes 掻く with kana-written 書く/描く. Kanji 掻く is #51963. Phrase entry 汗をかく #13368.
items.notes: The same kaku goes with embarrassment: haji kaita (I embarrassed myself).

items.use: A caring remark to someone who looks ill, kaoiro warui yo, usually followed by daijoubu? Ga often drops, and when they look better it's kaoiro yoku natta ne.
items.verbSense: bad, in poor condition
items.trap: Not kao ga shiroi, which sounds like fair skin: 'you look pale' is kaoiro ga warui (kaoiro warui yo). Kao ga aoi also works and sounds stronger; kao ga massao is white as a sheet, from shock, fear or feeling very sick.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)

example.ja: 顔色悪いよ。大丈夫？
example.english: You look pale. Are you OK?

examplePolite.romaji: kaoiro ga warui desu yo. daijoubu desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔色が悪いですよ。大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: You look pale. Are you all right?

items.freqNote: 顔色 #2897; 悪い #139; phrase entry 顔色が悪い #13422.
items.notes: Kaoiro o ukagau (read someone's face) is a separate idiom: checking their mood before you act.

items.use: Said to someone flushed from drink, a fever or embarrassment, often teasing: kao akai yo. Ga usually drops; going red as it happens is kao ga akaku naru (kao akaku natteru).
items.verbSense: red
items.trap: 'Blush' has no single everyday verb: the face goes red, kao ga akaku naru, or you tereru (get bashful); sekimen suru is bookish.
partners: me (eyes: me ga akai = red eyes)

example.ja: 顔赤いよ。酔った？
example.english: Your face is red. Are you drunk?

examplePolite.romaji: kao ga akai desu yo. yotta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 顔が赤いですよ。酔ったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Your face is red. Have you been drinking?

items.freqNote: 顔 #174; 赤い #1711; 真っ赤 makka #5350 (kao ga makka = bright red).
items.notes: Tereru (get bashful) is the verb behind most blushing: tereteru no?

blocks.label: Seasons
blocks.rationale: Sets that mark the year in daily talk: blossoms out in spring, summer heat and cicadas, snow lying in winter.
blocks.interference: semi ga naku uses naku (鳴く, an animal's call), not naku 'cry' (泣く), and pairs with kaminari ga naru: animals naku, things naru. atsusa ni yowai is the osake ga yowai idea with ni (samusa ni yowai for cold), and snow furu as it falls but tsumoru once it lies.

items.use: Mostly about cherry blossoms in spring: sakura saita? (are they out?), mou saiteru (they're already out), mada saitenai. Saiteru is the flowers being out now, not still opening. Ga is usually dropped.
items.verbSense: bloom, open (of flowers)
items.trap: 'The blossoms are out' points to deru, but flowers that are out are saiteru (sakura saiteru); hana ga deru isn't said. Hiraku is the petals opening, mostly in description, not the everyday word. Blossoms coming down are chiru: mou chitchatta (petals already on the ground are ochiteru).

example.ja: ベランダの花、咲いたよ。
example.english: The flowers on the balcony have come out.

examplePolite.romaji: beranda no hana ga sakimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: ベランダの花が咲きましたよ。
examplePolite.english: The flowers on the balcony have come out.

items.freqNote: The phrase 花が咲く is listed as a set expression at #8654. Kana はな also covers 鼻 (nose, #2627), so the kanji rank is used. 桜 is #3953, and its partner verb 散る is #5348.
items.notes: Peak bloom is mankai (ima mankai da tte), and going to see them is ohanami: ohanami ikanai?
