items.use: Said about yourself or someone else in summer: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne (I'm no good in the heat). The cold version, samusa ni yowai, is just as common. The ni stays.
items.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
items.trap: Atsusa takes ni: atsusa ga yowai isn't said (with osake, ga and ni both work). Atsui no nigate (I can't do heat) is just as everyday.

example.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 暑さに弱いんだよね。
example.english: I'm no good in the heat.

examplePolite.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑さに弱いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I'm no good in the heat.

items.freqNote: 暑さ #11178; 寒さ is #7547. 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. No corpus hits for the pair, so commonness is a judgement.
items.notes: The opposite is atsusa ni tsuyoi; atsusa is atsui + -sa (the heat), like samusa from samui.

items.use: Summer small talk, mostly semi naiteru (the cicadas are going) or semi nakihajimeta ne (the cicadas have started). Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: make its call (an animal, bird or insect)
items.trap: English has a verb per creature (sing, chirp, buzz, meow), but Japanese uses naku (鳴く) for nearly all of them, and it sounds the same as naku 'cry' (泣く). Tori ga utau is poetic; in talk it's naku.

example.ja: セミ鳴き始めたね。
example.english: The cicadas have started up.

examplePolite.romaji: semi ga nakihajimemashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: セミが鳴き始めましたね。
examplePolite.english: The cicadas have started up.

items.freqNote: セミ #14340 is the usual spelling (蝉 #48270). Kana なく is mostly 泣く 'cry' (#407), so the kanji 鳴く is used. Foreign films barely mention cicadas (2 hits for セミが鳴く, 7 more for セミの鳴き声), so commonness is a judgement.
items.notes: Autumn nights have mushi ga naku (crickets and other insects); a barking dog is usually hoeru.

items.english: snow settles, lies on the ground
items.use: Mostly as yuki tsumotteru (there's snow on the ground) or tsumoru kana? (will it settle?). Tsumotteru is the snow lying there, while snow still coming down is yuki futteru.
items.verbSense: pile up, build up (snow, dust)
items.trap: English 'the snow's sticking' points to tsuku, but snow building up on the ground is tsumoru; tsuku is snow stuck on things: kuruma ni yuki tsuiteru. Nokotteru is old snow that hasn't melted yet.

example.ja: 朝起きたら、雪積もってた。
example.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.

examplePolite.romaji: asa okitara, yuki ga tsumottemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 朝起きたら、雪が積もってました。
examplePolite.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.

items.freqNote: 積もる #9027 also covers the figurative tsumoru hanashi (lots to catch up on). How often the set comes up depends on region and season, so commonness is a judgement.
items.notes: Melting is tokeru: yuki mou toketa ne.

blocks.label: Your place
blocks.rationale: Talking about where you live: renting, a cramped room, keeping a pet, parcels arriving.
blocks.interference: Renting uses kariru, the 'borrow' verb, and a cramped room is usually semai (narrow) rather than chiisai. The kau of keeping a pet sounds like kau 'buy', and parcels todoku (reach you) rather than tsuku (arrive) like people.

items.use: For renting a place to live as the tenant: hitorigurashi de heya karita (I rented a place of my own). Casual speech drops o, and heya here usually means the whole flat.
items.verbSense: borrow; use something that is someone else's, free or paid
items.trap: There's no separate 'rent' verb: the tenant kariru (borrows) and the landlord kasu (lends), so heya o kasu means letting it out. rentaru suru is for cars and kimono, not flats.

example.romaji: eki no chikaku ni heya karita n da.
example.ja: 駅の近くに部屋借りたんだ。
example.english: I've rented a place near the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no chikaku ni heya o karita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の近くに部屋を借りたんです。
examplePolite.english: I've rented a place near the station.

items.freqNote: 借りる #673 counts every kind of borrowing; 貸す kasu (lend, let out) is #658.
items.notes: The monthly rent is yachin (yachin takai = the rent's high).

items.use: Rooms and flats are usually judged semai (cramped) or hiroi (roomy): semai heya da kedo, douzo. As a comment it's heya ga semai, usually without ga: kono heya semai ne.
items.verbSense: narrow, cramped; small in floor space
items.trap: 'Small' points to chiisai, but a room that feels cramped is semai, and a roomy one is hiroi: kono heya semai ne. chiisai heya is fine for a room's size (chiisai heya ga futatsu aru), just not as the complaint.

example.ja: 狭い部屋だけど、どうぞ。
example.english: It's a tiny place, but come in.

examplePolite.romaji: semai heya desu kedo, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 狭い部屋ですけど、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: It's a small room, but please come in.

items.freqNote: 狭い #1805; its opposite 広い hiroi is #1347.
items.notes: The host's set line is semai tokoro da kedo, douzo (politely semai tokoro desu ga); the visitor's compliment is hiroi ne! semai also covers narrow roads.

items.use: Almost always in the -teru form: inu katteru (I have a dog), nanika katteru? (do you have any pets?). inu ga iru (there's a dog) also works for 'I have a dog'.
items.verbSense: keep, raise (an animal); sounds the same as kau 'buy'
items.trap: Not inu o motte iru: pets are kept with kau, the sound-alike of 'buy'. inu ga iru also works.

example.ja: うち、犬飼ってるんだ。
example.english: We've got a dog at home.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa inu o katte iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは犬を飼っているんです。
examplePolite.english: We have a dog at home.

items.freqNote: The homophone 買う (buy) is #238.
items.notes: katteru also means 'have bought'. In standard Tokyo speech kau 'keep' is accented on ka (KAtteru) while kau 'buy' is flat; context does the rest.

items.use: For deliveries and online orders, mostly in the past: nimotsu todoita (my parcel came), or still waiting: mada todokanai. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: reach, get to (someone); also reach with a hand
items.trap: 'Arrive' points to tsuku, which is people and trains arriving (eki ni tsuku). Things sent to you mostly todoku, 'reach you', the same verb as for letters and messages; nimotsu ga tsuku is heard but less usual.

example.ja: 昨日頼んだ荷物、もう届いた。
example.english: The parcel I ordered yesterday already came.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou tanonda nimotsu ga mou todokimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日頼んだ荷物がもう届きました。
examplePolite.english: The package I ordered yesterday has already arrived.

items.freqNote: 届く #738 also counts reaching (te ga todokanai = can't reach); 届ける todokeru (deliver, hand in) is #1208.
items.notes: A missed delivery means asking for saihaitatsu (redelivery).

blocks.label: Worries and advice
blocks.rationale: Talking a problem through: having something on your mind, asking for advice, hearing someone out, and saying what you really think.
blocks.interference: soudan ga aru (can I ask your advice?) is the side with the problem and soudan ni noru (I'll hear you out) is the friend's side; neither uses adobaisu. honne o iu is saying what you really feel, where shoujiki ni iu is just being frank.

items.use: Mostly heard as the caring question nanka nayami aru no? (is something bothering you?) or the offer nayami ga aru nara kiku yo (if something's on your mind, I'll listen). nayamigoto means the same, and koi no nayami is love trouble.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, problems, something to bring up)

example.ja: なんか悩みあるの？
example.english: Is something bothering you?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika nayami demo aru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か悩みでもあるんですか？
examplePolite.english: Is something on your mind?

items.freqNote: 悩み #2043; ある #21. 悩み事 (nayamigoto) #9993. Written 悩みがあ 16.
items.notes: The verb nayamu means to agonise or be torn: dotchi ni suru ka nayanderu (I can't decide which). shinpai is worrying about what might happen; nayami is a problem you keep turning over. nayami o motsu and nayami o kakaeru (be carrying worries) say the same in a more written style.

items.use: Opens a talk about something you need help deciding, and usually trails off: chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo... ga is usually kept, as with hanashi ga aru and onegai ga aru, though soudan aru n da kedo is heard too.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
items.trap: soudan sounds like a formal 'consultation', but it's the everyday word for running something by a friend. 'Can I ask your advice?' is chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo; adobaisu kudasai sounds abrupt.

example.romaji: chotto soudan ga aru n da kedo, ii?
example.ja: ちょっと相談があるんだけど、いい？
example.english: Can I ask your advice about something?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto soudan ga aru n desu kedo, ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと相談があるんですけど、いいですか？
examplePolite.english: Could I ask your advice about something?

items.freqNote: 相談 #560 counts every soudan use (soudan suru, soudan ni noru); ある #21. No phrase entry. Written 相談があ 18.
items.notes: The listener answers un, nani? or ii yo, soudan noru yo (sure, I'm listening).

items.use: Said by the one giving support, as an offer (nanka attara soudan ni noru yo) or a request (chotto soudan notte kurenai? = can I run something by you?). It means listening and helping think it through, not just telling someone what to do.
items.verbSense: ride, get on; here, get on board with someone's problem
items.trap: English 'give advice' leads to adobaisu suru, which is fine for passing on tips. Offering to hear someone out and help them think it through is soudan ni noru, and asking for that is soudan suru.

example.ja: いつでも相談に乗るよ。
example.english: I'm always here if you need to talk.

examplePolite.romaji: itsudemo soudan ni norimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いつでも相談に乗りますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm happy to help anytime.

items.freqNote: 相談 #560; 乗る #439 (載る #2368 is a different verb). Phrase entry 相談に乗る #3754, high for a phrase.
items.notes: The asker opens with soudan ga aru n da kedo, or says senpai ni soudan shita (I went to my senpai for advice). noru also means go along with: sono hanashi noru (I'm in), sasoi ni noru (take someone up on an offer).

items.use: Two everyday uses: honne o iu to... opens a frank admission (to be honest...), and honne itte yo asks someone to drop the politeness and tell you straight. honne is the real feeling behind tatemae, the polite surface.
items.verbSense: say

example.romaji: honne o iu to, chotto iya da na.
example.ja: 本音を言うと、ちょっと嫌だな。
example.english: To be honest, I'm not too keen.

examplePolite.romaji: honne o iu to, chotto iya na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 本音を言うと、ちょっと嫌なんです。
examplePolite.english: To be honest, I'd rather not.

items.freqNote: 本音 #3070; 言う #28. Phrase entry 本音を言う #14580; 建前 (tatemae) #19759. Written 本音を言 31.
items.notes: honne to tatemae (real feelings vs the polite front) is a pair every Japanese person knows; shoujiki ni iu to also means 'to be honest'.

blocks.label: Using your time
blocks.rationale: The jikan o verbs for what you do with time: put it into something, set it aside, make it, kill it.
blocks.interference: English spend, take, make and kill map to kakeru, toru, tsukuru and tsubusu (crush), never korosu; how long something takes stays jikan ga kakaru, and spending time with people is sugosu.

items.english: put time into, take time over
items.use: For spending time on something on purpose, mostly as kakete before another verb: jikan kakete tsukutta (I put real time into making it). With an amount, jikan drops: sanjikan kaketa. 'Take your time' is usually yukkuri de ii yo; jikan kakete ii yo is for a task: jikkuri jikan kakete ii yo.
items.verbSense: hang; put on; spend (time or money on something)
items.trap: 'I spent three hours on it' is sanjikan kaketa (or kakatta), not sugoshita: sugosu is for spending time somewhere or with someone.
partners: tema (effort: tema o kakeru = go to the trouble)

example.romaji: kore, kekkou jikan kakete tsukutta n da.
example.ja: これ、けっこう時間かけて作ったんだ。
example.english: I put quite a lot of time into making this.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa kekkou jikan o kakete tsukutta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: これはけっこう時間をかけて作ったんです。
examplePolite.english: I put quite a lot of time into making this.

items.freqNote: かける #244 is the kana form across every sense (call, sit, put on glasses); 掛ける #2742. Phrase entry 時間をかける #5443. Pair count 191.
items.notes: Its intransitive partner jikan ga kakaru is how long something takes; kakeru is you choosing to spend it.

items.english: set aside time, take up time
items.use: Mostly in thanks and apologies: jikan totte kurete arigatou (thanks for making time), ojikan torasete sumimasen (sorry to take up your time). It also means setting time aside: kondo chanto jikan toru ne.
items.verbSense: take; get (here: take or set aside time)
items.trap: English 'it takes an hour' leads to toru, but how long something takes is kakaru: ichijikan kakaru. toru is someone setting time aside, or taking up yours: jikan totte kurete arigatou, ojikan torasete sumimasen.

example.romaji: kyou wa jikan totte kurete arigatou.
example.ja: 今日は時間取ってくれてありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for making time today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ojikan totte itadaite, arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はお時間取っていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for making time today.

items.freqNote: 取る #228 (撮る, take a photo, is #649). Phrase entry 時間を取る #24464. Pair count 89.
items.notes: jikan toreru? asks if someone can spare time. A short polite thank-you, (kichou na) ojikan o arigatou gozaimashita, is also fine, and formal thanks use saku: ojikan o saite itadaite.

items.use: Said when promising to fit someone in, often in the potential: raishuu nara jikan tsukureru yo. In thanks it's jikan tsukutte kurete arigatou.
items.verbSense: make; create

example.ja: 来週なら時間作れるよ。
example.english: I can make time next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu nara jikan o tsukuremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 来週なら時間を作れますよ。
examplePolite.english: I can make time next week.

items.freqNote: 作る #146 covers every sense of make and cook. Phrase entry 時間を作る #16575. Pair count 52.
items.notes: Close to jikan o toru: tsukuru stresses squeezing time out of a busy schedule. Both work in thanks (jikan tsukutte kurete arigatou / jikan totte kurete arigatou).

items.use: Said when you're early or waiting for someone: kafe de jikan tsubushiteru ne. The noun himatsubushi (something to pass the time) is just as common: himatsubushi ni sumaho miteta.
items.verbSense: crush, squash; use up (time); ruin
items.trap: Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush'.

example.romaji: hayaku tsuita kara, kafe de jikan tsubushiteru.
example.ja: 早く着いたから、カフェで時間潰してる。
example.english: I got here early, so I'm killing time in a café.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku tsuita node, kafe de jikan o tsubushitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 早く着いたので、カフェで時間を潰してます。
examplePolite.english: I got here early, so I'm killing time in a café.

items.freqNote: 潰す #2027 also covers 'crush' and 'ruin'; the kana つぶす is #4184. Phrase entry 時間を潰す #32831; 暇つぶし #12575. Pair count 35.
items.notes: tsubusu also means flatten (akikan o tsubusu). A day off that gets eaten up is yasumi ga tsubureta.

blocks.label: Getting work done
blocks.rationale: The work itself: using your head, delivering results, taking notes, ideas coming to you, stamping papers.
blocks.interference: kekka o dasu (you deliver results) is not kekka ga deru (results come out); ideas come to you with ga ukabu, while notes are taken with o toru.

items.english: use your head; make you think
items.use: Said as a blunt scolding (chotto wa atama tsukae yo, use your head for once) and about brain-heavy games and work: atama tsukau shigoto. Casual speech often drops o.
items.verbSense: use

example.romaji: kono geemu, kekkou atama tsukau ne.
example.ja: このゲーム、結構頭使うね。
example.english: This game really makes you think.

examplePolite.romaji: kono geemu wa kekkou atama o tsukaimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このゲームは結構頭を使いますね。
examplePolite.english: This game really makes you think.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 頭を使う has its own entry in the drama list at #12701 (頭 #375, 使う #171). In the subtitles 74 of 88 hits keep o.
items.notes: Not ki o tsukau, which means being considerate.

items.use: Said about performance at work, in sport or in study, often as a must: kekka dasanai to (I need to show results). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put out, take out, send out; here: produce
items.trap: 'Get results' tempts kekka o morau. Results you achieve are put out: kekka o dasu. Results being announced is kekka ga deru, and kekka o morau only fits being handed a results sheet.
partners: kiroku (record: kiroku o dasu = set a record)

example.ja: 今年は絶対結果出す。
example.english: This year I'm going to get results, no matter what.

examplePolite.romaji: kotoshi wa zettai kekka o dashimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今年は絶対結果を出します。
examplePolite.english: This year I'm going to get results, no matter what.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 結果を出す has its own entry in the drama list at #8074 (結果 #626, 出す #163). In the subtitles 52 of 63 hits keep o.
items.notes: Learn it beside kekka ga deru: kekka deta (they're out) vs kekka dashita (I delivered).

items.use: Said in class, meetings and on the phone: chotto matte, memo toru kara. Casual speech drops o, and memo suru means the same and is at least as common.
items.verbSense: take; take down (a record)

example.ja: ちょっと待って、メモ取るから。
example.english: Hang on, let me write that down.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, ima memo o torimasu node.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、今メモを取りますので。
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, let me write that down.

items.freqNote: メモ #2955, 取る #228. No phrase entry. In the subtitles メモする has 53 hits against 16 for メモを取る; ノートを取る adds 6.
items.notes: A note left for someone is memo o nokosu.

items.use: Mostly in the negative, while brainstorming or choosing a gift: nanimo ukabanai (nothing comes to mind). When one arrives, ii aidea ukanda! Casual speech drops ga.
items.politeJa: アイデアが浮かびます
items.verbSense: float; come to mind
items.trap: 'I've got an idea!' is ii kangae ga aru! (or ii aidea aru!, omoitsuita!). ukabu is for ideas coming, or not coming, to mind: nanimo ukabanai.

example.ja: 全然いいアイデア浮かばない。
example.english: I can't come up with any good ideas.

examplePolite.romaji: zenzen ii aidea ga ukabimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 全然いいアイデアが浮かびません。
examplePolite.english: I can't come up with any good ideas.

items.freqNote: アイデア #2472 (アイディア #21121), 浮かぶ #2420, 思いつく omoitsuku #1957. No phrase entry. About 20 subtitle hits across both spellings; 考えが浮かぶ adds 24, and いい考えがある has 88.
items.notes: omoitsuku is the active twin: ii koto omoitsuita!

items.use: Heard at the bank, the city office, at work and for deliveries: koko ni hanko oshite kudasai. Casual speech drops o; for deliveries a signature usually works too: sain de ii desu ka?
items.verbSense: push, press
items.trap: 'Stamp' leads to sutanpu, which means a rubber stamp for fun or a chat sticker. A personal seal is a hanko (formally inkan), and you press it: hanko o osu.

example.ja: ここにハンコ押してね。
example.english: Stamp your seal here, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: koko ni hanko o oshite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: ここにハンコを押してください。
examplePolite.english: Please stamp your seal here.

items.freqNote: ハンコ #9936 (はんこ #13175, 印鑑 inkan #12048), 押す #1149. No phrase entry. Only 2 literal subtitle hits (one a sound-effect caption); 判 + 押す adds 13, some of them the idiom 太鼓判を押す. Paperwork is under-counted in foreign films.
items.notes: Banks and contracts want the registered inkan; deliveries usually accept a sain (signature).

blocks.label: When it hits you
blocks.rationale: Reactions to a big moment like a concert, a sad film or big news: tears come, goosebumps rise, it hasn't sunk in yet.
blocks.interference: Each reaction is the subject with its own verb: namida ga deru (not naku, which is crying outright), torihada ga tatsu (stand, not deru). jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in) sounds close to wakannai (I don't get it).

items.use: Tears that come on their own, mostly past: namida deta after a yawn, onions, laughing too hard or a moving film, with ga often dropped. namida dete kita is welling up as it happens, and namida desou (I'm going to cry) comes at a moving scene; crying outright is naku.
items.verbSense: come out, appear
items.trap: Learners use naku (cry) for any tears, but naku is crying from emotion. Watery eyes from a yawn, onions, hay fever or laughing are namida ga deru: akubi shitara namida deta. At a moving film both work: naita, or the softer namida deta (I teared up).

example.ja: 笑いすぎて涙出た。
example.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

examplePolite.romaji: waraisugite namida ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 笑いすぎて涙が出ました。
examplePolite.english: I laughed so hard I teared up.

items.freqNote: The phrase has its own entry, 涙が出る #6982; 泣く naku is #407. Subtitle pair count 25 (ga 22).
items.notes: namida ga tomaranai means the tears won't stop, from a sad film or from hay fever.

items.use: Mostly past as a reaction, with ga dropped: torihada tatta! after a great song, a scary story or a cold blast of air. mite, torihada tatteru (look, I've got goosebumps) shows them as they happen.
items.verbSense: stand, rise; here the bumps on your skin stand up
items.trap: 'Get goosebumps' pulls learners toward morau or dekiru, but goosebumps 'stand up': torihada ga tatsu. It's the plain word for all goosebumps: cold, fear or being moved.

example.ja: 今の歌、鳥肌立った！
example.english: That song just gave me goosebumps!

examplePolite.romaji: ima no uta, torihada ga tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今の歌、鳥肌が立ちました。
examplePolite.english: That song just gave me goosebumps.

items.freqNote: 鳥肌 #19017; phrase entries 鳥肌が立つ #23053 and the ga-less 鳥肌立つ #25477. Subtitle pair count 9, plus 4 kana たつ hits the tokenizer filed under 経つ. As a reaction to songs and live shows it is likely more common in life than in scripts (a judgement, not data).
items.notes: Once only for cold, fear or disgust; for being moved it's now standard. torihada mono (goosebump-worthy) is the casual compliment.

items.use: Mostly negative, after big news like passing an exam, a new job, a wedding or a baby: mada jikkan wakanai (it hasn't sunk in yet). jikkan nai says the same, and the polite mada jikkan ga wakanai desu is a stock line in interviews. Once it does sink in: yatto jikkan waite kita.
items.verbSense: well up, spring up (water, feelings)
items.trap: Learners reach for mada wakaranai or rikai shite nai, which sound like you don't understand the news. Japanese says the real feeling hasn't welled up: mada jikkan wakanai. mada shinjirarenai (I still can't believe it) also works.
partners: imeeji (imeeji ga wakanai: can't picture it)

example.ja: まだ全然実感湧かない。
example.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.

examplePolite.romaji: mada zenzen jikkan ga wakanai desu.
examplePolite.ja: まだ全然実感が湧かないです。
examplePolite.english: It still hasn't sunk in at all.

items.freqNote: Phrase entries 実感が湧く #28148 and 実感がわく #51487; 湧く #3148. The subtitle pair count is 9, filed under 沸く 'boil' because the tokenizer lemmatises わく that way (the subtitles mostly write 湧く); film dialogue likely under-counts the interview line.
items.notes: Don't mix up wakanai (doesn't well up, from waku) with wakannai (don't get it): one n apart.

blocks.label: Seasonal outings
blocks.rationale: The two big outings of the Japanese year: cherry-blossom viewing in spring, and the first shrine visit at New Year, where you draw a fortune slip.
blocks.interference: In speech hanami is nearly always ohanami. omikuji o hiku uses hiku 'pull, draw', as in kuji o hiku (draw lots), not toru. It sounds the same as piano o hiku but is a different verb.

items.use: The spring outing everyone talks about: ohanami ikou, ohanami itta? Casual speech drops ni. It is mostly a picnic under the cherry trees with food and drinks, not just looking. Plain hanami is heard mostly in compounds like hanami kyaku (blossom-viewing crowds).
items.verbSense: go (hanami = hana 'flowers' + mi 'viewing', here with polite o-)

example.romaji: raishuu, minna de ohanami ikou yo.
example.ja: 来週、みんなでお花見行こうよ。
example.english: Let's all go see the cherry blossoms next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu, minna de ohanami ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、みんなでお花見に行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's all go cherry-blossom viewing next week.

items.freqNote: 花見 #10548; お花見, the form you hear most, has no entry of its own. Films barely mention it (7 lines, 4 of them お花見), but it is a fixture of every Japanese spring.
items.notes: The blossoms coming out is sakura ga saku, and full bloom is mankai.

items.english: make the year's first shrine visit
items.use: Asked by everyone in early January: hatsumoude itta? It means the year's first visit to a shrine or temple, usually in the first few days of the year. Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: go (hatsumoude = hatsu 'first' + moude 'visit to a shrine')
items.trap: 'Visit' pulls toward houmon suru, which is a formal call on a person or company. Visiting a shrine is just going: hatsumoude ni iku, or on other days jinja ni omairi ni iku. hatsumoude suru (hatsumoude shita?) is also fine.

example.ja: 初詣、もう行った？
example.english: Been to the shrine for New Year yet?

examplePolite.romaji: hatsumoude ni wa mou ikimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 初詣にはもう行きましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you made your New Year shrine visit yet?

items.freqNote: 初詣 #22266 never appears in the film subtitles, yet hatsumoude itta? is one of the most-asked questions of early January.
items.notes: At the shrine most people also draw a fortune: omikuji o hiku.

items.use: Said at shrine and temple visits, especially at New Year: omikuji hiita? and then what you got (daikichi datta!). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: pull; also draw lots, a card or a raffle
items.trap: English 'draw' leads to kaku, which is drawing a picture. Drawing lots, a card or a fortune is hiku (pull): omikuji o hiku, kuji o hiku. It is the hiku of kaze o hiku, not the one in piano o hiku.

example.ja: おみくじ引いたら、大吉だった！
example.english: I drew a fortune slip and got great luck!

examplePolite.romaji: omikuji o hiitara, daikichi deshita!
examplePolite.ja: おみくじを引いたら、大吉でした！
examplePolite.english: I drew a fortune slip and got great luck!

items.freqNote: 引く #1039 covers every 'pull' sense, including kaze o hiku. 大吉 (daikichi, great luck) is #15710. Films use おみくじ only 6 times.
items.notes: Fortunes run from daikichi (great luck) down to kyou or even daikyou (bad, very bad luck), and a bad one is tied to a rack at the shrine and left behind.

blocks.label: Moving your body
blocks.rationale: Body instructions heard in class, at the doctor or at a massage: raise your hand, close your eyes, relax.
blocks.interference: Eyes take tojiru, not shimeru (which is for doors and windows). chikara o nuku pulls the strength out and is the opposite of chikara o ireru. te o ageru can also mean raising a hand to someone (hitting them).

items.use: Heard in class, at meetings and at events as a request: shitsumon aru hito, te agete. With ni and a person it means raising a hand against them: kodomo ni te o ageru (hit a child).
items.verbSense: raise, lift up; the same-sounding ageru also means give

example.ja: 質問ある人、手挙げて。
example.english: Anyone with a question, put your hand up.

examplePolite.romaji: shitsumon ga aru kata wa, te o agete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 質問がある方は、手を挙げてください。
examplePolite.english: If you have a question, please raise your hand.

items.freqNote: 手 #259; 挙げる #2605 is the spelling for raising a hand (挙手 kyoshu #13383 is the formal word). 上げる #837 is also written, and is the usual spelling for 'hands up!' and for hitting someone; kana あげる #668 is mostly 'give'. Phrase entries 手を上げる #8267 and 手を挙げる #11089.
items.notes: Films inflate the count with police shouting te o agero (hands up!). Putting it down is te o orosu.

items.use: Mostly heard as a request, me tojite: at the dentist under the lamp, with eye drops, or before a surprise. Photos are the opposite: me tsubutchatta (I blinked). Casual speech uses me tsubutte just as much, and o often drops in both.
items.verbSense: close, shut (eyes, a book, an app); doors and windows take shimeru instead
items.trap: Doors and windows take shimeru, so learners say me o shimeru. Eyes take tojiru, or the casual tsuburu: me tsubutte.

example.romaji: ii tte iu made, me tojitete ne.
example.ja: いいって言うまで、目閉じててね。
example.english: Keep your eyes shut till I say so.

examplePolite.romaji: ii to iu made, me o tojite ite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: いいと言うまで、目を閉じていてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please keep your eyes closed until I say so.

items.freqNote: 目 #216; 閉じる #3880, with the casual つぶる #8069 not far behind. Phrase entries 目を閉じる #6910 and 目をつぶる #7140 are almost level.
items.notes: Opening them again is me o akeru. Me o tsuburu also means 'let it slide' (overlook a fault).

items.use: Heard as an instruction at massages, the doctor's, sport and yoga: chikara nuite, or motto kata no chikara nuite. O often drops in the request.
items.verbSense: pull out, take out (a tooth, a plug); let out (air, tension); also skip (a meal)
partners: kuuki (air: let air out of a tyre)
ki (attention: ki o nuku = let your guard down)

example.romaji: motto chikara nuite. sou, sono kanji.
example.ja: もっと力抜いて。そう、その感じ。
example.english: Relax more. Yes, like that.

examplePolite.romaji: motto chikara o nuite kudasai. hai, sono kanji desu.
examplePolite.ja: もっと力を抜いてください。はい、その感じです。
examplePolite.english: Please relax a bit more. Yes, that's it.

items.freqNote: 力 #456; 抜く #1432; phrase entry 力を抜く #17281.
items.notes: The opposite is chikara o ireru (put strength in). Rirakkusu shite is the other everyday instruction; chikara nuite targets a tense part (kata no chikara nuite), and kata no chikara o nuku also means 'stop trying so hard'.

blocks.label: Body and fitness
blocks.rationale: What someone's body can do: see, run, play sport, keep going; often said about yourself in the negative (me warui, tairyoku nai).
blocks.interference: English adjectives (short-sighted, fast, athletic, fit) all become noun + ga + word: the eyes are bad, the legs are fast, the motor nerves are good, the stamina is there. Speed is hayai, coordination is ii, and stamina takes aru/nai, not ii.

items.use: Said about yourself to explain glasses or squinting: me warui kara... Casual speech drops ga. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta.
items.verbSense: warui: bad, in poor condition
items.trap: Not warui me o motteru ('have bad eyes'): Japanese makes the eyes the subject, me ga warui. English 'short-sighted' has no everyday one-word match either: kinshi and shiryoku ga warui are the terms you hear at eye exams. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta, not warui ni natta.

example.romaji: me warui kara, megane nai to nanimo mienai n da.
example.ja: 目悪いから、メガネないと何も見えないんだ。
example.english: My eyesight's bad, so I can't see a thing without my glasses.

examplePolite.romaji: me ga warui node, megane ga nai to nanimo mienai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 目が悪いので、メガネがないと何も見えないんです。
examplePolite.english: My eyesight is poor, so I can't see anything without glasses.

items.freqNote: 目 #216; 悪い #139; 視力 shiryoku #11362; 近視 kinshi #61905.
items.notes: The opposite, me ga ii, means good eyesight. 'Has a good eye' (for people or things) is miru me ga aru.

items.use: Said about kids, classmates and athletes: ano ko, ashi hayai ne, often with ga dropped. Japanese puts the speed in the legs, ashi ga hayai; hashiru no ga hayai also works. The opposite is ashi ga osoi (a slow runner).
items.verbSense: hayai: fast; the same word also means early
partners: shigoto (shigoto ga hayai: a fast worker)
henji (henji ga hayai: quick to reply)

example.romaji: ano ko, kurasu de ichiban ashi hayai n da.
example.ja: あの子、クラスで一番足速いんだ。
example.english: That kid's the fastest runner in the class.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa kurasu de ichiban ashi ga hayai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの子はクラスで一番足が速いんです。
examplePolite.english: That child is the fastest runner in the class.

items.freqNote: 足 #707; 速い #2346 (speed). The kana はやい also covers 早い #396 (early), so the kana rank overstates this sense. The phrase itself is listed under the other spelling, 足が早い #89256, and the opposite as 足が遅い #58166 (足速い #37273 is ashibayai, 'brisk-paced', a different word). The film count (22) is filed under 早い too, pooling both spellings.
items.notes: ashi ga hayai also means food spoils fast (namamono wa ashi ga hayai).

items.use: The everyday 'athletic, coordinated': ano hito, undou shinkei ii yo ne, with ga dropped. The opposite, undou shinkei ga nai, is common self-deprecation, and so is undou onchi (uncoordinated).
items.kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not asurechikku (in Japanese that's an obstacle-course playground): say undou shinkei ga ii. supootsu ga tokui and undou ga dekiru (good at sports) are also natural.

example.romaji: undou shinkei ii ne! nanka supootsu yatteta?
example.ja: 運動神経いいね！なんかスポーツやってた？
example.english: You're athletic! Did you use to play a sport?

examplePolite.romaji: undou shinkei ga ii desu ne! nanika supootsu yatteta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 運動神経がいいですね！何かスポーツやってたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You're really athletic! Did you play a sport?

items.freqNote: 運動神経 #12050 as a whole compound. It occurs almost only in this phrase and in undou shinkei ga nai / warui, so the phrase is more common than the rank suggests. 運動音痴 undou onchi #37364.
items.notes: Literally 'motor nerves are good'.

items.use: Heard most in the negative, about age or being out of shape: mou tairyoku nai (I've got no stamina left), with ga dropped. Tairyoku aru ne praises someone who keeps going, and a drop in stamina is tairyoku ga ochita.
items.verbSense: aru: there is; have (things, qualities)
items.trap: 'Fit' isn't fitto (in Japanese that's how clothes fit). genki covers 'well, healthy' (mada genki = still going strong), but for stamina and being in shape use tairyoku: tairyoku aru / tairyoku nai.

example.romaji: saikin undou shitenai kara, tairyoku nai n da.
example.ja: 最近運動してないから、体力ないんだ。
example.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I've got no stamina.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin undou shite inai node, tairyoku ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近運動していないので、体力がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I have no stamina.

items.freqNote: 体力 #3077; ある #21, ない #43. The film count (6) is too low to use, so commonness is judged. 体力的 tairyokuteki #20161; スタミナ #13386; 運動不足 undou busoku #19482.
items.notes: tairyoku o tsukeru (build up stamina) is the usual resolution: tairyoku tsukenakya.

notes: Out of scope by design: figurative idioms (te o kasu, ki ga au, atama ni kuru) — saved for a separate idiom list; grammar patterns (hitsuyou ga aru, shikata ga nai); plain noun + suru verbs (shinpai suru); free combinations; sets common only in film plots.
Not repeated from the versatility list: ki ni naru, ki ni suru, ki ga suru, ki o tsukeru, renraku suru.

Two workflows: the first gathered 595 candidates by topic and gap hunts and wrote the first list; the second counted every noun + verb pair in the subtitle corpus, sorted the 1,848 most frequent typical pairs (520 new everyday sets, 175 idioms saved), and re-selected the list on commonness and typicality with three judges (data, everyday Japan, complete sets). New entries were reviewed four ways (native naturalness, whether each trap is really a mistake, meaning and register, romaji and data).
The corpus is mostly subtitles for foreign films, so Japan-specific daily life (konbini, warikan, kasa o sasu) is under-counted; those sets were judged on native commonness instead.

cuts.trap: English 'disturb/bother' has no matching verb: it is jama (o) suru, and entering someone's home is the set phrase ojama shimasu.
cuts.reason: A plain suru verb (jama suru, 1342 hits); ojama shimasu is a greeting you learn on its own.

cuts.trap: Not shitsumon o kiku: 'ask a question' is shitsumon (o) suru, and kiku alone means 'ask' without the noun.
cuts.reason: Really the suru verb shitsumon suru; the kept shitsumon ga aru already handles asking questions.

cuts.trap: 'Have time' uses aru, not motsu.
cuts.reason: Very common (725), but it is just jikan ga nai with aru, so learning that one gives you this.

cuts.trap: Not ki o tsukeru: caring for a pet, child or plant is sewa o suru (inu no sewa).
cuts.reason: The added mendou o miru says 'look after' for kids, pets and juniors; sewa suru is a plain suru verb.

cuts.trap: 'Interested' is an adjective in English; Japanese says kyoumi ga aru/nai.
cuts.reason: Just the negative of the kept kyoumi ga aru, so kyoumi nai comes with it for free.
Free combination: miru goes with anything you look at; kao mitai is just 'want to see you'.

cuts.trap: Getting out of bed is okiru; me o samasu is coming awake.
cuts.reason: Same 'wake up' as me ga sameru, which is on the list and is the form people say more.

cuts.trap: Not tatakau, which means battle: a fight or argument between people is kenka suru (kare to kenka shita, with to).
cuts.reason: A plain suru verb (kenka suru, 507 hits); learn it as one verb: kare to kenka shita.

cuts.trap: No single verb for 'ruin'; say dainashi ni suru/naru.
cuts.reason: Means 'ruin, spoil' (a day off, a dinner, a surprise). Film drama inflates its 466 hits, but sekkaku no ... ga dainashi is everyday talk.
Common (463): sorosoro shigoto ni modoranakya, 'I'd better get back to work'. Films inflate it, but offices say it every day.

cuts.trap: Not kao o tsukuru: wearing an expression is kao o suru, as in hen na kao shiteru or sonna kao shinaide.
cuts.reason: Making a face is X na kao o suru (435 hits for kao + suru): sonna kao shinaide, iya na kao shita.

cuts.trap: 'Call' meaning summon is yobu; denwa suru is only phoning.
cuts.reason: Crime films inflate it (379 hits); judged only 2 for daily life.

cuts.trap: A voice you just happen to hear is koe ga kikoeru.
cuts.reason: Mostly 'I wanted to hear your voice' on the phone (koe kikitakatta, 58 hits); judged 3.

cuts.trap: The place you leave takes o: ie o deru.
cuts.reason: Means the same as uchi o deru, and uchi is the everyday word for home.

cuts.trap: 'Be helpful' is tasuke ni naru, not tetsudau.
cuts.reason: Says the same as the kept yaku ni tatsu; people also just say tasukaru.

cuts.trap: 'Leave me alone' is hitori ni shite, not oite iku.
cuts.reason: Hitori ni shite ('leave me alone') is mostly a drama line.

cuts.trap: No single everyday verb for 'breathe'; say iki o suru.
cuts.reason: Real 'breathe' (310 hits), but outside 'iki shite!' in a scare or at the doctor's, daily talk rarely needs it.
'Let go of my hand!' is a stock film-scene line (283 hits); everyday life rarely calls for it.

cuts.trap: Not kokoro o kaeru: changing your mind is ki ga kawaru, with ki as the subject (ki ga kawattara itte).
cuts.reason: A ki phrase ('change one's mind'), so it goes on the idiom list with the other ki sets.

cuts.english: wrap up, call it a day
cuts.trap: Ending a session is owari ni suru; owaru alone is intransitive.
cuts.reason: Common (279) and typical: kyou wa kore de owari ni shiyou ('let's call it a day') ends classes, shifts and practice.

cuts.trap: 'Talented' is an adjective; Japanese says sainou ga aru.
cuts.reason: The usual way to say someone is talented (sainou aru yo). Film pep talks push up its 275 hits, but it is still frequent.

cuts.english: light the stove or a fire; light a cigarette
cuts.trap: English 'light' has no obvious verb; it is tsukeru, the same verb as for lights, and hi o tsukete sounds like ki o tsukete (be careful).
cuts.reason: Lighting the stove uses the same tsukeru as denki o tsukeru, which already lists hi (fire) as a partner. The high count (256) is mostly films lighting fires and cigarettes.
Romance-plot phrasing inflated by films; judged 2 for daily talk.

cuts.trap: 'I had a scary experience' is kowai omoi o shita, not kowai keiken o motta: the feeling is the object of suru.
cuts.reason: Very common (246 hits) and closely paired. Kowai omoi o shita means 'I had a scary time'. It only missed because it always needs a feeling word in front.
Same meaning as the kept youji ga aru (have something to do).

cuts.trap: English 'have problems' leads to motsu; Japanese says kakaeru or mondai ga aru.
cuts.reason: Drama-plot phrasing; daily talk says mondai ga aru.

cuts.trap: English 'hit' leads to tataku or naguru; bumping your own head is utsu.
cuts.reason: Hitting your head comes up now and then; most of its 231 hits are accident scenes, and atama o butsukeru is the everyday 'I bumped my head'.

cuts.trap: Not kanjiru for 'it feels like...': the everyday form is ~ kanji ga suru (or ~ tte kanji).
cuts.reason: A sentence frame (... kanji ga suru, 'it feels like...') that works like ki ga suru on your versatility list. It is not a noun + verb set.
Very frequent (218) and typical: tegami is mostly written. It only missed because people write fewer letters now (judged 3).

cuts.english: go back to how it was
cuts.reason: The added moto ni modosu (put it back) teaches the same phrase. Modoru is just the version where it goes back on its own.

cuts.trap: English 'call me' leads to yobu (summon); a phone call is denwa (o) kureru or denwa shite.
cuts.reason: This is the same call as the kept denwa o kakeru. Kureru only adds 'to me', and people mostly say denwa shite or denwa kurete.

cuts.trap: English 'be interested' is an adjective; Japanese uses the noun kyoumi with motsu or ga aru, and ni for the topic.
cuts.reason: Means the same as the kept kyoumi ga aru, which is the everyday way to say you're interested.

cuts.trap: English 'affect' is one verb; Japanese uses the noun eikyou with ataeru (or ukeru for being affected).
cuts.reason: Means 'have an influence on' but sounds like the news (judged 2). In conversation people say eikyou suru or eikyou ga aru.

cuts.trap: English 'oneself' leads to jibun o mamoru; the set uses mi.
cuts.reason: Formal, news-style 'protect oneself' (judged 2/5); casual speech rarely uses it.

cuts.trap: Not just renraku dekinai: 'I can't reach him' is renraku ga torenai (or renraku ga tsukanai).
cuts.reason: The can-form of the kept renraku o toru (renraku ga torenai = can't reach them).

cuts.trap: English 'I didn't mean it' leads to imi; Japanese says warugi wa nakatta.
cuts.reason: Mostly heard in drama apologies (warugi wa nakatta, 197 hits); judged 3.

cuts.trap: Not tsukau, which treats time as a resource you use up. Spending time with people, or spending a weekend, is sugosu (shuumatsu dou sugoshita?).
cuts.reason: High in films (190), but wordy ('spend a pleasant time'). In talk people name the activity or say shuumatsu dou sugoshita without jikan.

cuts.trap: Particle is ni, not o; noru covers every vehicle.
cuts.reason: Real (186 hits), but boats rarely come up in daily life, and the car, bus and train sets on the list already teach noru with ni.

cuts.trap: English 'answer' leads to kotae, which is an answer to a question; replying to a person, message or call is henji (o) suru.
cuts.reason: A plain suru verb (henji suru); for messages the kept meeru o kaesu does the job.

cuts.trap: English 'leave' leads to saru or hanareru; leaving a place is o deru.
cuts.reason: Same 'place + o deru' pattern as uchi o deru, with the room in place of the house.

cuts.english: blame (someone else), pin it on someone
cuts.trap: Not semeru, which means 'criticise, attack'. To pin the blame on someone is X no sei ni suru.
cuts.reason: Blaming is X no sei ni suru (139 hits as written, judged 4): ore no sei ni suru na.

cuts.trap: Not himitsu o motsu or tamotsu. You keep a secret with mamoru (protect), the same verb as yakusoku o mamoru.
cuts.reason: The kept naisho ni suru covers keeping something secret in everyday talk.

cuts.trap: English 'wear' is one verb; Japanese splits it: kiru for suits and tops, haku for trousers and shoes.
cuts.reason: A suit is just another thing you kiru; fuku o kiru already gives you the verb.
Real (169 hits) but judged 3; rumours are a narrower topic than the kept talk sets.

cuts.trap: English 'it smells good' sends learners looking for a verb; Japanese says ii nioi (ga suru).
cuts.reason: The kept nioi ga suru already teaches ii nioi (suru), 'it smells nice'.
Real (168), but mostly apologies, news and drama showdowns. People say it far less in daily life.

cuts.english: make a hole; get (one's ears) pierced
cuts.trap: Not ana o tsukuru. Making a hole is akeru, and getting your ears pierced is piasu (no ana) o akeru.
cuts.reason: Most of the 159 hits are about drilling or punching holes, and only a few are ear piercings, so it rarely comes up in daily talk.

cuts.trap: English 'in the sky' leads to de; moving through the sky takes o.
cuts.reason: People say it about birds, planes and daydreams, not about trips. Most of the 159 hits come from fantasy and action films.

cuts.trap: English 'follow' suggests tsuite iku; instructions take shitagau with ni.
cuts.reason: 'Follow orders' is a military and crime-plot line (156). Real workplaces rarely say it.

cuts.trap: English 'too late' leads to osoi; for something past saving it is teokure.
cuts.reason: 'Too late to save' is mostly said in medical and rescue scenes.

cuts.trap: 'I can't explain it' is setsumei ga tsukanai, not a form of setsumei suru.
cuts.reason: 155 hits, but most are mystery plots ('it can't be explained'). Daily talk uses it less than the kept sets.

cuts.trap: 'Get a chance' is kikai ga aru, not kikai o morau.
cuts.reason: Common (153). Kikai ga areba ('if I get the chance') is an everyday line, and it only just missed.

cuts.trap: 'I have a bad feeling about this' is iya na yokan ga suru, not warui kimochi ga aru, which sounds like nausea.
cuts.reason: The 'I have a bad feeling about this' movie line. Most of its 152 hits come from film plots.

cuts.trap: 'Do my best' is zenryoku o tsukusu or ganbaru, never suru.
cuts.reason: Speech and pledge language (152). In conversation people say ganbaru.

cuts.trap: 'Pack your things' is matomeru (gather up), not tsumeru.
cuts.reason: Most of the 152 hits are the film line 'pack your things and get out'. In real life it comes up much less.

cuts.trap: 'Get out of the car' is oriru (step down), not deru.
cuts.reason: Getting out of a car uses the same oriru as the kept densha o oriru.

cuts.trap: English 'close' suggests shimeru; mouths and eyes take tojiru.
cuts.reason: 'Close your mouth' is rare in real talk (judged 2/5); people just say damatte.

cuts.trap: 'Make a mistake' is not tsukuru; say machigai o okasu or just machigaeru.
cuts.reason: Formal (150). Everyday speech says machigaeta or misu shita.

cuts.english: speak up; say it out loud
cuts.trap: English 'speak up' pushes toward hanasu. Japanese 'puts out the voice': motto koe dashite.
cuts.reason: Real (148 hits, judged 3); the main use is motto koe dashite.
Calling for help is an action-film situation (judged 2).

cuts.trap: 'I can't breathe' is iki ga dekinai; there is no single verb 'breathe'.
cuts.reason: Almost always 'iki ga dekinai!' (I can't breathe) in emergency scenes, far more in films than in daily life.

cuts.trap: 'I can't imagine' is usually souzou mo tsukanai, not souzou dekinai.
cuts.reason: Common (146 hits) in everyday talk: souzou tsuku, souzou mo tsukanai ('I can't even imagine'). It only just missed.

cuts.trap: 'Ask for opinions' uses kiku, not tanomu.
cuts.reason: Meeting language (145): minna no iken o kiku. Much rarer in daily talk than the kept hanashi o kiku.
The pair of me o tojiru (now added), but said less than it (145 vs 353 hits); you hear it mostly at the eye doctor or when waking someone.

cuts.trap: 'I have a favor to ask' is tanomi ga aru, not a form of kiku.
cuts.reason: Same as the kept onegai ga aru, with a more casual noun.

cuts.trap: 'Make trouble' is okosu (raise), not tsukuru.
cuts.reason: 'Cause trouble' in the plot sense; inflated by crime and drama.
The kept meeru o okuru uses the same verb for any message, LINE included.
The stiff, written way to say 'ready'. The kept junbi ga dekiru is what people say.

cuts.trap: Also means to apologize or ask humbly, not just a physical bow.
cuts.reason: Bowing or apologising humbly (141 hits, judged 3); more narration than talk.

cuts.trap: Not namae o ageru: you 'attach' a name (namae o tsukeru).
cuts.reason: Naming a baby, pet, file or group is everyday (119 hits as written, judged 4), and the verb is tsukeru.
Plots inflate the 138. Casual talk more often says nanka atta? or mondai aru?

cuts.trap: 'Can you hear me?' is kikoeru?, not kiku: kiku is deliberate listening, and the thing heard takes ga.
cuts.reason: The same set as the added koe ga kikoeru, with a sound in place of a voice. The kept oto ga suru also covers hearing a noise.

cuts.trap: 'Make way' is akeru (clear), not tsukuru.
cuts.reason: 'Make way!' gets shouted in crowd and chase scenes. In real life people say sumimasen or toorimasu.

cuts.trap: 'This medicine works' is kouka ga aru or kiku, not hataraku.
cuts.reason: The everyday way to ask whether a diet, cream or study method works (kouka aru?), with 137 hits. The added kusuri ga kiku only covers medicine.
The kept gakkou ni iku with a different noun, and daigaku ni hairu (being added) covers starting university.

cuts.trap: 'Live a happy life' is jinsei o okuru (send), not ikiru with jinsei.
cuts.reason: Bookish (judged 2); conversation just says ikiru.

cuts.trap: 'I don't remember that' is often kioku ga nai, not only oboete inai.
cuts.reason: 128 hits, but 'I don't remember' is mostly oboetenai. Kioku nai sounds more dramatic.

cuts.trap: 'Look around' needs mawari (surroundings) as the object; there is no 'around' particle.
cuts.reason: In subtitles, 'look around' is mostly action-scene direction, and the literal pairing is easy to build yourself.
You hear 'kuchi akete' mainly at the dentist or doctor.
Means 'polite, well-mannered'. It is real, but people describe someone this way less often than the kept sets (judged 3).

cuts.trap: yakusoku isn't only 'promise': it means any arrangement to meet, so kyou wa yakusoku ga aru = I'm meeting someone today.
cuts.reason: 'I'm meeting someone' is close enough to yotei ga aru.

cuts.trap: 'Take responsibility' is sekinin o motsu or toru, not ukeru.
cuts.reason: A formal variant of 'take responsibility' (120), said less than sekinin o toru, which also missed.

cuts.trap: 'Leave a message' is nokosu, not deru or saru.
cuts.reason: Its 119 hits come from answering-machine scenes. Few people in Japan leave voicemail now.

cuts.trap: 'Take someone' is tsurete iku; motte iku is only for things.
cuts.reason: Taking a child or parent to the doctor is everyday family talk (119 hits, judged 4/5). It only just missed.
Its 119 hits come from films about writers. Few people ever talk about writing a book (rated 2).

cuts.trap: 'I'm not sure I can' is jishin ga nai, not wakaranai.
cuts.reason: It comes with the added jishin ga aru: jishin nai is simply its negative.

cuts.trap: 'I have no experience' is keiken ga nai, not motte inai.
cuts.reason: Just the negative of keiken ga aru, which is being added.

cuts.ja: お悔やみを申し上げる
cuts.trap: 'I'm sorry for your loss' is okuyami moushiagemasu, not sumimasen.
cuts.reason: A funeral condolence formula only.
Same drink + nomu as osake o nomu, which lists biiru as a partner.

cuts.trap: "Are you hurt?" is kega wa nai?, not itai desu ka.
cuts.reason: 'Kega nai?' is just the question form of kega o suru, which is on the list.
The polite form of the kept hanashi ga aru.

cuts.trap: "Get some fresh air" is soto no kuuki o suu; suu (inhale) does the work of 'breathe'.
cuts.reason: 'Get some fresh air' is now on the list as kaze ni ataru; kuuki o suu is the less common way to say it.

cuts.trap: No adjective for 'confident'; say jishin o motsu or jishin ga aru.
cuts.reason: The added jishin ga aru says 'be confident' and is what people actually say. The motsu version sounds like a speech.
Real (111 hits, judged 3) but said less than the kept talk sets.

cuts.trap: 'Take responsibility' is sekinin o toru; ou means carry it on your back.
cuts.reason: Formal and written (111). Rare in conversation.

cuts.english: step away (from one's desk or the table)
cuts.trap: Not seki o deru. Stepping away for a moment is hazusu ('remove'), as in the phone line tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu.
cuts.reason: Mostly the office phone line tadaima seki o hazushite orimasu ('they've stepped away').

cuts.trap: 'Panic' is a verb in English, so learners say panikku suru; natives say panikku ni naru.
cuts.reason: People do say it, but thriller scenes inflate its 110 hits. Casual speech often shortens it to panikutta.
'Take leave' in office words. The kept yasumi o toru says the same thing.

cuts.trap: No 'look' verb: 'looks familiar' is mioboe ga aru (have a memory of seeing).
cuts.reason: Mostly the detective line 'do you recognise this?'. It is uncommon in daily conversation.

cuts.trap: 'Sit on' takes ni, not ue ni or de.
cuts.reason: Frequent (106 hits) and strongly paired (typical 0.27). It's the standard 'sit on a chair', though people often just say suwatte.

cuts.english: be shocked, be hurt (by news, a remark)
cuts.trap: Not shokku suru: you receive a shock, so shokku uketa. Shokku datta is the other natural way.
cuts.reason: Common (104 hits) and closely paired: half of all shokku in the corpus is shokku uketa ('I was shocked, it hurt'). It is ordinary casual speech.

cuts.trap: 'Smell this!' is kaide mite: actively smelling is kagu, not nioi o suru or kiku.
cuts.reason: Judged 2: actively sniffing (kaide mite, 'smell this') comes up much less than the kept nioi ga suru.

cuts.trap: 'Have a party' is suru (or hiraku), not motsu.
cuts.reason: Fine (103 hits, judged 3), but suru is generic here.

cuts.trap: 'Empty' has no verb form; say kara ni suru (make empty).
cuts.reason: Natives rate it only 2/5, and the pairing is loose.

cuts.trap: 'Rely on' is not shinrai suru (trust); it is tayori ni suru.
cuts.reason: Real (102 hits, judged 3) but said less than the kept people sets.
Same drink + nomu as osake o nomu, which lists wain as a partner.

cuts.trap: 'Have a heart attack' uses okosu (set off), not motsu.
cuts.reason: Heart attacks and seizures are medical-drama plot points, rare in everyday talk.

cuts.trap: English passive leads to eikyou sareru; natives say eikyou o ukeru (receive influence).
cuts.reason: Formal and written-leaning (99 hits, judged 3).
With jikka ni kaeru now added, that is the everyday way to say you're going home for the holidays. Kokyou sounds bookish.

cuts.trap: Not kakkou o kiru: 'dressed like that' is sonna kakkou shite. Kakkou means outfit or look.
cuts.reason: Commenting on how someone is dressed (sonna kakkou de iku no?, kawaii kakkou shiteru) comes up all the time in casual talk; sonna/konna kakkou alone has about 185 hits.

cuts.trap: 'Take an interest' uses motsu (hold), not toru.
cuts.reason: A more formal way to say you're interested. The kept kyoumi ga aru is the everyday version.

cuts.trap: English 'wave' is one verb; Japanese shakes the hand, te o furu.
cuts.reason: Waving (96 hits, judged 3) is described more than said.

cuts.english: have a complaint, got a problem
cuts.trap: 'Complain' is monku o iu; nanka monku aru? is 'got a problem?'
cuts.reason: The kept monku o iu covers it; nanka monku aru? uses the same noun.

cuts.trap: 'Wear' splits by body part: kiru for dresses and tops, haku for skirts and trousers.
cuts.reason: Just fuku o kiru with a dress as the garment; nothing new to learn.

cuts.trap: 'Any idea where it went?' is kokoroatari aru?, not aidia.
cuts.reason: A detective-interview line ('any idea who did it?'). It is rare in ordinary conversation.

cuts.trap: There is no phrasal verb for 'make up': it is nakanaori suru ('mending the relationship'), never tsukuru.
cuts.reason: A plain suru verb (nakanaori suru).

cuts.trap: 'Do your best' is not besuto o suru; it is besuto o tsukusu (or ganbaru).
cuts.reason: Pep-talk language (94). In conversation people say ganbaru.

cuts.trap: yameru here is 辞める (resign), the same sound as 止める (stop doing something). Quitting a job is not deru or owaru.
cuts.reason: The kept kaisha o yameru with a different noun (94 hits); both say 'quit my job'.

cuts.trap: Not te o motsu: holding hands is 'linking' them with tsunagu, the same verb as netto ni tsunagu.
cuts.reason: Holding hands is always te o tsunagu (84 hits as written): te tsunaide, with kids or a partner.

cuts.trap: 'Are you serious?' is honki de itteru?, not majime (earnest by nature).
cuts.reason: Honki de itteru? ('are you serious?') is a stock question (120 hits with maji de, judged 4).

cuts.trap: Not me o shimeru: shimeru is for doors and windows. Eyes take tsuburu (casual) or tojiru (neutral).
cuts.reason: The casual twin of me o tojiru (now added), with the same meaning; once you have one you will recognise the other.

cuts.trap: Not oto o tsukuru: 'make a noise' is oto o tateru ('raise' a sound).
cuts.reason: Fairly frequent (92 hits). Oto tatenaide ('keep the noise down') is everyday flat and night-time talk, and the verb tateru can't be guessed.
'Have hope' is the language of speeches and drama, judged 2 for daily life.

cuts.english: have time or money to spare; be relaxed about it
cuts.trap: English 'can afford' or 'have time to spare' has no single verb here; Japanese uses yoyuu ga aru / nai for time, money and calm.
cuts.reason: The positive of yoyuu ga nai. Learn that one and you have this too.

cuts.trap: 'Raise your voice' tempts ageru; Japanese puts out (dasu) a big voice.
cuts.reason: Raising your voice is oogoe o dasu (86 hits as written, judged 4): oogoe dasanaide.

cuts.trap: 'Lead/live a life' uses okuru (send), not michibiku.
cuts.reason: Sounds formal (native rating 2/5). In speech people say ~na seikatsu o shiteru or kurasu.

cuts.english: drive (someone), offer to take the car
cuts.trap: Not unten suru when offering a lift: 'I'll drive' is kuruma dasu yo ('take the car out').
cuts.reason: The added kuruma ni noseru (nosete ageru yo) already covers offering someone a lift. Kuruma dasu yo is just a second way to say it.
Kaku is just the ordinary 'write', and the set lives mostly on forms (koko ni namae kaite).

cuts.english: be expecting, have a baby on the way
cuts.trap: Not kodomo o motsu: 'we're having a baby' is kodomo ga dekita. Kodomo ga iru means you already have children.
cuts.reason: 'We're expecting' (86 hits, judged 3); the added kodomo ga umareru is the stronger baby set.

cuts.trap: 'Have courage' is aru/nai, not motsu.
cuts.reason: Means 'not have the courage'. It is real but less everyday than the kept sets, and film drama pushes up its 86 hits.

cuts.trap: 'Throw/have a party': Japanese opens (hiraku) it.
cuts.reason: Formal 'hold a party' (judged 2); people just say paatii suru.

cuts.trap: 'Lose' is ushinau here, not nakusu.
cuts.reason: 'Lose consciousness' belongs to hospital and action scenes, not daily life (judged 2/5).

cuts.trap: 'Get treatment' tempts morau; Japanese receives it with ukeru.
cuts.reason: Formal, medical-sounding 'receive treatment'; in casual speech people say byouin ni iku.

cuts.trap: 'Take action' is not toru; Japanese raises (okosu) it.
cuts.reason: Speeches and plot climaxes (85). Rare in daily life.

cuts.english: work up the courage, be brave
cuts.trap: Not yuuki o motsu or mitsukeru: you 'put out' courage, yuuki o dasu (yuuki dashite itta), as in genki o dasu.
cuts.reason: Yuuki (courage) is already a partner of the kept genki o dasu, as in yuuki dashite ('I worked up the courage').

cuts.trap: Not iiwake o tsukuru: you 'do' an excuse, iiwake (o) suru.
cuts.reason: A plain suru verb (iiwake suru); learn it as one verb: iiwake shinaide.

cuts.english: show off, try to look cool

cuts.reason: Real (judged 3) but less frequent than the kept hanashi sets.

cuts.trap: English 'take' leads to motte iku; natives say dasu (send out), the same pattern as shuuri ni dasu.
cuts.reason: Only for one errand, taking clothes to the dry cleaner's (7 hits).

cuts.trap: Not hanashi ga kawaru or hanareru: a conversation that drifts 'veers off' (soreru), and hanashi o modosu brings it back.
cuts.reason: Real (judged 3) but less frequent; for a chat drifting off topic.

cuts.trap: 'Sigh' is a verb in English. Japanese uses a noun with tsuku, the same verb as uso o tsuku.
cuts.reason: 'Sigh' is mostly narration. People rarely say it about themselves in conversation (8 hits).

cuts.english: black out; one's memory goes blank (from drinking)
cuts.trap: Not kioku o nakusu (amnesia, formal): blacking out from drink is kioku ga tobu (nomisugite kioku tonda).
cuts.reason: Mostly heard in drinking stories (8 hits), and less often than the kept drinking sets.

cuts.trap: 'Fall' asleep is tsuku (or just nemuru), not ochiru.
cuts.reason: Literary 'fall asleep'; in speech people say nechatta.

cuts.trap: A pot goes 'onto the fire' (hi ni kakeru), even on an electric hob.
cuts.reason: Kitchen-only: putting a pot on the stove (8 hits, judged 3/5).

cuts.trap: A small face is a compliment in Japan (photogenic, stylish), not a criticism.
cuts.reason: A common compliment in Japan (kao chiisai ne), but not frequent overall (8 hits, judged 3).

cuts.trap: English has no matching set: a mood is 'repaired' (naosu). When it improves on its own it is kigen ga naoru (10).
cuts.reason: Real (7 hits as written, judged 3); the added kigen ga warui covers moods.

cuts.trap: Wagamama is said of demands: wagamama iwanaide (stop being demanding). The polite wagamama o itte sumimasen apologises for a request.
cuts.reason: Wagamama iwanaide is what parents and partners say all the time (judged 4).

cuts.trap: Assigned transfers are said to happen to you (Osaka ni tenkin ni natta), with no passive verb.
cuts.reason: Company-transfer talk only (8).

cuts.trap: A set business apology and thanks (otesuu o okake shimashita). Meiwaku o kakeru (kept) is the general form.
cuts.reason: The polite business form of the kept meiwaku o kakeru, with the same frame.

cuts.trap: Socks take haku like shoes and trousers, never kiru.
cuts.reason: kutsu o haku already lists socks as a partner, with the same haku.

cuts.trap: A skirt goes on from below, so it takes haku, not kiru. A dress (wanpiisu) takes kiru.
cuts.reason: zubon o haku already lists skirts as a partner, with the same haku.

cuts.trap: This kaeru is 替える (swap in a new one), with the same sound as 変える (alter).
cuts.reason: Changing a light bulb comes up rarely (8 hits).

cuts.english: have no change, have no coins
cuts.trap: 'Change' meaning coins is kozeni, while otsuri is the change handed back. 'Have' is ga aru / nai, not motsu.
cuts.reason: Useful at shop counters, but rare in films (8), which undercount shop talk.

cuts.english: decide what to do after school (university, job)
cuts.trap: English has no single word for shinro, the path after graduation. Learners say shourai o kimeru or michi o kimeru.
cuts.reason: School-leavers' talk only (8).

cuts.english: pray for someone's soul (on a death)
cuts.trap: No English formula matches it. 'RIP' is said as gomeifuku o oinori shimasu, and meifuku is used only in this set.
cuts.reason: A condolence formula for a death only.

cuts.trap: Kites are raised (ageru), not flown (tobasu).
cuts.reason: A children's New Year pastime (8 hits, rated 3).

cuts.trap: There's no separate verb for 'tan' or 'burn': the skin is 'grilled by the sun', hi ni yakeru, the same yakeru as niku ga yakeru.
cuts.reason: Tanning and sunburn come up mostly in summer, and people more often use the noun (hiyake shita).

cuts.english: take / drop someone to the station, see someone off
cuts.trap: Not just eki made tsurete iku: walking or driving someone somewhere is okuru (the 'send' verb), as in okutte iku yo.
cuts.reason: The added uchi made okuru teaches the same made okuru for walking or driving someone somewhere. Just swap in eki.

cuts.trap: English splits grill, roast, bake, toast and fry; Japanese uses yaku for all dry-heat cooking (pan o yaku = make toast).
cuts.reason: Pan o yaku, being added, teaches the same yaku for all dry-heat cooking. Meat is just another partner.

cuts.trap: Not kami ga sodatsu: hair grows = nobiru. 'Your hair's grown' is kami nobita ne.
cuts.reason: Means 'your hair's grown' (kami nobita ne). It is real but only comes up now and then (7 hits).

cuts.trap: Not tsumoru (that's for snow): work, chores and laundry pile up with tamaru.
cuts.reason: A real complaint (shigoto tamatteru), but rare in the corpus (7).

cuts.english: ruin one's health, make oneself ill (from overwork)
cuts.trap: English 'ruin your health' gives no verb; Japanese breaks the body: muri suru to karada kowasu yo.
cuts.reason: A real warning about overwork, but said less than the kept health sets (judged 3/5).

cuts.trap: A smell clinging to clothes tsuku (sticks), like shimi ga tsuku: yakiniku no nioi ga fuku ni tsuita.
cuts.reason: Said after yakiniku or a smoky bar (nioi tsuichatta), but not often (about 6 hits).

cuts.trap: Not suibun o nomu: you 'take in' fluids, suibun o toru, just as you say eiyou o toru for nutrition.
cuts.reason: Mostly health advice and summer heat warnings rather than casual chat (7 hits).

cuts.english: stick in one's mind, be memorable
cuts.trap: Not oboeyasui or kioku suru: 'the most memorable part was…' is ichiban inshou ni nokotta no wa…
cuts.reason: Useful for 'the most memorable part was...' but only 7 hits and judged 3.

cuts.trap: Not kyuuryou o morau, which is just 'get paid': a raise is the salary going up, kyuuryou agatta.
cuts.reason: Real, but it comes up only occasionally (7).

cuts.trap: Not deeta o nakusu: files and photos disappear, kieru (shashin zenbu kiechatta). Kesu is deleting them yourself.
cuts.reason: Losing data is a one-off mishap, not something people talk about routinely (7).

cuts.trap: Not taijuu o tsukeru or eru: weight is the subject and it increases, taijuu ga fueru. To lose weight is taijuu ga heru, or simply yaseru.
cuts.reason: In casual talk people say futotta instead.

cuts.trap: Setting off hand-held fireworks yourself is hanabi o suru. Watching a display is hanabi o miru (6 hits) or hanabi taikai ni iku.
cuts.reason: A summer staple (sparklers in the park or on the beach), rated 3. Films show only 7 hits because they under-count Japanese seasonal life.

cuts.trap: The stock reply to praise is oseji demo ureshii, or oseji ja nai yo.
cuts.reason: Real (judged 3) but rare as a set (15 hits as written); oseji demo ureshii is the main use.

cuts.trap: Volume goes up and down with ageru / sageru (boryuumu sagete).
cuts.reason: Real (7), but people say oto o ookiku suru and oto o ageru (11) more for the same request.

cuts.trap: Warnings 'come out' (deru). In Japan an ooame or bouhuu keihou often closes schools.
cuts.reason: Storm-day talk (7 hits). It matters when a warning closes schools and rarely comes up otherwise.

cuts.english: the end comes in sight, have a clear outlook
cuts.trap: No English twin: medo ga tatanai = we can't tell when it will be done. Medo is the outlook for finishing.
cuts.reason: Business and planning talk (7).

cuts.trap: Not kuruma de byouki ni naru: motion sickness uses you, the verb for getting drunk (kuruma yoi, fune ni you).
cuts.reason: One situation: getting carsick (6 hits).

cuts.trap: Same tsukeru as lights, and eakon o kakeru (run it) is equally natural; not on ni suru or mawasu.
cuts.reason: Same tsukeru as denki o tsukeru. It carries straight over to the AC.

cuts.trap: Not taiko o hiku or suru: drums are hit, tataku, and a drum kit works the same way (doramu o tataku).
cuts.reason: Mostly about festival drums (6 hits, rated 3).

cuts.trap: Not 'sugu byouki ni naru hito' as the default: 'gets sick a lot' is karada ga yowai. Karada ga joubu is the sturdy opposite.
cuts.reason: Means 'be sickly, get ill a lot'. It is a natural everyday phrase but not a frequent one (6 hits, judged 3).

cuts.trap: Not kabi ni naru: mould 'grows' the way hair does (haeru).
cuts.reason: Real but rare (6 hits). It comes up mainly in the rainy season.

cuts.trap: Not just yotei ga ippai: a full schedule is 'stuffed' (tsumaru), like a blocked nose. Example: raishuu wa yotei ga tsumatteru.
cuts.reason: A nice image, but said less than yotei ga aru / hairu (6).

cuts.english: have the same tastes, share interests
cuts.trap: English 'we share hobbies' points to a sharing verb, but Japanese says your tastes 'match' (au), as in saizu ga au.
cuts.reason: Real (judged 3) but less frequent than the kept people sets.

cuts.english: be perceptive, quick to catch on, have good instincts
cuts.trap: English 'sharp' leads to atama ga ii, which means clever. Picking up on things is kan ga ii.
cuts.reason: Means 'perceptive, quick to catch on'. It is real but said less than the kept sets (6 hits).

cuts.english: run a fever, come down with a fever (of a person, often a child)
cuts.trap: Not netsu o morau: with the person as subject it is netsu o dashita (musuko ga netsu dashite). Netsu ga deta is the same event from the fever's side.

A free combination: netto de goes with any verb, and kau is the plain verb for buying (6).

cuts.trap: Notes are 'taken' (toru) with nooto or memo. Kaku sounds like writing in a notebook.
cuts.reason: Same act and verb as memo o toru, being added (6 hits against 16).

cuts.english: leave your child (at daycare, with someone)
cuts.trap: Leaving a child with daycare or grandparents is azukeru, the same verb as checking luggage.
cuts.reason: Only for parents leaving a child at daycare or with family (6 hits).

cuts.trap: 'Serve' or 'offer' suggests ageru. Guests are given tea with dasu (okyaku-san ni ocha dashite).
cuts.reason: Mainly for serving tea to guests or office visitors (6 hits, judged 3/5).

cuts.trap: 'Make plans' is tateru (stand up), not tsukuru.
cuts.reason: Same tateru as keikaku o tateru, now added, which people say far more (128 vs 6).

cuts.trap: For a complaint, a noise that bothers you is urusai, not oto ga ookii.
cuts.reason: Only 6 hits. A noise complaint is usually urusai! on its own, and the kept oto ga suru covers hearing the noise.

cuts.trap: Pedalling is kogu, the same verb as rowing a boat. Noru is just being on the bike.
cuts.reason: Riding a bike is the added jitensha ni noru. Kogu just adds the detail of pedalling.

cuts.trap: 'Something in my eye' uses gomi (rubbish, dust) + hairu: me ni gomi haitta.
cuts.reason: Getting something in your eye happens now and then (6 hits).

cuts.trap: Confidence 'attaches' (tsuku): renshuu shite jishin ga tsuita. Learners say jishin o eru.
cuts.reason: Builds on the added jishin ga aru (jishin tsuita = I've gained confidence). Only 6 hits.

cuts.trap: Not kaze o ageru: you 'transfer' a cold, kaze o utsusu (kaze utsushichatta, gomen).

cuts.trap: Not tebukuro o kiru: gloves 'fit on' (hameru), like rings; tebukuro o suru is also everyday.
cuts.reason: masuku o suru already lists gloves as a partner (tebukuro shiteru, the everyday form); hameru is stiffer.

cuts.trap: Not michi o tanomu or michi o shitsumon suru: asking the way is kiku, the verb for listening.
cuts.reason: Rare in the counts (5 hits). People usually ask the way with michi o oshiete kudasai.

cuts.trap: Not jikan ni tsuku or dekiru: making it in time is maniau, with ni on the deadline or train (densha ni maniatta).
cuts.reason: The low count comes from the tokenizer splitting ma ni au. Densha ni maniau already teaches the verb.

cuts.trap: Intransitive half: 'the kettle's boiled' is oyu ga waita, not oyu ga wakashita.
cuts.reason: The intransitive half of oyu o wakasu, which is being added. Oyu waita follows from it, and it has only 5 hits.

cuts.trap: Not taiyou ga tsuyoi or taiyou ga atsui: strong sun is hizashi (sunlight) ga tsuyoi.
cuts.reason: Said on hot summer days, but it has only 5 hits. People more often just say atsui.

cuts.trap: No 'stuffy' adjective: the nose clogs, hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru).
cuts.reason: A stuffy nose is one of the most common cold and hay-fever complaints, next to hanamizu ga deru (now added). It only just missed.

cuts.trap: A topic that's on the test 'comes out' in it, kore tesuto ni deru?, not shiken ni aru.
cuts.reason: Exam season only: kore tesuto ni deru? (5).

cuts.trap: Not kami ga hikui: hair length is mijikai. Hikui is only for height (se ga hikui).
cuts.reason: Swap nagai for mijikai in the added kami ga nagai. The short version is also said less (5 hits).

cuts.trap: Not mezamashi ga deru or ga iku: alarms, phones and bells ring with naru (鳴る), which sounds like naru, 'become'.
cuts.reason: Natives rate it 3/5. The kept mezamashi o kakeru is said more.

cuts.english: a stain or dirt comes out
cuts.trap: Not yogore ga deru: stains 'fall off', so kono shimi ochinai. Removing them is yogore o otosu.
cuts.reason: Stains rarely come up (5 hits).

cuts.trap: Not shimi o morau: a stain 'attaches', so shimi tsuichatta. Getting it out uses ochiru.
cuts.reason: Stains rarely come up (5 hits).

cuts.trap: Not just atatakai fuku o kiru: 'wrap up warm' is one noun, atsugi ('thick wearing'), plus suru.
cuts.reason: This is the suru verb atsugi suru, and it's fairly uncommon too (judged 2).

cuts.trap: The stomach rings: naru (鳴る), the verb for a phone or alarm, not the naru that means 'become'.
cuts.reason: A rumbling stomach comes up occasionally (judged 3/5).

cuts.english: get a belly, have a paunch
cuts.trap: English 'get a gut' or 'put on weight' gives no clue: the belly deru (sticks out), usually onaka dete kita.
cuts.reason: Means 'get a belly' (onaka dete kita). It is real but only comes up now and then (5 hits).

cuts.trap: Not botan o shimeru or kakeru: buttons are tomeru (fasten); undoing them is hazusu.
cuts.reason: Doing up or undoing buttons is rarely said (about 11 hits for both, judged 2).

cuts.english: a queue forms, there's a line
cuts.trap: Not gyouretsu ga aru: a queue 'comes into being', gyouretsu ga dekiteru. Joining it is narabu.
cuts.reason: Only 5 hits. People usually just say naranderu (people are lining up).

cuts.trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru. Muscle is 'attached' with tsukeru, the transitive half of kinniku ga tsuku.
cuts.reason: Gym and diet talk, rated 3 with only 5 hits.

cuts.trap: Getting chilled is hieru, not samui: people say hiechau yo (you'll get chilled). The same verb is used for cold drinks (biiru hieteru).
cuts.reason: 'Karada hiechau yo' (you'll get chilled) is a constant everyday warning in cold weather and air-conditioned rooms (judged 4/5); the film count (5) undersells it. It only just missed.

cuts.trap: The naitei (informal offer) is a Japanese job-hunting stage with no English word.
cuts.reason: Job-hunting season only (5).

cuts.trap: Rain stopping can be agaru as well as yamu (on the list). Small talk and forecasts use both.
cuts.reason: Means the same as the kept ame ga yamu, which is the more usual way to say the rain has stopped (agaru: about 5 hits).

cuts.trap: Attending is deru (go out to), as in kaigi ni deru.
cuts.reason: Weddings only (5 hits).

cuts.trap: 'Write / type a message' is utsu (hit the keys), not kaku. Moji o utsu and LINE utsu work the same way.
cuts.reason: Typing a message is real (5), but people mostly say meeru o okuru or LINE suru.

cuts.trap: A habit 'sticks' (tsuku): neru mae ni sumaho miru kuse ga tsuita. English 'get into' does not carry over.
cuts.reason: Means 'get into a habit'. It is real but rare next to kuse ga aru (3 to 5 hits).

cuts.trap: Not keshou o nugu or toru: makeup is 'dropped' with otosu, the same verb used for dirt and stains.
cuts.reason: A nightly-routine phrase (meiku otoshite kara neru) that films rarely show (4 hits); otosu is the same verb used for stains.

cuts.trap: Not michi ga karappo or michi ga hima: an uncrowded road or train is suiteru, the same suku as in onaka ga suku.
cuts.reason: People mention heavy traffic far more often than clear roads (4 hits).

cuts.trap: When the money is the subject the verb is tamaru (okane tamattara = once I've saved up), not transitive tameru.
cuts.reason: The intransitive half of okane o tameru, and you learn it with that one.

cuts.trap: Not yotei o tsukuru or oku: you 'put in' a plan (raishuu ni ireta = I put it in for next week).
cuts.reason: The transitive of yotei ga hairu, and rarely heard (4).

cuts.trap: Not kami o kawaku or fuku: drying it yourself is the transitive kawakasu, while kami ga kawaku means it dries.
cuts.reason: Rarely said aloud (4 hits).
Weather-forecast wording (4 hits). In conversation people say atsuku naru.

cuts.trap: Not kami o sodateru: growing your hair out is nobasu ('lengthen'), e.g. ima kami nobashiteru.
cuts.reason: Means 'grow your hair out'. It is real but said less (4 hits).

cuts.english: sleep lightly, be a light sleeper
cuts.trap: Not karui nemuri: sleep is 'shallow', asai. Deep sleep is nemuri ga fukai.
cuts.reason: Comes up only when talking about how you sleep.

cuts.trap: There's no verb for 'scratch': a scratch 'attaches' (kizu ga tsuku).
cuts.reason: A real set for scratches on phones and cars, but rare (4).

cuts.trap: Not only nakusu: losing a wallet or phone while out is usually otosu ('drop'), and the police ask where you dropped it.
cuts.reason: One mishap: losing your wallet or phone while you're out (4 hits).

cuts.trap: Not isha o miru (that means looking at the doctor): to see a doctor is isha ni kakaru, or isha ni mite morau.
cuts.reason: Same 'see a doctor' as byouin ni iku, which is on the list and is what people usually say.

cuts.trap: Not sakujo suru in speech: 'delete that photo!' is sono shashin keshite. Kesu means erase as well as switch off.
cuts.reason: Sono shashin keshite ('delete that photo') is everyday phone talk (judged 4). Films under-count it at 4.

cuts.trap: Not mise ga aku (that's opening for the day): a shop that has just opened is atarashii mise ga dekita.
cuts.reason: Real (atarashii mise dekita), but said less often than the kept mise ga aku.

cuts.trap: Not kusuri o nomu or tsukeru: creams, ointment and sunscreen are 'spread' on (nuru); nomu is only for swallowing.
cuts.reason: Putting on cream or ointment comes up only now and then (judged 3/5).

cuts.trap: English 'unplug' is one verb; Japanese pulls out the konsento (plug/socket). Plugging in is konsento ni sasu.
cuts.reason: Unplugging rarely comes up (4 hits).

cuts.english: a bug turns up (in the house)
cuts.trap: Not mushi ga iru for the moment of seeing it: pests (and ghosts) 'come out', gokiburi ga deta!
cuts.reason: One situation: a bug turning up indoors.

cuts.english: have a meal now, make it mealtime
cuts.trap: English 'let's eat' pushes to gohan o tabeyou. At home people say sorosoro gohan ni shiyou (let's switch to the meal), and ofuro ni suru? gohan ni suru? asks which comes first.
cuts.reason: This is the general 'X ni suru' (go with X) pattern, as in koohii ni suru, not a set tied to gohan.
Only 4 hits. The everyday invitation for a drink is nomi ni iku, which is being added.

cuts.trap: Soaking is tsukaru (be immersed). People contrast shawaa dake (shower only) with yubune ni tsukaru.
cuts.reason: Taking a bath is covered by ofuro ni hairu (kept). Yubune ni tsukaru is the narrower 'soak instead of just showering' (4 hits).

cuts.trap: Moving along on a bench or seat is tsumeru (pack in): sumimasen, tsumete moraemasu ka? It is not ugoku.
cuts.reason: One situation: moving along a bench or row of seats to make room (4 hits).
Massaging someone's shoulders comes up now and then (4 hits, judged 3/5).
Real (native rating 4/5) but rare in the counts (4 hits), and said less than nimotsu ga todoku (now added).
